title: Good Citizenship and Youth: Understanding … (ICCS 2016-based chapters on citizenship norms and related outcomes)
authors: E. Treviño, D. Carrasco, C. Villalobos, M. J. Morel, D. Torres Irribarra, D. Miranda, C. Miranda, L. Muñoz, D. Carrasco, A. Pavón Mediano, M. M. Isac, E. Claes, A. Sandoval-Hernández, A. Sandoval-Hernández, N. Savvides
outcome_summary: This book compiles multiple empirical chapters using ICCS 2016 grade 8 data to study citizenship norms profiles and their relationships with civic learning, school climate, political culture, and tolerance-related outcomes. The core measurement approach uses a multigroup latent class model to generate five citizenship norms profiles (comprehensive, socially engaged, duty-based, monitorial, anomic) from 12 ICCS citizenship-norm items, with binary recoding of importance. Across chapters, outcomes include profile membership (modeled with multilevel multinomial logistic regression), support for authoritarian government practices (modeled with clustered regression using IRT/WLE scores), tolerance of corruption (modeled with multilevel models using IRT-based tolerance scores), and political tolerance (modeled with multiple-group multinomial logistic regression). The analyses explicitly incorporate ICCS’s complex sampling design using Taylor Series Linearization and rescaled survey weights to ensure equal country contribution; however, the excerpt does not provide a complete missing-data procedure for PVs/IRT scores, so missing-data handling cannot be fully audited. Overall, the findings emphasize that civic learning opportunities and open classroom discussion are consistently associated with more comprehensive citizenship norms and lower tolerance of corruption/authoritarianism, though the comparative approach is correlational and does not establish causality.

title: Young People’s Perceptions of Europe in a Time of Change
authors: Bruno Losito, Gabriella Agrusti, Valeria Damiani, Wolfram Schulz
outcome_summary: This document is an IEA ICCS 2016 European regional report focused on young people’s perceptions of Europe within a broader civic and citizenship education framework. The excerpt states that ICCS 2016 provides data on students’ civic knowledge, attitudes, and engagement, and that the European option included regional questionnaire components covering European identity, recent European political/social events (e.g., immigration and freedom of movement), and European economic conditions and foreign policy. The report is designed to support comparisons across countries and over time (ICCS 2009 vs. ICCS 2016) and to examine variation within and between countries. However, the provided text does not include the methodological details needed to specify the analytic sample, scaling approach (PV vs. WLE/theta), missing-data strategy, or any predictive/ML modeling results. Therefore, no ML performance metrics or target-variable-specific effects can be extracted from the supplied section.

title: Teaching Tolerance in a Globalized World: An Introduction
authors: M. M. Isac, A. Sandoval-Hernández, D. Miranda
outcome_summary: This excerpted volume is a multi-chapter report using ICCS 2009 to study tolerance as attitudes toward equal rights for immigrants, ethnic minorities, and women. The chapters apply measurement invariance testing (CFA/MGCFA) to ensure cross-country comparability of latent attitude constructs, then use multilevel regression and multilevel path/structural equation modeling to examine how student, school, and country-level factors relate to these outcomes. Reported results include: scalar invariance of the three tolerance scales across 38 countries; evidence that most variance in attitudes lies at the student level rather than between schools; and consistent positive associations between open classroom discussion and egalitarian attitudes, with additional moderation effects that are context-specific (e.g., a buffer/booster effect in Austria). The segregation chapter finds generally low immigrant segregation (Duncan index) and limited predictive power of segregation for attitudes in most contexts. The excerpt does not provide a single unified ML prediction pipeline or performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) because the analyses are primarily psychometric and multilevel modeling rather than machine-learning prediction.
all_datasets_used: ICCS 2009 microdata with a nested sampling design

title: Skolēnu pilsoniskā izglītība Latvijā un pasaulē. Starptautiskā pētījuma IEA ICCS 2009 pirmie rezultāti
authors: Ireta Čekse, Andrejs Geske, Andris Grīnfelds, Andris Kangro
outcome_summary: Grāmatā apkopoti ICCS 2009 (International Civic and Citizenship Education Study) pirmie starptautiskie un Latvijas rezultāti, balstoties uz skolēnu kognitīvo testu un vairākiem aptauju instrumentiem (skolēnu, skolotāju un skolas aptaujas, kā arī nacionālā konteksta aptauja). Skolēnu tests sastāv no 80 jautājumiem 7 klasteros (C01–C07) un 7 testa variantiem; katram skolēnam tika izpildīts viens variants. Rezultāti tika skalēti, izmantojot IRT pieeju, un valstu vidējie rādītāji tika pārrēķināti uz 500 punktu skalu (SD=100), kā arī sadalīti kompetences līmeņos (1. līmenis 395–479, 2. līmenis 479–563, 3. līmenis ≥563). Latvijā 8. klases skolēnu vidējais rezultāts bija 482 punkti, kas bija statistiski nozīmīgi zemāks par visu dalībvalstu vidējo; aptuveni 48,4% Latvijas skolēnu nepārsniedza 1. kompetences līmeni. Papildus tiek ziņotas attieksmju skalas (piem., dzimumu līdztiesība, attieksme pret valsti) un saistības ar konteksta faktoriem (urbanizācija, mācību valoda, diskusiju vide klasē, vecāku interese, līdzdalības aktivitātes), bet šajā izvilkumā nav aprakstīta PV apvienošana vai trūkstošo datu apstrāde.

title: Morgendagens samfunnsborgere
authors: Rolf Mikkelsen, Dag Fjeldstad, Jon Lauglo
outcome_summary: This Acta Didactica Oslo report synthesizes Norwegian students’ responses and scale scores from ICCS 2009 (International Civic and Citizenship Education Study), focusing on democratic readiness and engagement. It uses ICCS scale metrics with international benchmarks (affective scales mean 50, SD 10; cognitive knowledge/skills mean 500, SD 100) and reports results for 8th and 9th grade, including gender and Nordic comparisons across Denmark, Finland, and Sweden. The report describes the ICCS cognitive test structure (80 items; 4 content areas; knowing vs analysing/reasoning) and provides descriptive outcomes such as Norway’s high cognitive scores (e.g., 515 for 8th grade and 541 for 9th grade) and high endorsement of democratic values and school participation. It also reports associations (e.g., correlations between knowledge and political self-concept, and between classroom openness and knowledge) and trend comparisons with CivEd 1999. Methodologically, the manuscript does not present an ML predictive modeling framework, does not document plausible-values handling, and does not specify missing-data procedures, limiting reproducibility for any PV-based reanalysis.

title: Northern Lights on Civic and Citizenship Education
outcome_summary: This volume chapter set uses IEA ICCS 2009 and ICCS 2016 Nordic data to describe and explain patterns in civic and environmental citizenship. For principal aims (Chapter 3), it uses school-level questionnaire responses with the ICCS school weight TOTWGTC and reports descriptive percentages and 2009–2016 percentage-point changes, with significance assessed via chi-squared tests. For student outcomes (Chapters 5 and 6), it models student-reported civic learning opportunities and civic competence using multilevel regression (two-level structure: students within schools) and factorial ANOVA for environmental citizenship, applying student weights and jackknife repeated replication for standard errors. Civic knowledge is measured using five plausible values with IRT scaling, and the models use Mplus with full information maximum likelihood for missing data. The evidence is cross-sectional, so the authors caution against causal interpretations; moreover, the study emphasizes that unequal access and differential effects can reproduce or mitigate SES-based inequalities.

all_target_variables: and explain patterns in civic and environmental citizenship achievement

title: Reflections on the Development of the IEA Civic and Citizenship Education Studies
authors: Wolfram Schulz
outcome_summary: This chapter provides a methodological reflection on how the IEA civic and citizenship education studies evolved from CIVED 1999 to ICCS 2009 and ICCS 2016, and what is planned for ICCS 2022. It explains content-domain expansion (e.g., increased emphasis on participation and reasoning/applying), design changes (e.g., rotated booklets, linkage items, and shifts in teacher questionnaire sampling from subject-specific to all teachers at the target grade), and method changes (e.g., introduction of plausible value methodology in ICCS and use of IRT-based scaling). It also discusses quality assurance procedures (translation verification and international quality monitoring) and the implications of questionnaire format changes for comparability across cycles. The chapter does not report predictive model performance metrics or an empirical ML pipeline; its contribution is guidance for interpreting and using ICCS/CIVED data for secondary analysis and for understanding comparability constraints across time and delivery modes.

title: Rapport national Luxembourg — ICCS (International Civic and Citizenship Education Study) 2009
authors: Réginald Burton, Claude Houssemand
outcome_summary: This national report for Luxembourg uses ICCS 2009 data to describe students’ civic knowledge and their affective/behavioral perceptions and engagement. The cognitive test administered to grade-8 students lasted 45 minutes and included 79 items (multiple-choice and constructed-response), with items rotated across seven test booklets; a European module was also administered in Luxembourg (12-minute cognitive test plus a 17-minute questionnaire). The report reports Luxembourg’s civic knowledge mean score as 473 points (significantly below the international mean) and interprets the distribution across performance levels, highlighting a large share of students at Level 1 and below (22% below Level 1; 30% at Level 1; 19% at Level 3). For non-cognitive outcomes, it reports questionnaire-based scales with a conventional mean of 50 and SD of 10, including democratic values, gender equality attitudes, immigrant rights attitudes, trust in civic institutions, interest in political/social questions, and civic participation intentions/behaviors. It also links family context indicators (e.g., birthplace, parents’ socioeconomic status, test language, parental interest and discussion frequency) to variation in civic knowledge and interest, and discusses curriculum expectations versus implemented curriculum using document analysis and stakeholder perceptions. The report is descriptive and interpretive; it does not provide an ML model-estimation procedure or performance metrics for predictive algorithms.

title: ICCS 2009 Asian Report
outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 Asian Report presents results from the Asian regional module of the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS). The report draws primarily on student data from lower-secondary students in five Asian participating education systems/countries (Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong SAR, Indonesia, Republic of Korea, Thailand), with Grade 8 as the target grade except where Grade 9 is used due to age criteria. Data collection combines an international cognitive test (80 items measuring civic knowledge, analysis, and reasoning; scaled using Rasch Partial Credit Model with weighted likelihood estimates) and student questionnaires including an additional 15-minute Asian questionnaire focused on region-relevant constructs such as trust in institutions, perceptions of government and the legal system, attitudes toward corruption and authoritarian practices, and beliefs about traditional culture, obedience to authority, and Asian identity. The report uses two-stage cluster sampling (PPS school sampling and intact class selection) and reports results as item percentages and questionnaire scale scores, including reliability (Cronbach’s alpha) and item-by-score maps. It also flags that Hong Kong SAR does not meet minimum participation requirements, so its results are excluded from the computation of the ICCS Asian average.
all_target_variables: Asian regional module of the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study

title: Young People’s Civic Attitudes and Practices: England’s Outcomes from the IEA International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS)
outcome_summary: This DfE report uses ICCS 2009 England (Year 9) data to describe pupils’ civic knowledge and attitudes and to model associations between these outcomes and pupil, home, and school factors using multilevel modelling. The report finds that civic knowledge is a strong predictor of positive democratic values, gender equality attitudes, and support for equal rights for ethnic groups and immigrants, while some classroom and school ethos variables show mixed directions (e.g., pupil influence at school is negatively associated with civic knowledge). For gender equality, normalized coefficients are reported for civic knowledge (37.5), being female (28.1), and openness in class discussion (8.2). For in-school participation, normalized coefficients are reported for civic knowledge (17.0), home literacy (14.9), parent interest (13.1), and openness (10.2), and for future voting intention civic knowledge (29.7) and parent interest (25.3). No machine-learning algorithms are evaluated, and the report does not provide a missing-data handling strategy for the modelling results.

title: Národní zpráva z Mezinárodní studie občanské výchovy
authors: Petr Soukup (ed.), Simona Křečková, Jan Schubert, Martina Ševců, Antonín Staněk, Lucia Truksová, Světlana Zeipeltová
outcome_summary: This ICCS 2009 Czech national report uses ICCS 2009 8th-grade data (4,630 students from 144 schools) to describe and model civic knowledge and civic/political attitudes. Although the report is not an ML study (no ML algorithms are trained), it estimates multilevel regression models (HLM) and simple regressions to explain outcomes. For civic knowledge, the multilevel model explains 83% of between-school variance and 33% of between-student variance; key positive predictors include frequent TV news viewing (+15.1 points), future voting participation (strongest effect), expected education years (+7.5 points per year), and higher parents’ occupational status, while attending basic schools is associated with lower scores (~-37.4 points). For European civic knowledge, explained variance is 52% between schools and 18% between students, with motivation and media exposure again positive and home language Czech strongly positive. For attitudes, democratic values support is positively related to civic knowledge (about 10% explained in simple regression), and planned voting participation is best predicted by civic knowledge and political interest (full model explains ~37%). Methodological caveat: the report does not document missing-data handling or PV-style procedures, and it does not provide ML-specific validation/metrics because no ML models are used.
all_datasets_used: ICCS 2009 Czech Republic main study data collected
all_target_variables: 83% of between-school variance and 33% of between-student variance achievement

title: ICCS 2009 Encyclopedia
outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 investigated how countries prepare young people for civic roles by measuring students’ civic and citizenship knowledge, understanding, and reasoning, alongside student attitudes, perceptions, and activities related to civics and citizenship. The student cognitive test comprised 80 items across seven item-clusters administered via a balanced rotated design across seven booklets, with 45 minutes for the assigned booklet, and a 40-minute student questionnaire capturing background and perceptions. Data collection occurred in 38 countries between October 2008 and May 2009, with additional teacher questionnaires (30 minutes) and school/principal contextual instruments. The encyclopedia volume presents qualitatively oriented national-context chapters (for 35 of 38 countries) and uses these contexts to help interpret the quantitative ICCS 2009 survey results reported elsewhere. The excerpt does not provide any model-based performance metrics or PV/missing-data handling for empirical estimation within this volume.

title: Indagine Internazionale sull'Educazione Civica e alla Cittadinanza. Quadro di Riferimento
authors: Wolfram Schulz, Julian Fraillon, John Ainley, Bruno Losito, David Kerr
outcome_summary: Questo volume è un Quadro di Riferimento metodologico per ICCS 2009: non analizza dati studente e non stima modelli predittivi/esplicativi, ma definisce come dovrebbero essere misurati i risultati e i fattori di contesto. La rilevazione prevede una prova cognitiva internazionale (item a scelta multipla e risposta aperta) e un questionario studenti (item Likert, risposta multipla, chiusa e alcune risposte aperte codificate), oltre a questionario insegnanti, questionario scuola e una rilevazione online sul contesto nazionale. La prova cognitiva è organizzata tramite rotazione di cluster di item nei fascicoli e le scale risultanti coprono quattro ambiti di contenuto e due ambiti cognitivi (conoscenze; ragionamento e analisi). Sono inoltre definiti ambiti affettivo-comportamentali (convinzioni di valore, atteggiamenti, intenzioni di comportamento, comportamenti) e una griglia multilivello di condizioni preesistenti e processi (comunità nazionale, scuola/classe, studente, ambiente familiare).

title: ICCS: MARCO DE LA EVALUACIÓN
authors: Wolfram Schulz, Julian Fraillon, John Ainley, Bruno Losito, David Kerr
outcome_summary: Este documento presenta el marco de evaluación del ICCS, describiendo qué se mide y cómo se organiza la instrumentación, más que resultados empíricos. El estudio evalúa (i) rendimiento cognitivo del alumno mediante un test con ítems de elección múltiple y algunos de respuesta abierta, y (ii) percepciones/actitudes y comportamientos mediante cuestionarios tipo Likert y otros formatos. El marco define dominios de contenido (sociedad y sistemas cívicos, principios cívicos, participación cívica, identidades cívicas) y dominios cognitivos (conocimiento; razonamiento y análisis), además de dominios afectivo-comportamentales (creencias sobre valores, actitudes, intenciones de comportamiento y comportamientos). Se emplea un diseño rotativo de cuadernillos para ampliar cobertura del marco sin aumentar el tiempo individual, y se indica que la puntuación se apoya en TRI. También se detallan escalas contextuales derivadas de cuestionarios del alumno, profesor y centro, y la existencia de módulos regionales (Europa, Latinoamérica y Asia).

title: ICCS Assessment Framework International Civic and Citizenship Education Study Assessment Framework
authors: Wolfram Schulz, Julian Fraillon, John Ainley, Bruno Losito, David Kerr
outcome_summary: This ICCS assessment framework specifies how civic and citizenship education is operationalized for large-scale measurement, including the structure of the civic and citizenship framework and the contextual framework. It defines content domains (civic and citizenship content), affective-behavioral domains, and cognitive domains, and describes how items are mapped to these domains. The document also outlines assessment design elements such as the ICCS instruments, test booklet design, item types, and how contextual scales are reported. Because it is a framework rather than an empirical analysis, it does not provide model performance metrics, benchmarks, or predictive results. Consequently, it should be used to understand what constructs ICCS measures and how instruments are organized, not to infer effects of predictors on student outcomes.

title: ICCS 2009 European Report
outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 European Report summarizes findings from the ICCS 2009 European module administered to Grade 8 students (or Grade 9 when Grade 8 average age was below 13.5) in 24 European countries, using a two-stage cluster sample (PPS school sampling, then intact class sampling). Students completed an international cognitive test (80 items in rotated booklets), an international student questionnaire, and a European cognitive test and European questionnaire; the European cognitive test was not scaled into a common EU knowledge scale due to unsatisfactory scaling properties, so EU-related item results are reported separately. The report also uses teacher, school principal, and national contexts survey data to contextualize civic and citizenship education. Outcomes include both cognitive knowledge (e.g., percentages correct on EU laws/policies and euro items) and affective/behavioral questionnaire scales (standardized to mean 50, SD 10 for equally weighted national samples meeting participation requirements). The report emphasizes cross-country variation and associations between constructs (e.g., self-reported EU knowledge and civic knowledge; European identity and attitudes), while noting that the excerpt does not document PV or missing-data handling procedures for any analytic model.

title: ESTUDIO INTERNACIONAL DE EDUCACIÓN CÍVICA Y FORMACIÓN CIUDADANA ICCS 2009 Primer informe nacional de resultados Chile - Junio 2010
outcome_summary: Este primer informe nacional de ICCS 2009 (Chile) es principalmente descriptivo y no entrena modelos de aprendizaje automático. Para el conocimiento cívico (escala IRT única), Chile obtiene 483 puntos, levemente por debajo del promedio internacional (500) y se ubica en el puesto 24 de 36 países con puntajes válidos. En el análisis jerárquico lineal multivariado, el modelo que incluye género y nivel socioeconómico a nivel de estudiante y el nivel socioeconómico promedio del establecimiento explica 21% de la varianza del puntaje; la dependencia no mantiene un efecto independiente al controlar por nivel socioeconómico. En desagregaciones, las mujeres obtienen puntajes significativamente mayores que los hombres (490 vs 476) y los estudiantes de nivel socioeconómico alto superan a los de nivel medio y bajo (538 vs 485 vs 450). El documento no reporta métricas ML ni detalles de ponderación/replicación, por lo que no es posible evaluar desempeño predictivo ni consideraciones de leakage o validación ML.

title: Initial Findings from the IEA International Civic and Citizenship Education Study
authors: Wolfram Schulz, John Ainley, Julian Fraillon, David Kerr, Bruno Losito
outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 is an IEA large-scale comparative study of civic and citizenship education conducted in 38 countries, collecting data from more than 140,000 students, about 62,000 teachers, and over 5,300 schools. The report excerpt frames the study’s purpose and organization and outlines the initial findings that will be reported in subsequent sections: variations in civic knowledge across countries, changes in civic content knowledge since earlier IEA civic studies, and students’ attitudes and civic engagement (including trust, interest, and participation). It also highlights the roles of schools and communities (e.g., classroom climate and implementation of civic education) and the influence of family background (including immigrant background and parental occupational status). The excerpt does not provide the technical scaling, sampling-weighting, or missing-data procedures, nor does it report model-based performance metrics, so the findings should be interpreted as descriptive comparative results rather than as outputs from an explicitly specified predictive ML pipeline.

title: Prvotní zjištění z Mezinárodní studie občanské výchovy
authors: Wolfram Schulz, John Ainley, Julian Fraillon, David Kerr, Bruno Losito
outcome_summary: Tato zpráva poskytuje prvotní (ne-ML) výsledky z ICCS 2009 pro 38 zemí, založené na škálování kognitivního testu (Rasch; mezinárodní průměr 500, SD 100) a škálování Likertových postojů (průměr 50, SD 10). V poskytnutém textu nejsou uvedeny žádné strojově-učící algoritmy ani ML metriky (Accuracy/AUC/RMSE), takže nelze určit „best ML model“. Zjištění ukazují, že průměrné občanské znalosti se mezi zeměmi pohybují přibližně v rozmezí 380–576 bodů a že dívky dosahují vyšších skóre než chlapci (v průměru rozdíl 22 bodů). V porovnání s CIVED 1999 (15 srovnatelných zemí) došlo k statisticky významnému poklesu obsahu občanských znalostí o zhruba 4 body. Metodologicky je třeba upozornit, že chybějící data a jejich ošetření nejsou v poskytnutém výřezu popsána a že jde o deskriptivní/regresní šetření, nikoli o prediktivní ML pipeline.

title: ICCS 2009 IDB USER GUIDE
outcome_summary: This ICCS 2009 IDB User Guide documents how to use the ICCS 2009 International Database and the IEA IDB Analyzer to compute weighted descriptive statistics, regression coefficients, benchmark/proficiency percentages, percentiles, and correlations. It explains that ICCS 2009 provides student, teacher, and school data files, including achievement scores for civic knowledge represented as five plausible values (PV1CIV–PV5CIV) and that achievement analyses should use these plausible values with appropriate sampling and imputation variance. The guide details the complex sampling design and the need for correct sampling weights (e.g., TOTWGTS for student-level) and Jackknife Repeated Replication (JRR) replicate variance estimation using jackknife zone/replicate variables. It also specifies how special missing-value codes (omitted, invalid, not administered, not reached, not applicable) should be interpreted and how analysts can exclude missing grouping variables in the software. No predictive ML modeling is evaluated in this document.

title: Resultados iniciales del Estudio Internacional de Educación Cívica y Ciudadana de la IEA
authors: Wolfram Schulz, John Ainley, Julian Fraillon, David Kerr, Bruno Losito
outcome_summary: Este informe presenta resultados iniciales del ICCS 2009, un estudio comparativo de educación cívica y ciudadana de la IEA en 38 países. La evaluación cognitiva del conocimiento cívico se basó en una prueba de 79 ítems (con 6 de respuesta construida y 73 de selección múltiple) administrada en siete cuadernillos con diseño de rotación balanceada; cada estudiante respondió un cuadernillo en 45 minutos. El conocimiento cívico se escaló mediante un modelo Rasch y se reporta en una métrica con media 500 y desviación estándar 100, usando valores plausibles (cinco por estudiante) para estimar el desempeño. Además, el cuestionario del estudiante (40 minutos) midió actitudes y compromiso cívico en escalas tipo Likert calibradas a media 50 y desviación estándar 10. El muestreo fue por conglomerados en dos etapas (escuelas PPS y una clase aleatoria por escuela) y el informe indica que todas las muestras nacionales fueron ponderadas; se reportan tasas de participación y el uso de reemplazos cuando fue necesario. No se reporta un análisis predictivo con algoritmos de ML; los resultados se describen principalmente con estadísticas comparativas y modelos de regresión para asociaciones.

title: INFORME LATINOAMERICANO DEL ICCS 2009 Actitudes y conocimientos cívicos de estudiantes de secundaria en seis países de América Latina
authors: Wolfram Schulz, John Ainley, Tim Friedman, Petra Lietz
outcome_summary: Este informe del ICCS 2009 (módulo regional latinoamericano) describe resultados descriptivos y de asociación para seis países (CHL, COL, DOM, GTM, MEX, PRY) con una muestra total cercana a 30.000 estudiantes de 8º/9º grado en más de 1.000 escuelas. El conocimiento cívico (escala ICCS) muestra promedios nacionales entre 380 y 483 puntos, con 32% de estudiantes por debajo del Nivel 1 y 23% en el Nivel 3; los países con mayor IDH tienden a tener mayores niveles de conocimiento cívico. En actitudes, los hombres muestran mayor aceptación de gobiernos autoritarios y de prácticas corruptas que las mujeres, y el patrón general indica que mayor conocimiento cívico se asocia con menor aceptación de autoritarismo, corrupción y justificaciones para desobedecer la ley (sin implicar causalidad). En convivencia pacífica, las mujeres reportan más empatía y los estudiantes con actitudes más positivas hacia la diversidad presentan niveles más altos de conocimiento cívico; aun así, una proporción importante justifica la justicia por cuenta propia cuando las autoridades no actúan. No se reportan modelos de machine learning ni métricas predictivas; el análisis se basa en escalas construidas con Rasch/IRT y comparaciones nacionales.

title: ICCS_2009_International_Report
outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 International Report documents the ICCS study design and the measurement framework for civic and citizenship education. The student cognitive test comprised 80 items (79 used in analysis) covering four content domains (civic society and systems, civic principles, civic participation, civic identities) and two cognitive processes (knowing; reasoning and analyzing), with items administered via a balanced rotated booklet design (45 minutes per student). The report also describes affective-behavioral outcomes measured through a 40-minute student questionnaire using Likert-type items, with questionnaire scales set to an international metric (mean 50, SD 10 for equally weighted national samples). Sampling was two-stage cluster sampling with PPS school selection and intact-class selection within schools, targeting Grade 8 (or Grade 9 when average Grade 8 age was below 13.5). Results presented include country comparisons of civic knowledge scale scores (mean 500, SD 100 for equally weighted national samples) and proficiency-level distributions, plus descriptive cross-country patterns for democratic values, trust, civic engagement, and related attitudes.

title: ICCS_2009_Technical_Report
authors: John Ainley, Wolfram Schulz
outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 is a comparative international survey of civic and citizenship education administered to Grade 8 (or equivalent) students, complemented by teacher and school principal questionnaires and a national contexts survey. The cognitive test used Rasch-based item response modeling to derive civic knowledge scores from 79 (of 80) items, and the report uses plausible value methodology with five separate estimates per student for reporting civic knowledge. The final reporting scale was standardized to an international metric (mean 500, SD 100 for equally weighted national samples), with proficiency levels defined by scale-point cut-points. The survey employed two-stage cluster sampling (PPS school sampling and intact classroom sampling) across 38 countries, with sampling weights and jackknife repeated replication (JRR) used to estimate sampling variance. For multivariate analyses, missing data were handled via dummy-variable adjustment and mean/median substitution, and standard errors incorporated both sampling and imputation components for plausible-value-based outcomes.

title: ICCS 2009 Latin American Report
outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 Latin American Report summarizes results from the Latin American regional module of the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS 2009) for six participating countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Mexico, Paraguay). The student assessment combined an international civic knowledge test (80 items; 79 used for scaling) with a Latin American regional cognitive test (16 multiple-choice items) administered after the international test; students also completed international and Latin American questionnaires. Civic knowledge was scaled using Rasch modeling for the international test and calibrated regional items onto the international civic knowledge scale, with proficiency levels defined on the international metric (mean 500, SD 100; levels spanning 395–478, 479–562, and 563+). Questionnaire constructs were scaled using IRT (Rasch Partial Credit Model) and reported as standardized scale scores (mean 50, SD 10) for equally weighted regional databases. The report reports national percentages and scale averages (with standard errors) and compares Latin American averages to the international ICCS average, finding relatively low civic knowledge in the region and systematic associations between civic knowledge and attitudes toward authoritarianism, corruption, and disobeying the law, while also documenting empathy, identity, diversity attitudes, and reported aggression/violence experiences.

title: ICCS 2009, Internationale hovedresultater
authors: Jens Bruun
outcome_summary: ICCS 2009 is an IEA international comparative study of civic and citizenship education among lower secondary students (target age ~14; typically grade 8). The report describes a complex sampling design with schools and one sampled class per school, and it presents international results across 38 countries using a cognitive test (ICCS Civic Knowledge Test) and extensive questionnaires on values, attitudes, and participation. The cognitive test is scaled using a Rasch model and reported on an international scale with mean 500 and SD 100; the report also notes the use of plausible values in the underlying scoring. For the attitudinal and participation domains, the report uses scale scores (often with an international mean set to 50) and item-based percentages, and it highlights that the tables are primarily descriptive rather than ranking claims of “better” outcomes. Correlational findings show small-to-moderate associations between knowledge and engagement measures, notably school democracy participation (r=0.27) and future electoral participation intentions (r=0.44), while other scales show no significant relationship. Methodological caveat: the report does not document PV handling or missing-data handling, and it does not provide ML evaluation metrics or model validation procedures because no ML prediction pipeline is used.

title: ICCS 2022 – nacionalni izveštaj o rezultatima međunarodnog istraživanja o građanskom obrazovanju i učestvu u modernom društvu
authors: Branislav Ranđelović, Daniјela Đukić, Taњa Trboјević, Srdjan Zrnić, Bojana Marković
outcome_summary: ICCS 2022 in Serbia was implemented as a standardized, multi-stage large-scale assessment of Grade 8 students (about age 14) using paper-based testing in the national cycle. The study administered a cognitive test (141 items; 45 minutes) measuring civic knowledge across four content domains and two cognitive domains, alongside contextual questionnaires for students, teachers, and school directors. The report describes IRT-based scaling and the use of ICCS reference levels (A–D) with reported national mean achievement on the ICCS 2022 scale (Serbia: 464 points; ICCS 2022 average: 508). It also reports extensive descriptive results for gender differences, socioeconomic gradients (e.g., SEI and parental education), and multiple civic engagement/attitude indicators (e.g., environmental concern and expected participation), including participation rates and documented exclusions to ensure comparability. Limitations are that this national report does not present an ML predictive modeling pipeline; therefore, no ML performance metrics, PV-combining procedures, or missing-data imputation strategies for modeling are provided.

title: Unges europæiske identitet: Det europæiske modul ICCS 2022
authors: Jens Bruun, Jonas Lieberkind
outcome_summary: Rapporten præsenterer hovedresultater fra ICCS 2022’s europæiske modul, som er et kort spørgeskema til elever på 8. klassetrin. Modulet måler elevernes europæiske identitet, oplevet undervisning om Europa og EU, holdninger til europæisk samarbejde (inkl. arbejdskraftens fri bevægelighed og miljø/klima), forventet valgdeltagelse til Europa-Parlamentet, tillid til EU-institutioner samt positive og negative forventninger til Europas fremtid. Data dækker 19 lande (med Tyskland som to delstater) og omfatter samlet over 66.000 elever, heraf godt 4.300 danske elever fra 134 skoler. Resultaterne rapporteres som IEA-udviklede skalaer (med europæisk gennemsnit sat til 50 og SD=10) og som procentandele for Likert-kategorier, og rapporten sammenligner over tid mellem ICCS 2009, 2016 og 2022, hvor det er muligt. Der rapporteres ikke ML-modeller eller PV-/missing-data procedurer i teksten, og derfor er resultaterne primært deskriptive/komparative frem for modelbaserede kausale estimater.

title: IEA International Civic and Citizenship Education Study 2022 Assessment Framework
authors: Wolfram Schulz, Julian Fraillon, Bruno Losito, Gabriella Agrusti, John Ainley, Valeria Damiani, Tim Friedman
outcome_summary: ICCS 2022 is the third cycle in its current form and the fifth IEA study of civic and citizenship education, designed to measure students’ civic knowledge and their civic attitudes and engagement, alongside contextual information from students, teachers, schools, and national contexts surveys. A key implementation feature is the option of computer-based delivery for the student survey (with about two-thirds of participating countries choosing it), including computer-enhanced modules that simulate participatory real-world scenarios with interactive feedback. The framework also emphasizes comparability across paper and computer modes and across cycles (2009, 2016, 2022), while broadening content to sustainability, digital civic engagement, diversity, young people’s views of the political system, and global citizenship.

title: Starptautiskā pilsoniskās izglītības pētījuma IEA ICCS 2022 Eiropas aptaujas pirmie rezultāti

Publikācija neapraksta mašīnmācīšanās modeļus vai prognozējošu modelēšanu; tādēļ secinājumi ir deskriptīvi un interpretējoši, balstīti uz aptaujas atbilžu sadalījumu, nevis uz ML veiktu cēlonisku vai prognozējošu analīzi.

title: Education for Citizenship in Times of Global Challenge

The report emphasizes that results are reported with caution when countries do not meet IEA participation/technical standards, and that comparisons across ICCS cycles are limited to countries meeting those standards for all data points. Scaling/equating procedures and detailed scoring methodology are referenced as being provided in the ICCS 2022 technical report, which is where PV handling and missing-data procedures would be specified. title: ICCS 2022 Technical Report
authors: Wolfram Schulz, Tim Friedman, Julian Fraillon
outcome_summary: ICCS 2022 is a cross-national study of civic and citizenship education that collects student civic knowledge (via an international test administered on paper or via a computer-based delivery platform), along with student, teacher, and school questionnaires capturing contextual and affective-behavioral constructs. The technical report describes an assessment framework with four civic knowledge content domains and two cognitive processes (knowing; reasoning and applying), plus an attitudes and engagement framework organized into attitudes and engagement constructs. The study uses stratified two-stage cluster sampling: schools are selected with probability proportional to size (PPS) and intact classrooms are randomly selected within schools; principals are nested within sampled schools. Scaling procedures are used to construct civic knowledge scores and questionnaire indices, including equating and mode-effect adjustment when computer-based delivery is used, supported by bridging studies in countries that switched modes. Weighting procedures and variance estimation methods are specified to support population-representative reporting, with results interpreted cautiously for countries not meeting IEA participation standards.

title: ICCS National Report Malta 2022
authors: Liberato Camilleri
outcome_summary: This ICCS 2022 national report for Malta uses the ICCS civic knowledge scale (derived from Rasch scaling of test items) and relates it to engagement-related questionnaire predictors using regression analysis. For the engagement predictor model, the report reports that the twelve engagement predictors explain 33.0% of the total variation in ICCS civic knowledge scores, with most predictors significant at p < 0.05. The strongest predictor is students’ expected participation in illegal protest activities (lowest p-value), with a negative regression coefficient (−3.425). The report also notes that two engagement aspects—participation in wider community groups/organisations and willingness to participate in school activities—were not significant. No machine-learning algorithms are trained; therefore, ML technique fields are empty and the analysis is conventional regression rather than predictive ML.

title: Mednarodna raziskava državljanske vzgoje in izobraževanja (IEA ICCS 2022) : nacionalno poročilo – prvi rezultati

Poročilo opisuje zasnovo ICCS 2022 (vključno s prehodom na računalniško podprto izvedbo, bridge study in standardi realizacije vzorca) ter rezultate za več vsebinskih sklopov: državljanska vednost (lestvica z zahtevnostnimi ravnmi A–D), razlike po spolu in socialno-ekonomskem statusu (SES), ter kazalnike družbeno/državljanskega delovanja (angažiranost), stališča in pričakovanja prihodnje participacije. Za državljansko vednost so predstavljena mednarodna primerjanja (npr. povprečje Slovenije 504 točk; deleži po ravneh, npr. ~25% na ravni A) in trendne spremembe med cikli 2009–2016–2022 (npr. Slovenija beleži padec med 2016 in 2022). Omejitev za interpretacijo v kontekstu “policy” je, da poročilo ne izvaja kauzalnih analiz in ne dokumentira PV/MI ali utežnih postopkov na ravni tega nacionalnega dokumenta.

title: Młodzi w demokracji. Wyniki Międzynarodowego Badania Kompetencji Obywatelskich ICCS 2022
authors: Olga Wasilewska (red.), Wioleta Dobosz-Leszczyńska, Paweł Penszko, Michał Sitek, Paweł Szymborski, Jędrzej Witkowski
outcome_summary: Raport podsumowuje realizację i wyniki ICCS 2022 w Polsce (uczniowie klasy ósmej, zwykle ok. 14 lat) w ramach międzynarodowego badania IEA. Badanie obejmowało test wiedzy i rozumienia zagadnień z edukacji obywatelskiej oraz ankiety uczniów, nauczycieli i dyrektorów; w Polsce uczniowie rozwiązywali test w formie papierowej, a ankieta nauczyciela była online. Dobór próby miał charakter losowania warstwowo-zespołowego: losowano szkoły, następnie oddziały klasy ósmej i nauczycieli, a wyniki uogólniano na populację z użyciem wag (school/class base weights oraz weight adjustments). Skale wyników konstruowano w oparciu o IRT/Rasch, a dla porównywalności między edycjami i formami (papier/komputer) stosowano procedury skalowania oraz uwzględniano mode-effect poprzez bridging study. Raport prezentuje średnie na skali (np. dla wiedzy i rozumienia w Polsce 554 punkty) oraz rozkłady na poziomach osiągnięć (A–D), wraz z błędami standardowymi i informacją o spełnieniu wymogów realizacji próby.

title: Politisk og demokratisk dannelse i en krisetid (ICCS 2022)

The cognitive test covers 121 items across domains such as institutions/systems, values/principles, interest/participation, and political/democratic identity; results are summarized as country means in scale points and as proportions of students at ICCS proficiency levels (A–E). L’échelle est décrite en quatre niveaux (A à D, avec un niveau “en dessous de D”) et couvre quatre domaines (systèmes et institutions civiques, principes civiques, participation civique, rôles et identités civiques) ainsi que deux domaines cognitifs (savoir, raisonner et appliquer). Pour chaque item, le rapport fournit le cadre de référence, le type de tâche (interactif, question ouverte, QCM), des exemples de réponses attendues, puis des résultats descriptifs (pourcentages de réponses correctes/partielles/incorrectes et non-réponses) pour la France et des comparaisons internationales. title: Kako mladi vidijo Evropo – zaznave osmošolcev o Evropi in Evropski uniji: Nacionalno poročilo Evropskega regionalnega modula ICCS 2022
authors: Eva Klemenčič Mirazchiyski
outcome_summary: This national report presents first results from the ICCS 2022 European Regional Module (ERM) for Slovenia, focusing on Grade 8 students’ attitudes, perceptions, and self-reported behaviors related to Europe and the European Union. The report uses Likert-type questionnaire items (and derived scales) and compares Slovenian results to a European average benchmark (European average fixed at 50 with SD=10 for equally weighted national samples meeting sampling requirements). Across domains, Slovenian students show a stronger European identity than the European average, report relatively high opportunities to learn about the EU, and express generally pro-environmental cooperation attitudes, though overall sustainable behavior and some mobility attitudes are slightly below European norms. The report also documents item-level differences in political consumerism and higher-than-average negative expectations about Europe’s future. title: Preparing for Life in a Digital Age

CIL achievement is measured with a computer-based assessment comprising four thematic modules of discrete tasks plus a large open task (e.g., creating a poster), mapped onto a CIL scale with proficiency levels. The chapter reports cross-country distributions of CIL scores (country means spanning roughly 361 to 553 scale points) and describes how student access, familiarity, and learning experiences relate to CIL. For multivariate analyses, the authors estimate two-level hierarchical models (students nested within schools) using MPlus and apply sampling weights at student and school levels. Missing data are handled by excluding students with no student questionnaire data and imputing missing school/teacher-derived variables using national mean/median values with missing indicators. The chapter emphasizes that ICT resources matter partly through socioeconomic context, while students’ experience and regular use of computers show more robust associations with CIL.

authors: E. Gebhardt et al.
outcome_summary: This chapter uses ICILS 2013 grade eight student computer-based assessment of computer and information literacy (CIL) plus a student questionnaire administered after the test. Students completed two randomly allocated 30-minute test modules from four, yielding one-hour total assessment time, and CIL achievement was scaled on a metric with mean 500 and SD 100 using Rasch-based scaling and plausible value methodology with full conditioning. The chapter reports gender differences in (i) interest-enjoyment in ICT, (ii) associations between interest-enjoyment and CIL by gender using correlations and effect sizes, and (iii) gender differences in patterns of ICT use (productivity applications, social communication, exchanging information, recreation, and study purposes) and their relationships with CIL using bivariate correlations and multiple regression models with country-specific fixed effects (country means of predictors set to zero within each country). Analyses are conducted on weighted data with sampling weights and nonresponse adjustments; however, the excerpt does not specify missing-data handling for questionnaire items. Overall, male students report higher interest-enjoyment and show stronger positive associations with CIL than female students, while gendered ICT-use patterns do not consistently translate into systematic advantages in CIL achievement.

Knowledge is assessed via a rotating test design with about 140 items distributed so that each student answers roughly 35 items, and results are reported on a fixed scale anchored to ICCS 2009 (international mean 500, SD 100). Attitudes and engagement are measured through student questionnaires and summarized using IEA-developed scales/indices, with additional alternative measures based on the proportion agreeing with statements. The report emphasizes that it is not designed to explain causal mechanisms; instead, it documents statistically significant differences (5% level) across countries, time (2009/2016/2022), and student subgroups (gender, socioeconomic background, migration background). It also notes that the COVID-19 period may have affected participation and results differently across countries, and that the report cannot quantify the pandemic’s impact on achievement changes.

title: Svenska elevers syn på EU och framtiden

ICCS is administered to grade-8 students and combines cognitive test items with questionnaire items on attitudes and engagement; this sheet reports primarily attitudinal/engagement outcomes as percentages (e.g., trust in the European Parliament and the Swedish government, expected voting behavior in national and EU elections, and perceived threats such as climate change and war). For Sweden, the sheet reports that 3,263 students from 149 schools participated. It also notes that results are intended for classroom discussion and highlights that views tend to be more positive among students with higher socioeconomic background. title: ICILS_2013_IDB_user_guide
outcome_summary: This document is a user guide for the ICILS 2013 international database, not an empirical study estimating effects with machine learning. It describes the ICILS 2013 design: a multistage stratified cluster sample of schools with nested student and teacher samples, and a rotated computer-based assessment where students complete only subsets of test modules. Student achievement in computer and information literacy (CIL) is produced using IRT scaling and multiple imputation via five plausible values (PV1–PV5), requiring analysts to run analyses separately for each PV and combine results using Rubin-style rules. The guide also specifies complex-survey estimation requirements: analysts should use the appropriate total weights (TOTWGTS for students, TOTWGTT for teachers, TOTWGTC for schools) and jackknife repeated replication (JRR) replicate weights/zone variables for correct standard errors. It further documents coding conventions for missingness (omitted vs not administered vs not reached) and cautions against causal language because the design is observational and cross-sectional.

title: Main findings and implications for education policies in Europe
outcome_summary: ICILS 2013 is an international large-scale assessment of computer and information literacy (CIL) for grade 8 students (average age 13.5), with main fieldwork in 2013. The policy document reports results from nearly 60,000 students in 3,300+ schools across 21 education systems, including 9 EU countries, and uses a CIL achievement scale with a mean of 500 points (equally weighted national samples) divided into proficiency levels (below level 1 through level 4). The report also draws on student, teacher, and school questionnaires to describe computer use, attitudes, teacher ICT self-efficacy, and the pedagogical embedding of ICT. Key benchmarks are expressed as shares of students at low proficiency (e.g., 15–45% in participating EU countries) and very high proficiency (less than 5% in all participating EU countries). The document is a synthesis for EU policy dialogue and does not provide the technical PV/missing-data/weighting procedures used in the underlying international analyses.

title: Is the “Net Generation” Ready for Digital Citizenship? Perspectives from the IEA International Computer and Information Literacy Study 2013
outcome_summary: This IEA policy brief synthesizes findings from ICILS 2013, which assessed Grade 8 (or equivalent) students’ computer and information literacy (CIL) across 21 education systems. The underlying ICILS assessment used a four-part framework covering individual learner skills and contextual factors in home, in-school, and wider community settings, with contextual questionnaires also collected from around 35,000 teachers and additional school ICT-related staff. The brief reports that, on average across participating systems, only about a quarter of students could identify characteristics of an untrustworthy email and about a fifth could recognize biased or unreliable information, indicating limited critical use of digital information. It also highlights large cross-country variation in home access to computers and internet, and it reports that teacher confidence and ICT integration beyond basic tasks are limited. The policy implications emphasize targeted CIL instruction, alignment of in-school and out-of-school ICT use, and investment in teacher education and professional development.

title: Uruguay en el ICILS 2023
authors: Cecilia Oreiro, Jennifer Viñas
outcome_summary: El informe “Uruguay en el ICILS 2023” describe el desempeño de estudiantes de octavo grado en alfabetización computacional y manejo de información y en pensamiento computacional, y estima modelos jerárquicos multivariados para explicar asociaciones con variables de estudiante y de centro. En alfabetización computacional y manejo de información, el 36% supera el nivel 1 (y 0,5% alcanza nivel 4), y en pensamiento computacional el 45% supera el nivel 1 (con promedio de 421 puntos). En los modelos, los factores más fuertemente asociados incluyen la composición socioeconómica del centro, la expectativa de graduación universitaria y el uso diario de TIC; por ejemplo, en el Modelo 3 para alfabetización computacional y manejo de información, 'Use ICT daily' (39,0***) y 'Center socioeconomic composition' (37,7***) aparecen como asociaciones positivas relevantes. Para pensamiento computacional, también destacan 'Use ICT daily' (33,1***) y 'Center socioeconomic composition' (28,6***), mientras que algunas variables de aprendizaje autorreportado en clase muestran coeficientes negativos. Limitaciones metodológicas: el análisis de modelos se realiza con una submuestra (excluye ~30% por falta de información), se imputan promedio/moda a nivel de centro para cuestionarios de docentes/directores/referentes, pero no se imputan faltantes del cuestionario de estudiantes; además, el informe no presenta métricas de desempeño típicas de ML (Accuracy/AUC/R²) porque no se entrenan modelos de aprendizaje automático.

title: Compass 12-Computational thinking, socioeconomic gaps and policy implications_0
outcome_summary: This brief uses ICILS 2018 grade-8 (or grade-9 in some countries) data to compare socioeconomic gaps in computer and information literacy (CIL) versus computational thinking (CT). CT was an optional component and was administered in 9 of the 14 participating countries; the authors pool countries that took both CIL and CT and compute gaps as differences in average scaled test scores between high-status and low-status groups. Two socioeconomic proxies are used: parental tertiary education and parental professional/specialist occupation (ISCO-08 1–3). Across countries, students from more advantaged backgrounds score higher in both CIL and CT, with the CT gap typically larger than the CIL gap; pooled regression with country fixed effects yields an estimated CT gap of 52 points vs 45 points for CIL (education proxy) and 45 vs 40 points (occupation proxy), both statistically significant. The brief does not report ICILS plausible-values handling or missing-data procedures, and it does not document whether complex survey weights were applied, limiting interpretability of uncertainty and reproducibility.

title: IEA International Computer and Information Literacy Study 2018 Assessment Framework
authors: Julian Fraillon, John Ainley, Wolfram Schulz, Daniel Duckworth, Tim Friedman
outcome_summary: This publication provides the ICILS 2018 assessment framework, explaining the background, constructs, and design of the computer and information literacy (CIL) assessment and the optional computational thinking (CT) domain. It defines the CIL and CT constructs, specifies strands and aspects, and describes how test items and student/context instruments are mapped to the framework. The document also outlines the contextual framework used to classify contextual factors and variables at multiple levels (e.g., student, classroom/school, and system). As a framework, it does not report an empirical analytic sample, model estimation, or performance metrics; instead, it serves as the blueprint for how ICILS measures are operationalized and how participating systems can interpret results. Consequently, there are no ML-based predictive outcomes or PV/missing-data handling results to summarize here.

title: ICILS_2013_Technical_Report
outcome_summary: ICILS 2013 is a computer-based large-scale assessment of computer and information literacy (CIL) for lower-secondary students (target grade typically Grade 8; Norway used Grade 9). The student test comprised four 30-minute modules with two modules administered per student via a balanced complete rotation, and the CIL scale was derived using a Rasch model with proficiency levels and achievement statistics produced through plausible value methodology with full conditioning. The study used a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design: PPS systematic sampling of schools followed by systematic stratified sampling of students and teachers within schools, with explicit and implicit stratification variables varying by country. To support valid population inference, the report specifies final sampling weights that combine base selection probabilities and nonresponse adjustments, and it describes replicate-weight logic (jackknife repeated replication) for sampling variance estimation. It also documents stringent participation-rate and within-school response thresholds (e.g., discarding schools with <50% within-school response) to reduce bias from nonresponse and operational deviations.

title: ICILS2018_IDB_User_Guide
outcome_summary: This document is a user guide for the ICILS 2018 international database rather than an empirical ML study. It describes the ICILS 2018 design: a cross-sectional, observational assessment of computer and information literacy (CIL) for grade 8 (or equivalent) students, with an optional computational thinking (CT) component in participating countries. The guide explains that student achievement scores are produced using IRT scaling and represented via five plausible values (PV1–PV5) for each scale, requiring analysts to run analyses separately for each PV and combine results to obtain correct standard errors that incorporate both sampling and imputation uncertainty. It also details the multistage stratified cluster sampling design, the need for sampling weights (e.g., TOTWGTS for students) and jackknife repeated replication (JRR) variance estimation variables, and how to use the IEA IDB Analyzer to merge files and compute estimates correctly. Finally, it documents data cleaning, missing-code conventions (omitted/not administered/not reached/logically not applicable), and comparability constraints across countries.

outcome_summary: ICILS 2018 is an IEA large-scale assessment of lower-secondary students’ computer and information literacy (CIL) and, for participating countries, computational thinking (CT). Students in the target grade (typically grade 8, around age 14) completed computer-based CIL modules (five 30-minute modules with two randomly assigned per student) and, where implemented, two additional CT modules (two 25-minute modules in randomized order). The report documents a two-stage cluster sampling design: schools were selected using stratified PPS systematic sampling, and within schools students and teachers were selected using systematic stratified sampling via IEA WinW3S. Achievement scales were derived using Rasch item response theory, and CIL/CT summary statistics were produced using plausible values with full conditioning; proficiency levels for CIL were developed using scale cut-points. The report also specifies complex survey weighting with non-response adjustments and variance estimation via jackknife repeated replication (JRR), and it details data cleaning, scaling, and quality assurance procedures to support cross-national comparability.

title: De digitale geletterdheid van Nederlandse leerlingen in het voortgezet onderwijs
authors: Alexander Krepel, Merlijn Karssen, Marieke Buisman, Judith Conijn, Bieke Schreurs, Goan Booij, Kimberly Farzan
outcome_summary: This ICILS 2023 report provides descriptive and multilevel regression results for Dutch students in the second year of secondary education (N=1288 students across 46 schools). The two outcomes are Computer- and information literacy and Computational thinking, each summarized on ICILS proficiency scales with reported mean scores of 460 (CIL) and 440 (CT), both around the lower/baseline levels, and with CIL close to the ICILS average while CT is lower than the ICILS average. Multilevel analyses indicate that education track is the dominant predictor of between-class differences (e.g., >80% of between-class variation attributed to education track), while other student background variables (home language, migration background, parental education/occupation) show limited additional explanatory power after controlling for track. ICT self-efficacy is positively associated with both outcomes, and years of ICT experience is associated with Computational thinking. The report is not an ML predictive-modeling study (no ML algorithms or ML performance metrics are reported); it uses IEA weighting and plausible values (5 PVs) with replicate weights, but missing-data handling procedures are not documented in the provided text.

title: ICILS_Teacher_Panel
outcome_summary: This ICILS Teacher Panel report uses longitudinal teacher questionnaire data collected in 2020 with ICILS 2018 as baseline to study whether inequality of educational opportunity changed between low- and high-SES schools (defined via a school-level national SES index aggregated from student-level parental occupation/education and books at home). Across Denmark, Finland, and Uruguay, the report finds no clear systematic widening or narrowing of SES gaps from 2018 to 2020; most opportunity gaps remain small in both years. However, several isolated changes appear, including significant SES-gap changes in Finland for teacher preparation time and opportunities to develop ICT expertise, and significant SES-gap increases in Finland and Uruguay for students’ ICT use in explaining and discussing ideas with other students. The analyses are descriptive/regression-based (e.g., difference-in-differences) rather than machine-learning prediction, and inference accounts for the complex ILSA sampling design using TOTWGTT/TOTWGTC weights and Jackknife Repeated Replication replicate weights. The report also cautions that panel response rates are relatively low, which may limit generalizability.

title: Mednarodna raziskava računalniške in informacijske pismenosti (IEA ICILS 2023) : nacionalno poročilo - prvi rezultati
authors: Eva Klemenčič Mirazchiyski
outcome_summary: This national ICILS 2023 report presents first results for Slovenia on two achievement constructs: computer and information literacy (RI literacy/CIL) and computer thinking (RM/CT, optional module). The assessment uses computer-based, authentic modules: RI literacy is measured with seven 30-minute modules rotated across students (each student completes two modules), while RM is measured with four 25-minute modules rotated across students (each student completes two modules). Achievement scales are reported on an IEA metric with a mean of 500 and SD of 100 for the international reference, and country means are derived using plausible values rather than raw test-score averages. The report also provides distributional information (percentiles and proficiency levels) and contextual comparisons (e.g., gender, immigrant background, language at home, SES proxies such as parental education and books at home, and access to devices at home). Methodologically, it emphasizes that reported scores are population estimates for the school system and that PV-based scaling is required for valid comparisons; however, the national report does not specify the exact missing-data handling procedure for background variables.

title: An International Perspective on Digital Literacy
authors: J. Fraillon, Julian Fraillon, Daniel Duckworth, Alec I. Kennedy, Andrés Strello, Rolf Strietholt, Yuan-Ling Liaw, Rolf Strietholt, Julian Fraillon, Yuan-Ling Liaw, Rolf Strietholt, Alec I. Kennedy, Andrés Strello, Rolf Strietholt
outcome_summary: This ICILS 2023 report set (grade 8) provides descriptive and gap analyses for computer and information literacy (CIL) and computational thinking (CT) using PV-based proficiency estimation under a rotated test booklet design. It reports substantial cross-country variation in average CIL and CT, with CIL generally showing less within-country spread than CT. The report documents achievement gaps by gender, immigrant background, language spoken at home, socioeconomic status (parental education/occupation and books at home), and home ICT access (e.g., PC availability when needed, internet disruptions, and number of home PC devices). It also reports trends across cycles: CIL is typically lower in 2023 than in 2018/2013 in countries with comparable data, while CT changes are smaller and often not statistically significant. Finally, it quantifies the CIL–CT association using PVs, reporting an average within-country correlation of 0.76, and notes only slight changes in this association between 2018 and 2023. No machine-learning predictive modeling is evaluated in the provided text.

It specifies the study’s target population and sampling logic (PPS school selection and one intact class per school), and it describes the suite of instruments: student questionnaire, teacher questionnaire, principal questionnaire, ICT coordinator questionnaire, and a national contexts survey. Because this is a design framework rather than an empirical results paper, it does not report model performance metrics, benchmarks, or statistical effects. The report presents Finland’s scale-score results and proficiency-level distributions (including changes from ICILS 2018), plus subgroup comparisons (e.g., gender, home resources, language background) and contextual information from teacher, principal, and ICT-responsible surveys. V SR sa testovalo 3 034 žiakov z 166 škôl (8-GYM, ZŠ a ŠZŠ) elektronicky, pričom testovanie trvalo približne 3,5 hodiny vrátane prestávok; žiaci absolvovali dva CIL moduly (z 7) a dva CT moduly (z 4). CIL skóre SR dosiahlo priemer 499 bodov, čo je signifikantne vyššie než priemer krajín ICILS 2023 (476), a v porovnaní s cyklom 2013 je SR nižšie o 19 bodov. authors: Magdalena Rölz, Iris Höller
outcome_summary: ICILS 2023 is an IEA large-scale assessment of students’ digital competencies on grade 8, conducted in a five-year cycle (since 2013) and including an optional Computational Thinking domain since 2018. The report uses Rasch-based scaling to create competence scores and competence levels, standardizing the CIL scale (computer and information literacy) to a mean of 500 and SD of 100 internationally, and then reporting standardized national comparisons; competence levels are derived from score thresholds. Austria tested 3,448 students from 154 schools and applies complex survey weighting for student, teacher, and school-level questionnaire data. Results show Austria’s CIL mean of 506 points (above INT 476 and EU 493) and a Computational Thinking mean of 476 points (around INT/EU 483), with large shares of students at or below competence level 1 in both domains. The report emphasizes that the design is cross-sectional, so causal claims about national policies (e.g., the 8-point plan) cannot be made, and it flags limitations related to timing of policy implementation and COVID-19 disruptions.

title: Compass_brief_8
outcome_summary: This IEA brief reports descriptive international trends in reading attitudes among fourth graders and their parents using PIRLS questionnaire data collected in 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016. It constructs two scale scores from questionnaire items that remained unchanged across cycles: “students like reading” (three items summed to a 0–9 scale) and “parents like reading” (four items summed to a 0–12 scale). Across the 18 countries participating in all cycles (plus Ontario and Quebec as benchmarking participants), students’ “like reading” scores declined in most countries between 2001 and 2016, with only England and Iran showing increases; between 2011 and 2016, no country showed an increase. Parents’ “like reading” scores also declined in most countries between 2001 and 2016 and between 2006 and 2016, with no increases between 2011 and 2016. The brief emphasizes that these are trend descriptions and do not establish causal explanations for the declines, and it does not document a missing-data handling strategy for questionnaire nonresponse in the provided text.

title: Does increasing hours of schooling lead to improvements in student learning?
outcome_summary: This IEA policy brief uses PIRLS 2006 and PIRLS 2011 to examine whether increasing students’ time in school is associated with reading achievement at the fourth-grade level. Across 36 overlapping education systems, most countries increased classroom hours between 2006 and 2011, but changes in hours were not consistently associated with changes in average reading achievement. After addressing endogeneity and measurement error via instrumental variables (books in the home and children’s books as instruments), the effect of reading with children remains positive and statistically significant, whereas the effect of parents’ own reading becomes statistically insignificant in most samples; for Spain, reading with children moves students upward by roughly 5–7 percentile points depending on whether parental education controls are included. En Educación Infantil, asistir ≥3 años incrementa ~16 puntos en lectura y reduce la probabilidad de notas muy bajas en las tres materias. En TIMSS por grupos extremos, el impacto de dimensiones latentes (autoestima, gusto, posesiones, clima y limitaciones de enseñanza) difiere sustancialmente entre grupos de bajo, medio y alto rendimiento.

title: Assessment Framework PIRLS 2016 2nd Edition
authors: Ina V.S. Mullis, Michael O. Martin
outcome_summary: This PIRLS 2016 Assessment Framework (2nd edition) specifies the construct definition and measurement design for PIRLS, PIRLS Literacy, and ePIRLS rather than reporting empirical predictive results. PIRLS and PIRLS Literacy use a matrix sampling design: each student receives two 40-minute blocks from a set of passage/item blocks, enabling broad coverage with limited testing time per student. Achievement is placed on the PIRLS scale using item response theory scaling and linking across cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016). ePIRLS extends PIRLS to online informational reading using computer-based tasks in a simulated Internet environment, with task combinations randomly distributed and scaled via item response theory.

title: Mesurer l’ODD 4 : La contribution du PIRLS

Le PIRLS évalue les élèves en 4e année (et, selon les pays, en 5e ou 6e année via PIRLS Literacy) et fournit des données comparatives internationales sur plusieurs cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016). Les résultats présentés sont principalement des indicateurs descriptifs et des comparaisons entre sous-groupes (p. ex. sexe, fréquentation préscolaire, activités de lecture précoces, présence de livres à la maison, langue d’enseignement, harcèlement, formation des enseignants), ainsi que des évolutions temporelles. Le document ne rapporte pas de procédure de modélisation prédictive ML ni de métriques de performance (AUC/RMSE/F1), et ne détaille pas la gestion des valeurs manquantes ou l’usage de poids d’échantillonnage dans les analyses illustratives. Par conséquent, l’interprétation doit rester centrée sur l’usage des indicateurs PIRLS pour le pilotage et la planification, sans inférer de causalité.

title: Operational-Automatic-Scoring-of-Text-Responses-ePIRLS
authors: Hyo Jeong Shin, Nico Andersen, Andrea Horbach, Euigyum Kim
outcome_summary: This project report evaluates operationally feasible automatic scoring of 2016 ePIRLS constructed-response text using two approaches: fuzzy lexical matching (FLM) and a semantics-based supervised classifier using XLM-R embeddings with SVM. Across 50 CR items and 15 countries/regions, XLM-R achieved an average human-machine agreement of κ = .755 (5-fold CV repeated five times), while FLM achieved a high grand mean accuracy of .971 but only scored about 26.1% of responses automatically on average (median), with efficiency ranging roughly 17.1%–37.9%. Linguistic variance operationalized via STTR showed a significant negative relationship with XLM-R accuracy (Pearson r = −.235; Spearman ρ = −.314) and with FLM efficiency (Pearson r = −.393; Spearman ρ = −.230), whereas STTR did not significantly affect FLM accuracy. Multilevel analyses further showed that item characteristics (process, passage, position, maximum points, difficulty) explained substantial portions of STTR variability (e.g., marginal R² ≈ .501 for item-level STTR). The study does not report survey-weighted estimation and uses human scores as the gold standard, with noted human misclassification noise that may affect training and evaluation.
