title: ePIRLS 2016: South African Highlights Report
authors: Howie, S.J., Combrinck, C., Roux, K., Tshele, M., Mtsatse, N., McLeod Palane, N., Mokoena, G.M.
outcome_summary: This ePIRLS 2016 South Africa highlights report summarizes a multiple case study of online reading in Gauteng Grade 5 learners in English-language schools. A total of 277 learners in nine schools completed both paper-based PIRLS booklets and computer-based ePIRLS informational tasks, with mean online reading reported as 508 and mean paper-based reading as 503; the report states there was no statistically significant difference between online and paper-based achievement. Gender comparisons also showed no statistically significant differences in either ePIRLS or PIRLS. The report further finds a large difference by school computer-room utilisation: in schools where the computer room was used, both paper-based and online mean scores were reported as 541, compared with 454 and 448 respectively where it was not used (with a stated significant gap of roughly 93–100 points). Benchmarking indicates that 15–16% of learners did not reach the lowest benchmark in both modes, and a larger share attained advanced benchmarks online than on paper; the report also notes limited questionnaire return rates, which constrains contextual-factor analyses.

title: Läsförmågan hos svenska elever i årskurs 4 i ett internationellt perspektiv (PIRLS 2016)
authors: Peter Fredriksson, Agnes Tongur, Elina Ekberg
outcome_summary: PIRLS 2016 assesses reading literacy in grade 4 using both literary fiction and informational texts (sachprosa), with items mapped to four comprehension processes (explicitly stated information, simple inferences, interpretive integration, and critical evaluation). In Sweden, PIRLS 2016 was administered with paper-and-pencil tests; each student reads two texts and answers about 25–30 items, enabling reliable national-level estimates while not producing scores for each student on every item. The report uses PIRLS scaling to a common score scale (international mean 500, SD 100 in 2001) and reports uncertainty via confidence intervals and 5% significance testing. Sweden’s mean reading literacy score is 555, which is 16 points above the EU/OECD average (539), and the report describes a statistically significant improvement of 13 points since 2011. It also reports subgroup patterns: girls outperform boys; students with higher home resources for learning outperform those with fewer resources; and migration-related gaps largely attenuate after accounting for socioeconomic background. The report emphasizes that PIRLS is designed for national comparisons and that results should not be interpreted at the individual student or single-school level.

title: Vijftien jaar leesprestaties in Nederland: PIRLS-2016
authors: Joyce Gubbels, Andrea Netten, Ludo Verhoeven
outcome_summary: This PIRLS-2016 Netherlands report describes Grade 6 reading proficiency and its associations with student, teacher, school, and home context factors. It uses PIRLS plausible values (five PVs derived via IRT) and reports weighted results for reading proficiency, with an overall Netherlands mean score of 545 (SE=1.7) and an international rank of 14th. The report finds that girls outperform boys, students who (nearly) always speak Dutch at home outperform those who sometimes/never do, and students with higher reading engagement, enjoyment, and self-confidence have higher reading scores. At the school level, reading proficiency is lowest in schools with higher shares of economically disadvantaged students and lower shares of Dutch first-language speakers, and rural schools score highest compared with urban schools. No machine-learning predictive modeling is performed; therefore, no ML algorithm performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are applicable, and the study should be interpreted as descriptive large-scale assessment analysis rather than causal inference.

title: Norske tiåringers leseforståelse. PIRLS 2021 – Kortrapport
authors: Åse Kari H. Wagner, Olaug Strand, Hildegunn Støle, Knud Knudsen, Johanne Hovig, Christina Huru, Trond Hadland
outcome_summary: Denne kortrapporten oppsummerer PIRLS 2021 for norske tiåringer (5. trinn) og gir et nordisk perspektiv. Norge hadde en gjennomsnittsskår på 539 i lesing, som er en nedgang på 20 skalapoeng fra 2016, og Norge ligger fortsatt over internasjonalt gjennomsnitt (503). Rapporten viser også at kjønnsforskjeller består (jenter presterer bedre enn gutter), at sammenhengen mellom familiens sosioøkonomiske status (SØS) og leseprestasjoner er tydelig (omtrent 70 poeng mellom laveste og høyeste SØS), og at andelen elever på lavt/under lavt mestringsnivå øker til omtrent en femtedel i 2021. Videre beskrives endringer i lesevaner og holdninger (lavere leseglede og mindre fritidslesing) samt økt bruk av digitale enheter i skolen. Det rapporteres ikke ML-modeller eller ML-ytelsesmål; analysene er primært deskriptive og basert på PIRLS’ standard skåringsrammeverk.

title: ePIRLS 2016 Den digitala läsförmågan hos svenska elever i årskurs 4 i ett internationellt perspektiv
authors: Peter Fredriksson, Agnes Tongur, Elina Ekberg
outcome_summary: This Skolverket report summarizes ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 results for Sweden and compares them with other participating countries. Swedish students average 559 points in digital reading, which is 13 points above the EU/OECD average (547), and only Singapore, Norway, and Ireland score higher. The report finds subgroup differences: girls score higher than boys (567 vs 552, +15), and students with higher home resources for learning score substantially higher than those with lower resources (+43 points; 589 vs 546). Migration-background differences are reported to largely disappear after accounting for socioeconomic background (home resources). The excerpt does not describe any machine-learning model training or PV/missing-data procedures, so no ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are applicable here.

title: About PIRLS 2021
outcome_summary: PIRLS 2021 is a fourth-grade reading achievement assessment conducted every five years, with the 2021 cycle providing 20 years of trend results. The assessment was administered in 57 countries and 8 benchmarking entities, with data collection occurring over two years during COVID-19 disruptions. PIRLS 2021 introduced a transition to digital assessment for a subset of countries and implemented a group adaptive design that assigns students to booklets combining easy/medium/difficult text and item sets, improving measurement precision and reducing item non-response. Scaling procedures place results on the PIRLS trend scale using concurrent calibration and linking designs, including population-based linking between digital main and bridge samples. The report also documents quality assurance steps (translation verification, standardized procedures, and international quality assurance visits) and explains how delayed testing countries are annotated, emphasizing that PIRLS cannot establish causal effects of COVID-19 on achievement.

title: Assessment Frameworks PIRLS 2021
authors: Ina V. S. Mullis, Michael O. Martin
outcome_summary: This document provides the PIRLS 2021 assessment frameworks and design rationale rather than reporting predictive or causal results. It defines reading literacy as the ability to understand and use written language forms required by society and/or valued by individuals, emphasizing reading to learn, participate in communities of readers, and for enjoyment. The PIRLS reading framework is organized by two reading purposes (literary experience; acquire and use information) and four comprehension processes (focus on and retrieve explicitly stated information; make straightforward inferences; interpret and integrate ideas and information; evaluate and critique content and textual elements). For PIRLS 2021, the assessment is transitioning to a digital format (digitalPIRLS) and is designed to integrate with ePIRLS, which assesses online reading in a simulated internet environment. The framework chapter also describes assessment design elements such as the group adaptive design and booklet assignment within countries, enabling results to be reported on the same achievement scale across varying item sets and difficulty ranges.

title: An Analysis of PIRLS 2021 Mode Effects: Differences in Reading Achievement Related to the Assessment Mode for PIRLS 2021 in Croatia and Slovenia
authors: Eva Klemenčič Mirazchiyski, Plamen Vladkov Mirazchiyski, Ines Perović
outcome_summary: This chapter uses PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 reading data for Croatia and Slovenia, comparing digitalPIRLS against bridge PIRLS paper samples. Across overall reading and the main purpose/process subscales, the paper–digital mode differences were not statistically significant in either country (e.g., Croatia overall t-test p=0.523; Slovenia overall t-test p=0.900). Regression models (run separately by mode) show that ICT-related home resources and student digital self-efficacy are significantly associated with reading achievement subscales, while teacher/classroom ICT variables generally show limited relationships (with a small exception for device use to create presentations/videos in Slovenia). The analysis relies on PIRLS plausible values and weighted estimation via RALSA; however, the chapter does not report a missing-data strategy for covariates beyond PV handling, which limits interpretability of coefficient estimates.

title: Socioeconomic Status in PIRLS 2021: Insights from Parent, Student, and Principal Reports
authors: Dihao Leng, Deepthi Kodamala, Katherine A. Reynolds, Ummugul Bezirhan, Matthias von Davier, Eugenio Gonzalez, Ann Kennedy
outcome_summary: This PIRLS 2021 Insights report examines how socioeconomic status (SES) is conceptualized and measured using a new Home Socioeconomic Status scale derived from the Home Questionnaire completed by parents/guardians of fourth-grade students. The Home SES scale classifies students into higher, middle, and lower SES based on four parent-reported indicators (books, children’s books, parental education, and parental occupation), and the report evaluates its alignment with student-reported home resources (e.g., number of books, access to digital devices) and principal-reported school socioeconomic composition. Correlation analyses use sampling weights and show that the student-reported number of books has the strongest alignment with parent-reported Home SES (international average Pearson r = 0.46; η² = 0.23), while digital-device indicators show much weaker or near-zero associations. The report also uses hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) with random intercepts for schools to quantify how much variance in parent-reported Home SES can be explained by student- and principal-reported variables, finding substantial between-school variation in many countries (ICC up to 0.60) and an international-average total R² of 0.34 for the full Model 4. A key limitation is selection bias risk: Home SES response rates are lower for lower-achieving students in some countries, which can affect interpretation of alignment and explained-variance results.

title: COVID-19 RESEARCH RESOURCES IN PIRLS 2021
authors: Maya Komakhidze, Katherine Reynolds, Erin Wry, Bethany Fishbein, Ann Kennedy, Matthias von Davier
outcome_summary: This PIRLS 2021 Insights report compiles COVID-19-related contextual resources available in the PIRLS 2021 International Database. It explains that PIRLS 2021 reading achievement results cannot be used for causal inference about COVID-19 learning loss, but the contextual questionnaires support descriptive and within-country analyses of pandemic-related schooling conditions. The report details three instrument sources: the Home Questionnaire (parent/guardian reports on staying home, home-based learning resources, and perceived learning progress), the School Questionnaire (principal reports on disruption duration and remote-learning resources/supports), and the Curriculum/Encyclopedia contributions (country-level policy and practice descriptions of closures, decision-making, distance learning modalities, and supports). It also highlights comparability issues due to COVID-19-driven modifications to the PIRLS 2021 data collection timeline, including full-year and half-year delays for some countries. Finally, it provides item-level caveats such as filter logic and response-option limitations (e.g., ceiling effects for disruption duration).
all_target_variables: reading achievement | that PIRLS 2021 reading achievement results cannot be used for causal inference

title: PIRLS 2021-National Report Qatar
outcome_summary: This PIRLS 2021 national report for Qatar presents descriptive results for Grade 4 reading achievement and related contextual factors. The study is based on PIRLS 2021’s international reading assessment administered to students at the end of Grade 4, with Qatar participating in the 2021 cycle (and previously in 2006 and every five years). The report states that Qatar’s sample comprised 5,253 students from 259 participating classes/schools, selected via a two-stage clustered sampling design (schools/classes, then one class randomly selected within the target grade). It reports achievement on the PIRLS scale (international mean set at 500) and proficiency levels (400, 475, 550, 625), including differences by gender, nationality (Qatari vs non-Qatari), and school type (government, Ministry-standard private, international, expatriate/community). It also discusses COVID-19 impacts on administration and compares paper vs digital modes for the transition stage, reporting very small differences, and provides contextual associations from questionnaires (home resources, early literacy activities, school climate, engagement, and attitudes toward reading).

title: التقرير الوطني الأردني عن الدراسة الدولية للتقدم في القرائية 2021 (بيرلس2021) (PIRLS 2021)
authors: عبدهللا عبابنة, خطاب أبو لبدة, لؤي شواشرة, عماد عبابنة
outcome_summary: This Jordan national report for PIRLS 2021 (Grade 4 Reading literacy) reports that Jordan’s overall mean reading literacy score was 381, below the international mean (503) and below the Arab mean (429). The report also shows that females outperform males, and that private-sector students outperform public-sector students, with urban students outperforming rural students. For the explanatory analysis, the report uses multiple regression and hierarchical multiple regression: teacher factors alone explain 7.4% of the variance in reading achievement, adding principal factors increases explained variance to 15.6%, and adding student factors yields 40.4% total explained variance (student factors contribute 36.3%). The analysis is not framed as machine learning; therefore, no ML algorithms, PV-handling, or missing-data strategy are documented in the provided text.

file_name: PIRLS 2021  in Northern Ireland Full Report.pdf
title: PIRLS 2021 in Northern Ireland: Reading Attainment
authors: Rachel Classick, Katherine Aston, María José Guevara Duque, Lillian Flemons, Henry Faulkner-Ellis, Jose Liht, Sigrid Boyd, Juliet Sizmur, Liz Twist
outcome_summary: This NFER report summarises PIRLS 2021 reading attainment for Northern Ireland, where pupils were assessed at the start of Year 7 (internationally Grade 5) due to COVID-19 delays. The report reports an average reading scale score of 566 for Northern Ireland, significantly above the PIRLS international centrepoint of 500, and provides cross-country comparisons with six comparator countries (Finland, Poland, Singapore, Republic of Ireland, Australia, England) while cautioning that delayed testing periods complicate interpretation. It also reports benchmark attainment: 23% reached the Advanced benchmark (625), 3% were below the Low benchmark (400), and it describes distributional spread using 10th/90th percentile scores (461 and 665; gap 204). Contextual chapters summarise gender differences (girls higher by 24 points), socio-economic gradients (FSME gap 49 points), and COVID-19 schooling experiences (e.g., 92% of pupils attended schools where >8 weeks of teaching were affected). The report is descriptive and does not implement or evaluate machine-learning predictive models.

title: Student Well-Being and Reading Achievement in PIRLS 2021
outcome_summary: This PIRLS Insights report uses PIRLS 2021 reading achievement for fourth-grade students and PIRLS 2021 Student Questionnaire indicators to describe how multiple aspects of student well-being relate to reading performance across participating countries. It reports descriptive associations for five individual well-being indicators: sense of school belonging (categorized into High/Some/Little), bullying frequency (Never/Almost Never, About Monthly, About Weekly), feeling tired upon arrival (Never/Every day or almost every day/Sometimes), feeling hungry upon arrival (Never/Sometimes/Every day or almost every day), and frequency of absences (collapsed categories). Across countries, higher belonging and lower bullying and absence frequency are associated with higher average reading achievement, while tiredness and hunger show more complex, non-linear patterns that vary by country. The report also integrates the five indicators using multi-level latent class analysis to form four well-being profile classes and compares their average reading achievement, emphasizing that class proportions differ across countries. Limitations include the lack of documented missing-data handling and the fact that the analyses are not causal; the report explicitly notes that causality is not implied.

title: Mednarodna raziskava bralne pismenosti (IEA PIRLS 2021) Nacionalno poročilo – prvi rezultati
authors: Eva M. Klemenčič, Plamen V. Mirazchiyski
outcome_summary: This national report presents descriptive PIRLS 2021 results for Slovenia and international comparisons across 57 participating education systems (plus 8 reference participants). PIRLS 2021 measures reading literacy in the fourth year of schooling (typically fourth grade; some systems used a bridge sample to link digital PIRLS to paper-based trend tasks) and uses rotated test booklets (“bundles/zvezki”) so each student answers a subset of reading passages and questions. The report summarizes scale-score comparisons (e.g., Slovenia’s average reading score on the PIRLS scale), international benchmarks (400/475/550/625), and trends between 2016 and 2021, including the observed global decline in 2021. It also reports extensive questionnaire-based context results (home literacy activities, SES gradients, student attitudes toward reading, school climate, and peer harassment), but it does not implement or evaluate any machine-learning predictive model. Consequently, the document’s contribution is policy-relevant interpretation of assessment outcomes rather than ML-based causal or predictive inference.

file_name: Progress in International Reading Literacy Study_ Australia_s res.pdf
title: Australia’s results from Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS 2021)
authors: Kylie Hillman, Elizabeth O’Grady, Sima Rodrigues, Marina Schmid, Sue Thomson
outcome_summary: This report documents PIRLS 2021 reading literacy results for Australia (Year 4) and presents comparisons with international benchmarks and trends across cycles. PIRLS uses a matrix-sampling design with 18 booklets, each student completing one booklet containing two short texts (literary and/or informational) and associated multiple-choice and constructed-response items; achievement is scaled using item response theory to a reading scale with mean 500 and SD 100. The report uses PIRLS international benchmarks (Low 400, Intermediate 475, High 550, Advanced 625) to describe proficiency and reports the percentage of students meeting each benchmark. Sampling in Australia follows a 2-stage stratified cluster design (schools, then intact classrooms), and the report states that weights are used so sampled students represent the Year 4 population, including adjustments for design features and non-participation. Results are presented descriptively by demographic groups (e.g., gender, First Nations background), home and school context variables, and teacher/classroom factors, with standard errors and statistical significance notes; no predictive ML modeling is conducted.

title: PIRLS 2021: Reading results for Ireland
authors: Emer Delaney, Sarah McAteer, Mary Delaney, Gráinne McHugh, Brendan O’Neill
outcome_summary: This PIRLS 2021 national report provides descriptive achievement results for Ireland’s Start G5 cohort (autumn 2021), with 4,663 pupils participating in the PIRLS test. Pupils’ mean reading achievement was 577 (SE 2.5), significantly above the PIRLS scale centrepoint (500) and higher than most other Start G5 countries, though comparisons are cautioned due to the Start G5 vs End G4 design and COVID-19 disruption. Achievement shows strong equity gradients: girls scored 11 points higher than boys (583 vs 573), and SES is strongly associated with achievement (highest vs lowest SES quartile: 620 vs 536; High benchmark 88% vs 45%; Advanced 48% vs 10%). The report also finds relative strengths on Literary texts and Interpret/Evaluate processes, and relative weaknesses on Informational texts and Retrieve/Infer processes. Contextual questionnaire analyses indicate that reading behaviours and attitudes are positively associated with achievement, while wellbeing indicators (tiredness/hunger) and bullying are negatively associated; however, the report cautions against causal interpretation.

title: PIRLS 2021: National Report for England
outcome_summary: This England national report uses PIRLS 2021 Year 5 overall reading performance as the outcome and estimates a multiple regression (Table 14) on a complete-case analytic sample of N=3,479 (after removing cases missing any regression variable). The strongest predictor is Year 1 phonics screening performance: a 10-point increase on the phonics check corresponds to an approximately 36-point increase in PIRLS overall reading. Books at home show a graded positive association (e.g., >200 books vs 0–10: about +56 PIRLS points), and FSM eligibility within the last 6 years is negatively associated (about −23 points). Pupil age is statistically significant but weak by standardised effect size (about +1.2 points per month). The report does not present ML algorithms or ML performance metrics; it also cautions that the relationship between policy and PIRLS should not be treated as causal.

title: PIRLS 2021. Estudio Internacional de Progreso en Comprensión Lectora. Informe español
outcome_summary: El informe español de PIRLS 2021 presenta resultados de comprensión lectora para alumnado de 4.º de Educación Primaria (4.º grado) y contextualiza el rendimiento con información de cuestionarios de hogar, alumnado, profesorado y centro. El estudio se basa en TRI y genera cinco valores plausibles para estimar la destreza lectora en una escala común con referencia central de 500 puntos (fijada en 1995). La evaluación incluye 18 textos (literarios e informativos) con procesos de comprensión (localización de información explícita, extracción de conclusiones directas, interpretación e integración, y análisis y evaluación), y en países con digitalPIRLS se integra ePIRLS con tareas en entorno simulado. El informe también describe el diseño adaptativo por grupo y el impacto de la pandemia en la ventana de recogida de datos (octubre 2020–julio 2022). Para España, se reporta que los resultados del informe se basan en 8500 estudiantes del formato digital, y se comparan con promedios OCDE-28 y Total UE, además de analizar niveles de rendimiento y brechas por variables de contexto. No se aplican modelos de aprendizaje automático predictivo en este documento; por tanto, los hallazgos son descriptivos/estimativos bajo el marco psicométrico de PIRLS.

title: PIRLS 2026 Assessment Frameworks
authors: Matthias von Davier, Ann Kennedy
outcome_summary: PIRLS 2026 is the sixth cycle of the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study, assessing reading achievement among fourth-grade students and reporting trends over 25 years. The framework specifies that reading literacy is assessed through two purposes for reading—literary experience and acquiring/using information—combined with four comprehension processes: focus on and retrieve explicitly stated information, make straightforward inferences, interpret and integrate ideas/information, and evaluate and critique content/textual elements. PIRLS 2026 completes the transition to a fully digital delivery format, integrating interactive digital reading formats (ePIRLS blocks) while clarifying that the assessment is not a test of digital/internet skills. The framework also describes the group-adaptive assessment design and the use of automated scoring, and it outlines how online tasks use a teacher avatar to support navigation so that the focus remains on reading comprehension rather than navigation. No empirical performance metrics or model-based results are reported in this document.

title: PIRLS-2021: Trends in leesprestaties, leesattitude en leesgedrag van tienjarigen uit Nederland
authors: Nicole Swart, Joyce Gubbels, Melissa in ’t Zandt, Maarten Wolbers, Eliane Segers
outcome_summary: This PIRLS-2021 Netherlands national report presents descriptive trends in reading achievement, reading attitude, and reading behavior for grade 6 students. It reports that the average reading achievement score in 2021 was 527, a decline of 18 points from 2016, and that this is approximately equal to the average of the 21 Western comparison countries (531). The report also shows that reading achievement declined for both reading goals and both comprehension processes between 2016 and 2021, and that the distribution across proficiency levels shifted away from middle/high and especially advanced levels. For reading attitude, reading pleasure decreased (mean scale score 8.8 in 2021) while engagement slightly increased (9.2 in 2021) and self-confidence remained roughly stable (9.9 in 2021). For reading behavior, outside-school reading frequency was stable but time spent reading outside school decreased, with the share reading less than 30 minutes per day rising to 63% in 2021. No machine learning models are estimated; therefore, no ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/R²) are available.

title: PIRLS 2021: fundamentos teóricos
authors: Ina V.S. Mullis, Michael O. Martin
outcome_summary: This document specifies the theoretical and assessment framework for PIRLS 2021, including the definition of reading literacy, the two reading purposes (literary experience; obtaining and using information), and four comprehension processes (explicit locating/retrieval; direct inference; interpret/articulate ideas; evaluate/analyze critically). It also details the move toward digitalPIRLS (with paperPIRLS still available) and the integration of ePIRLS for online informational reading, including how ePIRLS tasks are embedded via rotation and hybrid test forms. The assessment design uses a group-adaptive approach: texts are organized into three text difficulty levels (easy/moderate/difficult) and combined into two test difficulty levels, with the proportion of harder vs. easier tests varying by a country’s expected reading performance. The framework further describes questionnaire coverage across home, school, classroom, student characteristics, and national contexts, and explains how these context data support interpretation of reading performance trends. No empirical model results, metrics, or PV/missing-data estimation procedures are reported in this text.
all_target_variables: reading literacy | how these context data support interpretation of reading performance trends

title: PIRLS 2021 – Läsförmågan hos svenska elever i åk 4 i ett internationellt perspektiv
authors: Peter Fredriksson, Cecilia Stenman, Jenny Wiksten Folkeryd, Åsa af Geijerstam, Maria Westman, Christian Tallberg, Anders Auer, Anita Wester
outcome_summary: This Skolverket report summarizes PIRLS 2021 reading literacy results for Swedish students in grade 4 and compares them to other participating countries (with Russia omitted from international comparisons). Overall, Sweden’s mean reading literacy score decreased by 12 points since 2016 to 544, while the share of low performers increased (e.g., those not reaching the intermediate level rose to 19%) and the share of top performers remained roughly unchanged. The report also finds that girls continue to outperform boys (about a 15-point gap in Sweden) and that home resources (hemresurser) remains the strongest correlate of reading achievement. In regression analyses, the effect of always speaking Swedish at home increased (17 points) and school composition (based on students’ average home resources) increased (42 points) between 2016 and 2021, while the home-resources effect was not significantly larger after adjustment. The study is not an ML predictive modeling paper; it uses survey-based statistical comparisons and regression/variance decomposition, and it notes that causal direction cannot be inferred from associations.

title: School Closure Policies and Student Reading Achievement
outcome_summary: The study combines PIRLS 2016 and PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade reading achievement data with UNESCO UIS measures of national school-closure duration across 29 countries. Using sampling (senate) weights and jackknife repeated replication, and combining PIRLS plausible values via Rubin’s rules, the authors estimate that one additional day of school closures is associated with a -0.14 PIRLS scale-point decline in reading achievement between 2016 and 2021 (S.E. 0.015). The effect is robust across alternative specifications (global trends and country-specific trends) and robustness checks excluding delayed-wave countries, excluding federal decentralized countries, and varying the weighting of partially closed days. Heterogeneity analyses show that the negative association is attenuated for students with higher Home Resources for Learning and is more negative for students without a computer at home, while gender and home language differences are not statistically significant. The paper is regression-based rather than ML-based, so no ML model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) are reported.

title: T99B_TR_Book.fm
outcome_summary: This technical report documents the TIMSS 1999 Benchmarking study’s assessment design and the psychometric and operational procedures used to produce comparable mathematics and science achievement results for eighth-grade students. It explains the two-stage stratified cluster sampling of schools and classrooms (with an extra district stage for large systems), the rotated matrix test design with eight booklets, and the use of IRT scaling (2PL/3PL for dichotomous items and generalized partial credit for polytomous items). Achievement reporting is based on plausible values: five imputed proficiency estimates per student are generated using conditioning on background variables and then combined using multiple-imputation logic, with uncertainty decomposed into sampling and imputation components. International benchmarks are defined via scale anchoring at the 25th/50th/75th/90th percentiles, and reporting procedures include jackknife-based standard errors and Bonferroni adjustments for multiple comparisons. The report is descriptive and methodological; it does not present predictive ML results.

title: TIMSS 1999 Technical Report
outcome_summary: TIMSS 1999 is a cross-national achievement study that assessed eighth-grade students in mathematics and science across 38 participating countries, with a focus on measuring trends since the 1995 TIMSS cycle (TIMSS-Repeat). The study used a rotated test design with eight booklets and 26 item clusters, ensuring that not all students responded to all items while maintaining broad content coverage. Achievement scaling relied primarily on item response theory (IRT), producing scale scores for mathematics overall and five mathematics content areas, and for science overall and six science content areas. To quantify uncertainty in proficiency estimates, the report describes plausible-value technology generating five separate estimates per student. The technical report also documents translation and verification procedures, extensive data cleaning and quality assurance, and the use of sampling weights and jackknife replicate methods for standard errors. International benchmarks were anchored using the 90th, 75th, 50th, and 25th percentiles.

title: How Chinese Taipei used TIMSS data to reform mathematics education
authors: Fou-Lai Lin
outcome_summary: This IEA Compass brief explains how Chinese Taipei used successive TIMSS cycles as an evidence base for mathematics education reform rather than reporting a new empirical ML model. It highlights TIMSS 2003 patterns at grades 4 and 8—especially a higher share of students in the “below intermediate” benchmark group and a larger proportion reporting low confidence and low enjoyment in mathematics compared with the international average. title: Coherence between Swedish grades and TIMSS 2015
outcome_summary: This IEA Compass report validates coherence between Swedish year-9 grades and TIMSS 2015 (year-8) test scores using merged TIMSS and register data for Sweden. Descriptively, TIMSS score distributions shift upward across final grade levels A–F, with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for mean TIMSS scores across grade levels. Correlations are moderately strong: final grades correlate with TIMSS mathematics at r=0.76 and with TIMSS science at r=0.64, while national test grades correlate at about r=0.65 (math) and r=0.62 (science). In linear regression, final grades alone explain 57% of TIMSS mathematics variance and 39% of TIMSS science variance; adding student background (gender, migration background, home resources) increases explained variance to 61% (math) and 49% (science). The manuscript does not report any ML modeling, PV handling, or a missing-data strategy, and it does not clearly document whether TIMSS complex-survey weights were applied.

Students’ overall mean score is 27 out of 60, significantly below the OECD average of 33, and the factsheet reports that 33% of the variation in creative thinking is uniquely explained by mathematics performance (correlations: 0.72 with mathematics and 0.67 with reading). It also reports proficiency distributions: 60% reach at least Level 3 (OECD: 78%) and 14% are top performers at Levels 5–6 (OECD average: 27%). The note flags COVID-19-related implementation issues for some countries/economies (asterisks), but it does not provide ML model performance metrics because this is a descriptive results publication rather than an ML study.

title: Are Students Smart about Money?
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief summarizes PISA 2018 financial literacy results for 15-year-old students across 13 OECD countries/economies and 7 partner countries/economies (about 117,000 students, representing around 13.5 million students). The brief also describes within-country and subgroup patterns: gender gaps (boys higher overall but over-represented at both ends), socioeconomic gradients (advantaged students higher by about one proficiency level), and immigrant-background differences after accounting for socioeconomic status. It further links financial literacy to related skills measured in mathematics and reading (about 80% of score variation reflects skills also measured there) and to learning/exposure channels (parental information, school exposure to financial literacy tasks, and use of financial products). title: School Factors Related to Quality and Equity (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PISA 2000 microdata to map school context, inputs, and processes to educational quality and equity, focusing primarily on reading literacy performance (with mathematical and scientific literacy used for stability checks). The analysis is based on a hierarchically structured dataset (students nested in schools nested in countries) and uses multilevel modelling to reflect the two-stage sampling design. Student and school weights are applied to address non-response and missing performance scores, and plausible values are incorporated using five plausible values per test score as an additional nested level. Missing data are handled differently by variable type: continuous variables are imputed using weighted school or country averages, while categorical variables are represented via dummy variables including explicit missing indicators. The report benchmarks equity and quality using between-school variance (and intra-class correlation) and the association between students’ socio-economic background and performance, concluding that school effects vary substantially by country and that socio-economic composition explains more between-school variation than measured school climate, policies, and resources.

title: Messages from PISA 2000
outcome_summary: This OECD policy summary reports key messages from PISA 2000, a three-yearly international assessment of 15-year-olds conducted in 2000 with pencil-and-paper tests and questionnaires. It highlights reading literacy as the central performance domain in the presented comparisons, including mean scores, proficiency-level distributions (Levels 1, 5, and below Level 1), and cross-country benchmarks relative to the OECD average. The document emphasizes multilevel patterns: student background (socio-economic gradient) is described as the strongest single factor associated with reading performance, while school climate and resources show smaller but policy-relevant associations. It also reports decompositions of variation into within-school and between-school components and discusses system-level features such as school autonomy, monitoring, and approaches to supporting low-performing students. Because this is not an empirical ML paper, it does not specify PV handling, missing-data procedures, or model-estimation details, and causal interpretations (e.g., autonomy → performance) are explicitly cautioned.

title: Student Engagement at School (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD chapter analyzes student engagement in PISA 2000 using two engagement dimensions: sense of belonging (six questionnaire items about acceptance and loneliness) and participation (absence, class-skipping, and late arrival in the two weeks prior to the survey). It constructs dichotomous benchmarks for “low sense of belonging” (below 3.0 on the unstandardised scale) and “low participation” (<=10 on the unstandardised participation scale), and reports prevalence, country means (OECD average fixed at 500 with SD=100), and within-country school variation. The chapter uses multilevel logistic regression null models to estimate how prevalence of disaffection varies among schools within each country, and it also reports multilevel correlations between engagement and literacy outcomes in a subsequent chapter. Key results show that about one in four OECD students are classified as having low sense of belonging and about one in five have low participation, with higher prevalence in non-OECD countries. The analysis is cross-sectional and does not support causal claims about whether engagement precedes literacy performance; it also does not document a missing-data strategy for engagement items.

title: The Experience of Middle-Income Countries Participating in PISA 2000-2015 (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesises the experiences of middle-income countries participating in PISA from 2000 to 2015, combining qualitative evidence (interviews with national project managers), descriptive statistics on participation and costs, and secondary evidence from PISA 2012 analyses. It documents financial deterrents (fees, travel, implementation and reporting costs), technical/operational challenges (translation, sampling in decentralised systems, computer-based assessment logistics, coding reliability), and contextual constraints (governance, regulatory environment, press freedom, and cultural factors affecting implementation and dissemination). For education quality and equity, it summarises PISA 2012 mathematics results across 18 middle-income countries and discusses multilevel correlates of performance, including the role of socio-economic background, school climate, instructional time, and opportunities to learn. The report also reviews evidence on how PISA informs policy dialogue, finding limited systematic public media agenda-setting in many middle-income contexts but more consistent use in private dialogue with development partners. Limitations include the lack of a single unified empirical ML pipeline and limited causal attribution of PISA effects on reforms.

title: What Makes School Systems Perform? Seeing School Systems through the Prism of PISA 2000
outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesizes what drives school system performance by “seeing school systems through the prism of PISA 2000.” It does not estimate predictive models; instead, it summarizes cross-national patterns and policy features across six reference countries (Canada, England, Finland, France, Netherlands, Sweden) and links them to themes such as reform and innovation, devolution of responsibilities, system monitoring, support systems, standards, classroom organization, integration of non-native students, and coping with under-achievement. The report uses PISA 2000 as an anchor for comparative performance and equity discussions, including mean score differences for native-born versus foreign-born students (Table 1), while also drawing on a multilateral qualitative analytical framework (Annex A) to structure country evidence. Because it is a synthesis, it does not report model-based metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) or document plausible-value combination or missing-data procedures for any re-estimation. Consequently, the findings are best interpreted as policy-relevant correlational/interpretive insights rather than causal or model-evaluated effects.

title: PISA 2003 Data Analysis Manual (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD manual explains how to analyze PISA 2003 microdata using the survey’s complex sampling design, plausible values (PVs), and replication-based standard errors. It describes the two-stage sampling procedure (schools selected with probability proportional to size, then students sampled within schools) and the need to apply student final weights (W_FSTUWT) for point estimates. For uncertainty, it specifies BRR with Fay’s modification (Fay factor 0.5) using 80 replicate weights (W_FSTR1–W_FSTR80) to compute sampling variances. For cognitive achievement outcomes, it explains that PISA uses Rasch scaling and PVs (typically five PVs per scale), and that population statistics must be computed separately for each PV and then combined; the final variance combines sampling variance and imputation (measurement) variance. It also provides guidance for deriving proficiency levels from PVs and for computing standard errors on differences, including between-country comparisons where covariance is expected to be zero.

title: Technical Feasibility of Reporting YITS 2010 Skill Assessment Results on the PISA 2000 Reading Scale (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD technical study evaluates whether YITS 2010 respondents (age ~25) can be scored on the PISA 2000 reading proficiency scale using a subset of PISA 2000 reading link items. The authors administer 28 PISA 2000 items to a YITS reassessment subsample and examine item suitability and test functioning across the older population, focusing on whether there is a ceiling effect and whether item difficulty patterns remain consistent. They scale YITS item responses onto the PISA 2000 reading scale using the PISA 2000 item parameter framework, treat “not-reached” responses as not applicable (missing at random) for proficiency estimation, and generate plausible values (10 per respondent) to support secondary analyses. They also replicate the conditioning and plausible-value generation logic using a reduced set of conditioning variables (principal component scores) and discuss limitations for interpreting YITS scores as “true PISA results,” including higher measurement variance due to fewer items and the need for careful variance estimation when computing change between PISA 2000 and YITS 2010.

title: Education in the Eastern Partnership: Findings from PISA (EN)

The report describes how PISA scores are interpreted (e.g., a 20-point difference approximates a typical annual learning gain) and how proficiency levels translate achievement into actionable task capabilities, including the baseline Level 2. Key descriptive patterns include EaP students trailing OECD averages, large shares of low performers, and substantial inequities by socio-economic status, alongside notable differences in belonging, safety, and educational aspirations. The report also cautions that COVID-19 school-closure questionnaire items have high non-response, limiting representativeness for those specific indicators.

title: PISA 2000: Sample Weight Problems in Austria
authors: Erich Neuwirth
outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper examines how Austria’s PISA 2000 results are biased due to inadequate coverage of students in combined school-and-work-based vocational programmes, relative to PISA technical standards. The paper explains that PISA country scores are computed as weighted means across 19 school-type strata, and that the sum and distribution of weights should match the target population. It shows implausible changes in total weights from PISA 2000 to PISA 2003 (about +21%) and large stratum-percentage differences, especially for the BS tech/gew (BStg) stratum, which is associated with gender composition and achievement differences. Using Austrian Ministry of Education school statistics, the author constructs corrected weights (“pop2000”) and demonstrates that applying them to PISA 2000 lowers country mean scores versus the original weights (e.g., Reading 507.1 → 492.1; Mathematics 515.0 → 502.5; Science 518.6 → 504.7). The paper recommends using the corrected weights for more reliable longitudinal comparisons and notes that BRR replicate weights should be adjusted accordingly for standard PISA analyses.

title: School Accountability, Autonomy, Choice, and the Equity of Student Achievement (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes how national school accountability, autonomy, and choice relate to the equity of student achievement across countries, using PISA 2003 microdata. The target equity concept is operationalized as how strongly student mathematics achievement depends on family socio-economic status (SES), measured by PISA’s ESCS index; the key estimands are interaction effects between country-level institutional features and student-level ESCS. The study constructs a student-level micro database (181,469 students in 27 OECD countries) and excludes France, Mexico, and Turkey for data comparability reasons, while dropping students with missing ESCS. Missing background questionnaire data are handled via conditional mean imputation with imputation dummies and interactions, and estimation uses weighted least squares with PISA sampling probabilities plus clustering-robust standard errors to respect the hierarchical survey design. Because institutional variables are measured at the country level, the analysis emphasizes between-country variation and avoids within-country self-selection, but it limits degrees of freedom and precludes detailed interactions among institutional features.

title: School Accountability, Autonomy, Choice, and the Level of Student Achievement (EN)

The cognitive outcome is PISA 2003 mathematics achievement (with science and reading analyzed in the basic model), estimated using cross-country student-level multiple regressions that include a large set of student, family, school-resource, and country controls. The institutional variables—external exit exams, assessment uses (retention/promotion, grouping, school comparisons), teacher monitoring, school autonomy in budgeting/staffing/salaries/course content, and choice/competition indicators (private operation, government funding, and proxies for public-school choice)—are measured primarily from PISA school background questionnaires and supplemented with country-level data. The report applies sampling-probability weights, uses clustering-robust standard errors to reflect the hierarchical sampling structure, and imputes missing questionnaire data with conditional mean imputation while including imputation indicators. Results show sizable positive associations with cognitive achievement (e.g., external exit exams and private operation) and also improvements in several non-cognitive outcomes, with no evidence of a tradeoff between cognitive and non-cognitive skills.

title: Analysis of PISA 2006 Preferred Items Ranking Using the Percent-Correct Method (EN)
authors: Ray Adams, Alla Berezner, Maciej Jakubowski
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper analyzes how stable PISA 2006 country rankings are when the ranking is recomputed using an approximate “average percent-correct” method rather than the full PISA scaling model. Each country’s experts rated science Field Trial items for priority of inclusion on a five-point scale; the study then forms multiple item subsets corresponding to each country’s preferred items and computes item percent-correct (weighted by PISA student weights) and country average percent-correct across those subsets. Rankings are compared across (i) all PISA 2006 science items, (ii) only new PISA 2006 items, and (iii) preferred-item subsets with and without the 22 score-linking items from previous cycles. The paper finds remarkable consistency with the OECD (2007) initial PISA 2006 ranking, with only a few countries showing systematic rank shifts that are small and comparable to sampling error, suggesting that PISA rankings are robust to reasonable differences in item preference. It also concludes that experts cannot reliably predict which items would advantage their country’s final ranking, and that robustness depends on having a sufficiently large item pool that accommodates diverse preferences.

title: Comparing the Similarities and Differences of PISA 2003 and TIMSS (EN)

It explains differences in country rankings using country-level regression analyses that relate PISA–TIMSS gaps to (i) differences in content balance between the two assessments (PISA’s item distribution across TIMSS content domains) and (ii) differences in population definitions, operationalized via age at TIMSS testing and an estimated number of years of schooling at PISA testing. The paper also examines reading load as an additional predictor of PISA mathematics differences and reports high explanatory power for combined predictors (e.g., up to 97% variance explained in predicting PISA mathematics country means). Beyond achievement, it compares gender differences and attitudinal indices (self-confidence and motivation) across the two surveys, finding stronger agreement for attitudes than for achievement gender gaps. The key implication is that cross-survey comparisons must account for framework alignment, sampling definitions, and test composition; otherwise, apparent performance differences may reflect measurement design rather than true differences in mathematics proficiency.

title: The Efficiency of Secondary Schools in an International Perspective (EN)
outcome_summary: The paper derives school efficiency measures using PISA 2012 data for 8,640 schools across 30 OECD countries (excluding Chile, Greece, Hungary, Mexico, and Turkey). Inputs are school-average ESCS, the inverse student-teacher ratio, and computers per student; outputs are mathematics and reading achievement based on PISA plausible values, with the baseline using pv1 and robustness checks using other PVs. Efficiency is estimated via bootstrap bias-corrected Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with an international frontier benchmark, then related to school-level factors using a second-stage Tobit regression (and quantile regression) with country fixed effects. The study estimates that, holding inputs constant, schools could raise achievement by about 27% on average using more efficient input-output combinations, with substantial within- and between-country variation. It finds no evidence of a trade-off between efficiency and inclusion: higher efficiency aligns with a lower proportion of students below proficiency Level 2 and better student attitudes (e.g., lower truancy). Limitations include the proxy nature of school-level efficiency (PISA is not designed for school representativeness) and the correlational interpretation of second-stage associations.

title: Gendered Career Expectations of Students (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper analyzes adolescent occupational expectations using PISA 2006, focusing on gender differences in science-related career plans (engineering/computing vs health sciences) and the broader vertical (status) and horizontal (field) segregation. For science achievement, they use plausible values and combine estimates across five plausible values using Rubin’s rules. Across countries, the gender gap in engineering/computing and health expectations is not substantially reduced by controlling for science performance, science course-taking, family socioeconomic/cultural resources, migrant status, vocational track placement, or students’ science self-efficacy/self-concept and career information/preparation. The paper reports model coefficients and odds ratios rather than predictive ML metrics, and it frames the remaining unexplained gap as consistent with cultural gender ideologies rather than measurement artifacts.

The paper also clarifies that PISA remains primarily an assessment of learning outcomes, while the well-being module adds a multidimensional portrait of students’ experiences at age 15. title: The science of teaching science (EN)

title: Introduction of multistage adaptive testing design in PISA 2018 (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates a multistage adaptive testing (MSAT) design implemented for the PISA 2018 main survey in the Reading domain. The MSAT administers three stages (Core, Stage 1, Stage 2) using testlets (units of items) and routes students based on performance on automatically scored items, grouped into low/medium/high using testlet-specific number-correct thresholds derived from test characteristic curves. Two routing designs are compared: Design A (Core > Stage 1 > Stage 2) administered to 75% of students and Design B (Core > Stage 2 > Stage 1) administered to 25% to mitigate potential position effects for Stage 2 items. Using a simulation with 245 dichotomous/polytomous items and IRT scaling via a multiple-group IRT model (2PL for dichotomous, GPCM for polytomous) estimated with marginal maximum likelihood, the MSAT design achieved parameter recovery comparable to the operational benchmark and improved measurement precision by about 4.5% on average, with gains up to ~10% at extreme proficiency levels. The study is based on a single simulated dataset, so additional simulation work is recommended to assess robustness (e.g., omission rates and item-by-country interactions).

The note does not analyze student microdata, does not estimate models, and does not report ML performance metrics or causal effects. Therefore, the “benchmarks” are OECD averages and cross-country comparisons presented in the figures, not statistical model outputs from this document.

title: Agency in the Anthropocene (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD framework proposes how PISA 2025 could measure “agency in the Anthropocene” among 15-year-olds, linking science education to knowledge, decision-making, hope, efficacy, and respect for diverse perspectives. The document defines three competencies: (1) explaining human interactions with Earth systems, (2) making informed decisions to act using evidence and systems/creative thinking, and (3) demonstrating hope and respect for diverse perspectives in seeking solutions. It outlines a draft cognitive proficiency scale (high/medium/basic/low) intended to be constructed from items aligned to Science Competency 1 and 2 with an environmental focus, while non-cognitive elements would be measured via an attitude questionnaire. It also provides example assessment item content and illustrates how the construct can be situated across socio-ecological crises and spatial scales (local to global). No empirical results, model performance metrics, or sampling/weighting procedures are reported because the document is not an analysis paper.

title: What matters for language learning? The questionnaire framework for the PISA 2025 Foreign Language Assessment
authors: Gabriele Marconi, Carla Campos Cascales, Catalina Covacevich, Tue Halgreen
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper develops a questionnaire framework for the PISA 2025 Foreign Language Assessment, intended to collect policy and contextual information to interpret and produce policy-relevant analyses of 15-year-old students’ foreign language proficiency. The framework is organized around four policy domains—Government and school policies, Students and learning, Teachers’ training and profile, and Teaching practices—plus two transversal topics: ICT and the use of the target language for instruction in other subjects. It specifies construct definitions, expected relationships to foreign language learning, and the measurement levels (student, parent, teacher, school, system) for each construct. It also outlines a methodology for determining policy relevance (“essential” vs “relevant”) based on ratings by PISA-participating countries/economies and expert consensus. The paper does not provide empirical model results, benchmarks, or performance metrics; its contribution is the planned measurement architecture for future PISA 2025 analyses.

title: England (United Kingdom) (EN)

The note also reports descriptive comparisons by age and education, and associations between numeracy proficiency and labour force participation, unemployment risk, and wages, as well as links to well-being and civic outcomes, while noting that doorstep respondents are excluded in cross-cycle comparisons. The report highlights substantial cross-country variation in mean proficiency and in the share of adults at low proficiency (e.g., at or below Level 1 in literacy or numeracy), and it emphasizes that low ICT skills and low literacy/numeracy can jointly constrain access to e-government and online services. It also reports adjusted differences from regression models (e.g., educational attainment advantages, immigrant/foreign-language disadvantages, age-related gaps) and uses odds-ratio style comparisons for risk of low proficiency among specific subgroups (e.g., inactive youth, low-educated adults). In the workplace chapter, it documents that skills-use indicators correlate only weakly with measured proficiency, that occupation is the strongest driver of skills use, and that mismatch between skills and job requirements is associated with wage penalties and “waste” of human capital. title: Results from TALIS 2024: Slovenia
outcome_summary: This OECD note summarizes TALIS 2024 results for Slovenia, focusing on lower secondary teachers and principals. The note reports only statistically significant differences or changes relative to an OECD average and highlights that some estimates may be affected by non-response bias. Substantive areas covered include teachers’ background (age, gender, experience), teaching for today’s world (student diversity, special education needs, social and emotional skills), technology use (including AI use), teachers’ learning opportunities (initial teacher education, induction/mentoring, continuous professional learning), teacher leadership/autonomy, professional relationships, status of the profession, employment terms, demands/stress, and teachers’ professional outcomes (e.g., stress, satisfaction, retention intentions). outcome_summary: This OECD thematic report (“Getting Skills Right”) describes trends in adult learning using new data from the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills, prepared under the OECD Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) Board of Participating Countries. It focuses on where, what, and how adults learn, examining participation in formal, non-formal, and informal learning, the content and intensity/modes of learning, and barriers that limit access—especially for disadvantaged groups. The report also links these patterns to how policies and practices could be redesigned to better support adult learners in a changing labour market. title: School Leadership for Learning (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesizes and analyses TALIS 2013 data to examine how school leadership “for learning” relates to professional learning communities and a positive learning climate. It operationalises instructional leadership (PINSLEADS) and distributed leadership (PDISLEADS) from principal questionnaire items, and constructs professional learning community dimensions from teacher questionnaire scales (reflective dialogue, deprivatised practice, collaborative activity, shared sense of purpose, collective focus on student learning). Learning climate is measured using teacher-reported classroom disciplinary climate (TCDISCS) and positive teacher–student relationships (TSCTSTUDS). Methodologically, it uses multilevel random-intercept models with teacher and school weights (TCHWGT and SCHWGT) and multilevel latent class analyses (Latent Gold) to classify principals into leadership types (e.g., integrated, inclusive, educational, administrative). Across chapters, the report finds that instructional leadership is more consistently associated with professional learning community features (especially reflective dialogue and collaboration), while distributed leadership is more consistently associated with positive teacher–student relationships; principals’ direct influence on disciplinary classroom climate is marginal, with teacher and student-population composition playing a larger role. The report also highlights cross-country variation and notes that leadership effects are indirect and embedded in institutional and legal contexts.

title: Supporting Teacher Professionalism (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes TALIS 2013 survey data on teacher professionalism and its association with teacher perceptions and satisfaction. Teacher professionalism is operationalised as additive indices (0–5 per domain; 0–15 overall) across three domains: knowledge base, autonomy, and peer networks, constructed from TALIS teacher and principal questionnaire items. The report estimates relationships using multilevel random-intercept regression models with teachers nested within schools, pooling across participating countries/economies, and explicitly accounts for TALIS’s complex survey design using final teacher weights and balanced repeated replicate (BRR) weights (Fay’s adjustment 0.5). Outcomes are four TALIS-based measures: perceived status, satisfaction with the profession, satisfaction with the work environment, and self-efficacy, standardised for comparability. Missing data are handled by school-mean imputation for teacher-level items during index construction, while school-level variables are list-wise deleted in regression analyses. The report also conducts equity analyses contrasting high-needs vs low-needs schools using principal-reported student composition thresholds.

title: TALIS Starting Strong 2018 Technical Report
outcome_summary: TALIS Starting Strong 2018 is a technical report describing how the OECD/IEA TALIS Starting Strong survey was designed and implemented to produce robust international indicators on ECEC centre staff and centre leaders, including their pedagogical and professional practices and the learning and well-being environments in centres. The survey covers two populations of interest: ISCED level 02 ECEC centres (typically ages 3 to entry into primary education) and U3 centres (children under three). Data collection occurred in three phases (pilot, field trial, main survey), with rotated questionnaire designs and built-in experiments during the field trial to test question formats and wording. The report specifies a two-stage sampling approach (centres, then staff within centres), excludes home-based settings from ISCED level 02 coverage, and uses weighted estimation for international reporting with Fay’s variant of balanced repeated replication (BRR) for standard errors. Complex scaling is conducted using multiple-group confirmatory factor analysis with measurement invariance testing to support cross-country comparability of scale scores.

title: TALIS 2018 Results (Volume I): Teachers and School Leaders as Lifelong Learners

The design is cross-sectional and explicitly based on self-reports, so it cannot measure causality; the report also cautions that trends across cycles require careful interpretation because the set of participating countries/economies changes over time. Results are presented as international comparisons and trends, with international averages computed as arithmetic means (or EU totals as weighted averages) across participating countries meeting adjudication standards. title: Who Needs Special Education Professional Development? International Trends from TALIS 2013
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes TALIS 2013 teacher survey data to understand professional development (PD) participation, perceived impact, and current need for special education among lower-secondary teachers. The analytic sample includes 121,173 teachers nested in 1,074 schools across 38 TALIS-participating countries and partners, using a two-stage probability design (schools selected with PPS of teachers; teachers randomly sampled within schools). Outcomes are teacher self-reports: participation in special education PD in the last 12 months (yes/no), impact of that PD (dichotomized to large impact vs other), and current PD need for teaching special needs students (dichotomized to high need vs not high need). The study fits two-level logistic regression models with teachers nested within schools and includes country fixed effects; it incorporates TALIS teacher and replicate weights to reflect complex survey design. Missing data in regression models are addressed via chained-equations multiple imputation pooled across five imputed datasets, with non-imputed results reported as consistent.

title: Statistical Matching of PISA 2009 and TALIS 2008 Data in Iceland (EN)
authors: David Kaplan, Alyn Turner
outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates statistical matching methods to create a synthetic cohort that combines PISA 2009 (student and school principal data) with TALIS 2008 (teacher and school principal data) for Iceland, where the surveys do not share the same units. Because the only common unit across surveys is the school, the study aggregates student- and teacher-level information to the school level and then matches schools using shared principal-reported variables. Six matching/imputation approaches are compared, including hot-deck distance matching (nearest-neighbor Euclidean distance) and multiple-imputation-based methods (stochastic regression imputation, predictive mean matching, Bayesian regression imputation via chained equations, Bayesian bootstrap predictive mean matching, and an EM bootstrap). Validity is assessed using Rässler (2002) criteria focused on preserving covariance/correlation structure (third level) and marginal distributions (fourth level). Results indicate that most methods reproduce marginal descriptive statistics reasonably well, while BBPMM and the EM bootstrap stand out as best at preserving the conditional covariance/correlation structure and producing the closest distributional shapes (e.g., Q-Q plots). The report frames this as a proof of concept for feasibility, while noting limitations such as aggregation to the school level and the need for further work on sampling variability and sensitivity to imputation error.

title: High-Quality Teacher Professional Development and Classroom Teaching Practices (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD paper analyzes TALIS 2013 teacher questionnaire data from 35 educational systems/economies to examine whether “high-quality” teacher professional development (TPD) is associated with teachers’ reported classroom teaching practices. The study distinguishes TPD content foci (subject matter, pedagogy, curriculum) from delivery features (collaboration, collective participation, active learning, and duration), including an overall index of effective professional development. Ten classroom teaching practices are operationalized as Likert-scaled ordinal outcomes reflecting frequency of reported implementation over the prior year, and the relationships are estimated using school fixed-effects ordinal regression models with teacher background controls. Results are presented as percentage changes in odds associated with one standard deviation increases in TPD exposure, and the paper also reports cross-national prevalence gaps by gender and initial training completion. A key limitation noted is that student outcomes are not included, so the analysis cannot establish whether TPD improves learning effectiveness beyond associations with reported practices.

title: Evaluating Measurement Invariance of TALIS 2013 Complex Scales (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper evaluates how measurement invariance of 11 TALIS 2008 complex contextual scales (10 teacher scales and 1 principal scale) is established across 23 countries when using two multiple-group CFA approaches: a continuous approach (treating ordered categorical items as continuous) and a categorical approach (WLSMV/Theta parameterisation for ordered categorical indicators). The study uses latent variable modelling to test configural, metric, and scalar invariance, with model-data fit assessed using CFI/TLI/RMSEA/SRMR (and WRMR for the categorical model) and invariance judged via changes in fit indices (e.g., |ΔCFI| and |ΔRMSEA| thresholds). Missing data on observed variables is handled model-based under MAR, and sampling weights are applied with PML in Mplus, with country weights rescaled so each country contributes equally in the multi-group analysis. Results show that all 11 scales achieve configural and metric invariance under both approaches, but scalar invariance is not achieved under the continuous approach for any scale; under the categorical approach, scalar invariance is achieved for three scales (TBTRAD, TCCOLLAB) and additionally for TSRELAT, CCLIMATE, and SELFEF (as reported in the narrative), enabling meaningful cross-country mean comparisons for those scales. The paper concludes that categorical modelling is more appropriate for inherently categorical response formats when cross-country mean comparisons are the goal.

title: Translation and adaptation processes in TALIS 2018
authors: Béatrice Halleux
outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper evaluates the translation, adaptation, and verification processes used for TALIS 2018 instruments, drawing on documentation analysis and country-reported experiences. It contrasts the field trial (FT) workflow—using the eAssessment system—with the main survey (MS) workflow—using Microsoft Word and national adaptation forms (NAFs), and it summarizes how verifiers applied sentence-by-sentence checks with severity codes and how post-verification decisions were documented. The paper reports that most countries found verifier checks useful, but that adaptation/translation work was time-consuming and sometimes difficult due to software constraints, tight timelines, and challenges in identifying/recording adaptations. It also highlights recurring issues around trend items, the need for clearer guidelines (including item-by-item guidance), and the value of a translatability assessment introduced for TALIS 2024. Overall, the study’s contribution is procedural: improving comparability depends on earlier detection of translation problems, better documentation tools, and more structured guidance for translators, reviewers, and trend handling.

title: How much time do adults spend on the PIAAC assessment and why does it matter?
outcome_summary: This OECD “Adult Skills in Focus” brief uses PIAAC computer-based assessment log files to study how much time adults spend on literacy and numeracy tasks, and how timing relates to item difficulty and disengagement. The analysis is restricted to participants assigned to the literacy and numeracy modules and computes descriptive indicators such as total time on task, within-item time percentiles, and T-disengagement rates (based on a minimum time threshold needed to attempt items). Large cross-country differences are reported: respondents in Austria, Finland, Germany, and Norway take about 50 minutes on average, while Ireland, Italy, Slovakia, Spain, and the UK take about 40 minutes. The brief also reports that time-on-task increases with age and education, is lower for respondents more familiar with ICT, and shows small gender differences. Finally, it estimates an average within-person causal effect of spending one additional second on an item on the probability of answering correctly (0.6 percentage points), while noting that PIAAC is low-stakes and disengagement can bias proficiency comparisons.

title: The Routine Content Of Occupations: New Cross-Country Measures Based On PIAAC

outcome_summary: This OECD Trade Policy Paper constructs a new cross-country measure of the routine content of occupations, the Routine Intensity Indicator (RII), using OECD PIAAC adult survey responses. The RII is built from four PIAAC questionnaire items capturing how frequently workers can modify task sequences, change task content, plan their own work, and organise their working time; respondents with missing answers on any component are excluded. The paper then aggregates individual RII values to 3-digit ISCO08 occupations using median RII values and classifies occupations into four routine-intensity quartiles (high, medium, low, non-routine) for 20 OECD countries (with Australia and Finland excluded at the 3-digit mapping step). Descriptively, about 46% of employed persons are in non-routine (18%) or low routine-intensive (28%) occupations, with substantial cross-country variation. Finally, it examines associations between routine intensity and workforce skill proxies (including numeracy skills) and finds a negative but not very strong relationship, and it applies the routine classification to labour force survey employment data to show that routine-intensive occupations are less resilient during business-cycle downturns.

title: Beyond Proficiency (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PIAAC log-file data to study how adults allocate time to items and how disengagement relates to performance in low-stakes, untimed computer-based testing. The excerpted chapters focus on timing indicators (time on task, time to first interaction, time since last action) and on disengagement indicators (rapid item skipping and T-disengagement) derived from item-level response processes. The analysis is restricted to computer-based literacy and numeracy modules, excluding PSTRE in the timing/disengagement sections shown, and it leverages the adaptive/rotated design to interpret module-order effects and item-position patterns. At the item level, time on task is strongly correlated with time to first interaction and increases with item difficulty; respondents spend less time on items in the second module, accompanied by lower correctness and higher missingness. At the respondent level, time allocation follows a rational pattern relative to ex ante probability of success, and time on task shows a positive but declining association with the probability of giving a correct answer, with higher returns in Module 2. The report emphasizes that log-based time is an imperfect proxy for effort and that causal interpretation is limited because time and performance are jointly determined and log files do not reveal the cognitive strategies used.

title: Report on Social Desirability, Midpoint and Extreme Responding in TALIS 2013 (EN)
authors: Fons J. R. Van de Vijver, Jia He
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper analyzes response styles in TALIS 2013 using teacher questionnaire data from 76,887 lower secondary teachers across 18 countries that administered a 10-item social desirability scale. The study first tests measurement invariance of a two-factor social desirability structure (positive and negative impression management) using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis, finding strong support for partial metric invariance but weak scalar invariance. It then integrates social desirability with extreme and midpoint responding into a general response style factor extracted via exploratory factor analysis, explaining 64% of variance, with social desirability and extreme responding loading positively and midpoint responding negatively. The paper correlates response-style factors with country-level socioeconomic and education indicators (including PISA 2012 achievement means and HDI) and with 17 core TALIS constructs at both individual and country levels. Finally, it applies ANCOVA-based correction procedures and finds negligible changes in the size and rank order of cross-cultural differences in the core constructs after controlling for response styles, suggesting limited impact on substantive country comparisons.

title: Skills on the Move: Migrants in the Survey of Adult Skills
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes migrants’ skills and integration outcomes using the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC). It documents that, on average across participating countries, foreign-born adults have lower assessed literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving proficiency than native-born adults, with large cross-country variation (e.g., gaps exceeding 50 points in Sweden and Finland, but under 8 points in Australia, the Czech Republic, Ireland, New Zealand, and Singapore). The report emphasizes within-country heterogeneity: migrant skill gaps vary by education level, where education was obtained, age at arrival, and duration of residence. A central mechanism highlighted is language disadvantage: the literacy gap between migrants and natives is much smaller when test-takers complete the assessment in their native language, and language penalties persist regardless of length of stay. The report further links skills to labour-market and non-labour-market outcomes, noting lower employment and earnings returns to education among migrants, and smaller differences in several well-being indicators such as self-reported health, alongside differences in trust and political efficacy in some countries.

title: How returns to skills depend on formal qualifications: Evidence from PIAAC
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes how the labour-market returns to cognitive skills depend on formal qualifications using PIAAC data from 21 countries.
