At the individual level, country-specific multilevel mixed-effects models of occupational status show that numeracy skills partly explain the occupational disadvantage of less-educated adults, but a substantial residual disadvantage remains after controls. At the country level, the remaining disadvantage increases with the aggregate skills gap and with internal homogeneity of the two educational groups, and the skills-to-occupational-status association is weaker among the less educated than among the intermediate group, consistent with employer statistical discrimination and qualification-based screening. The report also notes limitations: PIAAC captures general cognitive skills only, excludes literacy-related non-respondents, and cannot fully test causal mechanisms with the available data.

It compares two constant thresholds (3000 ms and 5000 ms) with two item-specific approaches: visual inspection of bimodal response-time distributions (VI) and a proportion-correct conditional threshold (P+>0%), where the threshold is the shortest response time associated with proportion correct greater than zero. Validity checks show that P+>0% performs slightly better than VI and constant-threshold methods, with disengaged responses exhibiting near-zero success rates. Using the P+>0% method, disengagement is low in Literacy (generally <5% of responses) and extremely low in Numeracy (often <1%), while Problem solving shows higher disengagement (typically >5% but usually <10%). Country differences are statistically significant with small-to-medium effect sizes, disengagement is highly correlated across domains, and disengagement is negatively associated with proficiency; subgroup differences by gender, age, education, and language are mostly insignificant or very small. The paper emphasizes that the design does not support causal inference and that disengagement detection based on short response times may miss disengaged behavior with long response times.

title: Who can log in? The importance of skills for the feasibility of teleworking arrangements across OECD countries (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC first-cycle adult skills microdata (respondents aged 18–64; data collected in three rounds between 2011 and 2017) from 38 countries to estimate the feasibility of teleworking in theory. The authors construct a binary “telework” indicator from 12 PIAAC questions across three domains: physical skills, job flexibility, and the intensity of ICT/reading/writing skills in workplaces. They report that about 31% of OECD workers could, in theory, work from home, with substantial cross-country variation and robustness checks via upper and lower bound specifications. Feasibility is strongly patterned by education (54% for tertiary-educated vs 18% without tertiary education) and by skills proficiency (literacy Level 4–5: ~57% vs Level 3 and below: ~28%; similar patterns for numeracy). The paper further shows large gaps by income quintiles (top 20%: ~56% vs bottom 20%: ~14%) and highlights that even after controlling for observed characteristics in a probit framework, higher-skilled workers are roughly twice as likely to be telework-compatible. The implication is that pandemic-era teleworking capacity may exacerbate labour-market inequalities, especially for lower-skilled and less-educated groups, though the study focuses on feasibility rather than actual telework uptake.

title: Examining a congruency-typology model of leadership for learning using two-level latent class analysis with TALIS 2018 (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD/TALIS 2018 study examines whether teachers and principals are aligned in their perceptions of core components of a “leadership for learning” framework across 47 countries/economies. Using TALIS 2018 data from lower secondary schools, it estimates a two-level congruency-typology model via multilevel latent class analysis, producing a three-group teacher typology and a three-group principal typology. The model is designed to capture misalignment through cross-level interaction and to relate typology membership to school context and covariates, including teacher and principal training and experience. The abstract reports the scale of the dataset (152,635 teachers; 9,079 schools) but does not provide predictive performance metrics because the analysis is typology-based rather than supervised ML prediction. Policy relevance is framed around identifying where leadership-for-learning capacity-building may need to be targeted differently across national contexts.
all_target_variables: whether teachers and principals are aligned in their perceptions of core compone

title: Measuring process quality in early childhood education and care through Situational Judgement Questions (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates the psychometric properties of Situational Judgement Questions (SJQs) designed to measure early childhood education and care (ECEC) process quality in the TALIS Starting Strong 2018 Field Trial. The study compares two SJQ response formats (Likert-scale vs forced choice) and multiple scoring approaches, including ranking, popularity-based scoring, and Nominal Response Modelling (NRM) within an IRT framework. Reliability is assessed via internal consistency and empirical reliability, and validity is examined through construct/criterion validity using correlations with related questionnaire items and staff background measures (notably staff self-efficacy and formal education). Measurement invariance is tested across two target populations (under-3 centres vs ISCED Level 02 centres), with scalar invariance largely met for Likert formats (except SJQ29 showing metric invariance), while forced-choice formats show poorer invariance. The report recommends using Likert-format SJQs and NRM scoring for the Main Survey, while noting limitations including small field-trial sample sizes that prevent invariance testing across countries and the absence of direct observation to rule out social desirability.

title: INTERVIEWERS, TEST-TAKING CONDITIONS AND THE QUALITY OF THE PIAAC ASSESSMENT
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper examines whether variation in PIAAC test-taking conditions and interviewer practices threatens the validity of cross-country comparisons. Using PIAAC paradata collected by interviewers (room of assessment and observed distractions/interruptions) and interviewer-linked indicators, the study describes substantial between-country differences in assessment environments and in interviewer assignment size. It then relates these variations to engagement/attention measures: (i) 'length complaint' (whether the respondent complained about interview length) and (ii) 'disengagement' (based on whether respondents failed to attempt at least 10% of assigned cognitive items, using computer-based timing). The results indicate that room-of-assessment and recorded interruptions are unlikely to create meaningful cross-country quality differences, while interviewer assignment size and interviewer effects may have only mild impacts. The paper also highlights limitations: no causal identification is attempted, and missing-data/paradata recording issues constrain deeper interviewer-effect analysis.
all_target_variables: whether variation in PIAAC test-taking conditions and interviewer practices thre

title: Working and learning: A diversity of patterns (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD paper uses PIAAC 2012 to document how often youth aged 16–29 combine work and study across 23 countries/regions, and how this combination is structured by apprenticeship status, VET programmes, and other (non-formalised) arrangements. It reports that 39% of youth on average work while studying, with large cross-country variation (from under 20% in Italy/Czech Republic/Flanders to over 60% in the Netherlands). Using pooled probit and multinomial logit models with country dummies, it finds that older youth (20–29) are more likely to work and study, and that literacy proficiency is associated with a lower likelihood of combining study and work. It also shows that labour-market institutions and labour demand conditions—such as employment protection strictness, the difficulty of using temporary contracts, part-time incidence, and the minimum-to-median wage ratio—are related to the probability of work-and-study. The paper further reports that, after controlling for education and individual characteristics, youth combining work and study score about 5 literacy points higher than those studying only, but it emphasizes that PIAAC cannot establish individual-level causal effects or future labour-market outcomes.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC 2012 and defines the baseline work-and-study p

title: Youth in Transition (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report compares literacy/reading and numeracy/mathematics proficiency across pseudo-cohorts by linking PISA (age 15) and PIAAC (young adulthood, ~24–27) for countries participating in both assessments. Because PISA and PIAAC were not designed to be psychometrically linked, the report does not estimate growth by directly comparing raw scores; instead it computes standardised performance gaps using a modified Cohen’s d across subgroups defined consistently in both studies (gender, parental education, and home resources proxied by number of books). The report finds that socio-economic disparities in literacy and numeracy generally persist and often widen from age 15 to young adulthood, especially at the bottom of the performance distribution, while gender gaps in literacy show strong convergence by age ~27 and numeracy gender gaps remain small but widen somewhat. It also provides a feasibility “proof of concept” for linking in Poland using statistical matching and concordance, highlighting that lack of an established PISA–PIAAC link limits precision and interpretability of growth claims. Limitations include the pseudo-cohort design (no true individual longitudinal tracking), exclusion rules and small subgroup samples in PIAAC, and the inability to establish causality from the observational comparisons.

title: The causes and consequences of field-of-study mismatch (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD analysis uses PIAAC 2012 Adult Skills microdata to quantify field-of-study mismatch and to estimate how labour-demand (field saturation) and labour-supply (skill transferability) relate to mismatch, then evaluates individual and national costs. The study applies PIAAC’s complex survey design using jackknife replicate weights and uses plausible values for literacy/numeracy-based measures where appropriate. Across pooled models, field saturation is a robust predictor of mismatch: a one-standard-deviation increase in saturation raises the odds of mismatch by about 64%, while skill transferability shows weak or context-dependent pooled effects. For consequences, the wage penalty is small when qualifications are adequate (~3%) but large when mismatch coincides with overqualification (~25%), and mismatch is associated with higher unemployment/out-of-labour-force risk (18.1% vs 13.4%). Limitations include reliance on observational, cross-sectional associations and the use of imputation for missing analytical variables, so causal claims cannot be inferred.

title: Adults with low literacy and numeracy skills (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper is a literature review focused on policy interventions for adults with low literacy and numeracy skills, drawing on evidence from multiple countries and programme types. It does not estimate predictive or causal models on PIAAC microdata; instead, it synthesises findings about what tends to motivate adults to join and persist, and which teaching approaches are described as promising (notably formative assessment, e-learning, and contextualised/embedded provision, especially in workplace and family settings). The review highlights that successful interventions are relatively uncommon and that evaluation evidence is often weak, with frequent limitations such as short follow-up windows and insufficient comparison groups. It also stresses that the low-skilled adult population is heterogeneous, implying that one-size-fits-all solutions are unlikely. The main policy implication is to translate emerging evidence on effective teaching and learning approaches into scalable programme design, while improving evaluation quality to better identify which levers work for which subgroups.

title: The skills of Polish emigrants (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes migrants’ skills using PIAAC 2011–12 adult literacy and numeracy test scores, focusing on differences between migrants and non-migrants in destination countries and highlighting the special case of Polish emigrants. The paper reports descriptive comparisons showing that Polish emigrants are young and relatively well educated, yet they are disproportionately employed in low-skilled occupations abroad. For skills, it finds that migrants from most higher-income OECD countries tend to have similar or higher literacy/numeracy scores than non-migrants in destination countries, while migrants from lower-income countries (including Poland) show lower average skill scores. A regression for literacy (Table 2) reports that literacy scores decrease with age and increase with educational attainment and recent training, while migrant status effects are strongly negative for migrants from lower-income countries and Poland. The analysis also emphasizes language proficiency and the language of testing as key mechanisms, but the excerpt does not document PV handling or missing-data procedures, limiting methodological reproducibility.

title: Adults with Low Proficiency in Literacy or Numeracy (EN)
authors: Anke Grotlüschen, David Mallows, Stephen Reder, John Sabatini
outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper synthesizes and analyzes OECD 2012 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) information to characterize adults with low literacy and/or numeracy proficiency and to examine how proficiency relates to engagement in reading, writing and numeracy practices, social/economic outcomes, basic reading component skills, and participation in adult education and training. “Low proficiency” is defined as scoring at Level 1 or below on PIAAC literacy or numeracy scales (with an estimated proficiency score threshold of less than 226). Across participating OECD countries, the paper reports that 12.3% of adults score at or below Level 1 in both literacy and numeracy, with additional shares scoring at or below Level 1 in only one domain. It finds that engagement in literacy practices is strongly associated with many outcomes and that low-proficiency adults participate less in adult education and training, with much of the participation gap explained by socio-demographic and employment characteristics. The excerpt does not report ML model performance metrics or document PV/missing-data handling procedures, so the results should be interpreted as descriptive and regression-based associations rather than as validated predictive ML evidence.

title: Labour Market Mismatch and Labour Productivity (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper links mismatch indicators constructed from OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) micro-data to industry-level labour productivity measures derived from firm-level ORBIS data. Mismatch is defined using qualification benchmarks (ISCED vs job-required qualifications) and skill mismatch using PIAAC proficiency scores with percentile-based thresholds; the paper aggregates mismatch to 1-digit industries and estimates country-industry fixed-effects regressions for 19 OECD countries. The productivity decomposition follows Olley–Pakes (within-firm productivity and allocative efficiency), and the baseline results show that higher qualification mismatch and skill mismatch are associated with lower labour productivity, with over-skilling and under-qualification accounting for most of the effects. The study reports economically significant magnitudes (e.g., a 1 SD increase in over-skilling corresponds to ~6% lower allocative efficiency) and robustness checks including market competition and managerial quality. The analysis is explicitly correlational rather than causal, and the econometric sample is limited by availability of productivity data, so counterfactual gains for countries outside the econometric sample are more speculative.

title: Estimating Cross-Country Investment in Training: An Experimental Methodology Using PIAAC Data
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper proposes an experimental, expenditure-based methodology to measure cross-country investment in human capital via workforce training, using PIAAC microdata linked to Labour Force Surveys and System of National Accounts. It distinguishes three training types—formal training, on-the-job training, and informal learning—and estimates both opportunity costs (foregone work/leisure time) and direct costs (employer/worker cost shares), discounted using PIAAC responses on training allocation and perceived usefulness. The approach produces comparable economy- and industry-level investment estimates for 22 OECD countries for 2011–2012, and also provides first-time estimates for private vs public sectors. Results indicate that average total investment in training is about 6.7% of gross value added (GVA), with on-the-job training around 2.4% of GVA on average, and substantial heterogeneity by country and sector. The paper validates robustness by recomputing the capitalisation factors (p and q) under alternative assumptions and reports very high rank correlations across methodologies, while noting limitations such as reliance on wage measures not assumed to equal marginal products and the need for further work to build time-series capital stock estimates.

title: Comparison of PIAAC and PISA Frameworks for Numeracy and Mathematical Literacy
authors: Iddo Gal, Dave Tout
outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper compares how PIAAC numeracy and PISA mathematical literacy are conceptualized and operationalized, focusing on assessment design choices that shape interpretation of proficiency results. It describes that both programs use nationally representative stratified random sampling, but differ in testing context (PISA: group testing of 15-year-olds in schools; PIAAC: individual household testing of adults aged 16–65) and in time constraints that affect item counts and item types. The paper explains that both assessments use IRT-based scaling to produce continuous proficiency scales and report proficiency levels/bands, while also highlighting differences in scale ranges, response probabilities, and the number of reporting levels (5 in PIAAC vs 6 in PISA). It further details differences in item formats, response/action classifications, and complexity schemes, including how PIAAC’s adaptive computer-based routing and automatic scoring constrain open constructed responses. Overall, it concludes that direct comparisons of reported proficiency levels across PISA and PIAAC require caution because the underlying measurement criteria and item difficulty distributions are not equivalent.
all_target_variables: numeracy and PISA mathematical literacy | that both assessments use IRT-based scaling to produce continuous proficiency sc

title: Cross-Country Estimates of Employment and Investment in Organisational Capital: A Task-Based Methodology Using the PIAAC Database
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper develops a task-based methodology to measure employment and investment in organisational capital (OC) using the OECD PIAAC background questionnaire task-frequency information. It operationalises OC as firm-specific organisational knowledge reflected in workers’ performance of OC-relevant tasks, then identifies OC-related occupations via a distribution-based top-quartile rule (mainly using 9 OC tasks) combined with hierarchical clustering of occupations using the full task set. The study covers 20 countries (2011–2012 PIAAC round) and estimates OC employment shares and OC investment as 20% of wages for OC-related occupations, expressed relative to value-added from OECD STAN. Key descriptive results include an average OC employment share of 16% (9.5% Denmark to 26% UK) and an average OC investment share of 2.2% (1.4% Czech Republic to 3.7% UK). The paper does not report ML model performance metrics because it is not an ML prediction study; it also does not document a missing-data strategy for the task-frequency inputs, and the 20% capitalisation factor is an assumption not validated within the paper.

title: Returns to Skills Around the World (EN)
authors: Hanushek, Schwerdt, Wiederhold, Woessmann
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses the PIAAC 2011–2012 adult skills survey to estimate how cognitive skills relate to labor-market earnings across the full working life, focusing in the baseline on prime-age (35–54) full-time wage and salary workers in 22 countries. Skills are measured in literacy, numeracy, and problem solving on 500-point scales, standardized within countries, and the regressions use the first plausible value of each domain score. A one-standard-deviation increase in numeracy is associated with about a 17.8% (≈18%) higher hourly wage on average across countries, with substantial heterogeneity: returns exceed 21% in six countries (largest in the United States at ~28%) and are below 15% in eight countries (including all Nordic countries). The paper reports robustness to alternative earnings measures (continuous vs decile medians; inclusion of bonuses; hourly vs monthly; adding self-employed) and to additional controls (e.g., parental education, migrant status, occupation/industry). Cross-country institutional patterns show systematically lower skill returns in countries with higher union density, stricter employment protection, and larger public-sector shares, while product-market regulation and minimum wages show weaker or conditional relationships. The study emphasizes that these associations are best interpreted as lower bounds due to measurement error in skills and that causal interpretation is not established.

title: Age, Ageing and Skills (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes age-related differences in information-processing skills using PIAAC (2012) literacy and numeracy proficiency, with additional discussion of problem solving in technology-rich environments where available. The study is cross-sectional, so observed age differences combine age, cohort, and period effects; it therefore uses adjustments for observable characteristics (notably gender and educational attainment/parental education) and, for a subset of countries, compares PIAAC with earlier IALS results to construct synthetic cohorts and estimate “age effects.” The report presents country-level age-skill profiles (e.g., average literacy and numeracy by age bands) and regression-based marginal effects linking proficiency and education to employment and occupational outcomes, as well as associations between training/skills use and proficiency gaps. It also examines policy-relevant correlates such as retirement status and effective retirement age. No machine-learning predictive modeling is reported; results are primarily descriptive and regression-based, and the manuscript does not provide a reproducible missing-data strategy.
all_target_variables: literacy and numeracy proficiency | policy-relevant correlates such as retirement status and effective retirement ag | proficiency gaps

title: How Technology Changes Demands for Human Skills
authors: Frank Levy
outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper is not an empirical large-scale assessment study; it is a conceptual argument that situates PIAAC-measured competencies within technology-driven changes in work. It proposes that a technology-rich workplace requires foundational skills (numeracy and literacy/reading) and an advanced problem-solving skill (Expert Thinking, aligned with PIAAC’s Problem Solving in Technology-Rich Environments), while also identifying an advanced communication skill (Complex Communication) that is not currently tested in PIAAC. The paper describes the breadth of the PIAAC frameworks for literacy, numeracy, and technology-rich problem solving, including the role of digital tools and metacognition in problem solving. It also frames PIAAC as an “early warning system” for countries’ preparedness for rapid technical change, while noting limitations of the current PIAAC version regarding Complex Communication and certain numeracy aspects. No model performance metrics, sampling design, or PV/missing-data procedures are reported because no ML or statistical estimation is conducted.

title: Using process data to understand adults’ problem-solving behaviour in the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PIAAC process data from the Problem Solving in Technology-Rich Environments (PSTRE) domain, focusing on the PS2 item cluster (seven interactive tasks) administered to adults routed to PS2 in five countries (England/N. Ireland (UK), Ireland, Japan, the Netherlands, United States). The study applies the longest common subsequence (LCS) sequence-mining approach to compare each respondent’s observed action sequence to expert-predefined reference sequences, producing indicators of similarity (mean LCS/reference overlap), consistency of similarity (standard deviation across items), efficiency (LCS/observed sequence overlap), and consistency of efficiency. Respondents with at least one nonresponse sequence pattern (“Start, Next, Next_OK”) are excluded from the LCS reporting sample (6,007). Results show that similarity varies significantly across countries (ANOVA), while consistency of similarity does not; similarity and consistency are associated with PSTRE proficiency level; and subgroup differences emerge by gender, age, and ICT familiarity. The report does not describe the use of PVs or a general missing-data handling strategy for the process indicators, and it does not incorporate action-timestamp information into efficiency.

title: Skills mismatch, productivity and policies (EN)
authors: Müge Adalet McGowan, Dan Andrews
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to construct a literacy-proficiency-based skills mismatch indicator that combines self-reported mismatch with quantitative proficiency thresholds by occupation (1-digit ISCO). It reports descriptive cross-country mismatch rates (e.g., New Zealand at 28% vs OECD average 25%, with over-skilling about 18% and under-skilling about 10% in New Zealand) and then estimates logit models for mismatch, over-skilling, and under-skilling using New Zealand baseline data (2015) and pooled cross-country regressions using PIAAC waves (2012 and 2015), excluding Indonesia, Singapore, and the Russian Federation. The paper’s policy results are expressed as marginal effects from logit regressions and scenario-based changes in mismatch probabilities, with pseudo-R2 values reported by policy panel. It does not report machine-learning model performance metrics because the empirical strategy is econometric (logit/OLS), and it also does not document plausible-value handling or missing-data procedures in the provided text, limiting transparency for replication.

title: Education, Labour Market Experience and Cognitive Skills (EN)
authors: Juan Francisco Jimeno, Aitor Lacuesta, Marta Martínez-Matute, Ernesto Villanueva
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC 2012 adult literacy and numeracy assessments (computer or paper administration) to study how formal education and labour-market experience relate to cognitive skills. The analysis focuses on eight countries with the largest samples (Spain, Italy, United Kingdom/England & Northern Ireland, Ireland, Norway, Sweden, Estonia, Netherlands), with additional regressions including several other countries. The baseline analytic sample is prime-aged adults (26–45), and some models use broader age ranges (16–45 or 16–65). The paper uses one of the ten imputations for each test score (preliminary results) and constructs work experience from years in paid work (≥6 months) and job task content from reported task frequency in the current/last job, distinguishing basic vs advanced numeracy and literacy tasks. Results indicate that experience is most strongly associated with numeracy early in the career for low-educated adults, and that performing basic numeracy/literacy tasks is linked to higher corresponding test performance mainly among the least schooled; overall, on-the-job learning is estimated to be about one-third of the contribution of compulsory schooling. The paper is regression/econometric rather than ML-predictive, and it does not report a full PV/missing-data combining strategy or survey-weight usage in the provided text, limiting strict comparability of effect sizes and uncertainty across countries.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC 2012 adult literacy and numeracy assessments

title: Measuring skill gaps in firms: the PIAAC Employer Module (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper introduces the PIAAC Employer Module as a new survey instrument intended to measure workplace skill gaps—imbalances between the supply and demand for skills—and to link these gaps to firms’ business strategy and hiring, training, and human resource practices. The document focuses on how the module complements worker-level information from the OECD Survey of Adult Skills, and it details key technical features such as questionnaire conceptual development, units of observation and coverage, mode of administration, and requirements for data cleaning and validation. No empirical model estimates, predictive performance metrics, or benchmark comparisons are reported in the provided text. As a result, the contribution is primarily methodological and design-oriented: it establishes what data will be collected and how it should be prepared for future analyses of skill gaps in firms.

title: Adaptive problem solving: Moving towards a new assessment domain in the second cycle of PIAAC
authors: Samuel Greiff, Katharina Scheiter, Ronny Scherer, Francesca Borgonovi, Ann Britt, Art Graesser, Muneo Kitajima, Jean-François Rouet
outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper outlines the conceptual model and assessment design principles for adaptive problem solving (APS) to be assessed in the second cycle of PIAAC, alongside literacy and numeracy. It defines APS as a cognitive and metacognitive process occurring at the interface between internal processes and an external information environment, emphasizing monitoring and regulation as conditions for adaptivity. The paper proposes assessment principles for task development, including coverage of problem-solving processes, use of interactive/dynamic information-rich problems, and the role of computer-based administration and log-file indicators (e.g., response times, action sequences, and strategy indicators such as VOTAT). It also discusses how APS should relate to ICT literacy and how a PIAAC background questionnaire could capture covariates and precursors (e.g., literacy/numeracy, cognitive precursors, and non-cognitive factors). Because it is not an empirical ML study, it does not report model performance metrics or PV/missing-data handling results.

title: The effects of vocational education on adult skills and wages (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PIAAC adult survey data to estimate the effects of vocational education (VET) versus academic education across ISCED levels on adult skills and labour-market outcomes. The authors define four main alternative treatments (vocational vs academic at ISCED 3–4 and at ISCED 5) and estimate average treatment effects in a multivalued treatment framework using IPWRA (inverse-probability weighting plus regression adjustment) under a conditional independence assumption. The analytic sample comprises 72,769 adults aged 25–59 (with 60–65 retained for fundamentals-skill analyses) across 17 OECD countries where vocational/academic distinctions are reliable in PIAAC. Outcomes include hourly earnings, employment status, NEET/NET status, time spent in paid work, health, civic behaviour, training incidence/intensity, and PIAAC foundation-skill proficiency (literacy, numeracy, and PSTRE problem solving). Results show small advantages for vocational education at ISCED 3–4 in employment-related measures, but clear disadvantages for earnings and foundation skills at ISCED 5, with additional negative associations for health/civic behaviour and for ICT-related problem solving proficiency. The report emphasizes that causal interpretation depends on selection-on-observables assumptions and that missing-data handling is explicitly discussed for PSTRE but not comprehensively documented for all outcomes in the provided text.

title: Assessing adults’ skills on a global scale (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD paper compares two international adult-skills surveys—PIAAC and STEP—highlighting similarities and differences in (i) survey and sampling design and (ii) survey instruments and assessment/proficiency estimation. The paper argues that differences in how data are collected and how proficiency is estimated can affect cross-country comparability when researchers jointly analyze or compare results across the two surveys. It also reports little evidence that the literacy assessment used in both surveys is inadequate for forming a valid basis for assessing adults’ proficiency on a global scale. The contribution is therefore methodological: it clarifies where comparability risks arise (design and scaling/estimation) and where concerns appear limited (core literacy assessment adequacy). The excerpt does not provide model performance metrics, PV/imputation rules, or an explicit weighted analytic sample, consistent with a design-comparison focus rather than an empirical predictive modeling study.

title: Education systems, education reforms, and adult skills in the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes adult numeracy skills using PIAAC microdata from the 2012 and 2014 rounds, where proficiency in literacy and numeracy is represented by 10 plausible values derived from calibrated and scaled cognitive item responses. The study first conducts correlational analyses linking country-level education-system characteristics (early tracking and vocational education orientation, constructed from cross-national education data around 2002) to average numeracy/literacy levels and percentile gaps for adults aged 20–35. It then estimates long-run associations of two reform types in 17 European countries—postponing tracking age and expanding university access for vocational-track students—using OLS and unconditional quantile regression to examine effects across the numeracy distribution (10th to 90th percentiles). The report finds that vocationally oriented systems are associated with higher average numeracy and more compressed upper-tail dispersion, while tracking-age postponement shows no significant average effect but benefits lower percentiles. Expanding university access is associated with higher numeracy, especially for individuals in the bottom deciles, reducing skill gaps. The manuscript does not document the exact missing-data handling beyond including missingness dummies for some background variables, and it does not present ML model performance metrics because the analysis is econometric rather than predictive ML.

title: Measurement Properties of Non-cognitive scales in the Polish Follow-up Study on PIAAC (POSTPIAAC) (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates the psychometric measurement properties of two non-cognitive scales—BFI-S (Big Five Inventory-Short) and Grit-S—in the Polish Follow-up Study on PIAAC (postPIAAC). The study uses a representative adult sample in Poland and applies IRT-based item diagnostics (graded response model), reliability analyses (e.g., omega coefficients), confirmatory factor analysis for structural validity, and multigroup measurement invariance testing (configural/metric/scalar/latent means using delta CFI). For discriminant validity, it compares personality factor scores against PIAAC literacy and numeracy proficiency, finding very weak associations, suggesting the constructs are distinct. For criterion validity, it estimates associations between personality traits and multiple life outcomes (education, labour market participation/employment, job satisfaction, wages, health, trust, life satisfaction) using multivariate regression models (linear, logit, ordered logit) with complex survey weights and plausible values for numeracy. The report concludes that measurement quality is only partially satisfactory (especially for reverse-worded items and full scalar invariance), but personality measures still add predictive power for several policy-relevant outcomes, with limited incremental gains beyond the Big Five for Grit.
all_target_variables: literacy and numeracy proficiency | multiple life achievement

title: Skill Mismatch and Public Policy in OECD Countries (EN)
authors: Müge Adalet McGowan, Dan Andrews
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC 2011-12 microdata for adults aged 16-65 in 22 OECD countries to study how policy environments relate to skill mismatch, defined as over- or under-skilling using an OECD construction that combines self-assessment with literacy proficiency thresholds by occupation. The empirical strategy estimates pooled cross-country logit models: first, mismatch is regressed on individual and job characteristics; then country-level policy indicators are added one at a time to avoid multicollinearity, and finally interaction models test heterogeneous effects for youth. The paper reports marginal effects and average effects (log-odds) with statistical significance, including economically meaningful scenario changes (e.g., bankruptcy cost reductions and housing transaction cost reductions). It does not report ML performance metrics (AUC/RMSE) and explicitly cautions that results are bivariate correlations rather than causal estimates due to cross-sectional data and policy endogeneity concerns.

title: Skills and Wage Inequality (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC (2012) to study how measured adult cognitive proficiency (literacy and numeracy) and formal educational attainment relate to labour-market outcomes, focusing on wage inequality across countries. It first documents inequality in proficiency and hourly wages using percentile dispersion measures (e.g., 90th–10th, 90th–50th, 50th–10th) and shows that the cross-country correlation between average proficiency and its dispersion is negative. It then estimates unconditional quantile regressions of log hourly wages on education and numeracy proficiency (with demographic controls), showing that education has a stronger and more inequality-enhancing profile—especially at the top of the earnings distribution—while proficiency returns are flatter above the median. Finally, it decomposes cross-country differences in wage inequality into composition effects versus wage-structure effects using an Oaxaca–Blinder-type quantile decomposition, finding that wage-structure differences dominate and that composition explains only a limited share of cross-country wage-inequality gaps. The paper’s cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation of how institutions shape returns over time.
all_target_variables: numeracy proficiency | only a limited share of cross-country wage-inequality gaps achievement

title: Skills and labour market performance in Sweden
authors: Margherita Bussi, Jon Pareliussen
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) 2012 for Sweden to describe adult literacy proficiency and to estimate how literacy and socio-demographic factors relate to employment and participation in adult education and training. The analysis reports multivariate OLS regressions for literacy determinants (R² = 0.39; n = 3687 after exclusions) and logit regressions for employment and AET participation. Across specifications, literacy is strongly associated with labour market outcomes: a one-standard-deviation increase in literacy corresponds to 85% higher odds of being employed (and 30% higher odds of participating in adult education/training). For immigrants, literacy and time since immigration are key predictors of literacy and employment, with employment gaps largely explained by lower literacy proficiency. Limitations include the absence of explicit documentation of plausible-value handling and missing-data strategy in the provided text, and the caution that reverse causality may exist between skills and employment.

title: A New Measure of Skills Mismatch (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD paper proposes a theory-based measure of skills mismatch using PIAAC first-wave data for adults aged 16–65, focusing on literacy and numeracy (problem solving is excluded due to higher missingness). It defines job-specific minimum and maximum skill requirements using self-reported “well-matched” workers and IRT-based proficiency scores, then classifies dependent employees into under-skilled, well-matched, and over-skilled groups. Across the pooled sample, about 86% are well-matched in literacy (4% under-skilled, 10% over-skilled) and similarly for numeracy. The study reports substantial cross-domain overlap (94% of literacy well-matched are also numeracy well-matched; Spearman ρ = 0.81) and subgroup differences by gender, education, age, and foreign status. Methodologically, it does not present ML model performance metrics because the approach is measurement/estimation rather than predictive ML, and it does not explicitly document missing-data handling beyond excluding problem solving and describing IRT-based proficiency imputation.
all_target_variables: problem solving and describing IRT-based proficiency

title: A new macroeconomic measure of human capital exploiting PISA and PIAAC: Linking education policies to productivity (EN)
authors: Balázs Égert, Christine de la Maisonneuve, David Turner
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper develops a new macroeconomic “stock of human capital” that combines the quantity of education (mean years of schooling) with the quality of education (student test scores from PISA linked to adult skills from PIAAC). The key methodological step is estimating the relative elasticities of adult test scores with respect to cohort-matched student test scores and mean years of schooling, and then using these estimated weights to cumulate quality and quantity across cohorts in the working-age population. The resulting human-capital measure is used in OECD QASR-style productivity regressions, including both cross-country time-series panel models for OECD countries and purely cross-sectional models for a broader set of countries. The paper reports that the new measure is robustly positively associated with multi-factor productivity and that simulated, sustained improvements in student test scores yield larger long-run productivity gains than comparable increases in mean years of schooling, though with very long lags (nearly five decades) for student-skill improvements to fully affect the working-age stock. The analysis is macro-aggregated and does not involve student-level ML or PV-based estimation, so survey-weight and PV-handling transparency is not applicable in the usual ILSA microdata sense.

title: Numeracy practices and numeracy skills among adults (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper analyzes the relationship between adult numeracy proficiency and the frequency/intensity of numeracy practices in everyday life and at work using PIAAC microdata. The report constructs an “intensity of engagement” index from eight ordinal questionnaire items on numeracy-related activities, using a two-parameter IRT approach to place individuals on a 0–1 scale and then classify engagement into three groups (limited, median, intensive). Numeracy proficiency is measured via a direct numeracy assessment reported on a 0–500 scale with proficiency levels (1–5 plus below 1). The analyses compare students vs non-students and examine how individual characteristics (e.g., age, gender, education, numeracy/literacy proficiency) and job characteristics relate to engagement, and how engagement relates to proficiency, employability, wages, and well-being (e.g., health). The report emphasizes “use it or lose it” patterns but does not provide a documented ML prediction pipeline; results are associational and may not identify causal direction.

title: Ageing and Skills: A Review and Analysis of Skill Gain and Skill Loss Over the Lifespan and Over Time
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper reviews and synthesizes evidence on how cognitive foundation skills relate to ageing, and it explains how repeated cross-sectional adult literacy measures from IALS (1994–1998) and ALL (2003–2007), together with future PIAAC observations, can be used to estimate skill gain and skill loss at the cohort level. It emphasizes that cross-sectional age differences are confounded by cohort and period effects, while longitudinal designs face retest and attrition biases; repeated cross-sections can help distinguish ageing effects (within-cohort change) from cohort effects (between-cohort change) when samples are representative. The paper reports that pooled IALS/ALL profiles show negative relationships between literacy proficiency and age across working-age adults (16–65), with education adjustment changing the pattern (differences become smaller from mid-20s to mid-50s). For Australia and the Netherlands, it describes statistically significant cohort and ageing effects at specific ages, but it does not provide ML model performance metrics or a documented PV/missing-data/weighting strategy for an original predictive analysis.

title: Pathways to Success (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report chapter set describes how PISA 2000 (reading as the focus domain in 2000) can be linked to Canada’s longitudinal Youth in Transition Survey (YITS) to study pathways from age 15 to young adulthood. The Canadian cohort consists of 29 687 students who participated in PISA 2000 and were followed every two years through YITS, with additional parent and school information collected in the initial wave. The report explains that PISA provides benchmarked cognitive proficiency on a scaled metric (OECD mean 500, SD 100) and, for reading, proficiency levels with cut-points used for policy interpretation. It also documents that attrition in the longitudinal follow-up was addressed using special weights applied to analyses, though the excerpt does not provide the exact weight variable names or missing-data rules for covariates. Across chapters, the report emphasizes predictive associations between early PISA achievement and later educational attainment, persistence, course choice, and labour market outcomes, while cautioning that cross-sectional PISA alone cannot support causal claims.

title: Strong Performers and Successful Reformers in Education: Lessons from PISA for the United States
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses the OECD Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) as an international benchmarking yardstick to characterize “high-performing” and “successful reformer” education systems and to draw policy lessons for the United States. It describes PISA 2009 as assessing 15-year-olds in reading (major focus), with updates in mathematics and science, using pencil-and-paper tasks (and in 20 countries, additional computer-based digital reading tasks), plus student and school questionnaires. The report emphasizes that PISA is designed to measure students’ ability to apply knowledge to real-world problems and to provide contextual indicators linking performance to student, school, and system characteristics. It reports cross-country comparisons such as mean scores, proficiency-level shares (e.g., below Level 2 baseline in reading), and equity indicators (e.g., variance explained by socio-economic background), and it discusses how these patterns relate to education system features (standards, teacher quality, accountability, autonomy, and resource allocation). Because the excerpted text does not present an original predictive modeling analysis, no ML performance metrics or PV/missing-data procedures are documented here.

title: Education in the Western Balkans (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report analyses PISA 2018 to benchmark learning outcomes and describe how schooling policies and system features in the Western Balkans relate to performance and equity. It uses PISA’s representative sampling of 15-year-olds (grade 7 or above) and reports reading, mathematics and science outcomes, including proficiency levels and subgroup gaps by socio-economic status, gender, language of instruction, and educational track (general vs vocational). The report also draws on PISA questionnaires to describe school resourcing (material resources and technological infrastructure), school network characteristics (school size and student-teacher ratios), and teacher practices/quality assurance mechanisms (teacher-directed vs adaptive instruction, teacher appraisal, certification and professional development). Reported associations are typically based on regression models (e.g., logistic regression for track selection; linear regression for performance differences), but the excerpt does not provide a replicable ML specification, PV-combining rules, or missing-data procedure. Policy implications emphasise fairer student assessment and tracking, more equitable resourcing, and more holistic teacher appraisal and professional development aligned with desired teaching practices.

title: Social Mobility and Inequality in Latin America and the Caribbean (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesises evidence on social mobility and inequality in Latin America and the Caribbean using results from PISA 2022 and PIAAC (first cycle), complemented by other OECD and partner indicators. For PISA 2022, it highlights low foundational performance in mathematics, reading, and science, with Level 2 treated as the minimum proficiency benchmark and large shares of students below that threshold across LAC countries. It also reports socio-economic disparities using PISA’s ESCS index (e.g., ESCS top–bottom differences and the strength of the socio-economic gradient), interpreting these as signals of fairness and system quality rather than as causal estimates. For PIAAC, it reports adult literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving in technology-rich environments (PSTRE) proficiency distributions and links low skills to labour-market vulnerability and informality. The report does not provide an original ML modelling pipeline, performance metrics for predictive algorithms, or explicit sampling/replicate-weight handling within the report.

title: Strong Performers and Successful Reformers in Education: Lessons from PISA for Mexico
outcome_summary: This OECD report is a descriptive benchmarking and policy lessons synthesis using PISA results for Mexico across multiple cycles (reading from 2000 onward, mathematics from 2003, and science from 2006). It reports Mexico’s mean country scores and proficiency distributions, including whether changes are statistically significant, and compares Mexico to OECD averages and to selected benchmark groups (OECD, G20, and countries with similar GDP per capita). The report also examines equity by relating performance to students’ socio-economic background using the PISA ESCS index and highlights changes in the strength of that association over time. For internal benchmarking, it uses school-level aggregates (school ESCS profiles and school performance) to show that performance varies substantially even among schools serving students with similar socio-economic backgrounds. The report does not conduct new student-level ML modeling; instead, it interprets published PISA estimates and links them to reform priorities for Mexico.

title: Strong Performers and Successful Reformers in Education: Lessons from PISA for Korea
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PISA 2009 as the central international benchmarking source to characterise Korea’s performance and to extract policy-relevant lessons for sustaining high achievement and improving equity. It reports Korea’s strong mean performance in reading and mathematics and its position among top performers in science, alongside trends since 2000 (e.g., increases in the share of top performers in reading and reductions in low performers in science). The report also summarises PISA-based evidence on equity (e.g., the proportion of variance in performance explained by ESCS, resilience among disadvantaged students, and school-level resource allocation patterns) and on learning environment factors (e.g., student-teacher relations and disciplinary climate). For digital reading, it reports Korea as the highest-performing country in the PISA 2009 digital reading option and contrasts digital vs print reading outcomes. title: Creative minds in action (EN)
authors: Sofia Bertolaja, Said Ettejjari, Natalie Foster
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PISA 2022 creative thinking assessment data to examine how 15-year-old students generate and express creative ideas across four domain contexts: written expression, visual expression, social problem solving, and scientific problem solving. It explains that the original PISA scoring awarded full/partial/no credit using coding procedures designed for cross-cultural comparability, but that this approach cannot identify the most creative responses within each participating country/economy. To address this, the report describes a rescoring project in which two more granular scoring methods—Holistic Judgement (1–7) and Criteria-Based scoring (appropriateness, originality, value, and flexibility where applicable)—were applied to a random sample of genuine student responses. The report then uses the rescored data to illustrate patterns in creative responses, including examples from disadvantaged students (lowest ESCS decile) and qualitative themes across tasks. The excerpt does not provide model-based performance metrics or specify PV/missing-data handling, so quantitative effect sizes and statistical uncertainty cannot be verified from the provided text.

title: Developing measures of engagement in PISA (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper develops and evaluates multiple indicators of student disengagement in PISA, drawing on PISA 2018, 2015, and 2012. It computes seven disengagement measures spanning three information sources: self-reported effort (Effort thermometer; perseverance; work mastery), questionnaire-based behavioural indicators (non-response, non-differentiation, inconsistency), and test-based behavioural indicators (performance decline and rapid guessing based on response times). The study finds low consistency across most measures (often small or even negative correlations), while rapid guessing and questionnaire non-response show relatively stronger associations. Disengagement is systematically related to student characteristics: boys, socio-economically disadvantaged students, and students with an immigrant background show higher disengagement in most countries/economies. Disengagement is also associated with lower PISA reading performance (using reading plausible values), but the paper emphasizes that cross-sectional data prevent causal interpretation and that engagement-related measurement issues can threaten score comparability.

title: Internships for secondary school students in general education (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD short paper reviews quantitative evidence on how internships/work placements during general secondary education relate to later career development and adult labour-market outcomes. It summarizes longitudinal findings across several countries: in Germany (NEPS), internships of several days in a company and additional voluntary internships are associated with lower NEET likelihood and higher earnings/job satisfaction at later ages; in the UK (BCS70), some placement perceptions (e.g., usefulness for career planning) are linked to higher wages and employment-related outcomes, while other associations are not statistically significant. In the US (ELS and NLSY97-based studies), results are mixed, with some studies showing employment gains and stronger effects for socially disadvantaged groups or young men, and weaker effects at longer follow-up horizons. The paper also uses PISA 2018/2022 to describe how internship participation varies by student characteristics (e.g., gender, performance levels, ESCS quartiles) and notes that participation is largely maintained during the COVID-19 period. Because this is a review rather than a single re-analysis, the excerpt does not provide a unified ML pipeline, PV handling, or missing-data/weighting procedures for the longitudinal estimates.

title: Teacher support for student learning: Insights from PISA
authors: Daniel Salinas, Gwénaël Jacotin, Miyako Ikeda, Cassandra Morley, Andreas Schleicher, Yuri Belfali
outcome_summary: This OECD policy paper synthesizes PISA evidence on teacher support for student learning, focusing on mathematics lessons in PISA 2022 and using earlier cycles (2003 and 2012) to describe trends up to 2022. Teacher support is measured from student questionnaire responses to four items (interest in every student’s learning, extra help when needed, help with learning, and continuing until students understand), combined into the TEACHSUP index (standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 across OECD countries). The report also examines how teacher support varies within versus between schools (with most variation occurring within schools) and relates teacher support to school learning environment factors (student-teacher relationships, disciplinary climate, and student persistence) and to teacher characteristics from the optional teacher questionnaire (time/work-life balance, job satisfaction, and adaptive instruction). It reports correlational associations and statistically significant differences, but explicitly notes that PISA data do not provide causal evidence for the policy interventions discussed. Due to COVID-19-related data collection challenges, some education systems are annotated for sampling-standard concerns, and the report uses confidence intervals and significance testing conventions to guide interpretation.

title: Do 15-year-olds know how to manage money? (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief reports descriptive results from PISA 2012’s first international financial literacy assessment. Across 13 participating OECD countries and economies, 10% of students can analyse complex financial products and solve non-routine problems, while 15% can at best make simple everyday spending decisions and recognise everyday financial documents such as invoices. Proficiency varies substantially: Shanghai-China has the highest mean score (603), and the gap between the highest- and lowest-performing countries/economies exceeds 225 points overall, with 75 score points (about one proficiency level) separating the top and bottom among OECD countries. Only 16% of between-country differences in mean financial literacy are explained by country wealth. The brief also highlights that financial literacy is distinct from mathematics and reading, and that gender differences are small on average but can favour boys among students with comparable math and reading performance in many systems.

title: Are 15-year-olds creative problem-solvers?
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief reports results from the PISA 2012 assessment of creative problem solving, administered on computer to about 85,000 15-year-old students across 44 countries and economies. Problem-solving competence is defined as engaging in cognitive processing to understand and resolve problem situations where the solution method is not immediately obvious, including willingness to engage and regulate problem-solving processes. The brief compares mean problem-solving performance across countries/economies and also reports “stronger-than-expected” versus “weaker-than-expected” performance, where expected performance is estimated from a regression model conditional on students’ mathematics, reading, and science scores. It finds that Singapore and Korea rank highest, with Japan also performing strongly, and that many students lack basic problem-solving skills (e.g., only 31% in OECD countries can troubleshoot an unfamiliar malfunctioning device at Level 4). The document is descriptive and does not provide an ML modeling pipeline or performance metrics for predictive algorithms, so implications are framed as policy-relevant patterns rather than causal effects.

title: OECD Reviews of Evaluation and Assessment in Education: Bosnia and Herzegovina (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD review chapter analyses how Bosnia and Herzegovina’s education system uses (or does not use) assessment and evaluation mechanisms to support learning, equity, and system improvement. It describes the country’s limited participation in international large-scale assessments (PISA 2018 and TIMSS 2019/Grade 8 and earlier TIMSS participation), and it contrasts this with the lack of state-level standardised testing and the fragmentation of assessment rulebooks across entities, cantons, and districts. The chapter documents that classroom assessment is largely summative and norm-based, formative assessment is inconsistently defined, and teachers often lack assessment literacy support (e.g., moderation, exemplars, and guidance). It also outlines policy pathways for strengthening assessment value (rulebook revisions, feedback practices, diagnostic assessments, and teacher training) and for improving external examinations and system evaluation capacity. No predictive modelling, PV estimation, or weighted statistical inference is conducted in this chapter.

title: Parental emotional support and adolescent well-being
outcome_summary: The paper uses PISA 2018 microdata of 15-year-olds to study how parental emotional support varies within countries by parents’ education level and by child gender, and how these patterns differ between countries. It further examines whether parental emotional support is associated with higher PISA achievement (reading, mathematics, science) and with students’ subjective well-being, reporting that the emotional-support–achievement and emotional-support–well-being associations are positive. The abstract indicates that differences in emotional support by parental education and gender are substantial but are largely explained by other characteristics, including family wealth, country of origin, and school urbanicity and private/public status. The excerpt does not report effect sizes, model specifications, PV combination rules, or missing-data procedures, so the magnitude of associations and the robustness of uncertainty estimates cannot be evaluated from the provided text alone.

title: Learning remotely when schools close: How well are students and schools prepared? Insights from PISA (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD policy note synthesizes evidence from PISA 2018 to assess how prepared students and schools are for remote learning during COVID-19 school closures. It reports descriptive indicators on students’ access to key home learning resources (quiet place to study, computer, and internet link) and on school preparedness (availability of computers and portability, teacher technical/pedagogical skills, time and professional resources for integrating digital devices, incentives/technical assistants, and whether an effective online learning support platform is available). The report highlights substantial within- and across-system inequalities, especially by socio-economic disadvantage at the school level, and emphasizes that technology access alone is insufficient without teacher capacity and guidance for students. It also notes a learning-relevant literacy finding from PISA 2018 (ability to distinguish fact from opinion) to argue that students may need structured teacher support to navigate online information. The document does not provide an ML modeling pipeline, PV estimation details, or explicit missing-data/weighting procedures for the reported percentages.

title: How does PISA assess science literacy?
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief explains how PISA 2015 assesses science literacy among 15-year-olds, emphasizing competencies rather than factual recall. Science literacy is defined as the ability to engage with science-related issues as a reflective citizen, operationalized through three skills: explaining phenomena scientifically, evaluating and designing scientific enquiry, and interpreting data and evidence scientifically. The brief highlights a major assessment change between PISA 2006 and PISA 2015: the move from pencil-and-paper to computer-based delivery for most participating students, enabling more extensive and nuanced measurement (including simulation-based enquiry tasks). It reports that about 540 000 students in more than 70 economies participated, with new participating economies including Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Guangdong (reported as B-S-J-G/China), Algeria, the Dominican Republic, Kosovo, and Lebanon. No model-based results, performance metrics, or causal/predictive estimates are presented because the document is not an empirical ML study.

title: Does money buy strong performance in PISA? (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief synthesizes PISA 2009 evidence to argue that national wealth and total education spending are not sufficient to explain differences in student performance. It reports threshold-like patterns: for per-capita GDP up to around USD 20,000, higher wealth is associated with higher mean reading scores, but above that level wealth is no longer a predictor. Similarly, cumulative education expenditure per student shows little relationship with performance after roughly USD 35,000 per student, with high-spending systems (e.g., Luxembourg, Norway, Switzerland, United States) performing similarly to lower-spending ones. The brief then highlights more actionable correlates in high-income economies: prioritizing teacher quality (e.g., teacher salaries and professional status) over smaller class sizes, and adopting inclusive systems with high expectations for all students (retaining/transfer/grouping practices linked to higher mean reading performance). Because the document does not provide a new ML model, PV handling, or missing-data procedures, the results should be interpreted as descriptive/associational policy messages rather than causal estimates.

title: Do countries with high mean performance in PISA maintain their lead as students age?
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief links PISA performance at age 15 to adult literacy and numeracy performance measured in PIAAC for the same birth cohorts, using published country-level means rather than student-level predictive modeling. It reports positive associations between PISA reading/mathematics scores and PIAAC literacy/numeracy scores for corresponding age bands 12 years later, with scatterplot fit statistics such as R²≈0.3549 (PISA 2003 reading vs PIAAC 2012 literacy, ages 23–25) and R²≈0.4713 (PISA 2000 mathematics vs PIAAC 2012 numeracy, ages 26–28). The brief emphasizes that no country shows higher-than-expected adult performance relative to its PISA starting point, suggesting limited “catch-up” after compulsory schooling. It also notes that the relationship is not deterministic at the individual level and that cohort growth can vary substantially within countries (illustrated with Canada and Denmark retesting examples). Limitations include reliance on country averages, differences in country composition contributing to OECD averages across studies, and the fact that the analysis is descriptive/associational rather than causal.

It explains that PISA for Schools (introduced in 2012) provides participating schools with confidential, school-level benchmarking aligned with PISA’s framework, covering performance in mathematics, reading, and science for 15-year-olds, and also addressing student motivation, perceptions of the school environment, and equity and inclusion. title: Are 15-year-olds prepared to deal with fake news and misinformation?
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief synthesises PISA 2018 evidence on whether 15-year-olds are prepared to deal with fake news and misinformation through in-school opportunities to learn digital reading and credibility skills. It reports that, on average across OECD countries, 54% of students were taught how to recognise whether information is subjective or biased, with large cross-country variation (e.g., over 70% in Australia, Canada, Denmark and the United States; under 45% in Israel, Latvia, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia and Switzerland). The brief also shows socio-economic gradients: students from advantaged backgrounds score higher on an index of knowledge of reading strategies for assessing source credibility, and about one-third (32%) of the reading-performance gap is indirectly associated with differences in this knowledge. Finally, it reports a strong association between opportunity to learn biased-information detection and performance on a PISA reading item distinguishing fact from opinion (R²=0.46 across OECD countries; weaker R²=0.15 across all participating countries), even after accounting for per-capita GDP or reading performance. The document is descriptive and does not re-estimate models with explicit PV or missing-data procedures, so causal interpretation is limited.

title: How are PISA results related to adult life outcomes?
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief synthesizes longitudinal evidence linking PISA reading performance at age 15 to adult life outcomes around age 25. It highlights that students in the top quarter of PISA reading performance are substantially more likely to complete university and to be in skilled employment, and less likely to be NEET, compared with students in the bottom quarter, with large cross-country differences reported for Australia, Canada, Denmark, and Switzerland. The brief also reports that accounting for PISA reading performance reduces gaps in skilled employment between advantaged (tertiary-educated parents) and disadvantaged youth, suggesting that school performance is an important mediator of later labour-market inequality. Additionally, students’ expectations for high-skilled work and self-reported perseverance/effort in school are associated with later educational attainment, even after accounting for reading performance in at least one example. The document does not provide model-based ML metrics or a transparent PV/missing-data estimation procedure within the brief, so the results should be interpreted as descriptive longitudinal associations rather than as newly estimated predictive models.

title: Cultivating Green Futures: Helping students understand and progress towards green jobs
outcome_summary: This OECD policy brief uses PISA 2018 as an evidence base to illustrate young people’s engagement with environmental issues and a gap between caring about climate change and perceived agency to contribute to solutions. It reports descriptive indicators such as the share of 15-year-olds expressing confidence in understanding climate change impacts (78% on average across OECD countries) and the smaller share who feel they can actively contribute (57%), alongside the finding that personal interest in environmental protection exceeds perceived agency in every country/economy. The brief also synthesises a scoping review of 87 green guidance programmes across primary to upper secondary education in 20 OECD countries, describing programme objectives and design features (e.g., career exploration, applied learning, employer/workplace experiences, and personalised guidance). Rather than estimating causal effects, it proposes a framework for “green guidance” grounded in broader OECD evidence on career readiness and employment outcomes. Limitations include the absence of an explicit student-level modelling design, no reported ML evaluation, and no documented PV/missing-data handling for an original analysis.

title: PISA for Development (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA for Development (PISA-D) results-in-focus brochure summarizes the school-based assessment conducted in seven low-to-middle-income countries (Cambodia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Senegal, Zambia). Approximately 37,000 students (representing about one million 15-year-olds in grade 7 or above) completed paper-based tests in reading, mathematics, and science, with a total testing time of two hours and a 35-minute student background questionnaire plus teacher and school principal questionnaires. The assessment was targeted to lower performance levels on the PISA scale, with more than two-thirds of items at Level 2 or below, and it used a mix of multiple-choice and constructed-response items. Reported outcomes include mean scores and the share of students reaching minimum proficiency (Level 2) in reading (~23%), mathematics (~12%), and science (~18%), compared with OECD averages (80%, 77%, 79%). The brochure also highlights equity patterns (gender, rural/urban, socioeconomic status, family resources) and policy-relevant “foundations for success” (resources, inclusive environments, learning time, quality instruction, family/community support), but it does not provide an ML modeling evaluation or technical PV/missing-data procedures.

title: What can we learn from the PISA reading-fluency test?
outcome_summary: This OECD “PISA in Focus” uses the PISA 2018 reading assessment, adding a three-minute reading-fluency task in which students judge the sensibility of short sentences (21–22 sentences total; 10–11 per block). Fluency is operationalised as total response time (seconds) to complete sensibility judgments, with multiple fluency scores per student and a scoring rule that excludes some speeded/inaccurate response patterns. The document reports that reading fluency is a significant predictor of PISA reading comprehension across major language groups, with fluency accounting for roughly 10–20% of the variation in reading proficiency for most language groups, and often exceeding 20% in multilingual environments. It also reports that more than one in five 15-year-olds score below Level 2 in reading proficiency on average across OECD countries, and that many of these low achievers are not yet fluent readers. Methodologically, the brief does not provide details on PV combining or missing-data handling, so uncertainty estimation and exact inferential procedures cannot be fully audited from the provided text.

title: How is students’ motivation related to their performance and anxiety? PISA in Focus #92
outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus #92 summarizes relationships between students’ motivation to achieve and two outcomes: performance in the PISA 2015 assessment and students’ test-related anxiety. Students in 55 education systems responded to five motivation statements (e.g., wanting top grades, wanting to be among the best, seeing oneself as ambitious). Across education systems, the brief reports that motivation is not strongly related to performance at the country level, but within almost every system motivation is positively associated with higher performance; this association is not statistically significant in Belgium and Singapore. The brief also reports that motivation is associated with higher anxiety, with the relationship varying by the type of motivation (extrinsic vs intrinsic) and by country. It further highlights that both motivation and performance are patterned by students’ socio-economic environments, suggesting that contextual factors may partly explain observed associations.
