title: What Do We Know about Young People’s Interest in Health Careers? (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD review synthesizes evidence on young people’s interest in health careers using PISA survey data on career aspirations of 15-year-old students and complements it with national administrative data on applications and admissions to nursing education programmes. The review organizes results around students’ aspirations to work in the health sector, aspirations to work as doctors, and aspirations to work as nurses, with additional attention to gender differences. It also reports evidence from an online search of data sources for a subgroup of OECD countries and discusses how administrative data are reported across OECD and non-OECD contexts. Because the document is a synthesis rather than a single empirical ML study, it does not report model-based performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/R²) or a unified predictive pipeline. Consequently, the implications are primarily descriptive and policy-oriented, highlighting where gendered patterns and data availability constraints may affect workforce planning and outreach strategies.

title: How does PISA measure students’ ability to collaborate?
outcome_summary: PISA 2015 introduced a new computer-administered assessment of collaborative problem solving, extending beyond the 2012 individual problem-solving framework. The assessment uses computer simulations in which students are placed in a team and must answer quiz-show-like questions about the fictional country of Xandar, with computer agents whose behavior can be controlled to standardize partner interactions. Competence is defined through four individual problem-solving processes plus three collaborative competencies, yielding 12 specific skills that are targeted by test items. The brief reports participation of around 125,000 students across 52 education systems, but it does not provide scoring benchmarks, model performance metrics, or an estimation strategy. It also summarizes evidence that computer-agent collaboration is a reasonable approximation of human-human collaboration, supporting the validity of the measurement approach.

title: Education for human flourishing (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD chapter develops a conceptual framework for “Education for human flourishing,” focusing on five learner competencies (adaptive problem-solving, ethical competence, understanding the world, appreciating the world, acting in the world) and a broader architecture linking them to foundational literacies, social-emotional skills, and well-being domains. It also proposes learning-environment design principles (curricular, pedagogical, aesthetic, social-emotional, exploratory-imaginative, digital, and physical spaces) and pedagogical features (teacher-guided learning and experiential learning), with illustrative technology-enabled examples (e.g., TEL tools and the Knowledge Building Design Studio). The document does not estimate statistical models, train ML predictors, or report performance metrics against an assessment outcome. Consequently, there are no benchmarks, effect sizes, or causal claims to evaluate; the contribution is normative and design-oriented, intended to inform future metric selection and assessment development rather than to test an empirical hypothesis.

title: Are Students Ready for a Technology-Rich World? What PISA Studies Tell Us
outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesizes evidence from PISA 2003 to describe students’ access to and use of ICT and to examine associations with mathematics performance. PISA 2003 assessed 15-year-olds in 41 countries (including all 30 OECD members) using mathematics as the main performance domain, with mathematics test booklets administered for 120 minutes per student across combinations totaling 390 minutes overall. ICT information comes from (i) student background questionnaires (35 minutes) and (ii) an optional 5-minute ICT questionnaire administered in 32 countries, plus a school questionnaire completed by principals. The report documents cross-country patterns in computer access (home vs school), frequency and type of ICT use (Internet/entertainment vs programs/software), attitudes, and confidence in performing routine, Internet, and high-level computer tasks. It emphasizes that observed relationships with performance do not establish causation and highlights equity concerns, especially for students lacking home computer access and for those with low confidence in routine/Internet ICT tasks.

title: Mathematics Teaching and Learning Strategies in PISA (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD chapter analyses PISA 2003 mathematics performance using student and school principal questionnaire indices capturing teaching and learning strategies (e.g., instructional time, homework, tutoring/out-of-school lessons, memorisation/elaboration/control strategies, competitive/co-operative learning preferences, and classroom climate such as disciplinary climate, teacher support, and student–teacher relations). The analysis is multilevel, partitioning achievement variance into between-student and between-school components and then estimating bivariate and multivariate associations (unique effects) for each factor while adjusting for a set of antecedent background variables (notably socio-economic background, motivation, anxiety, and self-beliefs). The chapter emphasizes that PISA is cross-sectional, so results are associations rather than causal effects. Missing data are handled using multiple imputation, and the text notes that some time-related indices were excluded from the final model due to inconsistencies in measurement. A key benchmark-like conclusion is that disciplinary climate shows the most robust positive association with mathematics performance, including at the school level, while many other strategy variables show inconsistent or attenuated effects once other factors are controlled.

title: PISA Computer-Based Assessment of Student Skills in Science (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report compares PISA 2006 science achievement delivered via computer-based assessment of scientific literacy (CBAS) versus the standard paper-and-pencil science test in three countries (Denmark, Iceland, Korea). The CBAS main study used a fixed-form computer test with 45 multimedia-extended items (final analyses on 42 items after dropping/combining specific items), administered on standardized laptops with two item orders split to reduce fatigue. Achievement scores were scaled on a PISA-like metric and re-standardised for comparability within the report; CBAS and paper scores were based on plausible values, and inference used PISA’s balanced repeated replication (BRR) with replicate weights. At the country level, overall performance did not change by modality, but gender differences did: males outperformed females on CBAS in all three countries, while gender patterns differed on paper. The report also documents that CBAS was less confounded by reading ability (weaker association with reading than in paper-based science) and that students reported higher enjoyment/motivation for CBAS, yet these engagement measures showed weak or non-existent associations with achievement on CBAS.

title: Learning Mathematics for Life: A Perspective from PISA (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD chapter provides an assessment-framework and item-characteristics perspective on PISA 2003 mathematics rather than training or evaluating machine-learning models. It explains how PISA defines mathematical literacy (mathematical literacy as functional use in real-world contexts) and structures the domain using the “ML + 3Cs” model (content, context, competencies), including competency clusters (reproduction, connections, reflection) and four overarching content ideas (change & relationships, space & shape, quantity, uncertainty). The chapter then illustrates how item difficulty is quantified using percent-correct, logit-based item difficulty, and the PISA mathematics scale (mean 500, SD 100) with six proficiency levels. It reports descriptive comparisons showing that question difficulty varies systematically with competency cluster, traditional curriculum topic, context type, word count (reading load), and item format, and it discusses omission rates as a function of item difficulty and format. Methodologically, it emphasizes scoring conventions (missing responses treated as incorrect for scoring) and notes limitations of PISA’s time constraints for observing the full “mathematisation” cycle.

title: Equally prepared for life? HOW 15-YEAR-OLD BOYS AND GIRLS PERFORM IN SCHOOL
outcome_summary: This OECD report documents the PISA 2006 science assessment framework and provides descriptive and comparative results on gender differences in science, reading, and mathematics among 15-year-olds. PISA 2006 involved about 400,000 students across 57 participating countries/economies, completing two hours of pencil-and-paper tasks; in three countries, some students received additional computer-based questions. The science domain used 37 science units (108 cognitive items) plus embedded attitudinal items, with items spanning multiple-choice and constructed-response formats and being organized around real-life science contexts (e.g., health, natural resources, environmental quality, hazards, frontiers). The report also links performance to student and school characteristics using questionnaire data and contextual indicators, including two-level regression structures (students nested in schools) and the use of the five plausible values in science as dependent variables. While the excerpt indicates complex survey weighting with normalized final student weights and normalized replicates, it does not specify missing-data handling for questionnaire variables in the provided text.

title: PISA Data Analysis Manual: SPSS, Second Edition (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD manual documents how to analyse PISA data correctly under the programme’s complex survey design and plausible-values framework. It explains that PISA uses a two-stage sampling process (schools, then students within schools), which increases standard errors relative to simple random sampling; therefore, analysts must use the provided student final weights (W_FSTUWT) and replicate weights (80 Fay’s BRR replicates) to compute unbiased sampling variance estimates. For achievement outcomes, PISA reports performance using plausible values: analyses should be run separately on five plausible values per student and then aggregated to combine sampling and imputation error. The manual also provides guidance on missing data handling for modelling examples, using a missing-dummy approach and imputation for individual/school-level predictors while not imputing system-level variables when the number of systems is small. It further describes the PISA 2006 rotated test design and the structure of the international database, including questionnaire instruments and available weights/replicates.

title: PISA Data Analysis Manual: SAS, Second Edition (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD manual explains how to analyse PISA 2006 data correctly under its complex sampling design and plausible value (PV) framework. It emphasizes that PISA uses a two-stage sample (schools then students), so standard errors must be computed using replicate weights rather than assuming simple random sampling; otherwise, standard errors are underestimated and non-significant results may appear significant. For achievement, PISA reports performance using five plausible values per student; analyses must be run separately on each PV and then aggregated using combining rules to incorporate both sampling uncertainty and imputation error (test unreliability). The manual also details SAS procedures for applying student final weights (W_FSTUWT) and using Fay’s BRR replicates for variance estimation, including guidance on variance divisors (VARDEF) for exploratory statistics. Finally, it documents a pragmatic missing-data strategy for multilevel modelling: missing dummies plus weighted mean imputation at student/school levels, with system-level variables left unimputed.

title: PISA Vocational Education and Training (VET) (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD framework chapter outlines the conceptual foundations and measurement strategy for PISA-VET employability skills, rather than reporting empirical model results. It defines problem solving using PIAAC Cycle 2 “adaptive problem solving” and task performance/collaboration using the OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills (SSES) constructs (conscientiousness and agreeableness facets). It proposes a three-pillar assessment approach: a generic stand-alone assessment for all four employability skills (Pillar 1), an occupationally embedded component primarily for literacy and problem solving (Pillar 2), and an occupation-specific skills assessment with minimal employability-skill overlap (Pillar 3). The framework also specifies how proficiency levels may be used (e.g., reduced granularity for time-constrained generic assessments) and how contextual questionnaires should support equity/equality analyses. No sampling, scaling estimation, PV computation, or predictive modeling performance is reported in the provided text.

title: Making Education Count for Development: Data Collection and Availability in Six PISA for Development Countries
outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates the current state of system-level data collection and availability (quality and completeness) for the PISA-D system-level questionnaire in six participating countries: Cambodia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Paraguay, Senegal, and Zambia. The system-level questionnaire is organized into ten worksheets covering education system structure, national assessments/examinations, instruction time, teacher training and salaries, educational finance (including enrolment), and national accounts/population data. Evidence is drawn from site visits conducted between March and May 2015, mainly meetings with National Project Managers and officials responsible for the relevant data domains, plus desk research for Cambodia. The report’s key results are qualitative/administrative: countries are generally able to provide the requested data, but challenges are uneven across themes—especially private education expenditure, sector coordination across ministries, and discrepancies between policy and implementation. The report provides technically sound options to improve international comparability and reduce respondent burden, rather than reporting student-level achievement metrics or ML model performance.

title: Does test-based school accountability have an impact on student achievement and equity in education?
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2006–2015 to study whether test-based school accountability affects student achievement and equity, and whether school autonomy moderates these relationships. The authors build a pooled country-level panel by merging student PV-based achievement scores (mathematics as the main dependent variable; reading and science in annexes) with student SES (ESCS) and school/head teacher questionnaire measures of accountability and autonomy. They estimate regression models using the Stata Repest command to account for PISA’s complex survey design and plausible values, and they cluster standard errors at the country level; for country-level uncertainty they bootstrap by leaving one country out at a time. Across all countries, they find no conclusive evidence that accountability is associated with achievement or inequality in mathematics (and broadly similar patterns for reading), while science shows a positive average association alongside increased inequality driven by lower- and middle-income countries. For low- and middle-income countries, accountability is associated with higher performance in mathematics and science, but with a trade-off of increased inequality, and autonomy in curriculum/assessment appears to strengthen the positive accountability–achievement association.

title: Education in Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD/UNICEF report analyzes PISA 2018 to describe education system performance and equity patterns across Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EECA). It uses PISA’s two-stage sampling of schools and students of age 15 (Grade 7 or above) and compares EECA averages to OECD benchmarks, focusing primarily on reading performance and related proficiency levels. The report documents that EECA reading performance is lower than the OECD average (421 vs 487 score points) but generally improving over time, with no decreases among earlier participants. It also highlights inequities: boys score lower than girls in reading (about 32 points on average), urban students outperform rural students with larger gaps than in the OECD, and socio-economic disparities are substantial (about 80 score points between advantaged and disadvantaged students). Beyond achievement, the report synthesizes evidence on school sorting/segregation, resource allocation, learning time, truancy, and teaching practices, translating these patterns into policy considerations for more equitable schooling and teaching.

title: Effective Teacher Policies: Insights from PISA
outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesizes findings from PISA 2015, including an innovation that integrates a teacher survey into the PISA assessment, and it also uses other related OECD databases and comparisons with earlier PISA cycles (notably PISA 2006). It focuses on three policy questions: (1) how high-performing systems select, develop, evaluate and compensate teachers; (2) how teacher sorting across schools relates to equity; and (3) how countries attract and retain people into teaching. The report provides cross-country descriptive comparisons and discusses statistically significant differences/changes, while noting that some indicators are missing when there are too few observations or when data do not apply. It reports several benchmark-style results such as the share of disadvantaged schools receiving smaller classes and/or lower student-teacher ratios, the inequitable distribution of teacher qualifications/experience, and the proportion of 15-year-olds expecting to work as teachers. The excerpt does not provide the technical estimation details (e.g., PV combination rules, exact missing-data method, or weighting variable names), so causal interpretation is limited and the statistical mechanics of the estimates cannot be fully audited from the provided text.

title: Ten Questions for Mathematics Teachers… and how PISA can help answer them
outcome_summary: This OECD teacher guide uses cross-sectional PISA 2012 mathematics results (for 15-year-old students) together with student background questionnaire responses about mathematics class experiences and teaching practices, and it also incorporates TALIS 2013 teacher questionnaire data on teaching practices and teacher self-efficacy. The report organizes evidence into ten classroom-focused questions, including how teacher-directed versus student-oriented strategies relate to students’ success across mathematics item difficulty, and how strategy use varies by student gender and socio-economic status. It emphasizes that PISA and TALIS are collected at one point in time and therefore cannot establish cause-and-effect relationships. The excerpt does not provide a technical ML modeling specification (algorithms, validation metrics, or PV/missing-data procedures), so the findings are presented as descriptive/correlational patterns and evidence-informed recommendations for teachers rather than as model-based predictive performance.

title: The Measurement of Socio-economic Status in PISA (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper examines how socio-economic status is measured in PISA, focusing on the index of economic, social and cultural status (ESCS) and its components. It reviews changes introduced over time in questionnaires (parental education, occupation, household possessions), scaling procedures, and field-trial experiments in 2021 that used alternative question formats. The paper also analyzes trends in ESCS components from 2015 to 2022 to assess whether observed changes reflect real shifts or measurement artifacts. Finally, it evaluates validity, reliability, and comparability of ESCS component measures, including differences between self- vs proxy reports, post-coded vs pre-coded occupation formats, and parent vs student reporting of household possessions. The excerpt does not provide student-level ML model performance metrics or explicit PV/missing-data handling, indicating the work is primarily measurement-focused rather than predictive modeling.

title: PISA for development technical strand c (EN)

It recommends a two-stage approach: first identify households reporting a 15-year-old, then revisit to verify age and schooling status and administer a filter, test, and contextual questionnaire. For sampling, it discusses probability sampling (with large household listing requirements) versus targeted sampling of marginal/vulnerable areas using poverty maps, and it highlights challenges in under-coverage of marginalised groups in standard household surveys. For measurement, it proposes a modular set of cognitive assessments (from PISA booklets to ASER/Uwezo-like basic literacy/numeracy and pictorial/verbal tasks) with filters to route respondents to appropriate difficulty levels, and it outlines linking strategies using Rasch/IRT models. The paper does not provide predictive ML results or PV-based achievement estimates; its contribution is methodological guidance for future implementation and instrument development.

Rather than estimating effects on achievement, it synthesizes the PISA questionnaire framework (student, classroom, and school contexts), reviews how contextual measures evolved across PISA cycles (2000–2012), and compares constructs used in other international assessments relevant to low- and middle-income countries. The paper identifies seven enhancement themes—early learning opportunities, language at home and at school, family and community support, quality of instruction, learning time, socioeconomic status, and school resources—and discusses options for extending existing PISA scales (especially ESCS) while maintaining international comparability. It also outlines psychometric and pilot-testing requirements (including IRT-based analyses) and emphasizes integration constraints such as questionnaire length and the PfD assessment design (e.g., rotation).

title: PISA For Development Technical Strand A (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD technical strand paper (Strand A: Enhancement of PISA Cognitive Instruments) identifies technical issues for adapting PISA reading, mathematics, and science instruments to developing-country contexts without developing new cognitive items. It reviews the existing secure item pool (517 items used across PISA 2000–2012; 337 secure items) and shows that item difficulty targeting and item-by-country interactions (country DIF) can be large, threatening cross-country construct comparability. The paper discusses test design constraints (rotated booklet design, domain coverage, item formats, and administration logistics) and evaluates options such as omitting more difficult items, using fewer booklets, and conducting equating studies to document comparability. It also reviews PISA proficiency levels and argues that current described levels—especially at the lower end—may be insufficiently informative for many partner countries, suggesting complementary approaches such as reading components or new lower-difficulty items in future phases. No predictive ML model is estimated; the outputs are technical recommendations and psychometric design considerations.

title: Teenage career development in Wales (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2022 to describe teenage career development in Wales (students aged 15–16) and compares Wales to OECD averages, with additional trend context from PISA 2015 and 2018. The analysis is based on student questionnaire responses on career development activities and career thinking (e.g., career certainty/uncertainty, occupational expectations coded to ISCO, educational ambitions aligned to ISCED), alongside principal questionnaire information about how schools organise career guidance. In Wales, career uncertainty is high (44% uncertain in 2022 vs 39% across the OECD), and occupational expectations are strongly concentrated in professions (e.g., 63% of students with an occupational plan expect professional occupations, compared with 22.5% of actual workers aged 30–34). The paper also reports equity-related patterns (gender and social disparities) and highlights opportunity to increase engagement in career development activities, especially for disadvantaged and low-performing students. title: PISA in Low and Middle Income Countries (EN)

It explains that PISA is designed to benchmark 15-year-olds’ reading, mathematics, and science performance using proficiency levels (e.g., Level 2 as a baseline) and contextual questionnaires, but it argues that effective policy use is constrained by implementation and capacity challenges. The paper reports descriptive cross-country patterns: students in many partner countries perform substantially below OECD averages, with large shares below baseline proficiency, and it highlights that coverage of 15-year-olds can be non-universal, reducing representativeness and comparability. It also discusses how national wealth (GNI per capita) relates to performance, noting a flattening relationship at higher income levels. title: Analysis of the Predictive Power of PISA Test Items (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper examines whether PISA 2003 mathematics and problem-solving item responses predict later educational qualifications, using the Australian LSAY cohort linked to PISA 2003. The study constructs a qualification-level outcome for 2007 and 2010 (five recoded categories derived from current and highest completed qualifications) and tests relationships between later qualifications and (a) single PISA items and (b) scales formed from newly proposed item classifications (16 new classifications) plus original PISA framework classifications. The main analyses use linear regression on student-level data, with models estimated both without conditioning and after accounting for overall performance using the first plausible value in mathematics or problem solving; additional conditioning models include gender, ESCS, and immigrant/language indicators. Item psychometric characteristics (difficulty and discrimination) are also considered, and item-based scales are standardized using weighted z-scores. The paper finds that statistics-related and rates/ratios/proportions/percentages-related mathematics item classifications are significantly related to later qualifications, and that reverse/flexible thinking items are significant predictors in both mathematics and problem solving, while some other classifications show weaker or domain-specific relationships. Limitations include the lack of labour-market outcomes (too early for most students) and the use of educational outcomes only, plus caution about conditioning/DIF interpretations and the use of only the first plausible value.

title: Do the Average Level and Dispersion of Socio-Economic Background Measures Explain France's Gap in PISA Scores?
authors: Hervé Boulhol, Patrizio Sicari
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2009 to test whether cross-country differences in students’ socio-economic background (ESCS) explain France’s relative performance. ESCS is computed at the student level from OECD’s ESCS components and then aggregated to each country as the mean ESCS and the dispersion (standard deviation) of ESCS across students. The paper estimates country-level regressions where the dependent variables are the average PISA score (reading, mathematics, science combined), the 5th percentile (P5), the 95th percentile (P95), and the P95/P5 inequality ratio. Results show that ESCS mean and especially ESCS dispersion are strongly associated with country differences in average performance, with ESCS explaining about 60% of the variance in average PISA scores across countries. After adjusting France’s average PISA score for ESCS differences, the France–best-performer gap (Finland, Korea, Japan, Canada) is reduced by about 50%, but not eliminated. The authors caution that endogeneity and the small country sample limit causal interpretation, and the paper does not document how PVs and missing data were handled when constructing PISA distributional statistics.

title: The Policy Impact of PISA: An Exploration of the Normative Effects of International Benchmarking in School System Performance
outcome_summary: This OECD report examines the normative impact of PISA on national/federal education policy-making using an expert questionnaire administered in July 2011 to PISA Governing Board representatives from 65 PISA 2009 participating countries/economies. The study collects perceptions of PISA influence (e.g., “very/moderately/extremely influential”), identifies which PISA result aspects (reading, mathematics, science, trends, equity, and attitudes) inspired policy or practice changes, and constructs a breadth-of-policy-impact index using “Yes/Partly/No” responses. It further reports how PISA is used in assessment and evaluation systems, curriculum standards, and performance targets, including examples of policy transfer and benchmarking. The report does not estimate student achievement models and therefore does not use PV-based scaling or ML prediction; instead, it provides descriptive cross-national evidence of policy uptake. Key limitations include one respondent per system, subjective judgments, and incomplete extended responses, which constrain the depth of country-specific examples.

title: THEORETICAL CONSIDERATIONS ON SCALING METHODOLOGY IN PISA
outcome_summary: This OECD report provides a mathematical review of PISA’s scaling methodology across three phases: (1) item scaling using IRT with fixed trend-item parameters to maintain cross-cycle comparability; (2) student prior distribution estimation using a latent regression model (LRM) that regresses latent proficiencies on questionnaire-derived covariates (Empirical Bayes); and (3) multiple imputations where plausible values (PVs) are drawn from the posterior distribution, using Laplace approximation for practical inference. It emphasizes scale robustness as the number of participating countries/economies grows, while highlighting the need to assess model–data fit and residual structures by sub-populations. The report also discusses nuisance factors (e.g., testlet effects and locally dependent items) and how they can be incorporated into the measurement model or residual covariance structure. While it confirms robustness in principle, it stresses that validity depends on correct model specification, appropriate parameter constraints, and careful DIF/residual diagnostics rather than on the scaling framework alone.

title: How a student’s month of birth is linked to performance at school (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2018 to study how month of birth relates to students’ relative age within their school-entry cohort and, in turn, to cognitive outcomes (reading, mathematics, science) and multiple non-cognitive outcomes (self-perceived competence and difficulty in reading, self-efficacy and fear of failure, motivation/attitudes toward competition, expectations to complete tertiary education, and bullying exposure). It also documents how school-entry regulations (cut-off dates and school-year start dates) vary across more than 45 participating countries/economies and how strictly they are applied, using contextual questionnaire information on students’ age at entry. The paper reports that being among the youngest in the grade cohort is associated with lower performance across PISA domains and with higher likelihood of repeating a grade in primary school, and in several systems with lower self-confidence and weaker future education expectations. It emphasizes that disentangling age-at-test, age-at-entry, and schooling duration is difficult and that identification relies on theoretical relative age derived from regulations, with caution about cross-country comparability and selection effects.

title: A tool to capture learning experiences during COVID-19 (EN)
outcome_summary: The OECD report introduces the PISA Global Crises Module as a tool to capture students’ learning experiences, school closure context, and related well-being during COVID-19 disruptions. It specifies that the module contains 62 student questionnaire items (grouped into 11 constructs) and 68 school questionnaire items (grouped into 14 constructs), developed through expert input, PISA National Centres, and small-scale cognitive interviews in three countries. The module is designed to help policymakers and researchers examine differential effects on learning and well-being and to document the degree and nature of educational interruption across education systems. The document does not report any student-level predictive modeling, scaling, plausible values, or performance metrics; instead, it provides the instruments and construct descriptions to support adaptation and implementation. Consequently, no benchmarks or effect sizes are reported in the provided text.

title: Parental Involvement in Selected PISA Countries and Economies
authors: Francesca Borgonovi, Guillermo Montt
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper analyzes cross-national patterns of parental involvement using PISA 2009, where 14 countries/economies administered an optional parental questionnaire. The study links parental involvement indicators to three student outcomes at age 15: reading performance (cognitive), enjoyment of reading (non-cognitive motivation), and awareness of effective summarising strategies (a metacognitive/learning-strategy indicator). It reports that some forms of involvement—especially reading to children when they are young, discussing complex social/political issues, and parents reading for enjoyment—show stronger positive associations with both cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes than more school-based or homework-help oriented involvement. The paper also documents substantial cross-country variation and within-country inequalities in parental involvement by socioeconomic status and immigrant background, and it frames how parental involvement may mediate performance gaps through composition and differential strength. Causality is not claimed because PISA is observational and the excerpt does not document PV estimation and missing-data handling details.

title: OECD Economic Surveys: Iceland 2025
authors: Hansjörg Blöchliger, Yosuke Jin, Natia Mosiashvili
outcome_summary: OECD Economic Surveys: Iceland 2025 is a policy-oriented macroeconomic assessment rather than an empirical large-scale assessment study. The excerpted text does not describe any student assessment instruments, sampling of schools/students, or statistical scaling of achievement scores. Consequently, there are no Plausible Values (PVs), no model-based predictive targets, and no reported ML performance metrics. The document specifies a data cut-off date (13 June 2025) and provides an executive summary and thematic chapters on growth, monetary policy, the financial system, and fiscal policy. Because the survey is not an ILSA-style microdata analysis, there is no methodological basis here for extracting weighting, missing-data, or ML evaluation details for education outcomes.

title: Creating Effective Teaching and Learning Environments: First Results from TALIS – ISBN 978-92-64-05605-3
outcome_summary: This OECD TALIS report (first round implemented in 2007–08) uses complex survey regression analyses to describe associations between teacher/school context variables and two key learning-environment indicators: the classroom disciplinary climate index and teachers’ self-efficacy index. The report does not use machine learning; instead it applies multiple regression and multilevel regression (random intercept models) where appropriate, run separately for each country, with BRR variance estimation and Fay’s adjustment. For missing data, earlier chapters use listwise deletion, while Chapter 7 imputes missing values using multiple imputation (five imputed datasets) under a missing-at-random assumption, then combines estimates across imputations. The analysis is weighted using teacher final weights (TCHWGT) and replicate weights (TRWGT1–TRWGT100) to reflect TALIS’s clustered sampling design. Because the study is cross-sectional and based on self-reports, the reported “effects” are statistical net associations rather than causal impacts.

title: Invariance analyses in large-scale studies
authors: Fons J.R. van de Vijver, Eldad Davidov, Bart Meuleman, Kimberley Lek, Rens van de Schoot, Jean-Paul Fox, Michael Eid, Francesco Avvisati, Noémie Le Donné, Marco Paccagnella
outcome_summary: This OECD report addresses measurement invariance in large-scale cross-cultural surveys (PISA, TALIS, PIAAC) and explains why conventional exact invariance tests (e.g., MGCFA scalar invariance, IRT DIF tests) can be overly strict or unstable when many groups are compared. It presents and applies proof-of-concept procedures using both real and simulated data: multigroup CFA with alignment optimisation, Bayesian approximate measurement invariance (BSEM/approximate MI with alignment), Bayesian marginal measurement invariance testing in a one-parameter IRT framework (using fractional Bayes factors), and multigroup/multilevel latent class analysis for categorical latent variables. Across demonstrations, the report shows that scalar invariance often fails under strict criteria, while alignment and Bayesian approximate/marginal approaches can still support meaningful cross-group comparisons by quantifying evidence for (approximate) invariance and by avoiding anchor-item dependence. For example, in the ESS-based ALLOW illustration, scalar invariance fit is poor under traditional MGCFA, whereas Bayesian approximate MI with alignment yields highly correlated factor-mean rankings (correlations >0.98) with sensitivity to prior variance for some country pairs. The report emphasizes that these methods are promising but not yet definitive standards, and it highlights limitations such as sensitivity to priors, computational complexity, and challenges incorporating complex survey weights.
all_target_variables: measurement invariance in large-scale cross-cultural surveys (PISA, TALIS, PIAAC

title: The analytical value of non-probability samples in the context of TALIS (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper reviews how non-probability samples have been used in comparative, cross-national survey research and what value they may have for policy, with a specific focus on potential roles within TALIS. It argues that non-probability sampling typically leads to biased estimates when selection into the sample is systematically related to the variable of interest, and that there is no general statistical theory that guarantees valid inference or design-based uncertainty quantification. The paper synthesizes mitigation strategies used in practice—especially the collection of theoretically grounded confounders, some control over sampling/eligibility, and post hoc adjustments such as post-stratification, raking, GREG weighting, and propensity scoring—while stressing that these methods cannot fully correct for non-coverage and uncontrolled selection. It concludes that non-probability approaches could be fit for purpose in TALIS mainly for exploratory relationship-focused modules, longitudinal complementary panels among volunteer participants, and instrument development/field-trial development phases, but not as a replacement for TALIS’s probabilistic core survey.
all_target_variables: non-probability samples have been used in comparative, cross-national survey res

title: LEARNING IN RURAL SCHOOLS: INSIGHTS FROM PISA, TALIS AND THE LITERATURE
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper synthesizes prior research and then uses OECD microdata from PISA 2015 (15-year-olds; science performance and educational expectations) and TALIS 2013 (lower secondary; teacher characteristics and professional development needs) to compare rural and urban learning contexts across OECD member and partner countries. Rural-urban differences in science performance are reported to largely disappear after accounting for students’ and schools’ socio-economic status, with an average rural-urban gap of 31 score points before adjustment (about one year of schooling). However, educational expectations show a persistent rural disadvantage: rural students are less likely to expect completing university even after accounting for socio-economic status (odds ratio decreases substantially but remains above/below parity depending on country). The paper also documents that rural schools often have smaller student-teacher ratios and more supportive teaching practices, while also facing non-universal challenges such as infrastructure and teacher quality concerns. Methodologically, the paper does not provide PV or missing-data handling details in the excerpt, and it relies on OECD reporting thresholds for rural/urban comparisons.

title: Improving accessibility in PISA: Guidelines for revising and designing PISA items
outcome_summary: This OECD report develops and operationalizes accessibility guidelines for revising and designing PISA items, drawing on Universal Design, Cognitive Load Theory, Accessibility Theory (TAMI/ARM), and WCAG principles. The guidelines were applied to 33 PISA 2025 Science items in an alternative PISA Science form that includes targeted digital accessibility tools (e.g., read-aloud, contrast and cursor/font options, zoom and spacing options) and revised item text/visual/layout features. The revised form was piloted in 2024 in seven countries (N=260) using an observational user-experience design: students completed the test and then provided 4-point Likert-scale feedback and focus-group input on clarity, navigation, and perceived accessibility. Results indicate that most students found images/graphs and texts clear (83% and 77%, respectively) and navigation easy (88%), with some remaining issues (e.g., read-aloud compatibility for visual text and lack of alternative text). The report emphasizes that this is not a causal or generalizable effectiveness evaluation and does not compare revised items to original PISA items in a controlled design.

title: OECD document d99e8c0a-en
outcome_summary: This OECD paper estimates learning gains over one school year for 15-year-olds in Austria and Scotland by combining multiple PISA cycles (2012, 2015, 2018) and exploiting changes in PISA testing dates across cycles. The dependent variables are PISA reading, mathematics, and science scores derived from item-response theory and analyzed using multiply imputed plausible values (PISA PVs). The core identification uses a difference-in-differences design comparing students grouped by month of birth across early- vs late-testing years, with year fixed effects and month-of-birth dummies; covariates include gender, immigrant background, and socio-economic status quartiles. The estimated grade-and-age effects are about one-fourth of a standard deviation (≈25 score points) in each subject, with robustness checks including parallel-trends placebos and leave-one-out by month of birth. Limitations include reliance on the common-trend assumption and the fact that PISA was not designed specifically to measure grade-and-age effects, leading to relatively large statistical uncertainty for subgroup comparisons.

title: How much do 15-year-olds learn over one year of schooling? An international comparison based on PISA
outcome_summary: This OECD study quantifies typical learning gains over one school year for 15-year-olds using PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 microdata in 18 countries/economies. Because PISA is cross-sectional, the authors exploit school-entry regulations to create an instrumental-variables design that uses expected grade (from month of birth) to identify the grade-and-age effect, under local linearity assumptions for age effects. The analysis uses multiply imputed test scores (plausible values) and reports standard errors that account for clustering and the complex sampling design via PISA replicate weights. Across countries, the average grade-and-age learning gain is about 19 score points (≈0.2 SD) in mathematics, reading, and science, with wide country-level confidence intervals and stronger gains in higher-income contexts. The estimates are local average treatment effects for “compliers” near cut-offs, so they provide benchmarks rather than fully generalizable causal effects for all students.

title: Teenage career development in Norway (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PISA 2022 to provide a snapshot of teenage career development in Norway, focusing on students’ occupational expectations, career certainty/uncertainty, educational and occupational ambitions, alignment/misalignment of plans, instrumental motivation, and participation in career development activities. The Norway sample comprises 6,611 students in 265 schools, with principals also completing questionnaires. For career-development activities, questionnaire design means only a random subset of students answered specific items (4–5 of 11), so participation estimates for each activity rely on that item-specific subsample. The report compares Norway to OECD averages and disaggregates results by gender, ESCS quartiles (advantaged vs disadvantaged), performance level (high vs low based on PISA proficiency thresholds), migrant status, and urban/rural location. It emphasizes that career uncertainty is very high in Norway (45% in 2022) and that while guidance participation is often higher than the OECD average, fewer than half report key workplace-experience activities by age 15.

title: Attendance in early childhood education and care programmes and academic proficiencies at age 15 (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PISA 2015 to examine whether students’ attendance in early childhood education and care (ECEC) programmes is associated with academic proficiencies at age 15. The abstract indicates that, on average across OECD countries, students who attended ECEC tend to score higher in later academic proficiencies, but the ECEC–proficiency differences become almost nil once students’ socio-economic status (SES) is considered. The report also finds that entering ECEC earlier than the typical starting time is associated with lower proficiencies at age 15, suggesting that earlier entry is not universally beneficial. Finally, the abstract reports that ECEC programme quality indicators are positively associated with later academic skills, and that these relationships vary considerably across PISA countries, emphasizing the role of country-specific policy context and programme quality rather than attendance alone.

title: Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic
authors: Alec I. Kennedy, Ana María Mejía-Rodríguez, Rolf Strietholt
outcome_summary: The study links ICCS 2016 and ICCS 2022 Grade 8 civic outcomes with national COVID-19 containment measures from OxCGRT (school-closure duration and an average stringency index) for 14 countries plus Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia. Civic knowledge is estimated using ICCS plausible values and combined across five PVs using Rubin’s rules, while trust and expected participation outcomes are ICCS linked scales. The authors estimate separate weighted regression models (sampling weights: senate weights; variance: jackknife repeated replication) and report standardized interaction coefficients rather than ML prediction metrics. Across outcomes, greater lockdown stringency and longer school closures are associated with larger declines in civic knowledge and trust in civic institutions, while they are associated with increases (or smaller declines) in expected protest participation (legal and illegal) and expected active political participation. Expected electoral participation shows inconsistent results, with no significant association for stringency but a negative association for closure duration. Limitations include a small number of countries, observational identification (no causal design), and measurement error from linking scales across cycles.

all_target_variables: Civic knowledge (Plausible Values) | Trust in civic institutions (INTRUST scale) | Expected participation in legal protest activities (LEGACT) | Expected participation in illegal protest activities (ILLACT) | Expected electoral participation (ELECPART) | Expected active political participation (POLPART)

title: Teenage career development in Malta (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2022 to describe teenage career development in Malta and to benchmark Malta against OECD averages. The analysis focuses on students’ occupational expectations and career certainty (including uncertainty when students do not provide a classifiable job expectation), educational ambitions (expectations to complete tertiary education), alignment between occupational and educational plans, and engagement in career development activities (e.g., job shadowing/work-site visits, job fairs, and speaking with a career advisor). Malta’s students show relatively high career concentration in a small set of occupations and strong expectations for tertiary education, but occupational expectations are poorly aligned with the actual labour market distribution in Malta. Engagement with career advisors is comparatively high, while direct employer engagement (internships, job shadowing/work-site visits, and job fairs) is lower than typical OECD patterns. The paper also reports that sceptical attitudes about how well schooling prepares students for adult life are more prevalent in Malta than in the OECD average, especially among disadvantaged and lower-performing students.
all_target_variables: teenage career development in Malta and to benchmark Malta against OECD averages

title: Academic resilience (EN)
outcome_summary: This OECD working paper defines academic resilience in PISA as the ability of 15-year-old students from socio-economically disadvantaged backgrounds to reach at least proficiency Level 3 in reading, mathematics, and science, using PISA proficiency levels as absolute benchmarks. Disadvantage is operationalised as being in the bottom quarter of ESCS within each country/economy, and the paper tracks trends in the share of resilient students across PISA 2006–2015. For determinants, it estimates multilevel logistic models with a random intercept at the school level, pooling PISA 2012 and PISA 2015 to obtain sufficient numbers of disadvantaged students and schools per country. The models use student and derived school weights, exclude schools without disadvantaged students, and handle missing data through imputation with missing-value dummy indicators. The paper reports cross-country patterns showing that resilience varies substantially across schools and is strongly associated with classroom disciplinary climate, while resource indicators show weaker or inconsistent relationships.
all_target_variables: mathematics, and science, using PISA proficiency

title: Discourse of contemporary chinese ideological and political education: Development directions and teaching methods
authors: Sulan Ji, Hao Li
outcome_summary: This paper evaluates teaching methods and perceived outcomes of ideological and political education among Chinese university students using a questionnaire adapted from the IEA ICCS model and supplemented by interviews. The study’s quantitative results are based on Likert-scale indices and descriptive distributions (e.g., method usage frequencies) plus inferential statistics (single-sample t-tests and a simple regression), not on machine-learning prediction of an achievement outcome. The reported metrics are mainly mean differences from a test value (e.g., trust and civic intention means significantly above 3 with p<.01 or p<.001) and a regression result showing Political Theory explaining 12.6% of variance in socio-political activity (R²=0.126; Beta=0.355; p<.001). The best-performing “model” in an ML sense is not applicable because no ML algorithms are trained or compared. Limitations include a single-university convenience sample, no survey-weight documentation, and no PV-based achievement measurement.

title: A decade of educational research with the German National Educational Panel Study: A systematic review
authors: T. Gnambs, M. Gnambs, T. Gnambs et al.
outcome_summary: This systematic review synthesizes how NEPS data have been used in empirical educational research between 2013 and 2024, rather than estimating effects on student outcomes. The authors built a comprehensive bibliometric database (initially 1492 records, reduced to 625 eligible peer-reviewed articles) using NEPS bibliography plus OpenAlex and Scopus searches, applying strict inclusion/exclusion criteria (empirical NEPS use, peer-reviewed journal, full text available, and publication up to 2024). The review’s main quantitative outputs are publication counts, journal prestige/impact indicators (JIF quartiles and FWCI), and topic-modeling results using BERTopic with transformer-based embeddings (SPECTER 2), dimensionality reduction (UMAP), clustering (HDBSCAN), and TF-IDF-based topic terms. Because no student-level predictive modeling is performed, there are no ML performance metrics, PV handling, or missing-data strategies for achievement scores. Limitations include reliance on text-based topic modeling (inherently exploratory) and exclusion of gray literature and non-peer-reviewed outputs, which may underrepresent certain research themes.

title: A critical review and meta-analysis of studies investigating the effects of the professional development teachers typically receive
authors: Jannika Lindvall, Nils Kirsten, Andreas Ryve, Jan-Eric Gustafsson
outcome_summary: This article is a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the effects of teachers’ typical professional development (PD) participation using nationally or state-representative datasets. It synthesizes 68 included studies and conducts meta-analyses for two outcome families: student achievement and teachers’ instructional practices/teaching practices, using Pearson’s r as the effect-size metric (converted to Fisher’s z and back to correlations) and robust variance estimation with a random-effects model. Across correlational studies, PD participation shows a significant positive association with instructional practices (r = .20, p < .001; 95% CI [.11, .29]) but a non-significant association with student achievement (r = .06, p = .11; 95% CI [-.02, .13]). Quasi-experimental studies (N = 7 for student achievement) are summarized narratively due to limited count, showing mixed effects closer to zero. The authors caution that most primary studies are correlational (87%), with frequent shortcomings in reporting/handling sampling weights, clustering/nesting, and plausible values, so the meta-analytic results should not be interpreted as causal PD effects.

title: Immigration status and adolescents’ voting intention in European countries: The importance of immigrant integration policy context
authors: H. Kim, M.H. Seltzer
outcome_summary: The study analyzes ICCS 2009 Grade-8 Voting Intention (an IRT-based scale standardized to mean 50, SD 10) for 17 European countries, comparing voting-intention contrasts between first-generation and native adolescents and between second-generation and native adolescents. Using a two-step multilevel meta-analytic approach (within-country two-level models with students nested in schools, then between-country HLM models), the authors estimate country-specific immigrant/native contrasts and relate their cross-national variation to MIPEX 2010 integration-policy dimensions. For first-generation contrasts, the education-policy dimension is the key predictor (education coefficient 0.068, SE 0.025, p < .05), explaining 51.3% of between-country variance in contrasts. For second-generation contrasts, citizenship-acquisition policy is the key predictor (0.034, SE 0.015, p < .05), with large reported variance explained (50.4%). The paper does not use machine learning algorithms and does not report a missing-data imputation/deletion protocol for individual covariates, so results should be interpreted as correlational rather than causal.
all_datasets_used: ICCS 2009 Grade 8 Voting Intention (Voting Intention scale, IRT; standardized mean 50 SD 10)
all_target_variables: First-generation/native voting intention contrast | Second-generation/native voting intention contrast

title: Adolescents' expected civic participation: The role of civic knowledge and efficacy beliefs
authors: S. Manganelli, et al.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes ICCS 2009 data for Italian eighth-grade students (N=3352) to explain adolescents’ expected civic participation using a measurement-and-structural modeling framework. Expected civic participation is operationalized as a latent construct indicated by four questionnaire indices: expected electoral participation, expected political activities, expected informal political participation, and expected legal protest. Civic knowledge is measured with a 79-item ICCS test spanning civic society/systems, principles, participation, identities, and knowing/reasoning/analysis; five plausible-value estimates are generated and used as indicators in the model. The authors report good measurement-model fit (CFA: χ²(2)=21.954; CFI=.991; RMSEA=.055; SRMR=.013) and acceptable structural-model fit (SEM: χ²(200)=1921.092; CFI=.954; RMSEA=.051; SRMR=.058), with the model explaining 61% of variance in expected civic participation. Missing data are handled via expectation-maximization, and sampling weights are applied due to the ICCS stratified two-stage design. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (no causal claims) and the absence of ML predictive modeling; results are based on SEM path estimates rather than algorithmic prediction metrics.

title: Unravelling the link between non-voting and political knowledge: An exploratory study
authors: Julia Schwanholz, Julia Rakers
outcome_summary: This paper is an exploratory qualitative study addressing how political knowledge relates to non-voting, using focus group discussions rather than quantitative ILSA microdata analysis. The empirical material comes from two German cases: non-voters in Duisburg’s 2020 municipal elections (five focus groups, 27 participants) and non-voters in North Rhine-Westphalia’s 2022 state elections (eight focus groups, 52 participants). The authors apply and extend Amnå & Ekman’s typology of passive citizens (disillusioned, unengaged, standby) to interpret “paths to participation” and identify where political knowledge deficits occur (e.g., understanding political system functioning vs. campaign/party communication). No ML models, PV-based achievement outcomes, or survey-weighted statistical estimates are reported; instead, coded qualitative themes are used to derive implications for civic education design. Limitations include restricted age coverage (excluding first-time voters and participants older than 70) and the inherent non-representativeness of focus group sampling.

title: Students’ multicultural attitudes and the role of background characteristics
authors: D. Michael, L. Kyriakides
outcome_summary: This study used a Cyprus secondary-school sample (n=450; 7th–8th grade) to validate and apply the adapted Greek Munroe Multicultural Attitude Scale Questionnaire (MASQUE) and to examine how students’ background characteristics relate to multicultural attitudes and social desirability bias. The analysis relied on CFA and SEM (not ML prediction), testing MASQUE’s three-factor structure (Know, Care, Act) and measurement invariance across gender, immigrant background, and home language, and then estimating structural paths. Gender was the only background characteristic with significant effects: females reported higher multicultural attitudes across all three MASQUE factors (e.g., Know β=.44, R2=.19) and slightly higher social desirability (β=.27, R2=.07). Immigrant background and home language showed no significant effects. Social desirability correlated positively with Care and Act (β=.34 and .43) but not with Know, suggesting response bias is more relevant for affective/behavioral components. Limitations include cross-sectional design, non-national representativeness, and no reported missing-data handling strategy.

all_target_variables: Multicultural attitudes (MASQUE factors: Know, Care, Act) | Social desirability bias (MCSDS–Form C) | Association between social desirability and multicultural attitudes (MASQUE factors)

title: Unpacking equity. Educational equity in secondary analyses of international large-scale assessments: A systematic review
authors: Lies Appels, Sven De Maeyer, Jerich Faddar, Peter Van Petegem
outcome_summary: This paper is an interpretive systematic review, not an empirical ML study. It synthesizes 25 peer-reviewed articles (selected via PRISMA-guided identification, screening, and eligibility steps) that conduct secondary analyses using ILSA data, focusing on how educational equity is conceptualized and operationalized. The review identifies five major equity approaches—ability equity, social equity, ethnic equity, gender equity, and equity of treatment—and describes how each approach links equity concerns to specific ILSA materials (achievement tests and student/parent/school questionnaires). It reports that most equity research relies on PISA (76%), with smaller shares using TIMSS (20%) and PIRLS (4%), and that equity is often operationalized through relationships between student background and achievement. Because no predictive models are trained and no performance metrics are computed, there are no ML accuracy/AUC/R² results to benchmark; the key contribution is a framework for interpreting equity measurement choices and their implications for policy reading.

title: The civic side of American charter schools
authors: Chrystal S. Johnson, Chenchen Lu, Godwin Gyimah
outcome_summary: This study analyzes NAEP Civics grade 8 restricted-use data for the United States across the 2006, 2010, 2014, and 2018 testing cycles, modeling student civics achievement using NAEP plausible values (5 PVs in 2006/2010; 20 PVs in 2014/2018). The authors use two-level cross-sectional multilevel modeling with students nested in schools, applying NAEP student and school sampling weights (origwt and spsrswt) and jackknife replicate weights for variance estimation. Across cycles, private schools show consistently higher civics scores than traditional public schools (e.g., 2006: γ02 = 18.57, p < .01; 2018: γ02 = 17.38, p < .01), while charter schools are generally not significantly different from traditional public schools. Teacher civics instructional time and teacher credential level are mostly not significantly associated with civics scores in the overall model. The study is explicitly correlational and cautions that differences across school types may reflect unmeasured prior academic preparation and other contextual factors.
all_datasets_used: NAEP Civics 2006 Grade 8 (US) | NAEP Civics 2010 Grade 8 (US) | NAEP Civics 2014 Grade 8 (US) | NAEP Civics 2018 Grade 8 (US)

title: Pre-service teachers' perceptions of teacher morality in China
authors: W. Ye, W.-W. Law
outcome_summary: This study surveyed 203 pre-service teachers in the ECNU Shanghai M.Ed. programme (2017–2018) using a questionnaire that included teacher-morality items and political-civic competence items adapted from ICCS (2009–2011) and related Chinese citizenship education work. The quantitative analysis used descriptive statistics and multiple regression (SPSS), not machine learning, to examine how political-civic competence perceptions relate to teacher morality perceptions and vice versa. For teacher morality perception, political identity (b=0.377), scientific spirit (b=0.249), and rule-of-law awareness (b=0.289) were significant predictors, with R²=0.586 (F(9,184)=28.905, p<.001). For political-civic competence perception, teacher morality perception was a strong predictor (b=0.695, p<.001) with R²=0.506 (F(6,187)=31.894, p<.001). The study is limited by its single-institution sample and by the absence of any reported missing-data strategy or PV/achievement scaling procedures.
all_datasets_used: ICCS-based questionnaire items (adapted) — China (ECNU M.Ed. pre-service teachers, 2017-2018 survey)
all_target_variables: Teacher morality perception (Likert scale) | Political-civic competence perception (Likert scale)

title: Opportunities or risks for civic education in electoral democracies? Evidence from Nigeria
authors: L. Demarest, L. Kuppens
outcome_summary: The study uses an original large-scale pencil-and-paper survey of 3,118 final-year secondary school students (average age 16) in Lagos State, Nigeria, collected in September–October 2019. It examines associations between socioeconomic status (SES), political knowledge, political engagement, democratic norms, and institutional trust, and five intended political participation outcomes measured on four-point scales: voting, party membership, campaigning, contacting politicians, and peaceful protest. The authors estimate multilevel linear regression models (students nested in schools) and then use latent class analysis (LCA) to identify three participation profiles, followed by fractional multinomial logistic regression to relate determinants to class membership. Reported effect sizes are generally very small (partial eta squared < 0.01 in the appendix), and the key pattern is that knowledge and democratic norms are positively related to voting/contacting/protesting but negatively related to party membership and campaigning, while institutional trust is positively related to all participation intentions. The paper does not report any machine-learning model performance metrics, and it does not document a missing-data handling strategy, limiting reproducibility and inference about robustness.

title: Adolescents’ transitions between different views on democracy: Examining individual-level moderators
authors: J. Šerek, L. Lomičová
outcome_summary: The study analyzes two waves of longitudinal data from 768 Czech high school students (T1: May/June 2014; T2: Nov/Dec 2015) to model adolescents’ democratic views as patterns across eight agreement items covering general democracy support, civil liberties, and majoritarianism/minority rights. Using latent class analysis and latent transition analysis in Mplus (with classroom clustering handled via the “complex” option), the authors selected a three-class typology at both time points: majority-oriented, conventional, and liberal. The liberal class was less stable (stay probability 0.61) than the other two (0.89 and 0.86), with transitions from liberal to majority-oriented (0.26) and to conventional (0.13). Predictors of transitions showed that males and adolescents with lower institutional trust were more likely to shift from liberal to majority-oriented, while lower civic participation predicted shifts from liberal to conventional. Missing item-level data were handled with full-information maximum likelihood (FIML), and the design is correlational (no causal identification).
all_datasets_used: Longitudinal democracy views (Czech high school students), T1 (2014)–T2 (2015), 9th/10th grade
all_target_variables: Latent transition from liberal to conventional view

title: Civic education, school climate, and gender in Latin American countries: A path analysis using ICCS 2016 data
authors: Kalie A. Chamberlain, Ryan Rarick, Jenette De Oliveira, Lorissa K. Nelson, Ryan T. Knowles
outcome_summary: This study uses ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data from five Latin American countries (Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Peru) to examine how school civic-education factors relate to three citizenship types and whether these relationships differ by gender. The authors first compute gender mean differences across seven civic education scales (standardized to mean 50, SD 10) and then select the five measures with the largest gender gaps for multilevel path analysis. The multilevel path models are estimated in Mplus7 using replicate weights and missing-data estimation to preserve cases, with students at level 1 and classrooms at level 2. Results are reported as standardized path coefficients and model fit indices (CFI, RMSEA, standardized RMR); for example, civic learning shows positive associations with all citizenship types, while civic knowledge has mixed/negative associations for conventional citizenship. The study is correlational (path analysis) and does not use ML algorithms, so findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
