all_target_variables: Personally responsible citizenship | Conventional citizenship | Social movement citizenship

title: Factors affecting youth citizenship in accordance with socioeconomic background
authors: H.J. Kim, J.Y. Chung
outcome_summary: This study analyzes youth citizenship participation using the Gyeonggi Education Panel Study (GEPS), focusing on eighth graders surveyed in 2016 (Korea). From an initial random sample of 6,314 students, the analytic sample comprised 4,785 students matched with parents after excluding cases with missing values. The authors first used latent class analysis to classify students into three socioeconomic background groups based on household income and parents’ educational attainment, then compared cognitive and affective-behavioral participation across groups and estimated within-class regression models. Cognitive participation differed significantly by class (Lower M=4.18, Middle M=4.27, Upper M=4.28; χ²=23.641, p<.000), and affective-behavioral participation also differed (Lower M=3.55, Middle M=3.66, Upper M=3.71; χ²=29.053, p<.000). The study reports adjusted R² values around 0.24–0.29 for cognitive and ~0.25 for affective-behavioral models, but it does not report survey weights or any plausible-values framework, limiting generalizability beyond the GEPS sample.
all_datasets_used: GEPS 2016 (Korea) Grade 8 citizenship participation (cognitive participation) | GEPS 2016 (Korea) Grade 8 citizenship participation (affective-behavioral participation)
all_target_variables: Cognitive citizen participation | Affective-behavioral citizen participation

title: Classroom emotions in civic education: A multilevel approach to antecedents and effects
authors: Elisabeth Graf, Lisa Stempfer, Krista R. Muis, Thomas Goetz
outcome_summary: This study used Austrian vocational-school survey data collected in 2021–2022 (N=1162 students; 19 schools; 89 classes) to test how an open classroom climate (measured with an ICCS 2016-based scale adaptation) relates to discrete classroom emotions (enjoyment, shame, anxiety, boredom) and how these emotions relate to political knowledge and intended political participation. The authors estimated multilevel SEM with doubly-latent mediation and random slopes, using Bayesian estimation and reporting explained variance (R²) and indirect effects with credible intervals. They found that open classroom climate predicted enjoyment at both within- and between-class levels and predicted anxiety and boredom at the within level (and boredom also at the between level). Emotions were significant predictors of political knowledge (within R²w: enjoyment=0.147; shame=0.197; anxiety=0.211; boredom=0.159), but mediation via emotions was not supported for knowledge. For participation, enjoyment showed a significant positive indirect effect (within β=0.137, CI [0.069, 0.228]), while anxiety showed a significant negative indirect effect (within β=-0.068, CI [-0.140, -0.016]) consistent with competitive mediation. Limitations include cross-sectional observational data and weaker between-level model fit for some outcomes.
all_datasets_used: ICCS-based open classroom climate (ICCS 2016 scale adaptation) in Austrian vocational schools (2021-2022), multilevel within-class and between-class
all_target_variables: Political knowledge | Intention to political participation

title: Are educated individuals more likely to be civically engaged? Evidence from rural Bangladesh
authors: Rubaiya Murshed, Ricardo Sabates
outcome_summary: This study uses the Bangladesh Integrated Household Survey (BIHS) pooled across three rural Bangladesh rounds (2011–12, 2015, 2018–19), restricting civic engagement questions to one male and one female adult per household, yielding a final analytic sample of 24,440 adults in Bangladesh. The dependent variables are directly observed civic engagement indicators (binary yes/no items and additive integrated count scores), so plausible values are not applicable. The analysis estimates logit models for binary outcomes and Poisson/negative binomial count models for integrated scores, and it also runs propensity score matching (nearest-neighbor with caliper 0.001) for consecutive education transitions. Across regression results (Table 4), education shows strong positive associations with civic speaking confidence and integrated community leadership/contributions, with reported likelihood increases up to ~31.2 percentage points and integrated score differences up to ~49.3 percentage points. The paper explicitly states the analysis is correlational (no causality), and it does not report a missing-data handling strategy, limiting transparency about how incomplete responses were treated.

title: Are life goals invariant across different sociocultural and economic conditions? A study on a representative sample of adolescents
authors: Sara Manganelli, Elisa Cavicchiolo, Fabio Lucidi, Fabio Alivernini
outcome_summary: This study analyzes ICCS 2016 questionnaire data for 3460 Italian eighth-grade students to test whether the Goal Content Theory bifactor structure of life aspirations is invariant across socioeconomic status, immigrant background, and gender. Using Mplus 8.7 with the “Type = complex” approach, the authors fit a bifactor CFA model (intrinsic/extrinsic general orientations plus six specific aspirations) and then conduct multi-group measurement invariance tests (configural, metric, scalar) with strict cutoffs (e.g., ΔCFI < 0.010; ΔRMSEA < 0.015; ΔSRMR < 0.030). Latent mean difference tests show that low-SES adolescents report lower intrinsic general orientation and higher wealth and appearance aspirations, while immigrant adolescents score higher on extrinsic general orientation; gender differences include higher intrinsic orientation for females and higher extrinsic orientation for males, plus gender-specific patterns for appearance and wealth. The paper reports standardized mean differences (e.g., extrinsic general orientation: natives vs immigrants d=0.153; females vs males d=0.530***; intrinsic general orientation: females vs males d=-0.460*), but it is cross-sectional, so causal claims are not supported.

title: Pedagogical practices and civic knowledge and engagement in Latin America: Multilevel analysis using ICCS data
authors: Ricardo L. Gómez, Ana María Suárez
outcome_summary: This Heliyon study analyzes ICCS 2016 civic knowledge and engagement (SCKE) for 13–14-year-olds in five Latin American and Caribbean countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru), using hierarchical linear modeling in HLM8. The cognitive outcome is scaled on a standardized metric (mean 500, SD 100) and modeled using five plausible values included in the analysis. The authors report that 23% of the variation in SCKE resides at the group (school) level (ICC = 0.23; χ2 (119) = 309.24, p < 0.001). Across countries, openness in classroom discussions and civic learning at school are positively associated with SCKE in multiple settings, while civic participation in the wider community is consistently negatively associated. The paper does not report ML model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) because it uses multilevel regression rather than predictive ML, and it does not document missing-data handling, limiting transparency about selection bias.
all_datasets_used: ICCS 2016 (cycle 2016), civic knowledge and engagement (SCKE), students aged 13–14 (grade 8/9 depending on country)
all_target_variables: Civic Knowledge and Engagement (SCKE; ICCS cognitive test, 5 plausible values)

title: How friendly are OECD countries towards children? Conceptualization and measuring issues
authors: N. Tarshish
outcome_summary: This paper conceptualizes and operationalizes a country-level Child Friendliness Index for OECD members using secondary cross-national indicators. It combines a nurturance-and-care sub-index (17 indicators; Z-scores averaged into child outcomes and budgetary commitment) and a self-determination sub-index (6 indicators; Z-scores averaged into personal-domain participation and public-domain participation), then averages the two Z-score sub-indices into the overall Child Friendliness Index. The study uses ICCS 2009 for civic knowledge and voting intentions and uses PISA/PIRLS/TIMSS-derived school achievement indicators as part of the nurturance-and-care component, but it does not run student-level ML models or PV-based achievement prediction. Results are presented as country rankings and correlation coefficients across indices and macro indicators (e.g., GDP per capita and Gini), with Nordic countries (e.g., Finland, Sweden, Denmark) scoring highest overall. Limitations include reliance on secondary data with uneven coverage, subjective indicator selection, and missingness handled via country exclusion thresholds rather than formal imputation.

title: Measuring education: Do we need a plethora of assessment studies or just a single score?
authors: O. Gladushyna, R. Strietholt
outcome_summary: This paper is not an empirical ML prediction study; it examines how different ILSAs relate by computing correlations between country mean scores across domains (mathematics, science, reading, civic education, computer and information literacy, and other PISA/TIMSS add-ons) and by visualizing similarity using multidimensional scaling. It reports a very high correlation between TIMSS 2019 mathematics and science country means (r = 0.94) for both Grade 4 and Grade 8, suggesting limited added value of a separate science score when a math score is already available. In contrast, correlations between TIMSS 2019 mathematics and ICCS 2016 (Grade 8) are described as driven by outliers, with some countries showing large discrepancies (e.g., Latvia vs Norway). The paper also finds that the hypothesized pattern of higher correlations for assessments closer in time is not supported for PISA reading (2000–2018), and it highlights PISA linking errors up to 2012 as a limitation. Overall, it argues that non-core domains (ICCS/ICILS) can change country interpretations beyond core domains (math/science/reading), informing policy decisions about which assessments to prioritize.
all_target_variables: science score | how different ILSAs relate by computing correlations between country mean scores

title: Is classroom diversity related to citizenship competences of ethnic minority and majority students?
authors: A. Munniksma, et al.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes ICCS 2016 Dutch data for grade 8 students (second year of Dutch secondary school), using a nested students-within-classrooms design across 119 schools and 2565 students after excluding four mixed-track classrooms and students with missing values. Citizenship knowledge is PV-based: the authors compute five plausible values and report model estimates as the average across the five PV models, while the four attitude outcomes are Likert/scale measures standardized in ICCS 2009. The authors estimate weighted multilevel models with student-level and school-level weights to account for non-participation bias and clustering. Results show no association between classroom ethnic diversity and citizenship knowledge, but diversity is negatively related to trust in civic institutions and positively related to support for gender equality and equal rights for all ethnic groups; diversity is unrelated to expected electoral participation. The study is cross-sectional, so causality cannot be inferred, and the analysis is not an ML predictive pipeline (no ML algorithms or ML validation metrics are reported).
all_datasets_used: ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Citizenship knowledge (knowledge test; PV-based scale) | ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Trust in civic institutions (attitude scale) | ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Attitudes towards gender equality (attitude scale) | ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Attitudes towards ethnic equality (attitude scale) | ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Expected electoral participation (attitude scale)
all_target_variables: Citizenship knowledge | Trust in civic institutions | Support for gender equality | Support for equal rights for all ethnic groups | Expected electoral participation

title: Gaining tolerance of immigrants through simulating migratory experiences: Quasi-experimental evidence from secondary school classrooms
authors: Markus Al-Afifi, Thomas Nygren
outcome_summary: This study evaluates a quasi-experimental, classroom-based intervention in Sweden using ICCS 2022-derived attitude scales for secondary/upper-secondary students (ages 14–19). Five teachers implemented a 60-minute browser-based simulation (“Real Lives”) in fall 2024, with pretest immediately before and posttest immediately after; the analytic matched sample comprised 148 students. Outcomes were attitudes towards immigrants (ATI; composite of political and social tolerance) and social tolerance separately, analyzed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and hierarchical regression (Jamovi). ATI increased significantly from pre to post (Mdn 38→39; W=4562, p=0.005, r=0.2995), and social tolerance also increased (Mdn 27→28; W=4432, p=0.002, r=0.3288), whereas political tolerance did not (p=0.927). In the final regression model, perceived learning and playing time (plus a prior-knowledge moderation interaction) were significant predictors of ATI posttest levels (interaction B=0.303, p=0.025). Limitations include no control group/randomization, convenience sampling, and missing-data handling not explicitly reported for inferential models.
all_datasets_used: ICCS 2022-derived attitude measures (Sweden; secondary/upper-secondary students aged 14–19; pretest-posttest)
all_target_variables: Attitudes towards immigrants (ATI) posttest score | Social tolerance towards immigrants posttest score

title: Political trust among European youth: Evaluating multi-dimensionality and cross-national measurement comparability
authors: Linde Stals, Maria Magdalena Isac, others
outcome_summary: This study uses ICCS 2016 to evaluate the dimensionality and cross-national measurement equivalence of political trust among grade-8 adolescents (about 14 years old) in 15 European countries/regions (N=52,788). Political trust is measured with six ordinal Likert items (trust in parliament, political parties, government, police, armed forces, and courts of justice) and analyzed using CFA for one- vs two-dimensional structures, followed by multi-group CFA (MGCFA) tests of configural and scalar invariance across countries. The two-dimensional model (trust in order institutions vs trust in representative institutions) shows acceptable configural invariance (RMSEA=0.043; CFI=0.997; TLI=0.993) but scalar invariance is rejected (RMSEA=0.074; CFI=0.975; ΔRMSEA=0.029; ΔCFI=-0.020). Because exact scalar invariance is not achieved, the authors use Alignment Optimization to obtain approximate measurement equivalence, finding an average non-invariance of 16.11% (below the 25% threshold) and enabling more defensible cross-country comparisons of latent means. Limitations include reliance on model-fit cutoffs and the fact that approximate invariance tolerates some non-invariance, so theoretical validity of comparisons may be compromised.

title: The impact of schooling on trust in political institutions – Differences arising from students' immigration backgrounds
authors: Johanna F. Ziemes, Katrin Hahn-Laudenberg, Hermann J. Abs
outcome_summary: This study uses ICCS 2016 data from North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), Germany, focusing on Year Eight students (N=1451 in 59 secondary schools). Trust in Political Institutions (TIPI) is measured with six Likert items and analyzed as a continuous scale score; civic knowledge is a timed test scored using ICCS-provided Weighted Likelihood Estimations (WLE) from Rasch partial credit models. The authors estimate weighted regression models (via IDB Analyzer) with jackknife sampling variables to account for ICCS complex survey design and stratification by school type and migration-background composition. They report that student-teacher and student-student relationship quality are positive predictors of TIPI, with stronger associations among students with immigration backgrounds, while victimisation is not a significant predictor. Civic knowledge predicts TIPI for non-immigrant students but not for students with immigration backgrounds, and national identity predicts TIPI in both groups with a stronger effect among students with immigration backgrounds. The analysis is cross-sectional, so causal claims cannot be made, and the paper does not document an explicit missing-data handling procedure.
all_target_variables: predicts TIPI for non-immigrant students but not for students with immigration

title: Measuring the civic duty to vote: A proposal
authors: Andre Blais, Carol Galais
outcome_summary: This paper proposes and validates a psychometric battery to measure civic duty to vote using a cross-national internet survey conducted immediately after the 2014 European Parliament election in seven countries (France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Austria, Greece, Portugal). The authors estimate an extended 13-indicator CFA model and then construct a reduced 4-indicator battery (CHOICE, GUILT, OPINION, COUNTRY), using multiple Bayesian imputations for missing responses. Model fit improves in the reduced model (RMSEA = .069; CFI = .98; df = 2; N = 22,072). For predictive validity, the duty latent construct is related to turnout (voted vs abstained) with standardized regression weights varying by country; the model shows good fit in each country (RMSEA never exceeding .08; CFI never below .94). Concurrent validity is tested via OLS regressions where political interest, parents’ socialization, and age explain between 15% and 26% of variation in the duty scale, with listwise deletion for missing data. Limitations include that the study is not an ML prediction paper and does not use survey-weight variables explicitly in the reported estimation pipeline.

title: Student teachers’ responsible use of ICT: Examining two samples in Spain and Norway
authors: G. B. Gudmundsdottir, et al.
outcome_summary: This study used a DICTE project Webquest survey administered to first-year student teachers in Spain (N=681) and Norway (N=563), adapting items from the ICILS 2013 questionnaire for privacy and cyberbullying constructs and from the Norwegian Monitor 2011 for digital content evaluation. The authors analyzed the three latent constructs using structural equation modeling and tested measurement invariance across the two country samples. Model fit was acceptable in both samples (e.g., Spanish: CFI=0.996, RMSEA=0.024, SRMR=0.024; Norwegian: CFI=1.000, RMSEA=0.000, SRMR=0.015). Correlations showed strong privacy–cyberbullying links (r=0.69 Spain; r=0.57 Norway), moderate privacy–evaluation links (r=0.34 Spain; r=0.43 Norway), and weak cyberbullying–evaluation links (r=0.19 Spain; r=0.21 Norway). The paper is not an ML prediction study (no ML algorithms, no PVs), and it reports no missing item responses, limiting concerns about missing-data bias but not about self-report validity or cross-country comparability.
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2013 (questionnaire adaptation) + DICTE Webquest survey (Spain & Norway student teachers, first-year)
all_target_variables: Perceived competence in privacy issues (SEM factor) | Perceived competence in handling cyberbullying (SEM factor) | Ability to evaluate digital content (SEM factor)

title: Social inequality in digital competencies among students in Germany: A trend analysis using ICILS data 2013-2023
authors: Markus Lörz, Birgit Becker, Jan Niemann, Kerstin Drossel, Birgit Eickelmann
outcome_summary: The study analyzes the German ICILS trend data for 2013, 2018, and 2023 (8th-grade students aged 14–16) using the computer-based CIL achievement scale (210–708 points) and plausible values (five PVs per student). The authors restrict to regular schools and apply student-level ICILS weights, multiple imputation for item non-response via MICE (30 imputed datasets), and Rubin’s rules to combine PV-based estimates; they also use cluster-robust standard errors at the school level. Across the period, average digital competencies decline, but socioeconomic disparities increase: the SES gap rises from 43 to 66 competence points (p < 0.001) and from 15.9 to 25.0 competence points per SD of ISEI (p < 0.001). The strongest changing associations are for the cultural home environment (books at home) and school track (upper secondary), while the digital home environment shows stable, small explanatory contribution in KHB decomposition. Limitations include reliance on observational trend comparisons and simplified measurement of cultural and school environments (e.g., books at home only).
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2013-2023 Germany Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL)

title: Are European regions on the right track to achieve the 2030 strategic education and training targets? A comprehensive performance assessment
authors: Maria João Durães, Flávia Barbosa, Giovanna D’Inverno, Ana S. Camanho
outcome_summary: This paper does not perform machine-learning prediction on ILSA microdata; instead, it develops and applies a robust Benefit-of-the-Doubt (BoD) composite indicator framework to benchmark European regions’ progress toward the ET2030 education and training targets. Using Eurostat indicators for 2019, it constructs five performance indicators (Y1 early childhood education, Y2 early leavers, Y3 tertiary attainment, Y4 adult lifelong learning, and Y5 a digital-skills proxy) and two contextual variables (Z1 unemployment and Z2 citizenship) at NUTS-I and country levels. The robust BoD model benchmarks regions against a best-practice frontier, while the robust conditional BoD reweights comparisons using contextual similarity (kernel-based sampling) to produce more equitable peer sets and realistic targets. Results show substantial differences between robust and conditional scores (e.g., conditional scores generally higher), with only 8 super-performers in the robust regional analysis and 35 conditional peers identified. Limitations include reliance on cross-sectional 2019 data, incomplete indicator coverage at granular level (excluding a PISA-supported basic-skills indicator), and the absence of explicit missing-data handling details beyond a complete-data requirement.

title: The development of ICT skills in adolescence at the intersection of gender and family background
authors: Alexandra Wicht, Corinna Kleinert
outcome_summary: The study analyzes NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Germany) longitudinal ICT skills measured in paper-pencil multiple-choice tests in grade 9 (wave 1, 2010/11) and grade 12 (wave 7, 2013/14). The analytic sample includes 14,137 ninth-graders in Germany across 523 schools, with grade-12 growth restricted to the academic track due to high missingness in the non-academic track; missing ICT data were handled via two-level multiple imputation (60 imputations) using Blimp 3.1 with random intercepts. ICT skills are scaled using Warm’s mean-weighted likelihood estimator (WLE) from an IRT model (WLE reliability: 0.81 in grade 9; 0.73 in grade 12). Results show small but consistent male advantages in grade-9 ICT skills (e.g., female vs male B = −0.05* non-academic; −0.11*** academic) and a larger male advantage in growth (female vs male B = −0.28*** in academic track), with the gender gap in growth decreasing as income increases. Limitations include the absence of ML modeling/metrics (the paper uses regression with interactions) and no explicit reporting of survey-weight application in the provided text.
all_datasets_used: NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Germany) Grade 9 ICT skills (wave 1, 2010/11) | NEPS Starting Cohort 4 (Germany) ICT skills growth Grade 9 to Grade 12 (wave 1 to wave 7, academic track only)
all_target_variables: ICT skills in grade 9 (WLE) | ICT skills change from grade 9 to grade 12 (WLE)

title: Advancing language education with ChatGPT: A path to cultivate 21st-century digital skills
authors: Amir Reza Rahimi, Ramin Teimouri
outcome_summary: This paper investigates how ChatGPT-related features shape Iranian high-school English learners’ self-reported 21st-century digital skills using a questionnaire-based PLS-SEM model (N=236; three schools; 2023–2024). The study does not use ILSA/PISA/ICILS achievement data or machine-learning prediction; instead, it estimates structural relationships among latent constructs representing ChatGPT personalization, anthropomorphism, digital self-authenticity, interactivity, and accuracy/responsiveness, and seven digital-skill outcomes (information management, evaluation, communication, collaboration, critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving). Key results show significant positive effects of personalization on information evaluation and creativity, interactivity on critical thinking and problem-solving (and also communication/creativity), and accuracy/responsiveness on information management and several other skills, while anthropomorphism reduces collaborative skills but supports problem-solving. Limitations include convenience sampling, gender imbalance, reliance on self-report, and no reported missing-data handling; therefore, causal interpretations are not warranted.
all_datasets_used: ChatGPT-assisted language learning (Iran, 2023–2024 high-school English classes)
all_target_variables: Information management (INFOM) | Information evaluation (INFOE) | Digital communication skills (DCM) | Collaborative digital skills (COL) | Critical-thinking digital skills (CRT) | Creative digital skills (CRE) | Problem-solving digital skills (PS)

title: Addressing 21st-century digital skills in schools – Development and validation of an instrument to measure teachers' basic ICT competence beliefs
authors: C. Rubach, R. Lazarides
outcome_summary: This paper develops and validates an instrument to measure teachers’ basic ICT competence beliefs using a German online teacher survey (DigiKompEL), with N=372 in-service teachers. The study does not use ILSA/PV-based achievement outcomes; instead, it estimates a multidimensional measurement model with six competence dimensions (information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety and security, problem solving, analyzing and reflecting) and tests higher-order structure. Model fit for the preferred higher-order six-factor model is reported as χ2=654.729 (df=441), CFI=0.960, TLI=0.955, RMSEA=0.036, SRMR=0.044, with factor loadings ranging from λ=0.58 to λ=0.92. Construct validity is supported by significant positive correlations between competence belief dimensions and ICT benefit values and ICT use, and negative correlations with ICT cost values. Limitations include cross-sectional, voluntary sampling and the fact that the work is psychometric validation rather than predictive ML of outcomes.

title: Assessing digital self-efficacy: Review and scale development
authors: A.-S. Ulfert-Blank, I. Schmidt
outcome_summary: This paper is primarily a scale-development and validation study rather than an ILSA predictive-ML study. The authors conducted (1) a scoping review of existing digital self-efficacy (DSE) measures (n=17 included studies) and (2) the development and validation of a new German-language multidimensional DSE scale aligned to DigComp 2.1. The validation study used a German web-based CASI quota sample with a planned-missing design (initial N=627; final analytic N=571) and excluded invalid response patterns based on ipsativized variance, Mahalanobis distance, and implausibly short response times. Using Mplus with robust maximum likelihood and FIML for planned-missing data, confirmatory factor analysis supported a first-order correlated-factor structure over a single g-factor model, with standardized factor loadings mostly >0.50. Reliability (McDonald’s Omega) was high for information/data literacy (Ω=0.887), communication/collaboration (Ω=0.749), digital content creation (Ω=0.811), and safety (Ω=0.921), and moderate for problem-solving (Ω=0.659). Measurement invariance across gender was supported via (partial) strict invariance, enabling gender comparisons using manifest scale scores.

title: Digital inequality in Austria: Empirical evidence from the survey of the OECD “Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies”
authors: Stella Sophie Zilian, Laura Samantha Zilian
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes digital inequality in Austria using the OECD PIAAC 2011/2012 survey, focusing on the PSTRE (digital problem solving in technology-rich environments) cognitive domain. The analytic sample includes employed and self-employed respondents aged 16–65 who have proven ICT knowledge and completed PSTRE (N=2542; Austria only). The authors estimate a linear regression (OLS) with PV-aware survey estimation via the R svyPV package, reporting coefficient estimates and significance rather than ML performance metrics. Key results show women’s PSTRE scores are lower by about 7.36 points on average, and PSTRE increases with socio-economic background measured by books at home at age 16; age is negatively associated and years of schooling positively associated. When ICT use in everyday life is added, gender becomes statistically insignificant and only the highest socio-economic category remains significant, suggesting ICT familiarity is closely linked to PSTRE but causality is unclear. The study also uses Eurostat ICT-use and self-reported digital-skill trends (2012–2019) descriptively, which is not directly comparable to PSTRE and may reflect response bias.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC 2011/2012 Austria (16–65) PSTRE digital problem solving

title: New technology, new role of parents: How parents' beliefs and behavior affect students’ digital media self-efficacy
authors: M. Hammer, Katharina Scheiter, Kathleen Stürmer
outcome_summary: This study does not use machine learning prediction on ICILS/PISA achievement scores; instead, it tests mediation relationships in a school-based longitudinal design in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Students’ digital media self-efficacy was measured at the first measurement point (before tablet provision) using a 7-item Likert scale adapted from PISA 2015, while parents reported task values (intrinsic, utility, attainment, emotional cost, opportunity cost) and two behavior pathways: modeling (average daily screen time on phone/tablet/computer) and provision (whether the child has each device and the age at which it was provided). The mediation models were estimated in Mplus with missing data handled via maximum likelihood estimation, and indirect effects were assessed using 10,000 bootstrap samples. Across five parallel mediation models, the only indirect effect consistently different from zero was through the age at which parents provided their child with a smart phone; other mediators (time spent on devices and provision ages for tablet/computer) did not robustly mediate the belief–self-efficacy links. The paper reports standardized path estimates and 95% confidence intervals (Table 5) rather than ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC). Limitations include the inability to infer causality due to the cross-sectional measurement of beliefs and self-efficacy at the same time point and potential measurement bias from self-reports.

title: Non-cognitive skills and social gaps in digital skills: Evidence from ICILS 2018
authors: Zbigniew Karpiński, Giorgio Di Pietro, Federico Biagi
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes ICILS 2018 8th-grade Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) plausible values (five PVs combined using Rubin’s rules) for 12 participating countries/regions/cities, with a final analytic sample of 40,403 students after listwise deletion of missing key variables. The authors estimate fixed-effects linear models with school-level mean-centering to address the nested design and apply ICILS survey design weights for point estimates, with replicate weights for standard errors, using the R survey package. The baseline model (only student characteristics) has low explanatory power (Adj. R² = -0.04), while adding non-self-reported non-cognitive proxies improves fit markedly (Adj. R² = 0.20–0.24; best in Model 5 with R² = 0.37). The strongest proxy is drop in response time, and including proxies reduces the gender and socioeconomic gaps; the immigrant gap also shrinks but remains statistically significant. Limitations include the absence of causal identification and the use of behavioral proxies that may partially reflect cognitive capacities.
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) test (plausible values)

title: Computer user profiles in early adolescence and digitally assessed mathematics: A latent class analysis
authors: Marta Desimoni, Donatella Papa, Cristina Lasorsa, Michela Milioni, Rosalba Ceravolo
outcome_summary: The study analyzes heterogeneity in out-of-school computer use among Italian grade 8 students using a person-centered latent class analysis (LCA) and then links latent class membership to digitally assessed mathematics. Mathematics was measured with five online test forms (41 items each) and scaled using a Rasch-calibrated item bank; AcerConquest generated five plausible values (PVs) per student, combined using Rubin’s method in Mplus. The analytic sample included 1,155 students from Italy participating in the INVALSI 2019 Field Trial, with missing LCA indicators handled via full information maximum likelihood and missing exogenous covariates handled via listwise deletion. Four computer-user profiles were retained (sporadic, multipurpose, educational, recreational). Mathematics results showed significant differences across profiles (M1 overall Wald χ²(3)=44.20, p<0.001; M2 overall Wald χ²(3)=35.61, p<0.001), with educational users outperforming other groups and recreational users performing worst; ESCS and gender also had significant direct associations with mathematics. Limitations include the absence of survey-weight reporting and the cross-sectional nature, so associations should not be interpreted as causal effects.
all_datasets_used: INVALSI 2019 Field Trial Grade 8 Mathematics (digitally assessed mathematics; PVs via AcerConquest)

title: Digital learning in schools: What does it take beyond digital technology?
authors: M. Sailer, J. Murböck, F. Fischer
outcome_summary: This study uses a representative teacher survey in German public secondary schools in Bavaria (N=410 teachers; telephone interviews, 24 minutes on average, March 6–April 10, 2017) to examine how teachers’ basic digital skills, technology-related teaching skills, and the availability of digital technologies relate to (a) the frequency of digital technology use during teaching and (b) the types of student learning activities teachers foster with digital technology (passive, active, constructive, interactive). The paper reports no machine-learning prediction pipeline; instead, it uses confirmatory factor analysis for latent constructs and structural equation modeling (robust maximum likelihood) to estimate standardized relationships. Teachers reported using digital technology in some way for 43.03% (SD=24.54) of lesson time; passive learning activities were most frequent (13.35%), followed by interactive (10.45%), constructive (10.05%), and active (8.92%). In SEM, basic digital skills were positively associated with frequency of digital technology use (b=0.41) and with passive (b=0.37), active (b=0.29), and interactive (b=0.34) learning activities, while technology-related teaching skills were positively associated with constructive learning activities (b=0.30). Digital technology availability in school was not significantly related to either overall frequency or any learning-activity type. Limitations include reliance on teacher self-report and incomplete documentation of missing-data handling beyond complete-response inclusion.
all_target_variables: predicting frequency of digital technology use during teaching

title: Classes of problematic smartphone use and information and communication technology (ICT) self-efficacy
authors: Xiaoxiong Lai, Chang Nie, Shunsen Huang, Yuanwei Yao, Yajun Li, Xinran Dai, Yun Wang
outcome_summary: This longitudinal person-centered study used Wave 2 questionnaire data from Chinese adolescents (grades 7–10) to identify six latent classes combining problematic smartphone use (16-item PSU scale) and ICT self-efficacy (13-item ICILS 2018-based instrument). The analytic sample included 1,275 adolescents from four Central China cities, with Wave 1 smartphone use content types (entertainment, interpersonal, information-seeking, utility, study) measured one year earlier. The best-fitting LCA solution selected six classes, including a small well-adjusted group (9%, n=111). Using regression mixture modeling with a three-step ML approach, entertainment use predicted lower odds of belonging to the well-adjusted class (e.g., OR=3.09, p<0.001 for Class 1 vs Class 4), whereas information-seeking and study use predicted higher odds (e.g., information-seeking OR=0.60, p=0.034; study OR=0.58, p=0.048). The paper does not report survey weights and cautions against causal interpretation, so findings should be treated as predictive associations for designing differentiated digital guidance.
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2018 (ICT self-efficacy questionnaire), Wave 2 (April 2019–July 2020), Chinese adolescents (grades 7–10)
all_target_variables: Latent class membership: PSU & ICT self-efficacy classes

title: What predicts studentsâ€™ future ICT literacy? Evidence from a large-scale study conducted in different stages of secondary school
authors: Nicolas Hübner, Thorsten Fahrbach, Andreas Lachner, Ronny Scherer
outcome_summary: The study uses NEPS Starting Cohort 3 longitudinal data to model ICT literacy development across two adjacent stages: Grade 6→9 (full sample N=6810) and Grade 9→12 (upper-secondary subset N=1776). ICT literacy is measured with an ICT literacy test administered in Grades 6, 9, and 12 and scaled using weighted likelihood estimates (WLEs), with measurement error handled via a single-indicator approach. The authors fit multiple regression models in Mplus with full information maximum likelihood for missing data and cluster-robust standard errors for students nested in schools, reporting standardized coefficients (β) and Benjamini–Hochberg corrected p-values. In the joint models, explained variance was R2=0.667 for Grade 9 and R2=0.622 for Grade 12. The strongest predictor in both stages was prior ICT literacy (β=0.389 for Grade 9; β=0.657 for Grade 12), while learning-background variables were more predictive in Stage 1 than in Stage 2, suggesting stage-dependent mechanisms; the paper does not report complex sampling weights, and the design is predictive rather than causal.
all_datasets_used: NEPS Starting Cohort 3 Grade 9 ICT literacy (development from Grade 6 to 9) | NEPS Starting Cohort 3 Grade 12 ICT literacy (development from Grade 9 to 12, upper secondary subset)
all_target_variables: ICT literacy in Grade 9 (WLE score) | ICT literacy in Grade 12 (WLE score)

title: Against all expectations? What are the differences between resilient and non-resilient schools in the CIL domain
authors: Markus Lörz, Kerstin Drossel, Birgit Eickelmann, Nadine Fröhlich
outcome_summary: The study conducts secondary analyses of ICILS 2018 for Germany, using the Grade 8 computer-based Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) test as the dependent variable. CIL achievement is modeled using five plausible values per student, combined using Rubin’s rules, with student-level weighting factors applied to account for unit non-response and jackknife repeated replication (JRR) used for standard errors. The analytic sample comprises 174 schools and 3,155 students after excluding schools with fewer than 10 cases and not imputing missing values on central school-level variables. The authors estimate weighted OLS regressions with clustered schools (level 2) and stepwise models (student characteristics, home conditions, and school digital conditions). In Model 1, resilient low-SES schools (Type II) show a +65.2 CIL-point advantage over non-resilient low-SES schools (Type I), and in the fully adjusted Model 5 the advantage remains +58.8 points; the overall explanatory power increases from R²=0.305 to R²=0.411. The results are predictive associations rather than causal effects, and the paper does not use machine-learning algorithms for prediction.
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) — Germany

title: To plan or not to plan: Technology integration in student teachers' lesson plans and their relation to dimensions of instructional quality
authors: Florian Hebibi, Isabell Runge, Rebecca Lazarides
outcome_summary: This paper is not an ILSA-based predictive ML study; it analyzes written lesson plans from 130 German pre-service teachers and codes 568 technology-integration instances using two frameworks: SAMR (substitution to redefinition) and three instructional-quality dimensions (cognitive activation, student support, classroom management). The study reports descriptive distributions and inferential associations using Spearman correlations, Kruskal–Wallis tests with Dunn–Bonferroni post-hoc comparisons, and binary logistic regression models predicting whether each instructional-quality dimension is addressed. Key results show that most integrations are at lower SAMR levels (substitution 61%, augmentation 27%), while cognitive activation is most frequent (28.7%), followed by student support (18.8%) and classroom management (17.6%). Associations are positive but modest: Spearman r values were 0.17 (cognitive activation), 0.37 (student support), and 0.10 (classroom management), and logistic regression McFadden pseudo-R² ranged from 0.02 to 0.14. Limitations include reliance on planned (not enacted) teaching and interpretive qualitative coding, with no survey-weighted estimation and no PV-based achievement outcomes.
all_target_variables: predicting whether each instructional-quality dimension is addressed

title: Understanding teacher ICT usage: Insights from ICILS 2018 Korea data
authors: Natthawin Cho, Chunhan Huang
outcome_summary: The study analyzes ICILS 2018 teacher questionnaire data and uses Korea as a case study (N=2127 teachers) to test a three-layer model (external factors, internal factors, and an action layer) using PLS-SEM in SmartPLS4 with 10,000 bootstraps. The dependent constructs are teachers’ ICT usage: ICTPRAC (assessment-related ICT use), USETOOL (digital learning tools), and USEUTIL (general utility software). Across the action layer, most external and internal constructs show significant direct and total effects, with PD and COLICT consistently predicting all three usage outcomes; RESRC (school ICT resources) shows no direct effects on any action-layer construct. Key path coefficients include PD→USETOOL β=0.305 (t=9.877, p<0.001) and EXP→USEUTIL β=0.322 (t=18.428, p<0.001). Missing data were handled via mean imputation (max 3.6% per variable), and the authors note that causal relationships are not thoroughly considered.
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2018 Teacher questionnaire (Korea) — teacher ICT usage constructs
all_target_variables: ICTPRAC (ICT use for assessment practices) | USETOOL (use of digital learning tools) | USEUTIL (use of general utility software)

title: Comparing tablet and print mode of a german reading comprehension test in grade 3: Influence of test order, gender and language
authors: S. Seifert, L. Paleczek
outcome_summary: This study compared tablet (digital app) versus print administration of the German reading comprehension test GraLeV for Grade 3 students in Spring 2021, using a within-student design across two measurement periods (digital and print) with test order counterbalanced across 16 classrooms. The analytic sample comprised 218 students (Germany) who completed both periods; teacher questionnaire data were available for 173 students used for validity correlations. The results showed significant overall mode effects, with print-mode scores higher for Word, Text I, and Text II, while Sentence showed no significant overall mode difference. Correlations between digital and print subtest scores were moderate to high (r≈.56 to .70), with Text II reaching the only acceptable test–retest reliability threshold cited. Gender and L1/L2 language background did not moderate the mode effect, but test order did, indicating that response-format familiarity and sequencing influence comparability. The paper uses repeated-measures MANOVA and correlations (no ML/PV framework), and missing-data handling for teacher questionnaires is not explicitly documented.
all_datasets_used: GraLeV (German reading comprehension) Grade 3 — digital (tablet app) vs print — Spring 2021
all_target_variables: Word subtest raw score (digital vs print) | Sentence subtest raw score (digital vs print) | Text I subtest raw score (digital vs print) | Text II subtest raw score (digital vs print) | Convergent vs discriminant validity (teacher ratings correlations)

title: How well does the digital home learning environment predict ICT literacy and ICT self-efficacy? Comparing the predictive power of adolescent and parent reports
authors: Martin Senkbeil
outcome_summary: This study uses a German grade-6 convenience sample (422 complete parent–child dyads from 16 schools in northern Germany; 2019) to examine whether a digital home learning environment (HLE) predicts two outcomes: ICT literacy (TILT-Grade 6 objective test scored with WLE) and ICT self-efficacy (10-item 4-point scale). The authors estimate predictive validity using Mplus regression/correlation models with controls for gender and educational level and account for classroom nesting via TYPE = COMPLEX. For ICT self-efficacy, adolescent reports of parental ICT values and monitoring/supervision show the strongest effects (ΔR2 = 0.27; β = 0.32* for values and β = −0.40*** for monitoring in M1), whereas parent reports add little (ΔR2 = 0.09). For ICT literacy, parent reports are more predictive (ΔR2 = 0.18), with parental ICT values as the strongest positive predictor (β = 0.38***) and monitoring/supervision as a negative predictor (β = −0.17*), while psychological support shows suppression effects. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (associations, not causal mechanisms) and the absence of documented survey-weighting for population generalization.
all_datasets_used: TILT-Grade 6 ICT literacy test (Germany, grade 6; 2019 data collection)
all_target_variables: ICT self-efficacy (latent scale) | ICT literacy (WLE competence score)

title: Multilevel analysis of the effects of principal support and innovative school climate on the integration of technology in learning activities
authors: Stefan Ninković, Olivera Knežević Florić, Marijana Momčilović
outcome_summary: This study uses Serbian teacher survey data (364 teachers in 17 schools) to validate the ICAP-TS scale and to examine multilevel associations between school context and four types of technology integration in learning activities (passive, active, constructive, interactive). The technology-use outcomes are measured with a 12-item ICAP-TS (five-point Likert frequency: 0=almost never to 4=almost every lesson), while principal support and innovative climate are measured with Likert-type scales. The authors used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) for construct validity and multilevel modeling with random intercepts (and attempted random slopes) to separate within-school and between-school variance. For passive use, principal support showed a positive within-school effect (γ10=0.164, p=.025) and innovative climate was also positive (γ20=0.224, p=.001), but in the final random-slope specification principal support became non-significant while innovative climate remained significant (γ20=0.219, p=.002). For active, constructive, and interactive use, innovative climate was consistently significant within schools (e.g., active: γ20=0.372, p<.001; interactive: γ20=0.393, p<.05), whereas principal support was not consistently significant. Limitations include the absence of a reported missing-data strategy and the fact that the study is correlational (no causal identification).

title: The relationship between information literacy and digital self-efficacy in teaching information literacy for new teachers in Lithuania
outcome_summary: The study uses Lithuania 2022 survey data (N=405) from two teacher-training groups—191 undergraduate students and 214 requalification programme teachers—to examine how perceived information literacy components relate to digital self-efficacy in teaching information literacy. Information literacy is operationalized via IL-HUMASS subcomponents (information seeking, evaluation, processing, dissemination) and digital self-efficacy via DSE items (DSE1–DSE6). Using SEM in AMOS, all four information literacy components show positive direct effects on DSE in both groups, with the strongest standardized paths from information evaluation and information processing (undergraduates: βIE=0.834, βIP=0.849; requalification teachers: βIE=0.821, βIP=0.774; all p<.01). Group comparisons via Mann–Whitney indicate requalification teachers score higher on internet search abilities and netiquette/privacy/copyright. Limitations include the absence of a documented missing-data strategy and the correlational nature of SEM (no causal identification).
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2018 (conceptual framework referenced; study uses Lithuania 2022 teacher survey) | Lithuania 2022 teacher survey (undergraduate vs requalification programme)
all_target_variables: Digital self-efficacy in teaching information literacy (DSE) — undergraduate students | Digital self-efficacy in teaching information literacy (DSE) — requalification programme teachers | Group difference in perceived DSE (H1)

title: Educational achievement among East Asian schoolchildren 1967–2020: A thematic review of the literature
authors: B. Boman
outcome_summary: This article is a thematic literature review (not an empirical ML study) synthesizing 99 included studies published between 1967 and 2020 on educational achievement among East Asian schoolchildren (Grade 5–10) in Japan, China, South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore. It does not train or evaluate machine-learning models, and it does not re-estimate ILSA outcomes from microdata; instead, it codes included studies into themes and sub-themes using a qualitative content/thematic analysis approach. The review reports that seven major themes with 53 sub-themes emerge, with cultural and educational-quantity factors dominating, followed by non-cognitive abilities, cognitive ability, educational quality (e.g., teacher competence), socioeconomic patterns, curriculum, and related system/process considerations. Because no PV-based achievement modeling is performed, there are no PV-handling, missing-data, or survey-weighting steps tied to ILSA scaling. Limitations include potential incompleteness of the included literature and the subjectivity/categorical overlap inherent in thematic coding.

title: Measuring digital literacy across three age cohorts: Exploring test dimensionality and performance differences
authors: K.-Y. Jin, F. Reichert, L.P. Cagasan, J. de la Torre, N. Law
outcome_summary: This paper develops and validates a performance-based digital literacy (DL) assessment aligned to DigComp 2.1 and administers it to Hong Kong students in three cohorts (Primary 3, Secondary 1, Secondary 3) in 2018/2019. The assessment uses 80 items across three test forms (45/50/50 items) with constrained response formats (multiple-choice variants, drop-down, drag-and-drop, short response, and click-image). Psychometric analyses fit unidimensional and multidimensional IRT models (2PLM vs M2PLM), finding that DL is essentially unidimensional: AIC/BIC favored 2PLM over M2PLM and latent correlations among the five modeled competences were high (0.83–0.95). After item purification (discarding low-discrimination items and one gender DIF item), the final 73-item pool produced good measurement quality (RMSD 0.007–0.077; EAP reliability ~0.84–0.86). Performance differences were significant across cohorts (ANOVA F(2,1986)=592.43, p<.001, η2=0.374) and gender effects emerged only in secondary cohorts (gender main effect F(1,1961)=20.93, p<.001, η2=0.011; gender×cohort interaction F(2,1961)=4.86, p<.01, η2=0.005). Limitations include the absence of a documented missing-data handling protocol and the fact that the study is psychometric/measurement-focused rather than ML predictive modeling.

title: Trends in international assessments and outcomes in adulthood
authors: S. Stemper
outcome_summary: The paper links adolescent math performance from PISA (math, age-based sample; PISA 2018 used for the linking scale) and TIMSS (Grade 8 math; TIMSS 2019 used for linking) to adult outcomes from PIAAC numeracy (2012/2014/2017) and harmonized SDR education and income measures. Scores are rescaled to a common PISA scale and then aggregated to country-by-birth-cohort averages; missing cohort test-score observations are imputed using the closest non-missing score within two birth years. In PIAAC, both PISA and TIMSS cohort math scores are positively associated with adult numeracy (Table 2: coefficients around 0.20–0.22 SD per 1 SD higher adolescent math; R² ≈ 0.94). In SDR outcomes, PISA shows stronger and more consistent associations with years of education and secondary completion, while bachelor’s completion shows no clear relationship; for income, PISA effects are larger (about 7–12 percentile points) than TIMSS (about 3–4). The study reports robust standard errors clustered by country and birth year and uses fixed effects, but it explicitly cautions that the estimates are associations, not causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC 2012/2014/2017 (adult numeracy), linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS 2015/2019 Grade 8 math (cohort-by-country averages) | SDR harmonized adult education outcomes linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (cohort-by-country averages) | SDR harmonized adult income outcomes linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (cohort-by-country averages)
all_target_variables: PIAAC numeracy test score (cohort average) | Years of education (adult, 16+ years old) | Complete secondary school (adult, 19+ years old) | Complete bachelors (adult, 24+ years old) | Household income percentile (adult, 24+ years old)

title: Technology-related knowledge, skills, and attitudes of pre- and in-service teachers: The current situation and emerging trends
authors: Sabine Seufert, Josef Guggemos, Michael Sailer
outcome_summary: This article is an introductory overview for a special issue on technology-related knowledge, skills, and attitudes (KSA) of pre- and in-service teachers. It does not perform an original empirical analysis with a defined ILSA dataset/cycle, nor does it train or evaluate machine-learning models on ILSA microdata. Instead, it specifies the conceptual basis (notably the TPACK framework), reviews how technology-related KSA are assessed (self-assessment vs. external/objective measures), and outlines directions for fostering these KSA, including future-oriented considerations such as artificial intelligence and “augmentation strategies.” Because no student-level achievement outcomes are modeled, there are no PV-based benchmarks, no reported predictive metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE), and no sampling/weighting or missing-data procedures for an analytic dataset. Consequently, the contribution is methodological and conceptual rather than results-driven.
all_target_variables: technology-related KSA are assessed (self-assessment vs achievement

title: 1-s2.0-S0360131521000476-main
authors: Qiwei He, Francesca Borgonovi, Marco Paccagnella
outcome_summary: This Computers & Education study uses PIAAC PSTRE process data from the second cluster (PS2) administered to adults in five countries (England/Northern Ireland, Ireland, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United States) on seven interactive PSTRE items. The authors derive four cross-item behavioral indicators from log-file action sequences using longest common subsequence (LCS) alignment to ex-ante optimal reference sequences: similarity (SM), consistency of similarity (SSD), efficiency (EM), and consistency of efficiency (ESD). They exclude respondents with at least one nonresponse (NR) shortest-sequence pattern from the LCS analysis, reducing the analytic sample from 7462 to 5302. Results show significant country differences in similarity (ANOVA F(4,5297)=39.52, P<0.001) and a strong positive correlation between PSTRE proficiency scores and similarity (r=0.79), while efficiency shows a weaker relationship. The paper does not report a general missing-data strategy beyond the NR exclusion and does not describe survey-weight usage, limiting population-representative inference.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC PS2 PSTRE (adult problem solving in technology-rich environments), 2012-2017, 7 interactive items (process data)
all_target_variables: Problem-solving proficiency (PSTRE score/level) predicted by behavioral patterns

title: Teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge: Development of a measurement instrument
authors: Sara Monteyne, Charlotte Struyve, Natacha Gesquiere, Tom Neutens, Francis Wyffels, Johan van Braak, Koen Aesaert
outcome_summary: This paper develops and calibrates a measurement instrument for lower-secondary teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge as part of ICILS 2023 in Flanders. The calibration used N=352 senior pre-service teachers from nine of fifteen teacher-training institutes, administered online via Qualtrics with standardized supervision and a 45-minute time limit; item responses were binary coded and analyzed using classical test theory and item response theory. The authors retained 16 items after item-quality screening and dimensionality checks, finding that a unidimensional model was viable and that the 2PL IRT model fit the data better than the Rasch model (e.g., SRMSR=0.043 vs 0.073; MADaQ3=0.048 vs 0.049; chi-square difference favoring 2PL). Reliability for the final 16-item scale was reported as EAP-based reliability α=0.78. The study is instrument-development rather than predictive ML, so no ML performance metrics, survey weights, or PV handling are reported; missing-data handling is also not documented.

title: Pre-service English teachers‘ approaches to technology-assisted teaching and learning: Associations with study level, self-efficacy and value beliefs
authors: Andreas Hülshoff, Regina Jucks
outcome_summary: This study uses a 2022 online survey of N=125 pre-service teachers from universities in North Rhine-Westphalia (Germany) to examine how transmissive (information transmission/teacher focus) and constructivist (conceptual change/student focus) approaches to ICT-assisted EFL teaching cluster together, and how these clusters relate to value beliefs and self-efficacy. The authors identified three clusters via two-step cluster analysis (silhouette=0.5; smallest/largest ratio=1.39) and then compared clusters using MANOVA/ANOVA and chi-square tests. Cluster allocation differed by study level (χ2(2)=15.05, p<.001; Cramer-V=0.35), with master students more often in the constructivist-dominant cluster. Clusters significantly differed for value beliefs (interest, utility, relevance) but not for assumed costs or self-efficacy domains (all self-efficacy p≥.08). Limitations include a convenience sample, multiple-testing risk, and correlational design that precludes causal claims.
all_datasets_used: Non-ILSA survey of pre-service teachers (Germany, North Rhine-Westphalia; 2022 online survey)
all_target_variables: Cluster membership (approaches to ICT-assisted EFL teaching)

title: Artificial intelligence, tasks, skills, and wages: Worker-level evidence from Germany
authors: Erik Engberg, Michael Koch, Magnus Lodefalk, Sarah Schroeder
outcome_summary: This paper uses German worker-level administrative data (SIAB) for 2010–2017 to study how occupation-level AI exposure (DAIOE, time-varying) relates to individual wages, alongside descriptive analyses of task and skill changes using BIBB-BAuA surveys (2006/2012/2018). The wage models are Mincer-type fixed-effects regressions with worker, plant, 4-digit occupation, and year fixed effects, and standard errors clustered at the 4-digit occupation level. In Table 2, the benchmark specification shows a positive association between AI exposure and log daily wages; a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure (SD=2.07) corresponds to about a 1.96% wage increase, with coefficients remaining similar under stricter stayers samples. Table 3 demonstrates heterogeneity across AI subfields (e.g., positive for image recognition and strategy games, negative for video games). The study is not an ML prediction paper (no ML algorithms are trained), and causal interpretation is limited because AI exposure is observational and identification relies on fixed effects and controls rather than randomized variation.
all_target_variables: Log daily wage | Log daily wage (AI subfield exposure) | Log daily wage (low vs high task churning occupations)

title: Firm training, automation, and wages: International worker-level evidence
authors: Oliver Falck, Yuchen Guo, Christina Langer, Valentin Lindlacher, Simon Wiederhold
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PIAAC microdata to examine whether employer-provided firm training reduces workers’ automation risk and improves wages. The main international analysis pools 37 countries using the 2012 wave and constructs an individual-level automation risk index (0–1) from PIAAC workplace task-use items, then estimates OLS models with country/industry/occupation fixed effects and entropy balancing reweighting to address selection into training. In the preferred specification (Table 2, column 5), firm training reduces automation risk by 3.8 percentage points (coefficient −0.0377; R²=0.24; N=91,470). In the wage model (Table 7, column 5), firm training increases log hourly wages by 7.1% (coefficient 0.0713; R²=0.38; N=91,470), and adding automation risk reduces the wage effect by about 15% (Table 7, column 6). Digital skills analyses (Table 6, column 5) show a +0.048 SD increase (N=72,180), interpreted as a mechanism, with the caveat that digital skills were optional and missingness is handled via lower-bound restriction and sensitivity imputations.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC 2012 (international pooled; adult workers 25–65), automation risk from workplace task use | PIAAC 2012 (international pooled; adult workers 25–65), log hourly wages | PIAAC 2012 (international pooled; adult workers 25–65), digital skills (standardized)
all_target_variables: Automation risk (individual-level, 0–1) | Log hourly wages | Digital skills (standardized)

title: The Effects of Artificial Intelligence on the Future of Employment
authors: Hicham Sadok
outcome_summary: This article is a narrative literature review focused on how artificial intelligence may affect employment, framed through an evolutionary techno-economic perspective. It does not perform an empirical machine-learning analysis on ILSA micro-data (e.g., PIAAC) and therefore does not estimate predictive performance metrics (such as accuracy, RMSE, or AUC) from an ML model. Instead, it summarizes prior forecasting approaches linking technology to job substitution risk and discusses global estimates from external sources (notably an ILO working paper) about automation exposure and job creation across countries and gender. Because no assessment dataset is analyzed, there is no plausible-values procedure, no missing-data strategy, and no survey-weighting scheme to evaluate. The main contribution is conceptual synthesis and policy-oriented discussion rather than measurement-based causal or predictive inference from student assessment data.

title: The evolution of gender gaps in numeracy and literacy between childhood and young adulthood
authors: Francesca Borgonovi, Alvaro Choi, Marco Paccagnella
outcome_summary: This paper studies how gender gaps evolve across the life course by combining cross-sectional large-scale assessments for a synthetic cohort (born 1984/85) observed at ages 9–10 (TIMSS 1995 for numeracy; PIRLS 2001 proxy for literacy), 15–16 (PISA 2000), and 26–27 (PIAAC 2011/12). The analysis uses survey weights and complex-design standard errors (Jackknife/BRR) and handles plausible values via repest, with scores standardized using the overall mean/SD across participating countries. The key results are descriptive: numeracy shows a growing male advantage (pooled gaps: -0.029 at age 9/10, -0.087 at 15/16, -0.332 at 26/27), while literacy shows an inverted-U pattern (0.185 at 9/10, 0.307 at 15/16, -0.019 at 26/27). Extended PIAAC regressions suggest that controlling for STEM-related careers halves the numeracy gap but does not make the literacy gap statistically significant. Limitations include the absence of ML prediction models, reliance on synthetic-cohort comparability across assessments, and no explicit microdata missing-data handling strategy reported.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 1995 (age 9–10) + PISA 2000 (age 15–16) + PIAAC 2011/12 (age 26–27) — Numeracy/Mathematics | PIRLS 2001 (proxy age 9–10) + PISA 2000 (age 15–16) + PIAAC 2011/12 (age 26–27) — Literacy/Reading
all_target_variables: Gender gap in numeracy (male–female difference in standardized scores) | Gender gap in literacy (female–male difference in standardized scores)

title: Measurements of skill and skill-use using PIAAC
authors: D. Kawaguchi, T. Toriyabe
outcome_summary: This paper constructs new, internationally comparable measures of literacy and numeracy skill and skill use using OECD PIAAC microdata from 24 countries (PIAAC Round 1: 2008–2013; Round 2: 2012–2016), restricting to prime-age adults (25–59), excluding the problem-solving module, and excluding observations with missing values in analysis variables. The authors do not use PIAAC-provided plausible values; instead, they estimate latent traits via IRT (two-parameter logistic for skills; general partial credit model for ordered skill-use frequencies) and normalize indices. Across applications, the study shows that skill use is strongly associated with wages within occupations (e.g., 9.8% vs 6.0% wage increases for one SD higher literacy use vs literacy skill, attenuating to 6.6% vs 4.8% after occupation controls). It further finds that parental leave length widens the gender gap in literacy use among modestly skilled women (with effects persisting at the intensive margin), and that immigrant wage penalties are partly explained by differences in literacy utilization (25–36% of the explained gap in key countries). Limitations include the absence of explicit survey-weight reporting and the fact that the analysis is not ML predictive modeling.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC Round 1 (2008–2013) & Round 2 (2012–2016) — literacy skill and literacy skill use (prime-age 25–59; problem-solving excluded) | PIAAC Round 1 (2008–2013) & Round 2 (2012–2016) — literacy skill use (prime-age 25–59; problem-solving excluded) | PIAAC Round 1 (2008–2013) & Round 2 (2012–2016) — wage gap by years since immigration (with literacy skill and literacy skill use controls)
all_target_variables: Immigrant-native wage penalty explained by gaps in literacy skill and literacy skill use (Gelbach decomposition) | Literacy skill use — effect of parental leave on the gender gap in skill use (censored Tobit; extensive + intensive margins) | Wage gap between immigrants and natives over years since immigration (and its decomposition)

title: Separating PIAAC competencies from general cognitive skills: A dimensionality and explanatory analysis
authors: L. Engelhardt, F. Goldhammer
outcome_summary: The study uses a German PIAAC 2012 subsample (N=903) from the PIAAC-L longitudinal design, combining PIAAC literacy and numeracy competence tests (administered in 2015 with adaptive testlet selection) with a reasoning test (number series) and a perceptual speed test (SOEP Symbol-Digit) administered in 2016. Rather than predicting outcomes with ML, the authors fit CFA/bifactor-(S−1) dimensionality models in Mplus (MLR estimator) to separate a common factor (interpreted as close to fluid reasoning) from nested domain-specific factors for literacy, numeracy, and perceptual speed. The best-fitting three-nested-factor model supports additional shared variance for literacy beyond overlaps with reasoning and perceptual speed (literacy nested variance σ2(SE)=2.88(1.00), p=.004), while numeracy’s nested variance is not significant (σ2(SE)=5.61(3.65), p=.124). In explanatory regressions, age predicts the common factor and perceptual speed but not the literacy/numeracy nested factors; learning opportunities significantly predict literacy nested factors (e.g., educational attainment β=0.33, p<.001) but not numeracy nested factors. Limitations include cross-sectional inference for age relations and the fact that results are validated for German adults only; additionally, the paper does not use PV-based achievement modeling, and missingness is handled via SEM/IRT under MAR assumptions for adaptive testlet selection.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC 2012 (Germany) literacy competence + reasoning + perceptual speed (PIAAC-L subsample; assessments in 2015–2016) | PIAAC 2012 (Germany) numeracy competence + reasoning + perceptual speed (PIAAC-L subsample; assessments in 2015–2016)
all_target_variables: PIAAC literacy latent factor (domain-specific nested factor) | PIAAC numeracy latent factor (domain-specific nested factor)

title: Job Tasks and Wages in Developed Countries: Evidence from PIAAC
authors: Sara de la Rica, Luis Gortazar, Piotr Lewandowski
outcome_summary: This paper uses PIAAC worker-level data for 19 developed countries to construct three job-task intensity measures (abstract, routine, manual) from questionnaire items and to estimate “task prices” in log hourly wages. The analytic sample comprises 37,607 employees aged 25–54 with wages between 0 and 150 USD (PPP), excluding non-profit firms, agriculture, self-employment, and cases missing task-item information. The study reports that within occupations, a one-standard-deviation increase in abstract tasks is associated with a 3.3-log-point wage premium, while routine and manual tasks are associated with 2.6- and 2.9-log-point wage decreases, respectively. Cross-country heterogeneity is explored via interactions with development and labor-market institutions; union coverage and employment protection legislation show significant relationships with abstract-task prices, and development/ICT conditions interact with routine and manual task prices. The paper uses complex sampling weights (countries weighted equally) and runs regressions across all plausible values for numeracy skills, but it does not apply machine learning algorithms; therefore, the findings are correlational rather than predictive/causal.
all_datasets_used: PIAAC (2012/2015 waves; developed countries; worker-level wages) — task prices for abstract tasks | PIAAC (2012/2015 waves; developed countries; worker-level wages) — task prices for routine tasks | PIAAC (2012/2015 waves; developed countries; worker-level wages) — task prices for manual tasks | PIAAC (2012/2015 waves; developed countries; worker-level wages) — cross-country heterogeneity in task prices
all_target_variables: Abstract task price (within-occupation wage premium, log hourly earnings) | Routine task price (within-occupation wage decrease, log hourly earnings) | Manual task price (within-occupation wage decrease, log hourly earnings) | Country-differential task prices (interaction effects with development and institutions)

title: Central exams and adult skills: Evidence from PIAAC
authors: L. Leschnig, G. Schwerdt, et al.
outcome_summary: The paper studies the long-run relationship between central exit examinations at the end of secondary school and adult outcomes using OECD PIAAC adult skills and labor-market data matched to country-specific exam-regime histories for 30 countries. The main identification is a two-way fixed effects / difference-in-differences panel design using cohort-country variation in central-exam exposure, with country fixed effects and country-specific linear trends, and standard errors clustered by graduation year × country. Across domains, central exams increase adult numeracy and literacy by about 7% of a standard deviation and problem-solving by about 9% (e.g., 0.068, 0.068, 0.092 in baseline specifications). In contrast, there are no significant effects on earnings, employment, or tertiary attainment; earnings effects are bounded such that larger effects than about 4.6% can be ruled out. The study uses PIAAC sampling weights (adjusted to give equal country weight) but does not document a dedicated missing-data strategy beyond including an education-missing indicator and outcome-specific sample restrictions.

title: The impact of ICT and robots on labour market outcomes of demographic groups in Europe
authors: Maciej Albinowski, Piotr Lewandowski
outcome_summary: This paper studies how ICT and industrial robots affect labour-market outcomes of demographic groups in Europe using EU-SES worker-level data merged with sector-level technology measures from Eurostat/EU-KLEMS (ICT capital) and the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) (robot exposure), covering 14 countries over 2010–2018. The authors estimate within-sector demographic-group models for employment shares, relative hourly wages, and wage-bill shares, using OLS and two-stage least squares (2SLS) with an instrumental-variable strategy that instruments technology growth using “technology frontier” growth in the United States. In 2SLS results (e.g., Table 3), ICT capital increases employment shares for young and prime-aged women but reduces employment shares for women aged 60+, while robot exposure reduces employment shares for young/prime-aged men in routine manual contexts and can increase employment shares for some older men. Relative wages show barely any statistically significant IV effects (Table 4), implying employment reallocation dominates wage effects. The study applies country-sector weighting based on 2010 sectoral employment shares (and alternative weights in robustness checks) and clusters standard errors at the sector-year level; it does not use PVs, and missing-data handling for micro records is not explicitly documented in the provided text.

title: The effect of compulsory education on non-cognitive skills: Evidence from low- and middle-income countries
authors: A.K. Entorf, T.J. Dohmen
outcome_summary: The paper estimates causal effects of compulsory schooling reforms on non-cognitive skills using World Bank STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam (urban residents aged 15–64), exploiting within-country birth-cohort cutoffs tied to reforms. The preferred specification uses a 5-year birth window around each pivotal cohort and linear cohort trends, with standard errors clustered on reform × birth-year; the study does not use machine learning models. Across the five reforms, compulsory education increases openness to experience (+0.14 SD) and decision-making patterns (+0.10 SD) and decreases emotional stability (−0.23 SD), grit (−0.14 SD), hostile attribution bias (−0.21 SD), patience (−0.06; about −6% probability), and willingness to take risks (−0.05; about −5% probability). The paper further links these skill changes to wages via augmented Mincer wage regressions, predicting an overall wage increase of 9%, with about 40% of the predicted increase attributed to non-cognitive skill changes. Limitations include short Big Five item sets, single cross-sectional measurement, and no reported missing-data strategy or survey-weight application.

title: Can older workers stay productive? The role of ICT skills and training
authors: J.-W. Lee, D.W. Kwak, Eunbi Song
outcome_summary: The paper uses the Korean sample from the OECD PIAAC adult assessment (2012) and restricts the analysis to full-time workers working at least 30 hours per week (N=2620), excluding self-employed respondents. The dependent variable is log hourly earnings, and the key ICT construct is a composite index combining standardized problem-solving in technology-rich environments proficiency with standardized workplace ICT use (equal weight 0.5). Missing ICT proficiency scores (25.9%) are handled via regression-based multiple imputation using literacy and numeracy as predictors, and literacy is also included in wage regressions as a proxy for unobserved ability. In Table 2, ICT skills show a positive wage association (coefficient 0.166 in Column 1), while job training has a significantly larger wage effect for ages 50–65 (interaction coefficient 0.154). In Table 3, the ICT skills returns for older workers are significantly higher when they are highly educated (ICT x 50–65 x High Edu = 0.137) or employed in skill-intensive occupations (ICT x 50–65 x Skill Occ = 0.129). Limitations include observational identification challenges and the fact that the analysis is econometric rather than ML predictive modeling.
