title: Examining adults’ web navigation patterns in multi-layered hypertext environments
authors: Y. Gao, Ying Cui, Okan Bulut, Xiaoming Zhai, Fu Chen
outcome_summary: Using OECD PIAAC 2012 PSTRE log data, the study analyzed adults’ clickstream navigation patterns in two simulated multi-layered hypertext web-search tasks: the book purchase task and the reliable site task. The analytic sample comprised 494 adults from the United States and 914 adults from the United Kingdom, after excluding participants who advanced without clicking any SERP links. The authors identified latent navigation pattern groups via latent class analysis on page-visit counts and then characterized typical behavior using full-path sequence analysis; they report task correctness differences across pattern groups using Pearson chi-square tests and post-hoc pairwise comparisons. For the book purchase task, the Satisficing pattern group achieved the highest correctness (US: 96.05%; UK: 93.55%), while for the reliable site task the Sampling pattern group was highest (US: 92.45%; UK: 92.90%). The study’s limitations include restricted task environments (restricted information space and two tasks only) and no reported use of PIAAC sampling/replicate weights for these log-based pattern and correctness comparisons.

title: Educational mismatch and wages: Evidence from a cross-country comparison
authors: H. Sun
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD’s PIAAC microdata from the first two survey rounds (2011–2014), restricting to employed workers aged 16–65 and excluding self-employed individuals. Educational mismatch is measured as overeducation/undereducation using self-assessed required education (main analysis), with realized-match alternatives based on occupational education distributions; skill mismatch is benchmarked using PIAAC numeracy scores and used to decompose genuine vs apparent overeducation. Baseline Heckman two-step estimates show pooled wage penalties of −13.8% for overeducation and premiums of +9.9% for undereducation, with larger overeducation penalties for women (−14.3%) than men (−12.6%). Propensity score matching (NNM/RM/KM) reveals substantial cross-country heterogeneity, with the largest overeducation penalties in Britain, Cyprus, and Japan and smaller penalties in Nordic countries. Mediation analysis indicates occupational sorting and cognitive skill utilization (ICT/influencing/writing) explain meaningful shares of mismatch wage effects. Limitations include lack of reported survey-weight usage and reliance on matching/selection corrections rather than randomized assignment.

title: Artificial intelligence and cognitive inequality
authors: Indira Puri, Laura Veldkamp
outcome_summary: The paper develops a theoretical model linking AI-enabled information targeting to cognitive divergence and potential long-run convergence at a lower cognitive level. Empirically, it provides suggestive evidence using (1) a text-analysis of Facebook posts from US political party accounts, where it computes the dispersion of Dale–Chall readability (a proxy for linguistic complexity) within months and finds statistically significant increasing trends in variance over time (with bootstrapped standard errors; point estimates around 0.13 for Democrats and 0.12 for Republicans). It also reports OECD PIAAC adult skills trends, describing declines in literacy and numeracy across most countries between 2012 and 2022, with a notable literacy decline in many settings (e.g., large negative changes for several countries). The evidence is descriptive and not a student-level, PV-based predictive ML analysis; therefore, no ML performance metrics, PV handling, or survey-weighted estimation details are provided, and causal identification is not established.

title: Output costs of education and skill mismatch in OECD countries
authors: Pietro Garibaldi, Pedro Gomes, Thepthida Sopraseuth
outcome_summary: The paper uses cross-country PIAAC (Survey of Adult Skills) microdata collected between 2011 and 2015 for 17 OECD economies, restricting the sample to currently employed adults. It constructs two mismatch measures—education mismatch (based on ISCED 5B+ attainment within 2-digit occupations combined with subjective self-assessments) and skill mismatch (based on literacy/numeracy proficiency relative to the median within occupations, again combined with subjective mismatch)—and then calibrates a vertical mismatch structural model to match five PIAAC-derived targets (under-/over-employment shares and three relative wage moments). Eliminating the frictions generating mismatch increases output by 2.9% on average for education mismatch and 3.8% for skill mismatch, with substantial cross-country variation (0.4%–7% and 1%–9%, respectively). The two output-cost measures are highly correlated (0.87), and the main determinant is not the mismatch incidence but the wage premium of well-matched workers (correlation 0.98). The study does not report a missing-data strategy or PV handling details because the analysis is calibration/simulation rather than PV-based predictive modeling.

title: Human capital investment and perceived automation risks: Evidence from 16 countries
authors: S. Innocenti, M. Golin
outcome_summary: The study uses an original online survey administered between February and March 2019 to working individuals aged 20–70 in 16 countries (Australia, Brazil, Finland, Germany, Hong Kong, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, Romania, Spain, Switzerland, UAE, UK, US). The main outcome is a binary indicator of intention to attend training programmes that would take up one evening per week of leisure time for six months, derived from a four-point Likert item. The key predictor is a binary indicator of being moderately or very worried about losing one’s job in the next five years due to automation. Using pooled logit models with country and occupation fixed effects, the authors report that fear of automation raises predicted retraining intentions from about 0.63 to 0.67 (≈+6%) after controlling for locus of control, risk aversion, impatience, and job characteristics. The paper does not report ML performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) and does not provide a detailed missing-data handling protocol, and it explicitly avoids causal interpretation due to cross-sectional data and potential simultaneity.
all_datasets_used: Original 2019 multi-country worker survey (16 countries), binary intention to retrain (Likert-based)

title: Understanding teaching professionals' digital competence: What do PIAAC and TALIS reveal about technology-related skills, attitudes, and knowledge?
authors: Raija Hämäläinen, Kari Nissinen, Joonas O. Mannonen, Joni Lamsa, Kaisa J. Leino, Matti Taajamo
outcome_summary: This study uses PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 (2011–2012) PS-in-TRE plausible values and TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire items to examine digital competence components—measured skills, self-reported attitudes, and self-reported knowledge—among teaching professionals pooled across 11 European countries. The authors apply survey-weighted descriptive statistics and regression models (logistic/linear) with complex-sample procedures, including fixed country effects; for PIAAC skills, they use the plausible-values methodology requiring multiple imputation. Key results show that only 11% of teaching professionals have strong PS-in-TRE skills (Level 3) while 42% are weak (Level 1 or below), and age is the most consistent predictor: older teachers are more likely to have weak skills and greater need for ICT professional development. Associations between skills and attitudes/knowledge are generally weak (e.g., Pearson r=0.11 between measured skills and perceived job-relevant computer skills). Limitations include that skills and attitudes/knowledge come from different surveys and different participants, and that the TALIS items’ intercorrelations were too low to form reliable composite scales, so single-item analyses were used.

title: Global motivation to learn and adult learning: A nomological network analysis and a four-year longitudinal study
authors: Julia Gorges
outcome_summary: This paper investigates global motivation to learn (MtL) using the MtL scale implemented in the OECD Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC). Study 1 (SoSci Panel convenience sample; N=747) tests a nomological network via confirmatory factor analysis and bivariate associations between MtL and motivational/personality constructs, and reports that MtL shows strong convergent correlations with mastery goal orientation, intrinsic task value, need for cognition, and academic self-concept, with smaller associations with openness and conscientiousness and a small negative association with agreeableness. Study 2 uses the German PIAAC 2012 sample and its longitudinal extension PIAAC-L (t1=2012, t2=2015, t3=2016; N=5465 at baseline, N=2502 at t2, N=2370 at t3) to test prospective predictive validity of MtL for participation in adult education and training (PAE) over up to four years. The authors estimate latent-variable models in MPlus with sampling weights, replicate weights, and literacy incorporated through 10 plausible values; binary participation outcomes are modeled with WLSMV (probit) and pair-wise deletion, while planned PAE uses FIML. Across multiple models, MtL is a significant positive predictor of PAE in most specifications, but effects attenuate when literacy is included; openness does not significantly predict subsequent PAE. Limitations include reliance on latent-variable modeling rather than ML prediction, and the fact that predictive associations do not establish causal effects.

title: From asking to observing. Behavioural measures of socio-emotional and motivational skills in large-scale assessments
authors: Francesca Borgonovi, Alessandro Ferrara, Mario Piacentini
outcome_summary: This study develops and validates behavioural measures of socio-emotional and motivational skills (PSEC) using PISA microdata, primarily PISA 2012, and compares them with self-reported PSEC indicators. It constructs behavioural indicators from questionnaire responses (item non-response, inconsistency, non-differentiation) and from test-taking behaviour (performance decline and, for a subset of countries, response time effort from computer-based log files). Across countries, behavioural and self-reported measures show weak-to-moderate convergence, but behavioural indicators are consistently negatively associated with contemporaneous achievement in reading, mathematics, science, and collaborative problem-solving (Table 3), with non-response showing the strongest relationship. For a longitudinal subset of Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, and Canada, performance decline predicts lower university completion by age 25 and retains significance after controlling for self-reported PSEC (Tables 4–5). The paper does not document a formal missing-data procedure beyond restricting to non-missing cases, and the evidence is correlational/observational rather than causal.

title: Revisiting gender differences in personality: New evidence on big five domains and facets with large-scale samples from 27 nations
authors: Beatrice Rammstedt, Matthias Roth, Lena Roemer, Clemens M. Lechner
outcome_summary: The study uses PIAAC 2023 (PIAAC 2nd cycle; fielded 2022–23) public-use data from 27 countries (total N=143,313) to quantify gender differences in self-reported Big Five personality domains and facets using population-representative adult samples. It reports multivariate gender differences aggregated across countries using Mahalanobis distance (MD), finding an overall effect of MD=0.67, with women scoring higher than men most notably on Neuroticism (d=0.40) and Agreeableness (d=0.35), and smaller advantages on Conscientiousness (d=0.19) and Openness (d=0.11), while Extraversion shows no substantial domain-level difference. Cross-country variation is substantial (MD SD=0.09), with smaller differences in Singapore (MD=0.41) and larger differences in Germany, Norway, and Estonia (MD≈0.80). Associations with country-level indicators show that only Hofstede’s individualism-collectivism index is significantly related to the aggregated multivariate gender difference (17% explained variance; MD r=0.41), and facet-level patterns (subset of 11 countries) further highlight which facets drive domain effects. The paper does not report any ML model training or PV/missing-data handling strategy, and the country-level correlations are based on only 27 countries, limiting precision and sensitivity to outliers.

title: Predicting cross-national sex differences in large-scale assessments of students' reading literacy, mathematics, and science achievement: Evidence from PIRLS and TIMSS
outcome_summary: This preregistered study uses PIRLS (2001–2016, grade 4 reading literacy) and TIMSS (1995–2019, grade 4 and grade 8 mathematics and science) to examine how country-level macro indicators predict cross-national sex differences in achievement. The dependent variables are country-level Cohen’s d sex differences computed from IEA-scaled plausible values; plausible-value-specific regressions are combined using Rubin (1987) rules. The paper reports standardized single-regression weights (β) rather than ML prediction metrics, and it does not train machine-learning models. Across domains, girls show consistent advantages in reading literacy, while mathematics and science sex differences are small on average but vary meaningfully by country and grade. The strongest and most consistent associations are observed for education investment and gender-related macro indicators in grade 4, with weaker or less systematic patterns for grade 8; limitations include correlational inference at the country level and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling for the macro predictor dataset.

title: Unraveling the nexus: Culture, cognitive competence, and economic performance across 86 nations (2000–2018)
authors: David Becker, Thomas R. Coyle, Heiner Rindermann
outcome_summary: The study analyzes cross-national relationships between national culture and student competence using PISA country-level results from 2000–2018 (seven waves) and constructs three PISA-derived outcomes: means (general factor across waves/competencies), spans (general factor of 5th–95th percentile differences), and tilts (math–reading difference). The authors do not use student-level PVs or ML prediction; instead, they apply Factor Score Regression with multiple regression and path analyses across 86 countries (PISA 2022 excluded). Culture measured via religious affiliations, Hofstede’s 6-D model (recoded to four dimensions), and an Axiological Cube (from World Value Survey items) explains substantial variance in PISA means (e.g., AXC culture-only R2=0.627) and smaller variance in spans and tilts, with Religiosity & Authority showing strong negative associations. In controlled path models, PISA tilt has a positive direct effect on economic growth (βDir.=0.272), while cultural effects largely operate indirectly through PISA means. Limitations include correlational design, country-level aggregation, and no survey-weight/PV-based uncertainty quantification at the student level.

title: 1-s2.0-S0160289622000848-main
authors: M. Zullo
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes Italy’s secondary academic tracking by comparing students in the Liberal Arts versus technical (STEM) track using OECD PISA test scores from 2012, 2015, and 2018 (15-year-olds; Italy only). The analytic sample contains 841 Liberal Arts and 1968 STEM students, and the study applies inverse probability weighting to adjust for observable track-selection differences using propensity scores based on student and parental characteristics (e.g., gender, grade repetition, immigration status, books at home, region, and location). After matching, STEM students score higher in math (−50.1 PISA points difference) and science (−32.9), while reading shows no trade-off and instead a larger negative gap for Liberal Arts (−22.0). Decomposition results indicate that math and science gaps are mainly explained by coefficients/returns effects, while reading’s endowments and coefficients components move in opposite directions. Limitations include the lack of a reported general missing-data handling strategy and the fact that the study’s causal interpretation relies on observational matching rather than randomized track assignment.

title: Employment and productivity in an ageing society: Japan in international perspective
authors: Christophe André, Peter Gal, Matthias Schief
outcome_summary: This article is not an empirical large-scale assessment (ILSA) machine-learning study. It provides an economic perspective on how population ageing affects labour supply, productivity, innovation, technology adoption (including AI/robotics), and public finances, with Japan as the focal case and comparisons to other OECD economies. The paper reports multiple descriptive statistics and decomposition-style results (e.g., GDP per capita growth decomposition, employment rates by age, dependency ratios, and spending shares) drawn from external datasets and prior literature rather than from a single ILSA microdata analysis. Because no student-level assessment dataset is modeled, there are no ML targets, no predictive performance metrics (e.g., RMSE/AUC), and no survey-weighted estimation procedure. Consequently, the methodological implications are about policy interpretation of demographic and productivity channels, not about model-based prediction or causal identification from ILSA data.

title: Reading fiction and theory of mind in early adolescence: concurrent and longitudinal relations
authors: Sanne W. van der Kleij, Ian Apperly, Laura R. Shapiro, Jessie Ricketts
outcome_summary: This paper is not an ML predictive modeling study; it examines concurrent and longitudinal associations between reading fiction and theory of mind (ToM) in a local longitudinal cohort of 236 children in Birmingham, UK (ages 11–13). Reading fiction and non-fiction time were measured using the PIRLS student questionnaire at Time 1 and Time 3, while ToM was measured at Time 3 (and Time 4 for robustness) using the Silent Films task scored 0–12. The authors used path analysis in Mplus with robust standard errors (MLR) and estimated models using all available data under a missing-at-random assumption. In the concurrent model, ToM at Time 3 was uniquely associated with fiction reading (b=0.26, SE=0.09, 95% CI [0.11, 0.40]) after controlling for verbal ability, reading motivation, age, gender, and parental education; non-fiction reading was not uniquely associated (b=-0.01, SE=0.07). In the longitudinal model, Time 1 fiction and non-fiction reading did not uniquely predict ToM at Time 3; instead, ToM was uniquely associated with receptive vocabulary, parental education, and gender. Limitations include the absence of prior ToM measurement and the use of a single ToM task, so causal direction cannot be inferred.

title: Reading more, achieving more? Long-term gender gaps in reading behavior and reading achievement
outcome_summary: This study links reading achievement and questionnaire-based reading behavior across six PIRLS-related cycles (1970–2016) to create a country-level longitudinal dataset of gender gaps at the end of primary school. The main outcome is the gender gap in reading achievement measured in Cohen’s d units on a common achievement scale, while the key predictor is the gender gap in free-time reading behavior (also in Cohen’s d units), computed from standardized questionnaire items across cycles. The authors estimate country-fixed effects regressions (unit: country-by-year; 192 observations after excluding high single-sex-school shares) and apply sampling weights and Rubin’s rules to combine results across five plausible values for achievement. The main model shows a positive association (b = 0.11, SE = 0.05, p < .05), with robustness across PIRLS-only cycles and models including time-varying controls, though the early-literacy control model loses statistical significance due to reduced sample size. Limitations include partial comparability of behavior items across early cycles, missing-data documentation for some controls, and causal interpretability constraints typical of fixed-effects observational designs.

title: Curriculum standardization, central exams and achievement inequalities in primary education: A cross-national longitudinal study
outcome_summary: The study uses PIRLS 2006, 2011, and 2016 microdata for fourth-grade reading literacy across 47 countries (analyzed in 89 country-year units with <30% missingness on key individual variables; ≈430,000 students). It constructs a continuous curriculum standardization index from PIRLS curriculum questionnaires (five items) and an indicator for whether primary education includes national/regional central exams covering the full population. Outcomes are estimated at the country-year level for mean reading achievement (using five PIRLS plausible values), educational poverty (below 400), interindividual inequality (interquartile range), and group gaps by gender and parental tertiary education. The authors then apply a two-step, three-level hierarchical meta-regression with country fixed effects to focus on within-country change over time. Across specifications and a Western-country robustness check, they find little consistent evidence that either curriculum standardization or central exams improve average performance or reduce inequality; apparent positive associations in simpler models attenuate after controls, suggesting limited within-country effects and emphasizing implementation and complementary drivers of early literacy.

title: Reading literacy decline in Europe: Disentangling school closures and out-of-school learning conditions during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Ulrich Ludewig, Rolf Strietholt, Nele McElvany
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2016 and PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 reading literacy across 18 European countries/regions (N = 187,386 students), using PIRLS plausible values for reading literacy and for six out-of-school learning condition constructs. It first documents changes in out-of-school conditions between cohorts (e.g., increases in ECEC participation and school-entry reading skills, and decreases in language of instruction at home, parental reading engagement, printed books, and essential learning conditions). For the adjusted trend (RQ2), it applies propensity score weighting to balance out-of-school learning conditions between 2016 and 2021 and finds the average reading literacy decline reduced from d = −0.16 (observed) to d = −0.11 (adjusted), remaining statistically significant. For the closure-duration association (RQ3), meta-regression shows that the adjusted decline is significantly related to school-closure days, at −0.0015 SDs per day (p = .014), with R2 = .29. Limitations include reliance on observational reweighting (not causal identification) and incomplete coverage of some parental background and remote-learning quality measures.

title: Comparing linear and nonlinear reading assessments in PIRLS 2016
authors: Purya Baghaei, Elpis Grammatikopoulou, Stefan Johansson, Rolf Strietholt
outcome_summary: The study uses PIRLS 2016 (paper-based linear reading) and ePIRLS 2016 (digital nonlinear reading) item-level data for fourth-grade students, restricting to the AUI purpose and to students who completed both tests. Across 16 participating countries/benchmarking entities, the authors estimate and compare unidimensional 2PL, correlated two-factor 2PL, and bifactor (S-1) IRT models using the mirt package in R. In the pooled analysis (n=85,075), the bifactor (S-1) model shows the best fit by AIC/BIC and yields a high general-factor explained common variance (ECV=0.870) alongside a smaller nonlinear-specific ECV (0.120), with general-factor reliability around 0.855 and nonlinear-specific reliability around 0.504. The paper also reports substantial cross-country variation in the nonlinear-specific ECV (e.g., ~0.050 in Singapore vs ~0.185 in Georgia) and notes that PIRLS design confounds delivery mode with construct structure, limiting causal interpretation of “nonlinear reading ability.”
all_datasets_used: PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 AUI (paper) + ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 AUI (digital), pooled across countries
all_target_variables: Latent dimensionality of reading (general vs nonlinear-specific factor)

title: Trends in reading teacher shortage: Using 20 years of evidence from PIRLS
authors: Gratia O'Rafferty, Nurullah Eryilmaz, Alec Kennedy, Rolf Strietholt
outcome_summary: This open-access study uses PIRLS school-questionnaire principal reports from five cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016, 2021) to track reading teacher shortages across 65 education systems. The key outcome is a dichotomized principal-reported shortage impact on schools’ capacity to provide instruction, aggregated into country-year percentages and into country-year-by-school-type percentages for SES (low vs high) and location (rural vs urban). Using fixed-effects regression with country fixed effects, the authors find significant average increases in teacher-shortage concerns in 2011 and 2016 versus 2001 (about +6.86 and +6.72 percentage points), with additional significant increases for low-SES schools (2006/2011/2016) and for both rural and urban schools (2011/2016/2021). The analysis is descriptive/associational (no ML prediction), does not use PV-based achievement outcomes, and does not report a formal missing-data rule for constructed aggregates beyond noting subgroup exclusions in the location model.

title: Evaluation of achievement change in Egypt using PIRLS data
authors: H.A. Patrinos, M. Jakubowski, T. Gajderowicz
outcome_summary: The study uses PIRLS Grade 4 reading microdata for Egypt across the 2016 and 2021 assessment rounds, contrasting Egypt’s change with global time trends estimated from pooled PIRLS rounds (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016, 2021) and then decomposing Egypt’s 2016→2021 gain. Model-based estimates show Egypt’s 2021 reading scores increased by roughly 55–61 points relative to other PIRLS-participating countries, with standard errors computed using jackknife repeated replication (JRR). Heterogeneity analyses indicate the largest gains occurred among the lowest-achieving students, particularly boys (about ~80 points for the lowest boys), alongside a reduction in reading-score dispersion (SD: 123.6→109.9 overall). The Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition attributes only about one-third of the improvement (≈15–18 points out of ≈46–48) to changes in observed explanatory variables, mainly higher SES, while the remainder is unexplained. Limitations include the non-causal design for the reform and reliance on a decomposition sample reduced by missing teacher/principal responses (addressed via chained-equations imputation).

title: Sex differences in variability: Evidence from math and reading assessment in Italy
authors: Lorenzo Esposito, David Giofrè, Enrico Toffalini, David C. Geary
outcome_summary: The study analyzes Italian INVALSI mathematics and reading achievement distributions from 2009–2023 for second-, fifth-, and eighth-grade students, using a meta-analytic approach where the unit of analysis is the province-by-year effect size for boys versus girls. It reports that boys show greater variability in mathematics than girls (overall VR=1.101; log VR=0.097), with VR increasing with the standardized mean difference (SMD) in meta-regression (b=0.271, p<0.001) and with small grade and north–south geographical gradient effects. For reading, variability differences are near zero overall (VR≈0.99–1.02), with SMD showing an opposite-direction association relative to mathematics (b=-0.093, p<0.001) and geographical gradient not significant (p=0.819). The paper does not document plausible-values handling or a missing-data strategy for the underlying INVALSI distributions, and it is not an ML predictive modeling study, so results should be interpreted as distributional evidence rather than causal effects.

title: Research engagement in the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study: A systematic review
authors: Jamie Stiff, Jenny Lenkeit, Therese Hopfenbeck, Heather Kayton, Joshua McGrane
outcome_summary: This systematic review synthesizes 221 PIRLS-related peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2004 and 2022, building on a prior PIRLS review database and adding new studies identified through multi-database searches (ERIC, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, Zetoc) for January 2015–May 2022. The review reports descriptive patterns in the literature rather than predictive modeling results: it quantifies how research engagement has changed over time, which PIRLS cycles are most used (notably 2011 and 2016), and how article “nature” (secondary analysis, critiques, impact/policy) and thematic foci vary. It also summarizes qualitative themes in three areas: teacher characteristics/instruction practices, socioeconomic predictors of reading outcomes, and critiques of PIRLS scaling/IRT practices. Because the study does not train or evaluate ML models on PIRLS microdata, there are no model performance metrics, no survey-weighted estimation, and no plausible-value handling for achievement outcomes.

title: Independent reading in rural China’s elementary schools_ A mixed-methods analysis
authors: Huan Wang, Hongyu Guan, Hongmei Yi, Emma Seevak, Reid Manheim, Matthew Boswell, Scott Rozelle, Sarah Kott
outcome_summary: This mixed-methods study analyzes rural China survey data from 13,232 students in 134 schools across Guizhou and Jiangxi provinces (grades 3–6). The quantitative component uses OLS regressions with county fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors at the school level to correlate independent reading behaviors and book access with standardized reading, math, and Chinese test scores (math/Chinese were randomly assigned within classes to half the students). Across the full models, students who reported spending ≥60 minutes/day on independent reading scored higher in reading (0.14 SD), math (0.13 SD), and Chinese (0.14 SD), while students whose caregivers bought books scored lower in all three domains (reading −0.34 SD; math and Chinese −0.19 SD). The paper reports R-squared values of 0.058 (reading), 0.061 (math), and 0.076 (Chinese). Because the design is explicitly correlational, the authors caution that self-selection may explain associations, and the study does not report a missing-data handling strategy beyond the by-design test assignment.

title: A to Z reading intervention for struggling second graders: a difference-in-differences quasi-experimental evaluation
authors: J. Lopes, P.S. Martins, C. Oliveira
outcome_summary: This study evaluates the “A to Z” (A to Z) reading intervention for struggling second graders in Portugal using a difference-in-differences quasi-experimental design with student fixed effects. The analytic sample includes 1009 second-grade students (182 intervention; 827 control) from 73 schools, with outcomes measured at three evaluation moments across the school year (September, January, May). Four reading-related dependent variables were analyzed: words per minute (WPM), log(WPM), reading accuracy (percentage correct), and reading expressiveness (ordinal 1–5). The intervention produced positive and statistically significant DID effects from Moment 1 to Moment 2 (e.g., +9.03 WPM; +7.09 accuracy points; +3.14 expressiveness units) and from Moment 1 to Moment 3 (e.g., +11.87 WPM; +9.04 accuracy points; +6.23 expressiveness units), with effect sizes around 0.42–0.47 SD for Moments 2 and 3. The paper does not use ILSA/PIRLS achievement PVs and does not report a formal missing-data strategy beyond describing attrition and exclusions; therefore, causal interpretation is limited by non-random assignment and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling.

title: The use of digital devices for schoolwork at home and reading achievement: Multilevel analyses of the PIRLS 2016 U.S. results
authors: Jeeyoung Min, Young S. Seo
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading achievement for the United States (N=4,425) to examine how tablet/computer use for schoolwork at home relates to reading performance. Using multilevel models in Mplus, the authors apply the student weight TOTWGT for national representativeness and handle missing covariate data with full information maximum likelihood (FIML). In the overall models, weekly and daily at-home device use is associated with lower reading achievement compared with non-use (Model 2: B = −8.62 for weekly and B = −24.74 for daily). Gender interactions show that these negative associations are more pronounced for male students than female students. Subgroup analyses by PIRLS 2016 reading benchmarks indicate heterogeneity: high-performing students show a negative association for daily use (B = −3.73), while advanced-performing students show a positive association for monthly use (B = 5.46). The authors caution that cross-sectional associations should not be interpreted causally.

title: The predictive validity of PIRLS and ePIRLS on later academic achievement: Insights from Sweden,
authors: E. Grammatikopoulou
outcome_summary: This study uses PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading scores (paper-based PIRLS and computer-based ePIRLS) in Sweden and examines how they predict later academic achievement measured as teacher-assigned grades in Swedish, English, and Mathematics plus GPA in grades 6 and 9. The results show moderate-to-strong correlations between early reading and later outcomes, with ePIRLS correlations generally slightly higher than PIRLS. In regression models, mean reading achievement is a consistent predictor across subjects and grades (e.g., Swedish Grade 6 β=.630; English Grade 9 β=.568; Mathematics Grade 9 β=.504; GPA Grade 9 β=.510). Adding the digital–paper difference (ePIRLS minus PIRLS) yields small incremental predictive effects mainly for language subjects in grade 6 and for Swedish/English in grade 9, while the digital advantage is not significant for Mathematics and GPA in grade 9. Limitations include optional ePIRLS participation (self-selection) and the lack of reported PV-combination and missing-data handling details, which constrains reproducibility and interpretation of effect sizes.
all_datasets_used: PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (paper) and ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (digital), Sweden
all_target_variables: Swedish grade (Grade 6) | Swedish grade (Grade 9) | English grade (Grade 6) | English grade (Grade 9) | Mathematics grade (Grade 6) | Mathematics grade (Grade 9) | GPA (Grade 6) | GPA (Grade 9)

title: Why are there differences across German states in student achievement and cognitive ability?
authors: H. Rindermann
outcome_summary: This Heliyon study examines differences across the 16 German federal states in student achievement and cognitive ability by aggregating published state-level results from PISA (2000/2003/2006), PIRLS (2001/2006), IQB (2009/2011/2012/2015/2016), and a Bundeswehr intelligence test (1998). The authors compute correlations, regressions, and cross-sectional/longitudinal path models (including cross-lagged effects) on state-level means rather than training ML models on microdata. The combined achievement/ability pattern is highly homogeneous (Cronbach-α = .93), and the strongest associations are with political orientation and education policy: votes/governments for burgher-civic-conservative-right parties correlate positively with cognitive ability (e.g., rCA ≈ +.82 to +.90) and student achievement (rSA ≈ +.78 to +.88), while Klafki proximity is strongly negative (r ≈ −.83). The paper reports standardized path coefficients (e.g., education policy β ≈ .63; education quantity β ≈ .29) and discusses robustness via partial correlations and outlier removal. Limitations include the small N of states, ecological inference risk, and the absence of PV-based estimation and formal missing-data handling for underlying microdata.

title: Reading as a catalyst for creative attitude: evidence from rural China and the cognitive pathways linking literacy and innovation
outcome_summary: This study uses a three-year longitudinal panel (2015–2017) of 3424 fourth-grade students from 120 rural primary schools in Jiangxi Province, China, to examine how reading achievement relates to creative attitude measured by the Creativity Attitude Survey (CAS). Reading achievement is assessed with a PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 reading test aligned to China’s curriculum, including overall standardized reading scores and four comprehension dimensions (retrieval, inferential, integration, evaluation). The main results come from two-way fixed effects models (school and year fixed effects), showing a positive association between reading and creative attitude (0.298 SD), supported by an instrumental-variables estimate using peers’ average standardized reading scores (0.403; first-stage F=25.98). Robustness checks using lagged reading and reading-dimension models also yield positive coefficients, and mechanism/heterogeneity analyses indicate stronger effects in supportive reading environments. Limitations include reliance on IV assumptions for endogeneity, no documented survey-weight use, and missing-data handling not fully specified.

title: The reading rainbow of young multilingual learners: Reading comprehension in the majority (Spanish), regional (Basque) and foreign (English) language
authors: Amparo Lázaro-Ibarrola, María Luquin, Hanne Roothooft
outcome_summary: This study analyzed 199 primary-school learners in Spain from five state-funded schools, comparing high-intensity CLIL exposure (HI; n=118) versus low-intensity Basque-immersion contexts (LI; n=81). Reading comprehension was measured with online tests in English and Spanish for all learners, and in Basque for LI learners; NVI was measured with Raven’s Progressive Matrices, SES via a regional SES questionnaire, and ER via self-reported out-of-school reading time. The key quantitative results show higher English reading in HI than LI (p=.001; d=.548), lower Basque than Spanish in LI (p<.001; d=.612), and strong cross-language correlations. Multiple regression indicated NVI as the most consistent predictor of reading scores (e.g., English HI: R2=.180; β_NVI=.344, p<.001), SES as a secondary predictor mainly in HI, and ER as non-significant across models. Limitations include the absence of PVs/weights (not ILSA microdata), no reported missing-data handling, and no causal identification strategy.

title: The role of home and classroom factors in shaping reading achievement: A multilevel study based on PIRLS 2021 Türkiye data
authors: B. Coşkun, S.A. G̈oktaş
outcome_summary: This study uses PIRLS 2021 Türkiye fourth-grade reading achievement (five plausible values) and estimates two-level multilevel models with students nested within classrooms (Level 1: student/home variables; Level 2: teacher/classroom variables). The analytic sample contains 4745 students from 250 classrooms after exclusions and complete-case handling of missingness (listwise deletion), with additional removal of students whose classroom identifiers could not be linked to the Level-2 file and exclusion of one classroom with inadequate data. The authors applied sampling weights (TOTWGT for students and TCHWGT for classrooms/teachers) and used HLM’s plausible value analysis with Rubin-type combining rules; replicate weights were not incorporated. No machine-learning algorithms were trained; results are reported as multilevel fixed-effect coefficients with robust standard errors. Key findings include significant positive associations for reading self-confidence (γ=12.32, p<.001), home socioeconomic status (γ=9.20, p<.001), early literacy activities (γ=2.75, p<.001), digital self-efficacy (γ=2.00, p<.05), and classroom digital device availability (γ=19.11, p<.05), alongside significant negative associations for bullying (γ≈-13.57, p<.001) and enjoyment of reading (γ≈-1.72, p<.05). Limitations include cross-sectional design (correlational interpretation only) and the additive multilevel specification without cross-level interactions.

title: The application of machine learning approaches in international large-scale educational assessments: A scoping review
authors: Ronnel King, Zhoutiao Li, Faming Wang
outcome_summary: This scoping review synthesizes 57 peer-reviewed empirical studies that applied supervised machine learning to data from international large-scale educational assessments. Across the included studies, the review reports that the most frequently used machine-learning approaches were Random Forests (N=38), boosting algorithms (N=24), and Support Vector Machines (N=23), and that machine learning was used mainly for feature selection/importance analysis (N=54), comparative subgroup analyses (N=16), and model benchmarking for predictive accuracy (N=16). The review also summarizes theoretical frameworks used in the included studies (e.g., socio-ecological theory, PPCT, opportunity-propensity) and highlights strengths such as handling high-dimensional predictors and non-linear relationships. Because this is not an original empirical analysis, no single assessment cycle, country sample, or predictive performance metric is re-estimated here; consequently, limitations relate to the review’s descriptive mapping rather than to model evaluation validity.

title: School-level digital support and reading achievement: Evidence from the PIRLS 2021 U.S. sample
authors: J. Baffoe, D. Asamoah
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2021 U.S. Grade 5 reading achievement using five plausible values (PVs) and a weighted multiple linear regression framework with multiple imputation across PVs. The analytic sample is nationally representative (1657 students from 78 schools). Results show a significant negative main effect of school internet connection on reading achievement (B = –57.07, p < .001) and a significant positive main effect of teacher technological support (B = 58.37, p < .001), with a reported pseudo-R² of .217. Moderation effects indicate that internet access is more effective when students receive early instruction in locating information within texts (Internet × Locating skill: B = 25.28, p < .001), while teacher support is less beneficial when locating instruction is delayed (Teacher support × Locating skill: B = –19.33, p < .001). The authors caution that associations are not causal and that PIRLS measures rely on principal-reported contextual information, with limited school/district granularity and a nested data structure that would ideally be handled with multilevel modeling.

title: Comparing parental and school pressure in terms of their relations with students' well-being
authors: Ruben Kleinkorres, Justine Stang-Rabrig, Nele McElvany
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2021 Germany field test data from 342 fourth graders (17 classes in 17 schools across three federal states) collected in early 2020. Students’ reading achievement was scaled using a 1-PL model and summarized as standardized weighted likelihood estimates (WLE reliability = .86), while students’ school-related well-being was measured with five facets: satisfaction, enjoyment, worries, physical complaints, and social integration. The authors used SEM in R (lavaan) with cluster-robust standard errors for students nested within classes and handled missingness via full information maximum likelihood (FIML). In separate SEMs, school pressure significantly predicted worries (β = 0.27, p < .001) and parental pressure significantly predicted satisfaction (β = -0.17, p = .047), worries (β = 0.26, p = .003), physical complaints (β = 0.13, p = .037), and social integration (β = -0.23, p = .045). When both pressure sources were included simultaneously, pressure effects largely attenuated to non-significance, and academic achievement showed significant negative associations with worries and physical complaints. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and the relatively high missing rates for pressure measures, plus the fact that SEM estimates are not ML predictive performance metrics.
all_datasets_used: PIRLS 2021 Germany Field Test Grade 4 Reading (WLE achievement; early 2020 administration)

title: Reading achievements among students in the United Arab Emirates: A multilevel analysis of PIRLS 2021
authors: Hanada Taha Thomure, Cherry Zin Oo, Myint Swe Khine
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 reading achievement for the United Arab Emirates, restricting the sample to students who took the English-language test (20,537 students in 507 schools). Using a multilevel (hierarchical linear) modeling approach with an unconditional model, a Level-1 student model, and a full Level-2 model, the authors estimate maximum-likelihood coefficients for student- and school-level questionnaire variables. In the final full Level-2 model, socioeconomic status, students’ confidence in reading, and students’ engagement in reading show strong positive associations with reading achievement (e.g., confidence beta = 42.37, p < .001), and girls outperform boys (beta = -5.61, p < .05). At the school level, teacher sending students to the library (beta = 8.88, p < .001) and school character (beta = 47.88, p < .001) are significant, while other school variables are not. The paper does not report a missing-data strategy or explicit PV combination rules, limiting replicability and interpretation of uncertainty.

title: Expecting less in hard times: How the state of the economy influences students’ educational expectations
authors: Jessica L. Arnup, Nicole Black, David W. Johnston
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA microdata for students aged 15–16 from 38 OECD countries across four waves (2003, 2009, 2015, 2018), merged with OECD macroeconomic data on real GDP growth (from the year prior to PISA administration). It estimates within-country fixed-effects regressions with year fixed effects and school-clustered standard errors, using educational expectations converted to expected years of schooling as the main outcome, plus binary indicators for homework, tutoring, and arriving late. The key results show that higher GDP growth is associated with higher educational expectations (e.g., +0.191 expected years per 1 SD higher standardised GDP growth; quintile 5 vs quintile 1: +0.388 years) and that expected returns to education strengthen in expanding economies (interaction term = 0.712, p < 0.001). The paper reports no ML models and does not document a PV-based outcome or a detailed missing-data strategy beyond missing-value indicators, so causal interpretation is limited to associations.

title: Does tracking increase segregation? International evidence on the effects of between-school tracking on social segregation across schools
authors: A. Strello, Rolf Strietholt, Isa Steinmann
outcome_summary: This study uses international large-scale assessment data to examine whether between-school tracking increases socioeconomic segregation across schools. It constructs pseudo-panel country-level datasets by combining primary-level PIRLS (grade 4) and TIMSS (grade 4 Population A) with secondary-level PISA (15-year-olds) and TIMSS (grade 8 Population B), then computes two segregation indices (D and H) from weighted proportions of advantaged vs disadvantaged students based on books at home and parental education. The main results (Table 3) show that early between-school tracking increases segregation: for D based on books at home, the weighted mean effect is 0.058*** (d = 0.892) with PISA secondary data and 0.019* (d = 0.268) with TIMSS Pop. B secondary data; for D based on parental education, effects are 0.026*** (d = 0.400) and 0.042** (d = 0.519), respectively. The approach is difference-in-differences with primary segregation as a control, but causal claims rely on assumptions that cannot be fully tested. Missing socioeconomic indicators are imputed via predictive mean matching (MICE), and robustness checks include school-size restrictions and alternative segregation measures.

title: Explaining the gender gaps in mathematics achievement and attitudes_ The role of societal gender equality
authors: Z. Eylem Gevrek, Deniz Gevrek, Christian Neumeier
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA microdata to explain cross-country gender gaps in mathematics achievement and mathematics-related attitudes through a two-stage semiparametric Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition. For the first stage, it analyzes the 2012 PISA mathematics domain (and 2012 reading for heterogeneity) using PV-averaged test scores and decomposes each country’s mean gender gap into an explained part (accounting for observable student/family characteristics and school fixed effects) and an unexplained part. The unexplained component is statistically significant in most countries for math achievement and math attitudes, generally favoring boys, while reading gaps favor girls in all countries. In the second stage, the authors relate the unexplained components to societal gender equity measures (GGI and domain-specific indicators) using pooled panel data across 2006, 2009, 2012, and 2015 waves for math and reading. They find that composite GGI is not significant, but gender equity in tertiary education access and wage equality significantly predicts a smaller boys-favoring unexplained math gap. Limitations include descriptive (non-causal) interpretation due to potential omitted-variable bias and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling beyond the self-concept index.

title: FairLens: Auditing black-box clinical decision support systems
authors: Cecilia Panigutti, Alan Perotti, André Panisson, Paolo Bajardi, Dino Pedreschi
outcome_summary: The paper introduces FairLens, an auditing pipeline for black-box clinical decision support systems that predict future diagnoses from sequential ICD-9/CCS histories. Using MIMIC-IV ICU data restricted to patients with at least two admissions, the authors train a GRU-based recurrent neural network (DoctorAI) on a training/validation split and audit performance on a held-out test set, excluding first visits when no prior history exists. Global model performance is reported via recall@k (0.481 @10, 0.623 @20, 0.712 @30). FairLens stratifies patients by Gender, Ethnicity, Age group, and Insurance type, then computes group disparity using Wasserstein distance between predicted and ground-truth CCS code distributions (disparity@k, default disparity@30). In the synthetic-bias validation, disparity@20/@30 increases for the under-sampled “Other” insurance group even when standard metrics (recall@k and microAUC) remain almost constant, highlighting the added value of group-disparity auditing. The study does not document missing-data handling in the provided text and does not use survey weights, limiting direct generalization beyond the MIMIC-IV setting.

title: Impacts of generative AI on student teachers' task performance and collaborative knowledge construction process in mind mapping-based collaborative environment
authors: S. An, S. Zhang, T. Guo, S. Lu, W. Zhang, Z. Cai
outcome_summary: This quasi-experimental study in a 2023 higher-education course (Pedagogical Applications of Information Technology) compared 10 student-teacher groups (n=30 students; 5 control MMCE, 5 experimental GMMCE) using a mind-mapping-based collaborative environment with or without the generative AI tool ERNIE Bot. Task performance was assessed via group product ratings on the TPACK gauge: GMMCE significantly outperformed MMCE on the instructional design (ID) task (M=28.8 vs 21.8; Mann–Whitney U=3.000, p=0.047), while differences on the multimedia courseware (MD) task were not significant (M=29.4 vs 24.6; U=4.000, p=0.076). Collaborative knowledge construction was analyzed with Ordered Network Analysis (ONA) on coded discourse transitions, showing GMMCE shifts toward cognitive negotiation/consensus patterns across stages. Student-teacher interviews indicated higher perceived usefulness for ID revisions than for MD, with limitations tied to ERNIE Bot’s constrained multimodal understanding. No ILSA PVs or survey weights were used; missing-data handling and any weighting strategy are not reported, and the evidence is limited to a single-site, small sample.

title: The effects of ICT-based social media on adolescents' digital reading performance: A longitudinal study of PISA 2009, PISA 2012, PISA 2015 and PISA 2018
authors: Jie Hu, Rushi Yu
outcome_summary: This longitudinal study analyzes PISA computer-based reading performance for 15-year-olds across four cycles (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018), covering 767,511 students from 57 participating countries/regions. The dependent variable is PISA-provided plausible values (5 PVs in 2009/2012; 10 PVs in 2015/2018), combined with multiple imputation for missing questionnaire data (predictive mean matching) and pooled using Rubin’s rules. The authors fit hierarchical linear models (random intercept, fixed slopes) to account for the nested student–school–country structure and report fixed-effect estimates (Gamma) with t-tests and p-values; no predictive ML metrics (AUC/RMSE) are reported because the analysis is not ML-based. Across cycles, recreational email, browsing for fun, and reading online news tend to be positive, while chatting and social-network gaming are often negative; perceived usefulness of social media is consistently positive. Limitations include reliance on frequency-based ICT/social media measures, cycle-specific questionnaire revisions, and the observational nature of PISA (no causal identification).

title: Does greater community involvement mean more parent-teacher interaction? Evidence from seven developing countries
authors: M. Hossain
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA-D 2015 data for seven low- and lower-middle-income countries (Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Cambodia, Senegal, Zambia) to examine whether school-based management community involvement is associated with parent-teacher interaction. The outcome is teacher-reported parent demand for personal meetings about students’ progress, converted to a school-level proportion (percentage of teachers receiving requests) and analyzed with country-specific OLS regressions (robust standard errors), with GLM logit models as robustness checks. Across models, community involvement is not significant in most specifications, while school ownership (private vs public) is significant in six of seven countries; instructional resources are significant when ownership is excluded but largely lose significance once ownership is included, consistent with mediation. SES does not moderate the ownership effect, but it moderates the resources effect in Guatemala, Honduras, and Senegal. The analysis is observational and relies on imputation for missing independent variables; the paper does not provide PV-handling details because the focus is on a non-PV outcome.
all_datasets_used: PISA-D 2015 (15-year-olds), seven countries; outcome from teacher questionnaire (meeting demand proportion)

title: National contexts and information and communication technology in education: A systematic review of PISA studies
authors: Minju Kim, Pey-Yan Liou
outcome_summary: This article is a systematic review of PISA-based studies examining how student- and country-level ICT factors relate to learning outcomes, and how national contexts moderate these relationships. It does not re-analyze PISA microdata; instead, it screens and codes 29 peer-reviewed English-language studies from Web of Science using PRISMA procedures. Across the included studies, the review reports that most evidence concerns cognitive outcomes (reading, mathematics, science), with fewer studies addressing affective and behavioral outcomes. The review synthesizes patterns such as generally positive associations for ICT attitudes (e.g., self-confidence, competence, interest, autonomy) and more mixed or often negative associations for ICT access/use depending on context (home vs school; classroom lessons vs outside lessons). It also summarizes country-level variance using reported ICC ranges and describes moderation types (facilitating, diminishing, buffering, exacerbating, minimal). Because no pooled ML model or PV-based scaling is estimated in this paper, the findings are descriptive of the literature rather than effect-size estimates from a unified dataset.

title: Public and private school efficiency and equity in Latin America: New evidence based on PISA for development
authors: M. Delprato, G. Antequera
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA for Development (PISA-D) 2017 data for four Latin American countries—Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Paraguay—restricted to students at grade 7 (15 years old) or above, then merged across student, teacher, and school/principal questionnaires. The analysis is conducted at the school level (705 schools: 207 private, 498 public) using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with outputs defined as school mean math, reading, and science scores based on the first plausible value (PV1) for each subject. Technical efficiency is estimated with variable returns to scale and bias-corrected via homogeneous bootstrapping (2000 repetitions), yielding mean bias-corrected efficiency of 0.88 for private schools and 0.82 for public schools in the pooled region. Second-stage regressions (Simar–Wilson two-stage DEA) relate efficiency to student, teacher, and school characteristics and to inequality/policy indicators. The paper does not report a missing-data handling strategy and does not describe the use of PISA-D sampling weights, so results should be interpreted as efficiency comparisons based on the constructed school sample rather than fully survey-weighted population estimates.

title: School efficiency in low and middle income countries: An analysis based on PISA for development learning survey
authors: M. Delprato, G. Antequera
outcome_summary: The study uses the 2017 PISA for Development (PISA-D) learning survey at grade 7 (15-year-olds) or above in seven LMIC/economies (Cambodia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Senegal, Zambia). It merges student, teacher, and school/principal questionnaires and conducts a two-stage Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA): first estimating output-oriented technical efficiency frontiers for cognitive outcomes (math/reading/science using the first plausible value) and for non-cognitive outcomes (factor-derived indices of socialisation, attitudes, and feelings), then regressing bias-corrected efficiency scores on student, teacher, school, policy, and inequality indicators. Across 1180 schools, mean TEBC is 0.801 for cognitive and 0.782 for non-cognitive, implying potential efficiency gains of about 20–22% with inputs held constant. The paper reports bootstrap confidence intervals and marginal effects with bootstrapped standard errors, but it does not provide explicit survey-weight usage; results are therefore best interpreted as associations rather than causal effects, consistent with the cross-sectional nature of PISA-D.

title: Examining the relationship between online chatting and PISA reading literacy trends (2000-2018)
authors: Hans Luyten
outcome_summary: This study analyzes country-level trend changes in PISA reading literacy for 15-year-olds across 2000–2018, focusing on shifts after 2009. The authors first estimate per-country reading literacy trend changes using multilevel modeling with cross-sectional repeated measures, then compute correlations and a path model (lavaan) among four focal constructs: online chatting trend change, reading fiction trend change, reading strategies awareness change (available only for 2009–2018), and reading literacy trend change. Across 39 countries (weighted by standardized country weights derived from W_FSTUWT), the strongest correlation is between online chatting and reading literacy trend changes (r = −0.698, p < 0.001). In the path model, online chatting has a negative direct effect on reading literacy (β = −0.378, p = 0.009), while reading fiction and reading strategies have positive effects (β = 0.219, p = 0.005; β = 0.386, p = 0.007). The model explains 64.1% of variance and shows favorable fit (χ² p = 0.998), but the design is correlational and uses country aggregates, so causal claims about individual students cannot be inferred.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2000–2018 Reading literacy (15-year-olds; country-level trend changes after 2009)

title: Teachers’ perceived societal appreciation: PISA outcomes predict whether teachers feel valued in society
authors: B. Spruyt, et al.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 (lower secondary, ISCED 2) teacher survey data from 25 countries/regions, 4,307 schools, and 66,593 teachers, with PSA measured on a 4-point Likert scale. It estimates three-level multilevel linear regression models (teacher, school, country) and reports standardized coefficients (Table 2), showing that satisfaction with salary is the strongest individual-level correlate of PSA (β=0.24, p≤0.001), while job satisfaction (β=0.10, p≤0.001) and participation in school policy (β=0.07, p≤0.001) also relate positively. At the country level, higher PISA science performance is positively associated with PSA (β=0.14, p≤0.10), with similar patterns for other PISA domains but weaker statistical support. For within-country change, correlations between PSA change (2018 vs 2013) and multiple PISA-change indicators yield a mean correlation of 0.29 and 14/20 significant correlations (one-tailed; p<0.01). The paper is correlational (no causal identification) and does not document survey-weight usage; additionally, PSA is not PV-based, so PV handling is not applicable.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (2018) Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — Perceived societal appreciation (PSA) | TALIS 2018 (2018) Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — Change in PSA (2018 vs 2013)
all_target_variables: Perceived societal appreciation (PSA) among teachers | Change in perceived societal appreciation (PSA) between 2013 and 2018

title: Adolescents want to be teachers? Affecting factors and two-decade trends in 39 educational systems
authors: L. Guo, K.-T. Hau
outcome_summary: The study analyzes two-decade trends in adolescents’ expectations to become teachers using OECD PISA microdata from 2000 and 2018 for 15-year-olds, focusing on 39 economies where teaching-expectation data were available in both cycles. The outcome is an open-ended ISCO-coded job expectation recoded dichotomously (expected teacher vs not), and predictors include ESCS, reading achievement, a combined math/science achievement measure (MS), enjoyment of reading, self-efficacy, parents’ teaching careers, family support, teacher support, and teacher enthusiasm (2018 only). The authors estimate multilevel logistic regression models with school-level random effects, apply multiple imputation for missing predictors, and use all plausible values for achievement outcomes combined via Rubin’s rules. They report predicted probabilities (Pr) and descriptive trend percentages rather than ML metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE), and the paper does not train ML algorithms; therefore, results are predictive associations and cannot establish causality.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2000 & 2018 (15-year-olds), Reading and MS achievement (combined) — 39 economies
all_target_variables: Teaching career expectation (dichotomous: expected teacher vs not)

title: The correspondence between PISA performance and school achievement in Finland
authors: Jonna Pulkkinen, Jari Rautopuro
outcome_summary: The study links Finnish PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 (grade 9, ages 15) to national register grades from end-of-basic-education certificates, using PISA proficiency levels in reading, mathematics, and science as predictors of corresponding subject grades. It first reports Pearson correlations between PISA proficiency scores and grades, finding correlations around 0.60 across domains (e.g., up to r=0.66 for science-related grades in 2015) and also non-corresponding grade correlations, suggesting limited discriminant validity. It then estimates ordinary least-squares regressions separately for each domain, using PISA proficiency levels (Model 1) and adding gender and ESCS (Model 2), concluding that PISA levels predict grades even after controlling for SES. The analysis uses PISA complex survey design with student final weights and 80 replicate weights and handles 10 plausible values by running analyses for each PV and aggregating. A key limitation is that linking external register data may bias PV-based estimates because PV estimation does not incorporate the added information, so results should be interpreted as predictive/associational rather than causal.

title: Tailoring a measurement model of socioeconomic status: Applying the alignment optimization method to 15 years of PISA
authors: V. Rolfe
outcome_summary: This paper is not an ML prediction study; it develops and validates a Sweden-specific measurement model of socioeconomic status (SES) using PISA background questionnaire items across six PISA cycles (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015). The authors first quantify change in item means over time (e.g., small declines for textbooks/books/poetry and a moderate increase for internet connectivity), then estimate a sequence of confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) models in Mplus and refine the final single-factor SES model (Model 3) using modification indices from the 2000 cycle. Measurement invariance testing shows configural and metric invariance are acceptable, while scalar invariance fails (scalar model fit: RMSEA=0.081, CFI=0.825). To enable cross-time comparisons despite non-scalar invariance, they apply alignment optimization, reporting trustworthy alignment via Monte Carlo simulations (factor-mean correlation r≈0.993 for n=5,000 and r≈0.997 for n=15,000). The study’s implication is that legacy home-possessions items can support a temporally stable SES construct in Sweden, but researchers should use alignment/measurement-model validation rather than assuming ESCS comparability across cycles.

title: Income inequality is associated with heightened test anxiety and lower academic achievement: A cross-national study in 51 countries
authors: Ronnel B. King, Yuyang Cai, Andrew J. Elliot
outcome_summary: This cross-national study analyzed OECD PISA 2015 data for 389,215 fifteen-year-old students across 51 countries to test whether national income inequality (Gini, 2014) is associated with test anxiety and achievement in reading, mathematics, and science. The authors used multilevel SEM in Mplus with random slopes to evaluate direct effects, mediation (test anxiety as mediator), and cross-level moderation (inequality strengthening the anxiety–achievement link), while accounting for school-level clustering. Results showed that income inequality significantly predicted higher test anxiety (β = 0.67, p < .001), and test anxiety significantly predicted lower achievement in all three domains (reading β = −0.08; math β = −0.10; science β = −0.10; all p < .001). Income inequality had a significant negative association with math achievement (β = −0.32, p < .001) but not reading or science after covariates, and mediation/moderation hypotheses were not supported. Limitations include cross-sectional design and incomplete reporting of PV/missing-data handling and survey-weight application, which constrains reproducibility and causal interpretation.

title: Education systems and social background inequality of educational opportunity: New evidence
authors: Yongxiang Xie
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students across 49 countries to examine how education-system features moderate the relationship between family background (ESCS) and academic achievement. Achievement is constructed from PISA plausible values by taking weighted averages across the 10 PVs for mathematics, reading, and science, then averaging across domains into an overall score. The analysis applies a country fixed-effects model with clustered standard errors at the school level, estimating interactions between ESCS and two system indicators: SGUSE (high vs. low stratification) and HST (presence of standardized, selective lower-to-upper transition exams). Results show that ESCS has a positive association with achievement and that ESCS×SGUSE and ESCS×HST interactions are statistically significant (Model 1: ESCS×SGUSE=6.832***; Model 2: ESCS×SGUSE=4.108*** and ESCS×HST=9.188***; R²≈0.47; N=181,727). Limitations include the lack of an explicit missing-data strategy and the fact that the approach is not ML predictive modeling (no ML algorithms, weights, or PV-combining method beyond PV averaging are reported).

title: School efficiency in Latin America before and after the COVID-19 pandemic: New evidence from PISA 2018 and 2022
authors: Marcos Delprato, Germán Antequera
outcome_summary: This study analyzes school efficiency in Latin America and the Caribbean using OECD PISA 2018 and PISA 2022. It constructs school-level DEA production-frontier models where outputs are school-average math, reading, and science scores using PV1 (first of ten plausible values), and inputs include family SES, physical and educational school infrastructure, and the student–teacher ratio. The pooled working sample covers nine countries with 2,552 schools in 2018 and 2,417 schools in 2022. Average bias-corrected technical efficiency (TEBC) is 0.753 in 2018 and 0.781 in 2022, with overlapping confidence intervals, implying no statistical shift in regional efficiency. Second-stage bootstrap regressions show that efficiency is higher when within-school inequality and exclusion are lower (e.g., Gini and level-1-or-below have negative marginal effects), and that COVID-19 engagement/support policies and ICT access are positively associated with efficiency. Limitations include correlational (not causal) interpretation from cross-sectional PISA and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling and survey-weight usage.

title: Adolescent Loneliness Trends and Contextual Correlates Across 38 Countries From 2000 to 2022
outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD PISA loneliness data for 15- and 16-year-olds across 38 countries and survey years 2000, 2003, 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2022 (final analytic population: 1,267,476 after excluding students who skipped any loneliness items). Loneliness is measured as a weighted mean of 6 (or 5 in 2022) sense-of-belonging items on a 4-point Likert scale. The authors use weighted multilevel piecewise regression to estimate time trends and Fairbrother-style decomposition to separate between-country and within-country associations. Adjusted loneliness trends show a non-significant slight decrease from 2000–2012 (beta=-0.007) followed by a significant increase from 2012–2015 (beta=0.045) and a smaller increase from 2015–2022 (beta=0.017). For correlates, COVID-19 mortality and stringency in 2022 are near zero and non-significant, while within-country increases in internet use (2012–2018) and unemployment (2000–2022) are associated with lower loneliness. Limitations include reliance on observational associations (no causality) and no explicit missing-data strategy beyond loneliness-item exclusion.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2000-2022 (15- and 16-year-olds), loneliness scale (sense of belonging questionnaire) | PISA 2022 (15- and 16-year-olds), loneliness scale (sense of belonging questionnaire)

title: The role of knowledge-rich curricula in promoting deep thinking and complex skill acquisition
authors: Claudio Vanhees, Jasper Nijlunsing, Daniel Muijs, Nuno Crato, Michiel Wils, Dylan Wiliam, Tim Surma, Paul A. Kirschner
outcome_summary: This article is not an empirical large-scale assessment study; it is a conceptual synthesis arguing that knowledge-rich curricula support deep thinking and complex cognitive skill acquisition. It does not analyze TIMSS/PISA/PIRLS microdata with machine learning or statistical models, and it does not report PV-based achievement modeling, missing-data treatment, or survey-weighted estimation. Instead, it draws on prior experimental and longitudinal evidence (e.g., knowledge-rich curricular interventions) and uses descriptive policy examples from countries such as Portugal and England, referencing trends in external assessments (PISA/TIMSS) to motivate the argument. Because no student-level predictive pipeline is estimated, there are no model performance metrics (e.g., RMSE/AUC) to extract, and causal claims cannot be evaluated within this paper’s own methods. The main contribution is policy-relevant: it translates cognitive-science principles (schemas, working memory limits) into curriculum design principles (content-richness, coherence, clarity).

title: The association between private tutoring and mathematics learning outcomes in primary and secondary schools: A three-level meta-analysis
authors: Yuhuan Zhang, Lijin Liu, Zijing Wang, Lidong Wang
outcome_summary: This paper is a three-level meta-analysis (not an ML prediction study) synthesizing 76 empirical studies published between 2000 and 2024, yielding 202 effect sizes for cognitive mathematics outcomes and 36 for non-cognitive outcomes. Across the included evidence, private tutoring shows a statistically significant but small positive association with overall mathematics learning outcomes (r = 0.110, p < 0.01). For cognitive outcomes, the association is stronger (r = 0.144, p < 0.01), driven primarily by mathematics achievement (r = 0.145, p < 0.01) rather than mathematics ability (r = 0.082, p > 0.05). No significant association is found for non-cognitive outcomes overall (r = 0.019, p > 0.05), and no moderator effects are detected for non-cognitive outcomes. Moderation analyses indicate significant heterogeneity for cognitive outcomes by test type (school tests only: r = 0.289, p < 0.001), school stage (secondary stronger: r = 0.206, p < 0.001), and geographical location (Asia: r = 0.189, p < 0.01). Limitations include reliance on reported statistics from primary studies and the inability to infer causal effects from correlational effect sizes.
all_datasets_used: ILSA literature synthesis (systematic review; no single student-level analytic micro-dataset)

title: Expectancy-value-cost motivational profiles in biology and physics: Their relations with gender, self-reported satisfaction of needs, and learning behavior
authors: Eve Kikas, Ita Puusepp, Kati Aus
outcome_summary: This study used a school-based assessment in Estonia (34 schools; N=1502; Grades 8–9) to identify latent expectancy–value–cost motivational profiles in biology and physics and to examine how these profiles relate to gender, perceived teacher need-support/need-thwarting, task persistence, and deep learning strategy use. The authors estimated a latent profile analysis with TYPE = COMPLEX clustered by classroom and selected a six-profile solution using AIC/BIC/aBIC, entropy (0.81), and VLMR (0.199). They found that most students belonged to subject-general profiles (Moderate 41%, Adaptive 30%, Maladaptive 9%, Indifferent 3%), while smaller subject-specific profiles existed (Biology-Adaptive 9%, Physics-Adaptive 8%). Significant profile differences emerged for teacher perceptions (all omnibus χ2 p<.001), task persistence (biology χ2=733.15; physics χ2=591.41), and deep strategy use (χ2=124.97). Limitations include reliance on self-report measures, voluntary participation, and no reported missing-data handling; results are cross-sectional, so motivational–behavior associations cannot be interpreted causally.

title: Managing Artificial Intelligence in Archeology. An overview
authors: G. Gattiglia
outcome_summary: This article is a conceptual overview of how artificial intelligence (including machine learning and deep learning) is used in archaeology, focusing on post-digitality, transparency, ethics, and technical challenges. It does not use any ILSA or national large-scale assessment micro-data (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS/NAEP) and does not define an assessment cycle, grade, or achievement domain. Consequently, there are no predictive targets, no trained ML models evaluated on an ILSA dataset, and no performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, AUC, RMSE) reported from an empirical modeling exercise. The paper discusses example accuracies from archaeological AI applications in general terms, but these are not tied to an ILSA dataset and are not part of a reproducible large-scale assessment analysis. Limitations therefore concern the absence of measurement, sampling, weighting, and missing-data procedures typical of ILSA-based empirical studies.

title: The ’picking the fittest’ approach and spatial dynamics in China’s artificial intelligence regional development
authors: Saverio Barabuffi, Jacopo Cricchio, Alberto Di Minin
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes a panel of 30 Chinese provincial-level regions from 2006–2021, using AI patenting performance (AI-related invention patents per million population from CNIPA) as the outcome and ICT specialization (RTA ICT based on ICT-related patent shares, standardized and smoothed with a three-year moving average) as the key explanatory variable. In fixed-effects and 2SLS specifications, ICT specialization is positively and significantly associated with AI patenting, with larger effects in candidate AI development zone regions (2SLS: RTA ICT β=0.6705 for AI zones; β=0.4984 for non-AI zones, both p<0.01). Spatial econometric results show negative inter-regional spillovers: the SAR spatial lag coefficient is β=−0.2162 (p<0.05) and remains negative in the control-function SAR (β=−0.2064, p<0.05). The study does not use ML algorithms or PVs, and it does not report a missing-data handling strategy, so transparency on data completeness is limited.

title: 1-s2.0-S2666374022000437-main
authors: R. Muench, O. Wieczorek
outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2000, 2009, and 2015 microdata for the UK (excluding Scotland in all waves; excluding Wales in 2000) and Germany, using the imputed PISA mean score across reading, mathematics, and science as the dependent variable. It estimates multilevel regression models with student- and school-level predictors, applying multiple imputation for missing data and OECD-provided student weights to correct standard errors and variance decomposition. Across all three waves, socioeconomic status is consistently associated with performance, but school-level socioeconomic inequality (school mean ESCS) is substantially stronger than student-level ESCS, with large model fit (e.g., Germany R2 full model ≈0.48 in 2000; UK ≈0.315 in 2000) and significant ICCs indicating between-school homogeneity. Governance variables (autonomy, leadership, accountability) show little explanatory power and do not remove socioeconomic associations. Limitations include the correlational design and potential bias from differential PISA participation coverage in the UK versus Germany, which the authors discuss as possibly affecting achievement-gap estimates.
