all_target_variables: PISA mean score (imputed across reading, mathematics, science)

title: Explorando la relación entre las actitudes ante las ciencias y el rendimiento en PISA
authors: G. Bidegain, J.F. Lukas Mujika
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 science literacy and four attitude indices (SEFISCI, PARTSCI, INTSCI, JOYSCI) using country-level means across 72 PISA participating countries/economies and Spain’s 17 autonomous communities. Rather than training ML models, it applies bivariate correlations plus Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and quantile regression to characterize how attitude–achievement relationships vary across the science-performance distribution. Across countries, OLS shows significant negative linear relationships (p < .05) with slopes ranging from −41 (SEFISCI) to −88 (JOYSCI), and PARTSCI correlates strongly negatively with science achievement (r = −.73). Quantile regression indicates that the negative association weakens at higher performance quantiles, with PARTSCI and JOYSCI slopes near zero (Qrm vs OLSrm: PARTSCI F = 2.09, p = .035; JOYSCI F = 3.43, p = .0007). Limitations include ecological inference risk from aggregated means and lack of documented PV/missing-data handling because the analysis uses released aggregated indices rather than student-level PV draws.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 Science literacy (national means; grades 7+) | PISA 2015 Science literacy (Spain regional means; 17 regions)

title: Effects of social cues of artificial intelligence-powered pedagogical agents: A multilevel meta-analysis
authors: Shunan Zhang, Yincen Li, Guangji Gan, Stevany, Sirui Pang, Jang Hyun Kim
outcome_summary: This multilevel meta-analysis (Educational Research Review, 2025) synthesizes 33 primary studies evaluating how social cues in AI-powered pedagogical agents (AIPAs) affect learning. The authors pooled a total of 185 effect sizes using a three-level random-effects meta-analytic approach (sampling error, within-study heterogeneity, and between-study heterogeneity) estimated via restricted maximum likelihood in R (metafor). Across outcomes, social cues showed statistically detectable positive effects on cognitive learning outcomes (g = 0.359, SE = 0.084, P < .001, 95% CI [0.191, 0.526]), affective learning outcomes (g = 0.519, SE = 0.147, P < .001, 95% CI [0.226, 0.812]), and behavioral learning outcomes (g = 0.458, SE = 0.139, P = .003, 95% CI [0.169, 0.746]). Cognitive load showed no detectable effect (g = 0.039, SE = 0.086, P = .663, 95% CI [−0.153, 0.230]). Moderators for cognitive outcomes included agent form, anthropomorphism, instructional setting, interaction type, and educational level; affective outcomes were moderated by publication type. Limitations include reliance on reported summary statistics from heterogeneous primary studies and no student-level PV/survey-weight framework.

title: A long road to educational equity: Tracking trends through PISA 2000–2018
authors: Ekaterina Enchikova, Tiago Neves, Cibelle Toledo, Gil Nata
outcome_summary: This paper conducts a secondary, country-level trend analysis of socioeconomic equity in education using PISA 2000–2018. The authors extract OECD-published R-squared indicators (the share of variance in PISA scores explained by ESCS) for Reading, Mathematics, and Science for each participating country, then compute an average R-squared across subjects as the main equity indicator. They fit simple linear regressions per country to estimate the direction and magnitude of equity change over time (year coded from 2000 onward), and they report standard errors and statistical significance when at least three observations are available. Across 87 countries (with 71 having at least two waves), more countries show positive equity trends than negative, but most trends are not statistically robust due to limited observations and periodic fluctuations. The study finds that the OECD average R-squared decreased from 15% to 12.8% between 2000 and 2018, while equity improvements are concentrated in a subset of countries (e.g., Malaysia shows a significant negative trend; several OECD and partner countries show significant positive trends). Limitations include reliance on a single equity indicator (R-squared), potential comparability issues across PISA waves, and the absence of student-level modeling (so no PV-based estimation or ML prediction performance is evaluated).

title: PISA 2022 insights on intellectual curiosity, perspective-taking, and science achievement: Examining the mediating pathways
authors: Othman Abu Khurma, Adeeb Jarrah, Nagla Ali
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 secondary data for UAE students (initial N=24,600; reduced to 21,510 after outlier screening) to examine whether intellectual curiosity predicts science achievement and whether perspective-taking mediates this relationship. Missingness was handled using EM-based imputation with Little’s MCAR test indicating non-random missingness (Chi-Square=242,472.600, DF=235,009, Sig.=0.000), and the authors report reliability/validity for the three constructs in a measurement model. Using SmartPLS 4 SEM-PLS with bootstrapping (5,000 resamples), the model shows R-square=0.09 for Science achievement. Intellectual curiosity has a significant direct effect on Science achievement (β=0.19, T=22.57, p=0) and a significant indirect effect through perspective-taking (β=0.09, T=18.69, p=0), while perspective-taking also directly predicts Science achievement (β=0.15, T=18.98, p=0). The paper does not report the use of PISA sampling/replicate weights, and the cross-sectional design constrains causal claims.

title: Change in socioeconomic educational equity after 20 years of PISA: A systematic literature review
authors: Ekaterina Enchikova, Tiago Neves, Cibelle Toledo, Gil Nata
outcome_summary: This paper is a systematic literature review (not an empirical ML study) examining how quantitative PISA-based research has assessed change in socioeconomic educational equity over roughly 20 years. The review protocol follows Petticrew & Roberts (2008) and PRISMA (Page et al., 2021), searching EBSCO, Web of Science, and Scopus, and updating the search in March 2024. It includes 33 original quantitative articles plus 5 official OECD PISA reports, covering PISA waves from 2000 to 2022 (and OECD comparisons using subject-rotated waves such as 2000–2009 for Reading, 2003–2012 for Mathematics, and 2006–2015 for Science). The synthesis finds no clear overall trend of equity improvement across participating countries, with substantial heterogeneity by equity dimension (opportunity, outcome, resilience, segregation) and by time frame. Limitations include reliance on how primary studies define and code “change” (often with weak or missing objective cut-off criteria) and the fact that the review does not re-estimate equity indices from microdata.

title: Conversation-based assessment: A novel approach to boosting test-taking effort in digital formative assessment
authors: S.N. Yildirim-Erbasli, O. Bulut
outcome_summary: This article is not an empirical large-scale assessment study; it is a conceptual discussion proposing conversation-based assessment (CBA) as a solution to non-effortful test-taking in low-stakes formative contexts. It does not analyze PISA (or any other ILSA) micro-data, does not define an analytic sample, and does not estimate predictive models or report performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, RMSE, AUC). Instead, it synthesizes prior literature on conversational agents, assessment formats (selected- and constructed-response), and the role of motivation/test-taking effort in validity threats. Because no dataset, countries, or ML pipeline are evaluated, there are no benchmarks to compare and no methodological details on PV handling, missing-data treatment, or survey-weight application. The main contribution is a policy/practice-oriented design perspective: CBA could be integrated into classroom and potentially large-scale low-stakes assessments to increase engagement and effort, though causal effects must be tested in future empirical studies.

title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence in K-12 education (2017–2022)
authors: F. Martin, Min Zhuang, Darlene Schaefer
outcome_summary: This systematic review (PRISMA-guided) synthesizes 66 peer-reviewed studies on AI in K-12 education published between 2017 and May 2022. It does not conduct a new student-level predictive modeling analysis on any single ILSA dataset; instead, it reports descriptive synthesis of publication trends, research methodologies, AI themes, data collection methods, and AI techniques used across included studies. The review finds that publication volume increased after 2018, with the United States and China leading by number of included studies, and that qualitative methods were most common among the reviewed studies. Across the synthesized literature, supervised learning dominated, while unsupervised and reinforcement learning were comparatively rare. Reported performance metrics (e.g., accuracies) appear only within the included studies’ examples rather than being re-estimated or meta-analyzed here, and the review does not provide ILSA-specific PV handling, missing-data procedures, or survey-weighted estimation.

title: What do university students know about Artificial Intelligence? Development and validation of an AI literacy test
authors: M. Hornberger, et al.
outcome_summary: The paper develops and validates a theory-based AI literacy knowledge test for German university students using a 30-item multiple-choice instrument plus a sorting task (steps of machine learning). The validation sample comprised N=1286 students recruited from six universities in southern Germany, after excluding 44 invalid cases (high missingness in the AI literacy test and implausibly fast completion). Measurement was analyzed with IRT, comparing Rasch, 2-PL, and 3-PL models; the 3-PL model showed the best fit (M2=815.5581, RMSEA=0.026, SRMR=0.039, TLI=0.964, CFI=0.966) and acceptable reliability (EAP r=0.85; Cronbach’s α=0.82). Validity evidence included significant correlations with AI self-efficacy, interest, and attitudes, and group differences by prior AI learning and discipline. Limitations include voluntary sampling and correlational validity evidence rather than causal inference.
all_datasets_used: AI literacy test validation (German university students; 6 universities; web-based pilot/validation)

title: The impact of the pandemic and school closures on non-cognitive characteristics: Evidence from PISA
authors: Jose Wilmar Quintero Pena, Louis Volante, Kristof De Witte
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA non-cognitive outcomes across 2012–2022 (sense of belonging) and 2018–2022 (growth mindset and frequently bullied) for Canada, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, and a set of European countries. Using weighted OLS regressions with country fixed effects, time trends, and OECD-recommended Balance Repeated Replication (RBB) procedures (standard errors clustered at the school level), the authors compare the 2022 cohort to earlier cohorts via a COVID-19 indicator. They find a short-term decline in sense of belonging (e.g., −0.040 SD for 2018–2022) but evidence of recovery in longer comparisons, a significant decline in growth mindset (COVID coefficient around −0.080 SD), and a significant reduction in the likelihood of being frequently bullied (about −0.050 in the 2018–2022 comparison). The paper does not report a missing-data strategy, and the analysis is not ML-based (no predictive algorithms or PV handling), limiting interpretability for causal claims about mechanisms.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2012–2022 (pooled), non-cognitive: sense of belonging (BELONG) | PISA 2018–2022 (pooled), non-cognitive: growth mindset | PISA 2018–2022 (pooled), non-cognitive: being frequently bullied
all_target_variables: Sense of belonging (BELONG index) | Growth mindset (standardized fixed-growth mindset proxy) | Being frequently bullied (binary, last decile of bullying index)

title: AI in essay-based assessment: Student adoption, usage, and performance
authors: David Smerdon
outcome_summary: This open-access case study examines AI tool adoption and its association with performance in an undergraduate economics research-proposal essay assessment in Australia (2023 cohort). The quantitative analysis uses a voluntary survey merged with administrative grading data for 69 students (two-thirds of respondents reported using AI). The main regression models predict the overall research-proposal mark (0–100) and five criterion subscores using “Used AI” plus ability controls (pre-semester GPA and earlier course test scores). The unconditional model shows a small, non-significant positive association (+5.391 marks), while models with ability controls estimate effects of less than 1 mark and report no significant AI effects on any criterion. The study also includes an intention-to-treat style cohort comparison (2023 vs 2022) and finds no evidence of performance gains. Limitations include non-random AI use, survey response bias (respondents were higher GPA), and no documented missing-data handling; moreover, the paper uses linear regression rather than ML algorithms.
all_datasets_used: Undergraduate economics research proposal (Australia, 2023 cohort; essay-based assessment)
all_target_variables: Final research proposal mark (0–100) | Individual marking criteria subscores (scaled out of 100)

title: Developing and validating measures for AI literacy tests: From self-reported to objective measures
authors: T.K.F. Chiu, Yifan Chen, King Woon Yau, Ching-sing Chai, Helen Meng, Irwin King, Savio Wong, Yeung Yam
outcome_summary: This paper develops and validates an objective AI literacy test for K–12 (grades 7–9) using a curriculum co-design process (AI4Future) and psychometric validation rather than predictive ML. The analytic sample includes 2,380 students from six Hong Kong secondary schools who completed a 30-minute online test consisting of 25 binary-scored multiple-choice items. Using a Rasch model in WINSTEPS, the authors report moderate internal consistency (KR-20/Cronbach’s alpha = 0.7), person separation coefficients below 2 (limited spread), and high item separation/reliability (item reliability coefficient approximately 1). Item fit statistics show infit mean squares and outfit mean squares mostly near the ideal value of 1.0 (IMNSQ ~0.89–1.16; OMNSQ ~0.78–1.27), with point-measure correlations ranging from 0.19 to 0.48 and acceptable exact/match congruence. Limitations include the absence of documented missing-data handling and the fact that the study does not use ILSA PV-based achievement outcomes or survey weights, so results support test validity/quality rather than cross-national achievement prediction.

title: Important-Things-to-Know-Before-Developing-Artific
outcome_summary: This study reports a small, school-based drone learning intervention in Taiwan (Taoyuan City) with 73 learners aged 11–15 who completed task-based drone activities using Blockly for Robolink. The main quantitative outcomes were (1) a researcher-developed pre/post attainment test of drone concepts and Blockly programming and (2) post-task questionnaires/checklists measuring motivated strategies (metacognition, effort regulation, critical thinking, self-efficacy) and computational thinking (creativity, algorithmic thinking, problem-solving, cooperativity). Programming attainment increased from M = 22.89 (SD = 9.75) to M = 48.63 (SD = 16.92), and multiple regression showed Problem-solving (β = .313, p < .01) and Creativity (β = −.276, p < .05) as significant predictors (R2 = 0.20). Motivated strategies differed by dimension, with self-efficacy significantly lower than other self-regulatory factors (ANOVA F = 27.97, p < .001). The computational thinking checklist similarly showed cooperativity as the highest dimension (ANOVA F = 50.09, p < .001). Limitations include the absence of ML model training/metrics, no reported missing-data handling, and no survey-weighting or PV framework because outcomes are not ILSA PV-based achievement scores.

all_target_domains: Composite / Multi-Domain | Non-Cognitive / Process Output | Digital/Computer Literacy
all_target_variables: Programming attainment (post-test score) | Motivated strategies dimensions (self-efficacy vs metacognition/effort regulation/critical thinking) | Computational thinking dimensions (cooperativity vs algorithmic thinking/creativity/problem-solving)

title: The immigrant paradox and math self-concept: An SES-of-origin-country hypothesis
authors: G. Basarkod, H.W. Marsh, P.D. Parker, T. Dicke, J. Guo
outcome_summary: This study analyzes Australian PISA extended datasets for 2003 (12,551 students; 321 schools) and 2012 (14,481 students; 775 schools), focusing on mathematics-related constructs for 15-year-olds. The outcomes are math self-concept (weighted total score from PISA items) and educational expectations (a combined scale from binary expectation items). The authors use survey-weighted multilevel random-intercept models with multiple imputation for missing data and plausible values for math achievement, pooling results via Rubin’s rules. Across both cohorts, immigrant students (first- and second-generation) show higher math self-concepts and educational expectations than native students, but the immigrant paradox is reduced when relative SES—operationalized as parents’ origin-country mean years of education—is included. Relative SES negatively predicts both outcomes and helps explain the expectation-achievement gap; school-average achievement shows the expected negative association with self-concept but does not account for the immigrant paradox. Limitations include cross-sectional design and the fact that the paper does not use ML prediction algorithms (it uses multilevel modeling rather than ML).
all_datasets_used: PISA 2003 Australia (15-year-olds) Mathematics — math self-concept | PISA 2012 Australia (15-year-olds) Mathematics — math self-concept | PISA 2003 Australia (15-year-olds) Mathematics — educational expectations | PISA 2012 Australia (15-year-olds) Mathematics — educational expectations
all_target_variables: Math self-concept (weighted total score) | Educational expectations (combined binary scale)

title: Control-value theory and enjoyment of science_ A cross-national investigation with 15-year-olds using PISA 2006 data
authors: F.C. Mercan
outcome_summary: This cross-national study uses PISA 2006 microdata for 15-year-olds across 57 countries (398,750 students) to test Control-Value Theory in the science domain. Enjoyment of science learning is modeled as a latent outcome predicted by perceived control (science self-concept), value appraisals (personal value of science in Model 1; utility value of school science in Model 2), and their latent interaction using SEM with latent interactions (SEM-LI) estimated in Mplus with robust maximum likelihood. Multiple imputation was used for missing questionnaire responses (five imputed datasets via Amelia II). Model fit was strong for both models (Model 1: CFI=0.986, RMSEA=0.009; Model 2: CFI=0.983, RMSEA=0.010). The key interaction effects were statistically significant but very small (Model 1 β=0.042; Model 2 β=0.036), and the structural relations were largely invariant across countries and genders, though country-level patterns varied. Because the design is cross-sectional and the analysis is not causal, the findings support theory-consistent associations rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2006 (15-year-olds) Science learning — enjoyment of science (context questionnaire)

title: Cognitive skills and economic growth in the twenty-first century: Evidence from PISA and cognitive ability studies
authors: Björn Boman
outcome_summary: The paper examines whether PISA 2000 cognitive skills are associated with subsequent economic growth, using country-level aggregation rather than student-level PV modeling. In the main analysis, it regresses average GDP per capita growth (2010–2019) on a composite PISA 2000 score (averaging math, science, and reading) plus macro controls for 31 OECD/OECD-related partner countries. The model reports adjusted R² = 0.227, with relatively large standardized effects for PISA 2000 (β = 0.422) and FDI inflow (β = 0.413), but no predictors are significant at p < .05. A robustness check using a composite cognitive ability score for 80 countries yields adjusted R² = 0.333, where the Middle East/non-Middle East region dummy dominates (β = 0.569, p < .001) and cognitive skills remain smaller (β = 0.206, p = 0.140). Limitations include the absence of ML methods, reliance on aggregated country data, and no reported missing-data handling strategy.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2000 (country-level averages; math/science/reading composite), OECD/OECD-related partners (31 countries) | Composite cognitive ability score (80 countries; robustness check), OECD/OECD-related partners not restricted

title: ChatGPT: The brightest student in the class
authors: E. Vázquez-Cano, José M. Ramírez-Hurtado, Jose Manuel Saez-Lopez, Eloy Lopez-Meneses
outcome_summary: This study used a PISA 2009 reading comprehension text (385 words) as the source for a classroom summary task administered to 30 Spanish secondary students (149e16) and compared their teacher-rated summaries with a ChatGPT-generated summary camouflaged among student work. Thirty Spanish language teachers (selected across five regions) scored each summary using a rubric with two dimensions: content and style. The results show that ChatGPT obtained higher ratings than students in both dimensions: style differences were all above 3 points and content differences were above 2.5 points. Gender and teacher age significantly moderated the ChatGPT9student gaps (content: gender p=0.019; age p=0.004; style: age p=0.000), while teacher experience did not. No machine-learning model was trained; therefore, findings are about human assessment differences rather than predictive performance, and missing-data handling is not fully documented.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2009 reading comprehension text (summary task), Spain (secondary students, 149e16)
all_target_variables: Style score difference (ChatGPT vs students) | Content score difference (ChatGPT vs students)

title: Measuring mathematics competence in international and national large scale assessments_ Linking PISA and the national educational panel study in Germany
outcome_summary: This study evaluates how NEPS grade-9 mathematics can be related to PISA 2012 mathematics by establishing a concordance between the two scales. Data come from a Germany-based linking study (spring/summer 2012) where 9th graders completed PISA 2012 mathematics on day 1 and NEPS-K9 mathematics on day 2; only five PISA booklets were used, and the reported linking analyses rely on the 1,270 students who took both tests. PISA mathematics was scored using Rasch with fixed item parameters and transformed to the international PISA 2012 achievement scale metric via WLE; NEPS mathematics was scored with a Rasch model using fixed item parameters from NEPS 2010 and WLE person separation reliability around 0.791–0.796. The linking function was created using equipercentile linking in LEGS 2.01 with cubic-spline smoothing (slim = 0.5). Results show substantial correlation between PISA and NEPS scores (manifest r = 0.68; latent ≈ 0.90), close reproduction of PISA score-equivalent distributional characteristics, and fair individual-level classification consistency (Cohen’s Kappa ≈ 0.26), with limitations including an unmodeled order effect and reduced exactness at score extremes.

title: Interpreting mathematics performance in PISA_ Taking account of reading performance
authors: H. Ding, M. Homer
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2009 China Trial data from Fangshan District of Beijing (academic-track 15-year-olds; N=607 after excluding 3 students with missing ESCS) to explain mathematics performance (PVs) using reading performance and reading subareas. The authors fit two-level multilevel models with students nested in schools, incorporating PISA plausible values via the five-PV approach and pooling results using Stata’s MI procedure, while applying sampling weights and replicate weights through IEA IDB Analyzer. The key result is that overall reading performance strongly predicts mathematics performance (β=0.833, p<0.001), and the association is concentrated in specific reading aspects (Integrate & Interpret; Reflect & Evaluate) and in reading non-continuous texts (β=0.436, p<0.001). The study reports no causal identification; it is observational and therefore cannot establish that reading causes mathematics outcomes, and it uses a single local context that may limit generalizability.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2009 China Trial (Fangshan District, Beijing) Mathematics literacy (PVs)

title: Bullying victimization, school belonging, academic engagement and achievement in adolescents in rural China_ A serial mediation model
outcome_summary: This study examines how bullying victimization relates to academic achievement in 15-year-olds in rural China, using a contract survey in G Province and administering Chinese versions of PISA reading, math, and science tests as a term exam. The analytic sample comprised 813 students (359 boys, 454 girls) from 102 rural classes, restricted to rural residents aged 15 who completed all surveys and tests. The study does not train machine-learning models; instead, it uses regression-based serial mediation (PROCESS 2.1) with bootstrapping (5000 resamples) to test whether school belonging and academic engagement sequentially mediate the bullying–achievement association, separately by gender. In the full sample, bullying victimization negatively predicted school belonging (β=-0.30, p<0.001), school belonging positively predicted academic engagement (β=0.46, p<0.001), and academic engagement positively predicted academic achievement (β=0.21, p<0.01). The serial indirect effect bullying victimization → school belonging → academic engagement → academic achievement was significant in the full sample (β=-0.03, 95% CI [-0.05, -0.01]) and in boys (β=-0.02, 95% CI [-0.05, -0.005]), but not in girls, where academic engagement did not predict achievement (β=0.15, p>0.05). Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal direction), self-report measures for bullying/belonging/engagement, and lack of explicit missing-data handling beyond complete-case exclusion.

title: Relationship between digital game experience and problem-solving performance according to a PISA framework
authors: Chuen-Tsai Sun, Kuan-Ting Chou, Hsiu Chen Yu
outcome_summary: This study used a PISA 2012 framework to design a computer-based problem-solving assessment and a separate Cataroundasia process task for 267 recruited 6th-grade students in Taiwan. It reports no machine-learning models; instead, it uses SPSS-based correlations, one-way ANOVA, and linear regressions to test relationships between digital game experience, self-regulated learning, and problem-solving performance. Students with more digital game experience scored higher on the 0–71 computer-based problem-solving performance (ANOVA F(4,262)=3.17, p=.014; experienced mean 62.6 vs inexperienced 52.8; t=−3.224, p<.001). Problem-solving process stages significantly predicted overall performance (R2=.296), with representation & formulation the strongest predictor (β=.344, p<.001) and monitoring & reflection also significant (β=.193, p=.001). The study is limited by its single-school convenience sample, author-created measures, and the absence of PV-based ILSA scaling/weights; additionally, self-report self-regulated learning showed weak negative correlations with performance.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving (6th grade, Taiwan)
all_target_variables: Computer-based problem-solving performance (0–71) | Problem-solving performance vs self-regulated learning (correlation) | Problem-solving process stages predicting dynamic vs static performance | Problem-solving process stages predicting technical vs non-technical performance

title: Engagement, achievement, and teacher classroom practices in mathematics: Insights from TIMSS 2011 and PISA 2012
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2011 (Grade 8 mathematics) and PISA 2012 (15-year-old mathematics) data from four focal countries—Singapore, Finland, Australia, and Romania—to examine how emotional/cognitive engagement (interest, self-concept, future utility beliefs) relates to mathematics achievement and teacher classroom practices. Teacher practices are measured as composites of structure, support, and challenge, reported by teachers in TIMSS 2011 and by students in PISA 2012. The models are estimated with CFA and path analysis using robust WLSMV for ordinal indicators, applying student sampling weights (totwgt in TIMSS; W_FSTUWT in PISA) and corresponding replicate weights (jackknife in TIMSS; BRR in PISA). Across both datasets, socioeconomic status is a strong predictor of engagement and achievement (e.g., SES → achievement β≈0.32–0.50 in TIMSS; β≈0.29–0.42 in PISA), while teacher-practice effects are heterogeneous: support is consistently positive for self-concept in PISA, whereas challenge is negatively associated with achievement in PISA. The findings are correlational due to cross-sectional secondary analysis and may reflect reverse causation and measurement differences between teacher- and student-reported practices.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (eighth graders; engagement in mathematics; teacher-reported practices) | PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; engagement in mathematics; student-reported teacher practices)
all_target_variables: Interest (latent engagement factor) | Self-concept (latent engagement factor) | Future utility beliefs (latent engagement factor) | Mathematics achievement level (outcome)

title: Exposure to crime and academic achievement_ A case study for Costa Rica using PISA data
authors: G. Gimenez, B. Barrado
outcome_summary: The paper studies the effect of criminal violence on academic achievement in Costa Rica using PISA 2012 microdata for 15-year-olds (grades 7 and higher) matched to district-level homicide rates for 2012. The analytic sample contains 4,580 students from 193 schools in 138 districts. Missing PISA responses are handled with a hot-deck Bayesian bootstrap procedure (Rubin & Schenkeeach) and PISA plausible values are incorporated using the PISA design; survey weights are included via Stata pweights. The authors estimate a two-equation simultaneous system where homicide is endogenous and the outcome equations are solved with LIML using IV, reporting baseline LIML results and heterogeneity by gender and district social development. They find homicide rates are negatively and significantly associated with math, reading, and science scores, with larger impacts in low social-development districts and additional gender heterogeneity for science. Limitations include reliance on the validity/strength of instruments and the use of district homicide rates as the violence exposure measure.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2012 Costa Rica (15-year-olds, Grades 7+), Mathematics | PISA 2012 Costa Rica (15-year-olds, Grades 7+), Reading | PISA 2012 Costa Rica (15-year-olds, Grades 7+), Science
all_target_variables: Math achievement (PISA test scores) | Reading achievement (PISA test scores) | Science achievement (PISA test scores)

title: Does all work and no play make elite students? Evidence from the China education panel survey
authors: Juan Yang, Xinhui Zhao
outcome_summary: The study uses CEPS baseline data from the 2013–2014 school year for middle school students in Grades 7 and 9 in China (N=19,487; sampled via 28 county-level units/city districts, 112 schools, and 438 classes). Academic performance is measured as standardized midterm exam scores in Chinese, mathematics, and English, summed into a total test score. Using generalized propensity score matching and a dose-response (dose-response function) approach, the authors estimate a stable “inverted U” causal pattern: best performance occurs at about 3 hours/day on weekdays and 8 hours/day on weekends, while longer study time hinders achievement. Mediation analyses show that the effect operates through perceived learning difficulty and self-efficacy, with meaningful mediated proportions (e.g., 10.21%/19.17% for learning difficulty and 6.99%/5.38% for self-efficacy on weekdays). Limitations include lack of explicit missing-data handling documentation and reliance on observational causal assumptions rather than randomized assignment.
all_datasets_used: CEPS 2013-2014 (China) Grade 7/9 Midterm standardized scores (Chinese, Mathematics, English)
all_target_domains: Composite / Multi-Domain | Other / Unspecified | Non-Cognitive / Process Output
all_target_variables: Academic performance (total test score) | Learning difficulty (mediator; weekday scale 1–4) | Self-efficacy (mediator; weekday scale 1–4)

title: Expectancy-value profiles in math: How are student-perceived teaching behaviors related to motivational transitions?
authors: R. Lazarides, et al.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes Germany’s PISA 2012 mathematics assessment and the national longitudinal extension PISA Plus 2012–2013, focusing on Grade 9 (t1, 2012) to Grade 10 (t2, 2013) motivational belief profiles. The analytic sample is n=2605 students in 198 classrooms across 121 schools, selected to keep the mathematics teacher constant from Grade 9 to Grade 10. Motivational constructs (self-efficacy, interest, utility value) are used to form three latent profiles at Grade 9, with high classification quality (average latent class probabilities p=.81–.88) and clear profile sizes (20.9%, 24.7%, 54.3%). Latent transition analysis shows strong stability across time (transition probabilities p=.832–.845; within-profile persistence ~83–85%). Perceived student-oriented teaching in Grade 9 is linked to more adaptive motivational transitions (OR=0.43, p=.005), while general teacher support does not affect transitions. Limitations include person-centered modeling rather than predictive ML, observational design, and reliance on multiple imputation for missing questionnaire data.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2012 (Germany) Grade 9–10 Mathematics; PISA Plus 2012–2013 longitudinal motivational profiles | PISA 2012 (Germany) Grade 9–10 Mathematics; PISA Plus 2012–2013 longitudinal motivational transitions
all_target_variables: Motivational profile membership (Grade 9 latent profiles) | Motivational transitions from Grade 9 to Grade 10 latent profiles

title: 1-s2.0-S0883035523000794-main
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2012 mathematics data for 15-year-olds in seven predominantly English-speaking countries, restricting analyses to students who completed questionnaire forms A and C (final N=40,429). Overclaiming is measured from three fake mathematics constructs using a partial credit IRT model and then standardised within country; mathematics achievement is represented by PISA mathematics plausible values combined using Rubin’s Rules. The main analysis estimates OLS regressions of the overclaiming scale on students’ relative mathematics achievement within school (plus demographic, school, peer, and familiarity controls), with BRR replicate weights and senate weights applied so countries contribute equally. A one SD increase in relative achievement is associated with about a 0.1 SD increase in overclaiming (dropping to ~0.08 after controlling for familiarity), and item-level logistic models show OR≈1.18–1.21 for two fake items. Limitations include cross-sectional design and potential attenuation from peer-measurement error due to PISA’s sampled students within schools.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; questionnaire forms A & C; overclaiming from fake math constructs) | PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; questionnaire forms A & C; fake math items)
all_target_variables: Overclaiming scale (standardised; IRT from 3 fake constructs) | Overclaiming scale by within-school achievement tercile | Odds of strong knowledge for each fake construct (logistic; proper number, subjunctive scaling, declarative fraction)

title: Does Inequality Stay in the Shadow? The Cross-national Effects of Educational Equity on Private Tutoring and Student Achievement
authors: Alexander W. Wiseman
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) mathematics, science, and reading achievement using five plausible values and applies total student weights with 80 replicate weights, supplemented by World Bank nation-level equity indicators. Across the cross-national weighted regressions, all three private tutoring types (commercial company, personal, family) show negative associations with achievement in every subject (e.g., PERT b=-5.33 in mathematics; COMT b=-2.90 in science; COMT b=-2.98 in reading; all p<.001). Hierarchical linear models further show that tutoring effects often remain negative, while school- and system-level equity indicators have largely non-significant or irregular moderation effects on the tutoring–achievement relationship. The paper does not report any machine-learning model training or predictive metrics; it uses regression/HLM rather than ML algorithms. Because the design is observational and cross-sectional, the negative tutoring coefficients should not be interpreted causally, and missing-data handling for non-PV variables is not fully documented.

all_target_variables: Mathematics achievement (PVs) | Science achievement (PVs) | Reading achievement (PVs)

title: Got math attitude? (In)direct effects of student mathematics attitudes on intentions, behavioral engagement, and mathematics performance in the U.S. PISA
authors: K. Gjicali, A.A. Lipnevich
outcome_summary: This study analyzes the U.S. sample of PISA 2012, focusing on mathematics performance (five plausible values) and noncognitive constructs grounded in the theory of planned behavior (attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, intentions, and mathematics work ethic). Using SEM in Mplus with WLSMV for categorical intention indicators, the authors report that attitude determinants explain 21.1% of variance in intentions (R² = 0.211), 59.4% of variance in behavioral engagement (R² = 0.594), and 30.7% of variance in mathematics performance (R² = 0.307). The strongest structural paths are perceived behavioral control → behavioral engagement (β = 0.719) and behavioral engagement → math performance (β = 0.255), with perceived behavioral control also showing an indirect effect on performance through behavior (β = 0.184). Limitations include reliance on cross-sectional PISA data and the use of SEM rather than ML prediction; causal claims are not identified, and the study uses FIML for background missingness under MCAR assumptions.
all_target_variables: Mathematics performance (PISA math plausible values) | Intentions to pursue mathematics | Behavioral engagement (mathematics work ethic)

title: Does ICT matter for complex problem-solving competency? A multilevel analysis of 33 countries and economies
authors: Fu Chen, Yichi Liu, Yizhu Gao, Ying Cui, Qin Wang, Chang Lu
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2012 student data (15-year-olds in grade 7 or higher) from 33 countries/economies to examine how ICT-related factors and psychosocial variables relate to complex problem-solving (CPS) competency. CPS is measured via PISA 2012 computer-based tasks and plausible values; the authors used all five plausible values and combined estimates using Rubin’s rules. Missing ICT familiarity responses (with missingness often around 30–40%) were handled using regression-based multiple imputation, and the nested structure of students within schools within countries was modeled using three-level multilevel linear modeling with robust standard errors. In the full model, openness for problem-solving showed a positive association with CPS (B=10.08, SE=1.10, p<.001), while ICT availability at home (B=−9.55, SE=1.35, p<.001) and use of ICT at school (B=−9.40, SE=1.39, p<.001) were negative. The study reports variance explained and model fit (AIC/BIC) but does not use ML algorithms; therefore, results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects, and the linear MLM specification may miss potential nonlinear ICT–CPS relationships.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2012 Grade 7+ Complex Problem Solving (CPS) achievement (5 plausible values)

title: Students' problem-solving skills in-depth: ready for ‘real life’?
authors: A. Calma
outcome_summary: This paper is a descriptive content-analysis study applying the OECD PISA problem-solving framework to management education: 188 university group assignments were coded at the paragraph level into four processes (EU, RF, PE, MR) and 21 core tasks. The results show strong evidence of EU and RF processes (EU: 3495 paragraphs, 43.25%; RF: 3232, 40.00%) and weaker evidence of PE and MR (PE: 19.28%; MR: 7.30%). Within core tasks, the highest coded proportion was MR3 (discussing solution impact for the decision maker/company), while weaker performance appeared for MR2 (other variables that could have been considered) and MR4 (limitations/restrictions). The study reports reliability using weighted Cohen’s Kappa (substantial agreement for EU/RF/PE; fair for MR). No machine-learning prediction model, PV-based achievement outcome, or survey-weighted estimation is used; therefore, findings describe observed alignment with the framework rather than predictive accuracy or causal effects.

title: For skilled comprehenders digital reading is a routine task, for unskilled comprehenders it is a problem
authors: Johannes Naumann, Liene Brandhuber, Frank Goldhammer, Beate Eichmann, Samuel Greiff
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment (CBA) data across 32 countries (N = 13,080) focusing on digital reading navigation and performance. Students’ comprehension skill, problem solving skill, and digital reading were represented using author-computed WLEs, while navigation was operationalized from log files as Precision (relevant vs irrelevant page access) and Adaptive processing (time on relevant pages adjusted to item difficulty). Using a survey-weighted path-analytic approach with replicate weights and country-wise estimation integrated via random-effects meta-analysis, the authors report that comprehension and problem solving both positively predict Precision and Adaptive processing, with a compensatory interaction for Precision (negative CS×PS interaction) but not for Adaptive processing. Digital reading performance is predicted by both skills (e.g., problem solving b = 0.31; comprehension b = 0.40) and partially mediated through navigation indicators. Limitations include correlational inference and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment (CBA) — Digital reading (WLE) and navigation indicators; grade not specified
all_target_variables: Precision (navigation indicator) | Adaptive processing (navigation indicator) | Digital reading (WLE)

title: Exploring complex problem-solving in vietnamese students: An investigation of performance data and process data
authors: De Van Vo, Viet Thanh Huynh, Greiff Samuel, Geraldine Mooney Simmie
outcome_summary: This study investigated complex problem-solving among 589 Vietnamese undergraduate students using CPS tasks aligned with the PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework, combining performance data (Rasch-scaled CPS scores from dichotomous item scoring) and process data (log-derived number of interactions, time-on-task, strategy frequencies, and spatial interaction patterns). The paper did not train machine-learning predictive models; instead, it used Rasch scaling plus Pearson correlations and t-tests to characterize relationships between engagement behaviors and achievement. Key results show that students performed better in knowledge acquisition than knowledge application (t(588)=7.33, p<0.001), and males outperformed females overall and especially in knowledge acquisition (overall t(543.67)=3.569, p<.001; d=0.30). In MicroDYN model-based tasks, more actions were weakly negatively related to knowledge acquisition (r=-0.087, p=0.04), while in the MicroFIN realistic Robot Cleaner task the association was positive (r=0.198, p<0.001). Time-on-task was generally not predictive (realistic r=0.005, p=0.895; model-based r=-0.053, p=0.226), and VOTAT-like “vary one variable” behavior (Change 1) correlated positively with achievement (r=0.343***). Limitations include a single-university convenience sample, no reported missing-data strategy, and no PV-based ILSA weighting or causal identification.

title: Teaching strategies influencing learning strategies: Exploration of teaching and learning practices in a higher education context in Pakistan
authors: Aiman Zahid, Ali Nawab
outcome_summary: This paper is a qualitative exploratory case study in a higher education institute in Northern Sindh, Pakistan, examining how teachers’ teaching strategies influence students’ learning strategies. Data were collected through semi-structured group interviews with 12 second-year BEd (Hons.) student-teachers (two groups of six) and supported by five semi-structured classroom observations involving two English teachers. The analysis used thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke) to identify dominant teaching strategies (e.g., group work/discussions, practical work, repetition, questioning) and corresponding learning strategies (e.g., note-taking, discussion for theoretical subjects, metacognitive adaptation from cramming to deeper understanding). No machine learning models, predictive metrics, or PV-based achievement outcomes are reported, and therefore no accuracy/RMSE/AUC-type performance can be extracted. The authors also note limitations in generalizability due to the small, single-institute sample and the reliance on a limited number of observations.

title: Are only children always better? Testing the sibling effects on academic performance in rural Chinese adolescents
authors: J. Shi, L. Li, D. Wu, P. Li
outcome_summary: This study used a matched rural Grade 9 sample from 102 schools in a single city in Guangxi, China, administering the Chinese version of PISA 2015 Math, Reading, and Science as a term exam. Academic outcomes were converted to standardized z scores using an IRT-based scoring approach with PISA difficulty parameters. The paper does not apply machine learning; instead it uses OLS and a two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variable strategy, plus hierarchical regression robustness checks. Across outcomes, only-child status showed a negative association with math in OLS (β = −0.114, p < .05) but was not significant in 2SLS (β = −0.195, p > .05), while reading and science were not significantly predicted by only-child status in the IV models. Key positive predictors included parents’ academic expectation and kindergarten level, and eyesight was consistently negatively related to achievement. Limitations include the cross-sectional design, self-reported covariates, and the lack of reported complex survey weighting.

title: The moderating role of parental support in the relationship between latent profiles of bullying victimization and sense of school belonging: A cross-national comparison
authors: Yoonsun Han, Hae Rin Kang, Ji Won Choe, Hyein Kim
outcome_summary: This cross-national study used PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old students from five Northeast Asian regions (B-S-J-G China, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan) and the United States (total N=38,292). Bullying victimization was measured with six offline bullying-frequency items and used to estimate latent victimization profiles via latent profile analysis; sense of school belonging was measured with six Likert items and parental support with four Likert items. Missingness was handled with FIML in the LPA and listwise deletion for key variables in the regression models. The regression results (Model 1) showed that belonging was significantly lower for students in low, medium, and selective victimization profiles versus the very low profile across regions, with coefficients reported in Table 5. Model 2 interaction results indicated that parental support’s buffering role was not consistent across all regions—strongest for Taiwan—highlighting cross-cultural heterogeneity and limiting causal interpretation due to the cross-sectional design.

title: The gendered playing field: Family socioeconomic status and national gender inequality in adolescents’ out-of-school physical activity
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old adolescents from 50 countries/economies (final N=316,657 after listwise deletion for missing national gender inequality or neighborhood urbanicity). The dependent variable is the self-reported number of days in the past seven days adolescents participated in out-of-school vigorous physical activity, modeled with multilevel negative binomial regression to address overdispersion (alpha≈0.303). Across countries, female adolescents report 28.8% fewer days of out-of-school vigorous PA than male adolescents, while a one–standard deviation increase in family SES is associated with an 8.0% increase in weekly PA. Importantly, the SES moderation of the gender gap diminishes as national gender inequality increases (three-way interaction coefficient about −0.129), and these patterns remain stable after adding controls (in-school PE, math score, school grade, urbanicity, GDP per capita, and Gini). Limitations include reliance on self-reported PA and the absence of explicit survey-weight variable reporting for the inferential models.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 (age 15) out-of-school vigorous physical activity (count of days in past 7 days)
all_target_variables: Out-of-school vigorous physical activity (days per week)

title: Small-class effects on science achievement in secondary education
authors: Ting Shen
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 science achievement for 15-year-old students in 26 countries/economies (24 European plus the U.S. and Canada), using teacher-reported class size and defining “small classes” as 20 or fewer students. Science achievement is measured with 10 PISA plausible values (PV1SCIE–PV10SCIE), and the authors estimate propensity score (ATT) models with inverse probability of treatment weighting combined with PISA sampling weights (W_FSTUWT), then combine PV-specific estimates using Schafer’s formula. Across all 26 country estimates, the fixed-effects meta-analytic effect of small classes is δ = −0.05 (SE = 0.01, p < 0.01; 95% CI [−0.07, −0.04]); among the 9 countries with significant effects, δ = −0.13 (95% CI [−0.15, −0.11]). The paper reports robust standard errors for clustering and checks covariate balance before/after PS weighting, but it does not explicitly document missing-data handling for covariates/outcomes. Overall, the results suggest small-class policies do not consistently raise secondary science achievement and may vary substantially by country context.

title: Measurements of performance gaps are sensitive to the level of test stakes: Evidence from PISA and a Field Experiment
authors: Y. Ofek-Shanny
outcome_summary: The paper combines PISA 2015 Mathematics observational evidence with a within-subject field experiment in Israel (spring 2017) to test whether low-stakes testing engagement biases minority-majority performance-gap measurements. In PISA 2015, minority groups show higher skip+rapid-guess rates (weighted by PISA senate weights), but motivation filtering based on skipping/rapid guessing does not meaningfully change minority-majority performance gaps (Table 1). In the field experiment (n=599 students; 577 in regressions), students perform better on naturally high-stakes tests; for Arab students, the high-minus-low grade difference is larger than for Jewish students (Table 3: Arab ΔGrade=6.40, ΔZ=0.18), implying that the Jewish–Arab gap would be about 60% smaller under high-stakes measurement (0.38 SD to 0.15 SD). The study uses OLS with wild bootstrap clustered by school and includes controls for parental education and misunderstanding of stakes; it does not train ML models, so no PV handling or ML performance metrics apply. Limitations include non-representative school selection and the fact that motivation filtering relies on strong assumptions about engagement–proficiency correlation.

title: Educational Data Mining_ Identification of factors associated with school effectiveness in PISA assessment
authors: F. Martínez-Abad, A. Gamazo, M.-J. Rodríguez-Conde
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 microdata for Spain (15-year-olds) to build school effectiveness models in two phases. First, multilevel models (one per domain: mathematics, reading, science) use only input variables to estimate school residuals; schools are then labeled high- vs low-effectiveness based on residual quartiles across all three domains. Second, the authors train a decision tree (J48/C4.5) using process variables from PISA 2015 context questionnaires aggregated to the school level, with the unit of analysis being schools. The resulting tree has 25 branches and 13 terminal nodes and shows strong classification performance: global COR ≈ 0.947 in training and ≈ 0.916 in 10-fold stratified cross-validation; Kappa ≈ 0.849 (training) and ≈ 0.747 (CV); RRSE ≈ 0.515 (training) and ≈ 0.647 (CV). The study applies sample weights (student/school weights in HLM; school weights in the tree) and uses robust estimators rather than replicate weights; however, the design is cross-sectional, so causal claims are not supported, and aggregation may mask within-school heterogeneity.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 (Spain) — school effectiveness classification (secondary students, aggregated process variables)

title: The assessment of collaborative problem solving in PISA 2015: An investigation of the validity of the PISA 2015 CPS tasks
authors: M. Stadler, et al.
outcome_summary: This study recruited 483 German secondary-school students (grades 9–10) from eight Gymnasium schools in Rhineland-Palatinate and Hesse to evaluate the validity of PISA 2015 collaborative problem solving (CPS) tasks. Students completed four of the seven original PISA 2015 CPS tasks in an individual-player H–A format, and a fifth CPS task in a co-player (face-to-face) format with a randomly assigned classmate; the co-player predictive analysis used one partner per dyad (N=228 observed individual scores). Construct validity was tested with SEM in MPlus (type=complex for students nested in classes), showing moderate associations between CPS performance and self-reported collaboration (r≈0.25–0.29) and teacher-reported collaboration (r≈0.20–0.33), with reasoning showing a robust relation (r≈0.38). Predictive validity was assessed via response surface analysis (RSQD), explaining 30.2% of co-player performance variance and revealing significant main and interaction effects of individual CPS performance. Limitations include the associative nature of results (no causal inference), a small non-PISA sampling frame, and missing-data handling not being specified in the provided text.

title: Do school resources reduce socioeconomic achievement gap? Evidence from PISA 2015
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-olds in 39 countries/economies (final analytic sample: 300,218 students) to examine whether school resources relate to achievement and whether those relationships differ by students’ socioeconomic status (SES) and OECD membership. Outcomes are mathematics, reading, and science plausible values (0–1000, mean 500, SD 100), and the authors use country fixed effects with standard errors clustered at the school level, applying PISA final student weights and 80 replicate weights and averaging across plausible values. In the average within-country models, neither computers per student nor the share of teachers with master’s degrees is significantly associated with achievement (R² around 0.46–0.53). However, human resources show significant positive interactions with SES (e.g., teachers × SES: 7.981 in math; 7.855 in reading; 11.372 in science, all p < 0.001), implying larger returns for higher-SES students and thus a widening socioeconomic achievement gap. The paper is cross-sectional and uses resource proxies, so causal claims are limited and measurement may not capture how resources are used.

title: ICT-related behavioral factors mediate the relationship between adolescents’ ICT interest and their ICT self-efficacy: Evidence from 30 countries
authors: X. Chen, Jie Hu
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) using the optional ICT Familiarity Questionnaire, restricted to 30 OECD countries that completed the ICT module (total N=201,652 students in 7,708 schools). The dependent construct is ICT self-efficacy (COMPICT), derived from five Likert items and scaled with IRT; the key predictor is ICT interest (INTICT), derived from six ICT-enjoyment items, also IRT-scaled. Missing data across all variables are imputed using an EM algorithm in SPSS 20, producing single imputed values. Using multilevel mediation (students nested in schools; models run separately per country), ICT interest shows a positive total association with ICT self-efficacy in all countries (B≈0.4377–0.5703; Beta≈0.4385–0.6335). Mediation is substantial (proportion mediated ≈19.25%–40.15%), with ENTUSE and SOIAICT significant mediators across all countries, while USESCH and HOMESCH are mostly non-significant. Because the design is correlational and mediation is not causal identification, policy should interpret effects as associations rather than guaranteed causal impacts.

title: Collaboration and socio-economic inequality: Estimating the effects of intra-school and inter-school inequality on collaborative problem-solving skills
authors: P.E. Sum, G. Bădescu
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 CPS performance for 15-year-olds in 46 countries (102,219 students across 12,510 schools), using a multilevel (HLM) framework to estimate how socioeconomic inequality at different levels relates to collaborative problem solving. CPS is operationalized as the proportion of correct answers to the PISA 2015 CPS human-agent items, and the authors exclude respondents with missing data; unanswered CPS and science items are scored as incorrect. Across four HLM specifications, intra-school SES inequality shows a negative and statistically significant association with CPS (b=-10.61 in M1; b=-15.02 in M2; remaining negative in M3 and M4 even after adding SCIENCE). Inter-school inequality is negative in models without SCIENCE but loses statistical significance once SCIENCE is included. The paper also reports small positive associations for generalized trust and moderation patterns with political equality, but it does not use ML algorithms or PV-based achievement scaling.

title: Deciphering socioeconomic inequality in science literacy: Evidence from PISA 2015 in Türkiye
authors: Betül Yediyıldız, Ulas Ustun
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 Türkiye microdata for 15-year-olds (science literacy as the major domain) and estimates science literacy using 10 plausible values, combining results across plausible values via HLM 7 and IDB Analyzer. The analytic sample reported in the results tables is N=5859 students from 187 schools, with student sampling weights applied (W_FSTUWT). Using a two-level hierarchical linear model (students nested within schools), the authors find a moderate SES–science literacy correlation (r=0.30, p<.001) but a non-significant student-level SES effect (B=1.33, p=.129) alongside a strong school-level SES effect (B=56.43, p<.001; L2 R2=0.494; ICC=0.551). SES–science literacy relationships vary by region at the school level (L2 R2 up to 0.833 in TR02), and SES sub-dimensions show that occupational status and home possessions (including ICT resources) explain more variance than parental education. Limitations include the correlational, cross-sectional design and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling for contextual covariates.

title: How context shapes the relationship between school autonomy and test-scores. An explanatory analysis using PISA 2015
authors: Christian Buerger, Jane Arnold Lincove, Catherine Mata
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 student-level data (math achievement) pooled across 34 countries selected for sufficient within-country variation in school autonomy. The dependent variable is the first plausible value for PISA math, and models are estimated with pooled OLS including country fixed effects, student controls (gender, age, nativity, mother’s education, wealth) and school controls (rural location, public funding, enrollment, and composition by wealth and mother’s education). The key results show that autonomy–achievement associations are highly sensitive to specification: unconditional models suggest sizable effects, but once selection-related controls and country fixed effects are added, most autonomy coefficients become null, with only budget autonomy showing a small positive association (~+4.62 points). For equity, gender, wealth, and parent-education gaps are substantial in non-autonomous schools, while autonomy and accountability effects on gaps are heterogeneous across countries. The paper is not an ML prediction study (no ML algorithms are trained), and causal interpretation is limited because the design explicitly focuses on associations and selection bias rather than causal identification.
