title: Does motivation towards science mediate the relationship between parental support and adolescent science achievement? A comparison of two countries
authors: Pey-Yan Liou, Ssu-Ching Huang, Eunjung Myoung, Sufen Chen
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 science literacy data for 15-year-olds from Korea (n = 5581) and the United States (n = 5712) to test a moderated mediation model. Parental support predicts adolescents’ science intrinsic motivation, science extrinsic motivation, and science self-efficacy, which in turn mediate the relationship between parental support and science achievement (science literacy measured via 10 plausible values). The authors pooled estimates across plausible values using Rubin’s rules and handled missingness with FIML under robust maximum likelihood (MLR). Country moderated the parental support–science achievement relationship: parental support was positively associated with science achievement in Korea (direct PS → SA B = 5.38, p = .002; total B = 10.15, p < .001) but not in the United States (direct PS → SA B = −2.14, p = .193; total B = 1.13, p = .491). Indirect effects were positive through intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy, but negative through extrinsic motivation in both countries. Limitations include the correlational nature of PISA and incomplete reporting of whether specific PISA sampling weights/replicate weights were applied in the Mplus models.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds), Korea and United States
all_target_variables: Science achievement (PISA science literacy; 10 plausible values)

title: Why don’t more boys want to become teachers? The effect of a gendered profession on students’ career expectations
authors: Seong Won Han, Francesca Borgonovi, Sergio Guerriero
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 student questionnaire data on 15-year-olds’ teaching career expectations, coded from an open-ended question about the job they expect to have around age 30. The dependent variable is binary (expect teaching career vs not) and is modeled using hierarchical Bernoulli logit models with students nested within schools and countries, incorporating PISA plausible values for math/reading/science controls by running models across 10 plausible values and combining estimates. The pooled HGLM analyses use BRR for standard errors in logistic regressions and senate weights to ensure equal country contribution in the multilevel models, with missing values handled via chained equations (ICE) in Stata. Results show boys are generally less likely than girls to aspire to teaching, and country contexts matter: higher shares of male teachers are associated with higher odds of expecting teaching (stronger for boys), while higher gender egalitarianism is associated with lower odds (also stronger for boys). The paper reports odds ratios and standard errors rather than predictive ML metrics, and the single-wave cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

title: The assessment of collaborative problem solving in PISA 2015_ Can computer agents replace humans?
authors: K. Herborn, et al.
outcome_summary: This study does not train or evaluate machine-learning models; it validates the PISA 2015 Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) human-to-agent (H-A) approach by reformatting CPS tasks into a constrained human-to-human (H-H) classroom condition. The authors collected data in Germany (Grades 9–10) in 2016 with N=386 main test takers across four task-order groups, using four CPS tasks per student and predefined chat options. For factorial validity (RQ1), they fit confirmatory factor models in MPlus (SEM/ML) and compared one-dimensional vs two-dimensional vs bifactor structures; the one-dimensional CPS factor fit substantially better than models separating H-A and H-H. For performance validity (RQ2), they used MANOVA (Pillai’s trace) and found no significant interface effect on CPS performance accuracy (V=0.02, F(4,186)=0.77, p=.548), but a significant interface effect on behavioral actions (V=0.11, F(4,186)=5.55, p<.001), with classmates producing slightly more actions on Tasks 1 and 2 only. Limitations include the constrained H-H design (predefined chat, only one agent replaced) and the absence of population-representative PISA weighting.

title: Overlearning is as ineffective as underlearning? A cross-culture study from PISA 2015
authors: X. Zhang, Y. Liu
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 science data for 15-year-old students from eight countries/regions (N=75,404) to examine how engaged science learning time (smins, standardized as ztime) relates to science achievement. Using multilevel modeling with schools nested within countries, the authors compare linear and quadratic specifications and find that quadratic models fit better (lower LL/AIC/BIC/aBIC) and yield an inverted U-shaped pattern: science achievement rises with learning time up to an optimal point and then declines. The optimal ztime differs by country/region (e.g., Japan 0.84 vs South Korea 4.42 in the full-time model). A culture interaction model (east vs west) shows similar symmetry axes (optimal ztime ~3.85 East vs ~3.92 West) but stronger moderation in the eastern group, with steeper changes after the peak. Limitations include the absence of reported PV and missing-data handling details and no explicit discussion of survey-weight application.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 Grade 10/15-year-old Science (science learning time smins; science achievement score) | PISA 2015 Grade 10/15-year-old Science (culture moderator; smins and science achievement)
all_target_variables: Science achievement (PISA 2015 science score) | Science achievement moderated by culture (east vs west)

title: “Hot-headed” students? Scientific literacy, perceptions and awareness of climate change in 15-year olds across 54 countries
authors: M.C. Oliver, M.J. Adkins
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-olds (grades 7+) across 54 countries, modeling students’ self-reported awareness of the increase in greenhouse gases (ST09201TA) as an ordered four-category outcome. The authors fit a Bayesian multilevel ordered logistic proportional-odds model with school- and country-varying intercepts, using senate weights to address cross-country sampling and non-response differences. Missingness is handled via complete-case analysis (multiple imputation was attempted but did not converge). Scientific literacy (PISA science score, modeled via 10 plausible values) is the strongest predictor: students scoring one SD higher are about 34.5% more likely to report being more informed (odds-ratio 4.91–5.96). Enjoyment of science and interest in broad science topics each show sizable positive associations (odds-ratios ~1.37–1.40), while females are less likely on average (odds-ratio 0.82–0.92). Limitations include reliance on self-reported awareness and the absence of causal identification.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds; grades 7+; ST09201TA awareness item)
all_target_variables: Awareness of increase in greenhouse gases (ordered categories)

title: Identifying emergent roles and their relationship with learning outcomes and collaborative problem-solving skills
authors: Ziqi Mao, Xiaoran Li, Yanyan Li
outcome_summary: This study used a small CPS experiment with 54 undergraduates and postgraduates from a Beijing normal university (China). Participants completed pre-questionnaires on achievement motivation and self-reported statistics knowledge, were assigned into 18 heterogeneous triads, and then completed a 120-minute CPS task (“migration of workers”) with pre/post mind maps scored by trained coders and turn-level coding of emergent roles. For learning outcomes, hierarchical regression showed Model 1 explained 6.6% of variance (adjusted R2 = 0.066) and Model 2 increased to 21.0% (adjusted R2 = 0.210), with knowledge seeker and distractor roles significantly predicting lower learning outcomes (p = 0.035 and p = 0.029). For CPS skills, epistemic network analysis reported co-occurrence patterns (e.g., information giver with maintaining team function; IS/IG/KP/OP with negotiation and coordination) without predictive metrics. Limitations include non-representative sampling, no survey-weighting, and no documented missing-data strategy.
all_datasets_used: CPS experiment (Beijing university) — emergent roles coding and mind-map learning outcomes | CPS experiment (Beijing university) — emergent roles coding and CPS skills ENA
all_target_variables: Learning outcomes (mind-map scores) | CPS skills (epistemic network analysis co-occurrence patterns)

title: The relationship between inquiry-based teaching and students’ achievement. New evidence from a longitudinal PISA study in England
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2015 science data for England (Year 11; N=5,194 pupils from 206 schools) linked to England’s National Pupil Database to obtain GCSE science pillar scores taken about six months after the PISA test. The primary outcome is GCSE science achievement, with PISA science scores used as a secondary outcome in robustness checks. The authors estimate OLS regression models with extensive controls for demographics, prior achievement (KS2 and PISA science), science course type, and additional student and school context; they apply PISA’s complex survey design using BRR weights and impute small item non-response. Across four model specifications, higher inquiry-teaching frequency shows at most a small (~0.1 SD) association that becomes non-significant once full controls are included. The paper reports no consistent positive effects across inquiry components, subgroups, or disciplinary-climate splits, with only tentative evidence that moderate inquiry combined with high teacher guidance may yield small gains. Limitations include reliance on observational associations (no causal identification) and the use of standardized GCSE/PISA measures that may not capture all inquiry-relevant skills.
all_target_variables: GCSE science achievement (pillar score) — disciplinary climate implementation proxy

title: Context-aware prompting for collaborative problem solving skill identification
authors: Mengxiao Zhu, Li Feng, Xin Wang, Wei Huang
outcome_summary: The study proposes CAP4CPS, a context-aware prompting framework for automated collaborative problem solving (CPS) skill coding from chat-message process data. It evaluates the approach on two experimental CPS datasets: Three-Resistor (378 U.S. university/community-college students) and Mondrian Geometric Fantasy (840 Chinese Grade 10–11 students; 51 teams excluded as invalid, leaving 229 valid teams). CAP4CPS uses BERT-based prompt embeddings with separate cognitive and social context extraction (historical dialogue windows) and an attention-based fusion module to predict CPS subskill labels. Across both datasets, CAP4CPS outperforms strong baselines, reaching Accuracy 81.04%/83.27%, Weighted-F1 80.78/83.17, and Cohen’s Kappa 75.33/78.37 (Three-Resistor/Mondrian). The paper reports stratified train/validation/test splits but does not provide a formal missing-data handling protocol beyond dataset-level exclusions, and it does not use ILSA PVs or survey weights, so results reflect task-dataset classification performance rather than population-representative achievement estimates.
ml_all_techniques: Naive Bayes, Random Forest, Random Forest, k-NN, k-NN, CNN, GRU, LSTM, BERT-finetune, BERT-prompt, Conditional Inference Trees, BERT-seq, BERT-prompt
all_datasets_used: Three-Resistor CPS task (PISA 2015-aligned skill matrix), university/community-college students, chat-message CPS skill coding | Mondrian Geometric Fantasy CPS task (PISA 2015-aligned skill framework), Grade 10–11 students, chat-message CPS skill coding

title: Examining the context of better science literacy outcomes among U.S. schools using visual analytics: A machine learning approach
authors: C. Ding
outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2015 science data aggregated to the school level for 238 U.S. schools, constructing 49 school-context variables from principal, teacher, and student questionnaires. It applied MDS preference analysis (a visual analytics approach) to map schools and variables into a two-dimensional space, then divided the plot into four quadrants and tested quadrant differences using one-way ANOVA. Schools in Quadrant 4—characterized by higher individualized teaching, student science self-efficacy, achievement motivation, enjoyment of science, creative extra-curricular activities, and a more qualified science teaching force—showed much higher science literacy outcomes than schools in other quadrants. Quadrant grouping explained 46% of the variance in school science literacy outcomes (F(4233)=50.24, p<.001), with Quadrant 4 differing from other quadrants (ps<0.001). Limitations include the absence of reported PV-handling and missing-data strategy, and the fact that the approach is primarily descriptive/visual rather than a validated predictive ML model.

title: AI advocates and cautious critics: How AI attitudes, AI interest, use of AI, and AI literacy build university students' AI self-efficacy
authors: Arne Bewersdorff, Marie Hornberger, Claudia Nerdel, Daniel S. Schiff
outcome_summary: The study recruited university students from the United States (n=494), the United Kingdom (n=499), and Germany (n=472) via Prolific and analyzed N=1465 after excluding attention-check failures, non-completers, and very fast responders. It used IRT scoring for AI literacy and then applied path analysis (SEM) to test relationships among AI use, AI interest, AI attitudes, AI literacy, and AI self-efficacy, reporting strong model fit across the total sample and country subsamples (e.g., total-sample χ²=3.102, p=.999; CFI=1.005; RMSEA=0.000). Key effects were AI use → AI interest (0.434, p<.01) and AI interest → AI self-efficacy (0.245, p<.01), with AI literacy also contributing modestly (0.144, p<.01). The authors also identified three student groups (AI Advocates, Cautious Critics, Pragmatic Observers) using Gaussian mixture modeling and found significant group differences (MANOVA Pillai’s trace=0.180, p<.01). Limitations include cross-sectional, non-representative sampling and no reported missing-data handling strategy.
all_datasets_used: Cross-national university student survey (US, UK, Germany; December 2023 recruitment)

title: Gender inequality and adolescent bullying victimization among 69 countries and its effect modification by corporal punishment prohibiting laws
authors: Mariko Hosozawa, Naho Yamane, Sumiyo Okawa, Hiromi Obara, Hiroyasu Iso, Ai Ikeda
outcome_summary: This study analyzed PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students across 69 eligible countries to explain cross-country differences in adolescent bullying victimization. The outcome was a composite total victimization score (6–24) based on six self-report items covering verbal, physical, and relational victimization over the past 12 months; one missing item (2.3%) was imputed using person-mean imputation, and students were included if they answered at least five of six items. Using three-level multilevel linear regression (students within schools within countries) with OECD BRR weights, the authors found that higher country-level gender inequality (GII) predicted higher victimization (b=0.52 per 1 SD GII; 95% CI 0.32–0.73), with a stronger association for boys (GII*sex b=-0.23). National laws fully prohibiting corporal punishment enacted within the past 10 years significantly attenuated the GII–victimization association (b=-0.43), while bans enacted for >10 years did not. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and ecological fallacy risk, plus restricted country coverage (PISA excludes low-income/African countries).
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) victimization composite score (verbal/physical/relational) across 69 countries

title: Adolescents’ meaning in life as a resilience factor between bullying victimization and life satisfaction
authors: Y. Seon, S. Smith-Adcock
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 nationally representative data for U.S. 15-year-olds to test whether meaning in life (MIL) functions as both a compensatory and protective resilience factor between bullying victimization and life satisfaction. Bullying victimization is measured with six frequency items (verbal, physical, relational), MIL with three comprehension/purpose/meaning items, and life satisfaction with a single 0–10 item. Using Mplus latent moderated structural equations (LMS) with TYPE = COMPLEX RANDOM and the final student weight, the authors report good measurement-model fit (CFI=0.982, TLI=0.968, RMSEA=0.043, SRMR=0.021) and a significant improvement from Model 0 to Model 1 (TRd=19.97, p<.001). The key moderation effect is significant (interaction B=0.231, SE=0.054, p<.001), with bullying victimization negatively related to life satisfaction (B=-0.369) and MIL positively related (B=1.861). Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal inference) and the use of non-PV self-report outcomes rather than achievement PVs.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 U.S. 15-year-olds (bullying victimization, meaning in life, life satisfaction)

title: 1-s2.0-S0191491X24000683-main
authors: L. Xiao, Kit-Tai Hau, Aohua Ni, Leifeng Xiao
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 reading-domain data from 26 economies selected by Global Competitiveness Index (15 high-GCI and 11 low-GCI), totaling 184,102 students from 6,397 schools. Reading achievement is analyzed using weighted likelihood estimates (WLE) derived from the OECD IRT scaling procedure, with 10 plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules. The authors fit multilevel hierarchical models (student and school levels) and report that both student ESCS and school ESCS are positively associated with reading achievement, with the SES effect larger in high-GCI economies (e.g., student ESCS β≈0.145 in high-GCI vs β≈0.075 in low-GCI). Disciplinary climate shows a positive direct effect and a significant moderation of the SES–reading relationship, while teacher support is associated with reading at the student level but does not significantly moderate the SES gradient. Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal inference) and unclear explicit use of named sampling/replicate weights beyond PISA WLE scaling.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (WLE; multilevel models across 26 economies selected by GCI) | PISA 2018 Reading (WLE; multilevel moderation models across 26 economies selected by GCI)
all_target_variables: Reading achievement (WLE scores) | Reading achievement (WLE scores) — moderation of SES by teacher support and disciplinary climate

title: The role of parental involvement in adolescents’ digital reading performance
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 digital reading performance (10 plausible values, PVREAD 1–10) for 15-year-old students in 12 countries (total N=83,043; 3,342 schools), linking student and parent questionnaire data and adding the country-level ICT Development Index (IDI). It estimates a three-level HLM (country–school–student) and handles missing parent-questionnaire data via multiple imputation, matching each imputed dataset to the corresponding plausible value and combining results using Rubin’s rules. In the full model, previous parental support in reading-related activities is positively associated with digital reading performance (β=0.021, p<0.001), while current parental support and school policies for parental behavioral involvement are negatively associated (β=-0.041 and β=-0.047, both p<0.001). Parental emotional support (β=0.055) and parental enjoyment of reading (β=0.060) are positively correlated with performance (both p<0.001), and only the interaction between previous support and emotional support shows a positive effect. Because the design is cross-sectional and the analysis is correlational, these associations should not be interpreted as causal impacts of parental involvement.

title: Exploring the relationship between educational ICT resources, student engagement, and academic performance: A multilevel structural equation analysis based on PISA 2018 data
authors: Yajing Wang, Yashuang Wang
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students from Finland, Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore, and the United States (N=26,405 after deleting missing values). Outcomes are reading, mathematical, and scientific literacy, each represented using 10 plausible values combined with Rubin’s rules. The authors estimate fixed-slope multilevel structural equation mediation models (student and school levels) linking school ICT resources (ICTSCH) and home ICT resources (ICTHOME) to achievement directly and indirectly through ICT-based student engagement (cognitive-motivational, curriculum-based, and non-curricular). Across domains, ICT resources show significant negative direct associations with achievement at the student level (e.g., reading: ICTSCH -0.037***; ICTHOME -0.054***), while mediation differs by level: student-level mediation is negative overall (driven by non-curricular engagement), whereas school-level mediation can be positive via curriculum-based engagement (e.g., reading: ICTHOME→CBE→AP 0.129*). Because the design is cross-sectional and the models are not predictive ML, results should be interpreted as correlational associations rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading literacy (10 PVs; multilevel mediation) | PISA 2018 Mathematical literacy (10 PVs; multilevel mediation) | PISA 2018 Scientific literacy (10 PVs; multilevel mediation)
all_target_variables: Reading literacy (academic performance) | Mathematical literacy (academic performance) | Scientific literacy (academic performance)

title: Measurement invariance of information, communication and technology (ICT) engagement and its relationship with student academic literacy: Evidence from PISA 2018
authors: Y. Ma, X. Qin
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 data from 16 countries/regions (KOR, JAP, HKG, USA, GER, FRA, ITA, COA, FIN, SWZ, TUR, AUS, NZL, BRA, CHI, HUN) to (a) test measurement invariance of the PISA ICT engagement questionnaire and (b) examine how four ICT engagement factors relate to student literacy in mathematics, science, and reading. The ICT engagement construct is modeled with a four-factor Likert-scale structure and tested via multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA) using WLSMV with theta parameterization; residual (strict) invariance is supported using fit-change criteria (e.g., ΔCFI = −0.005, ΔRMSEA = 0.000, ΔSRMR = 0.007). For literacy outcomes, each student receives 10 plausible values per domain, and the authors use the average of the 10 PVs. Associations are estimated with three-level models (students within schools within countries) including student, school, and country-level covariates and student sampling weights (W_FSTUWT). The paper reports total R² values of 0.17 (math), 0.12 (science), and 0.18 (reading), with perceived ICT autonomy generally positive and use of social media generally negative across countries; however, the design is cross-sectional so causal claims cannot be made.

title: The role of item format in the PISA 2018 mathematics literacy assessment: A cross-country study
authors: Kseniia Marcq, Johan Braeken, Erika Jassuly Chalén Donayre
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 mathematics literacy CBA item responses from students who received mathematics booklets in 71 countries/economies (total sample over 260,000). Using cross-classified mixed-effects logistic models estimated separately per country and then pooled via multivariate random-effects meta-analysis, it models item-level correctness as a function of item format (MC vs CR) and gender, including an interaction. Across countries, CR items were more difficult than MC items: the pooled logit effect was b1 = −1.13 (95% CI [−1.21, −1.05]) with average correct-response probabilities of 23% (CR) vs 48% (MC). Item format explained 12% of item variance on average, but the effect varied by country (larger in lower-performing systems). The gender moderation was small (interaction b12 = −0.09), suggesting limited within-country fairness impact. Limitations include lack of reported survey-weighting and missing-data handling for item responses, and the fact that the analysis targets item difficulty rather than PV-based achievement.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics literacy (CBA), item-level responses (rotated booklet; 71 countries/economies)
all_target_variables: Probability of correct response to a mathematics item (binary correctness) | Cross-country variation in item format effect (MC vs CR) by gender

title: The interrelationships between reading achievement, online reading activities, and metacognitive skills: Findings from PISA data
authors: A. Rohatgi, O.E. Hatlevik
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 reading-focused data for five Nordic countries (Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden; total N=27,170 students from 1,176 schools) to examine interrelationships among online reading activities for information search (ORA), reading achievement (RA; PV1READ–PV10READ), and online metacognition for assessing source credibility (MASC), alongside ESCS and covariates. The authors fit a multigroup multilevel structural equation model in Mplus with TYPE=TWOLEVEL and country as the grouping variable, reporting overall model fit (χ2(291)=2327.20, CFI=0.93, TLI=0.92, RMSEA=0.04, SRMR=0.057). RA was a consistent positive predictor of MASC across countries (RA→MASC: 0.39–0.51), while ORA’s association with MASC varied: direct effects were significant only in Norway and Sweden, but indirect effects through RA were significant in all countries. The analysis applies PISA sampling weights and uses full-information maximum likelihood for missingness; however, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation and the SEM assumptions (e.g., unidirectional paths) should be considered when translating findings into policy.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (15-year-olds), Nordic countries (DNK, FIN, ISL, NOR, SWE)
all_target_variables: Online reading activities for searching information (ORA)

title: School performance and inequality of opportunities in Latin America
authors: Juliane Borchers, Marina S. Cunha
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 student achievement in Latin America (10 countries: ARG, BRA, CHL, COL, CRI, DOM, MEX, PAN, PER, URY) using a multilevel educational production function framework with students nested in schools. Outcomes are PISA standardized reading, mathematics, and science scores, estimated using all ten plausible values and the 80 PISA replicates, with missing values replaced by each variable’s country average. The reported results are multilevel regression coefficients rather than ML predictive metrics: grade repetition shows large negative associations across all three domains, while family background is consistently positive. In mathematics and science, student-perceived teacher feedback is significantly negative, and instructional adaptation is positive for mathematics. The paper is cross-sectional, so findings describe associations and heterogeneity by socioeconomic context rather than causal impacts.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (15-16) Reading achievement (Plausible Values) | PISA 2018 (15-16) Mathematics achievement (Plausible Values) | PISA 2018 (15-16) Science achievement (Plausible Values)
all_target_variables: Reading achievement (PVs) | Mathematics achievement (PVs) | Science achievement (PVs)

title: Predicting adolescents’ environmental action: From individual to national-level factors using an explainable machine learning approach
authors: Bo Hu, Jing Gao, Yannuo Feng, Ziqian Xia, Kun Wang, Liuna Geng
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 (66 countries; final analytic sample 420,339 adolescents after excluding non-responders to the environmental-action items) to predict two binary targets: private-sphere and public-sphere environmental actions. Four ML algorithms were trained with a 90/10 train-test split and stratified 10-fold cross-validation on the training set, with Optuna hyperparameter tuning; missing values were imputed using MICE predictive mean matching, and class imbalance was addressed via SMOTE. For public-sphere actions, LightGBM was best, reaching test Accuracy = 0.700, F1 = 0.702, Recall = 0.702, and AUC = 0.767. For private-sphere actions, XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy/recall (test Accuracy = 0.833, Recall = 0.833, AUC = 0.718), while Random Forest slightly led F1. The models use SHAP for interpretability, but SHAP-based feature importance is not causal, and the manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights in the ML pipeline.
ml_all_techniques: LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, Neural Network
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) — environmental action items (public-sphere vs private-sphere)
all_target_variables: Public-sphere environmental action (classification) | Private-sphere environmental action (classification)

title: Does between-school tracking really result in more achievement homogeneous schools? Evidence from 40 countries around the globe
authors: Silvia Salchegger, Markus Hirczy
outcome_summary: This study uses a two-stage individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis combining TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 (math and science), PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 (reading), and PISA 2018 (age 15) across 40 countries (with PISA coverage ≥80%). The authors decompose achievement variance into within-school achievement variation (WSAV) and between-school achievement variation (BSAV) using multilevel variance decomposition, then compute DID-style differences in WSAV/BSAV from Grade 4 to age 15 and synthesize them with random-effects meta-analysis and mixed-effects meta-regressions. Across domains, WSAV reductions are small and statistically significant mainly for reading (early tracking μ̂ = -15.33, p < .05), while BSAV increases are large in early-tracking countries (reading μ̂ = 25.64; math μ̂ = 26.50; science μ̂ = 29.18, all p < .05). Tracking timing significantly moderates BSAV change (e.g., reading QM[2] = 12.11, p = .002), but WSAV moderation is weaker and domain-dependent. Limitations include the absence of a documented missing-data strategy and the fact that this is not ML prediction; causal claims are limited by the pseudo-panel DID assumptions and cross-assessment comparability.
all_datasets_used: PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading and PISA 2018 Reading (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change | TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Math and PISA 2018 Math (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change | TIMSS 2011 Grade 4 Science and PISA 2018 Science (age 15) — WSAV/BSAV change
all_target_variables: Within-school achievement variation (WSAV) change | Between-school achievement variation (BSAV) change

title: Competitiveness, country economic inequality and adolescent well-being: Analysis of 60 countries
authors: Y. Koyama, T. Fujiwara
outcome_summary: This cross-sectional observational study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-olds, analyzing 347,934 adolescents from 60 countries with complete competitiveness and well-being data and available country Gini index values. Outcomes are non-cognitive well-being composites: life satisfaction and purpose of life, standardized across OECD countries. The authors estimate multilevel linear mixed models with random intercepts for individuals and countries, applying school- and student-level sampling weights and handling missing covariates via multiple imputation (mice) with Rubin’s rules. Results show that individual competitiveness is positively associated with both life satisfaction (β = 0.087) and purpose of life (β = 0.214), while country competitiveness predicts purpose of life (β = 0.115) but not life satisfaction. The association between individual competitiveness and well-being is heterogeneous by national inequality, with the strongest effects in middle Gini countries. Limitations include self-reported measures and cross-sectional design, so causality cannot be inferred.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Well-being: life satisfaction | PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Well-being: purpose of life
all_target_variables: Life satisfaction (standardized composite score) | Purpose of life (standardized composite score)

title: Relations between academic boredom, academic achievement, ICT use, and teacher enthusiasm among adolescents
authors: F. Borgonovi, Magdalena Pokropek, Artur Pokropek
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 microdata from eight countries (Bulgaria, Georgia, Hong Kong, Ireland, Mexico, Panama, Serbia, Spain) to examine how academic boredom relates to achievement and how ICT use and teacher enthusiasm are associated with boredom among 15-year-olds. The authors model boredom in mathematics classes, language and literature classes, and self-study at home using multilevel models with students nested in schools, and they handle missing achievement data via multiple imputation combined with PISA plausible values using Rubin’s rules. They report standardized associations rather than ML performance metrics: ICT use for leisure shows positive associations with boredom (about +11% to +12% of a SD in math and self-study boredom on average), while teacher enthusiasm shows negative associations (about −12% in math, −31% in language/literature, and −11% in self-study on average). The key limitation is that the design is cross-sectional and correlational, so reverse causality and omitted-variable bias remain possible; additionally, the paper does not present survey-weight application details beyond stating weighted representativeness.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Reading and Mathematics — boredom in mathematics classes | PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Reading and Mathematics — boredom in language and literature classes | PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Reading and Mathematics — boredom during self-study at home
all_target_variables: Boredom in mathematics classes (self-reported) | Boredom in language and literature classes (self-reported) | Boredom during self-study at home (self-reported)

title: Patterns of cognitive returns to Information and Communication Technology (ICT) use of 15-year-olds: Global evidence from a Hierarchical Linear Modeling approach using PISA 2018
authors: Aditi Bhutoria, Nayyaf Aljabri
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 for 15-year-olds across 79 countries using a three-level HLM (students within schools within countries) to estimate how ICT-related online activity relates to cognitive outcomes in mathematics, science, and reading. The dependent variables are PISA plausible values, with the authors using pv2 for each subject, and they address missingness in variables with >5% missing via multiple imputation using MICE. The key result is consistent concave (inverted-U) patterns: Online Activity has positive coefficients (e.g., 36.87*** in math, 35.20*** in science, 44.38*** in reading) but negative quadratic terms (−4.845***, −4.607***, −5.551***), implying diminishing returns beyond a threshold. Heterogeneity analyses show that the interaction between Online Activity categories and ESCS indicates moderation by socioeconomic status, and country subgroups using the ICT Development Index suggest diminishing returns are more evident where ICT infrastructure is established. Because the design is observational, the findings indicate associations rather than causal effects, and the use of a single plausible value may affect precision relative to combining all PVs.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (pv2) for 15-year-olds | PISA 2018 Science (pv2) for 15-year-olds | PISA 2018 Reading (pv2) for 15-year-olds
all_target_variables: Mathematics achievement (Plausible Value pv2) | Science achievement (Plausible Value pv2) | Reading achievement (Plausible Value pv2)

title: Are schools digitally inclusive for all? Profiles of school digital inclusion using PISA 2018
authors: Hye Jeong Kim, Pilnam Yi, Ji In Hong
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 data for 15-year-olds across 27 countries, constructing school-level profiles of school digital inclusion (SDI) from 14 standardized indicators covering digital infrastructure, support for technology integration, and digital literacy (teacher skills and student digital literacy). Latent profile analysis identified three distinct SDI profiles: High (21.05%, n=1596), Medium (52.24%, n=3961), and Low (26.72%, n=2026), with significant between-profile differences across all 14 indicators (ANOVA F tests reported in Table 3). To explain profile membership, multinomial logistic regression showed that ESCS and school type were significant predictors: for example, ESCS increased the odds of high SDI membership versus low SDI (OR=2.476, p<0.001), and private schools were more likely to be in higher SDI profiles. The paper does not report a formal missing-data handling strategy beyond excluding 211 schools with missing values, and it does not discuss survey-weight application; additionally, the approach is profile-based rather than predictive ML with PV-based achievement outcomes.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) School ICT questionnaire — school-level SDI profiles
all_target_variables: School digital inclusion profile membership (3 profiles)

title: Material resources, school climate, and achievement variations in the Philippines_ Insights from PISA 2018
authors: J.E. Trinidad
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for the Philippines, restricting to 7233 15-year-old students nested within 187 public and private schools, and uses standardized reading and math test scores as outcomes. It constructs school-level indices for material resource constraints and school climate deficits (attendance and discipline) and includes student-level attendance, gender (female), and an OECD SES index. The authors fit hierarchical linear models and report that most variance is at the student level (reading: Level 1 variance 4090.88 vs Level 2 2183.69; math: Level 1 4266.70 vs Level 2 1902.70). For reading, material constraints and attendance problems are significantly negative (e.g., materials coefficient −20.42, p<0.001; attendance climate −19.03, p<0.001), while private school, female, and SES are positive (p<0.001). For math, attendance problems and material constraints are also negative (e.g., attendance climate −17.98, p<0.001; student attendance −17.66, p<0.001), with private school, female, and SES positive (p<0.001). Limitations include reporting only the first plausible value and not documenting missing-data handling or survey-weight application, so results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Philippines (15-year-olds) Reading | PISA 2018 Philippines (15-year-olds) Math
all_target_variables: Reading achievement (standardized test score; single plausible value) | Math achievement (standardized test score; single plausible value)

title: Technological resources, ICT use and schools efficiency in Latin America – Insights from OECD PISA 2018
authors: T. Agasisti, G. Antequera, M. Delprato
outcome_summary: This study analyzes school efficiency in Latin America using OECD PISA 2018 data from 10 countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Panama, Peru, Uruguay). The authors treat schools as decision-making units and estimate output-oriented technical efficiency via Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) using school-average math, reading, and science achievement (based on PV1) as outputs, and school infrastructure, student-teacher ratio (inverse), teachers’ availability/capacity, and family socioeconomic status as inputs. They then run a Simar–Wilson two-stage DEA second-stage regression where ICT availability (ICT resources index) and ICT use (ICT use index) are key environmental covariates, alongside admission criteria and system characteristics (private vs public, urban vs rural, and competition). Results show an average technical inefficiency of about 25% (mean TEBC ≈ 0.755) and substantial within-country dispersion. Across countries, higher ICT availability is associated with higher efficiency (e.g., positive marginal effects in the top ICT availability quartile for most countries), while ICT use effects are more heterogeneous and sometimes non-significant or negative (notably Colombia). The paper frames associations rather than causal effects and does not report a missing-data strategy beyond PV1 usage, nor does it document the use of PISA sampling weights in the DEA/second-stage estimation.

title: Predictors of students’ global competence in China, Germany, Turkey, and Mexico: A cross-cultural comparative study
authors: H. Zhang, H. Tang, Qianyu Zhou, Fuyan Wang, Hong Zhang
outcome_summary: This cross-cultural comparative study uses PISA 2018 global competence data (grades 7–12) from four economies: China operationalized via Hong Kong SAR (n=6037), Germany (n=5451), Turkey (n=6890), and Mexico (n=7299), totaling 25,677 students nested in 771 schools. The authors model four questionnaire-based global competence dimensions—self-efficacy, respect, awareness of intercultural communication, and global mindedness—using multilevel HLM (two-level student/school structure), not PV-based achievement. Across countries, cultural possessions (CULTPOS), perceived ICT competence (COMPICT), and perception of co-operation (PERCOOP) show consistent positive associations with self-efficacy and awareness, while their relationships with respect are negative and context-dependent. The paper reports multilevel regression coefficients (β) and standard errors but no predictive ML metrics (e.g., Accuracy/AUC/R²). Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling and no causal identification, so findings should be interpreted as correlational patterns rather than effects of interventions.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Global Competence (grades 7–12) — self-efficacy regarding global issues scale | PISA 2018 Global Competence (grades 7–12) — respect for people from other cultural backgrounds scale | PISA 2018 Global Competence (grades 7–12) — awareness of intercultural communication scale | PISA 2018 Global Competence (grades 7–12) — global mindedness scale
all_target_variables: Self-efficacy regarding global issues | Respect for people from other cultural backgrounds | Awareness of intercultural communication | Global mindedness

title: The influence of ICT competencies on English digital reading achievement
authors: Shing On Leung, Ronnel B. King, Lingyi Fu, Shuqiong Luo, Lijia Lin
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 digital reading achievement in English using PV1READ for 7703 15-year-old students from Macau (n=679), Hong Kong (n=348), and Singapore (n=6676). Missing data were addressed with MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS 26, and the authors estimate hierarchical regression models with gender and SES as controls, then add ICT literacy (ICT use during lessons; ICT use outside lessons) and ICT attitudes (interest, autonomy, competence, and ICT as a social-interaction topic). Across economies, SES shows a positive association with English digital reading achievement, while gender shows a negative association. ICT literacy effects are small and often negative (notably ICT use outside lessons in Macau), whereas interest, autonomy, and competence are positive predictors; ICT as a topic in social interaction is negative in all three economies. Limitations include the use of a single plausible value (PV1READ) and the absence of reported survey-weighting/replicate-weight procedures, so results may not fully reflect PISA’s complex sampling design.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) English digital reading (PV1READ) — Macau, Hong Kong, Singapore

title: Analysing ability grouping in secondary school: A way to improve academic performance and mitigate educational inequalities in Spain?
authors: José Manuel Amoedo, María Carmen Sánchez-Carreira, Bruno Blanco-Varela
outcome_summary: The study analyzes the effects of ability grouping on achievement in Spain using PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students. It constructs a treatment indicator (ABGROUP) from school questionnaire items and builds a synthetic socio-educational vulnerability index (SVI), then splits students into low/medium/high vulnerability groups using percentile cut-points. Propensity Score Matching (nearest-neighbour with exact matching) is used to create balanced treatment and control groups, and outcomes are computed as differences in weighted means for PISA plausible-value achievement measures (global, science, reading, mathematics). Across domains, the results show predominantly adverse effects: high-vulnerability students experience statistically significant declines in global performance, science, reading, and mathematics, while medium-vulnerability effects are generally non-significant. Reading also shows significant declines for low-vulnerability students. Limitations include reliance on PISA’s ability-grouping questionnaire (no direct information on within- vs between-class implementation) and the absence of reported complex-survey weight handling in the matching/uncertainty estimation.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Spain (15-year-olds) — Global competence (overall) | PISA 2018 Spain (15-year-olds) — Science competence | PISA 2018 Spain (15-year-olds) — Reading competence | PISA 2018 Spain (15-year-olds) — Mathematics competence
all_target_variables: Global performance (PISA plausible values) | Science performance (PISA plausible values) | Reading performance (PISA plausible values) | Mathematics performance (PISA plausible values)

title: Effects of individual attributes, family background, and school context on students’ global competence: Insights from the OECD PISA 2018
authors: Xi Wu, Yanan Zhang
outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 global competence for 15-year-olds using a hierarchical linear modelling approach to examine how individual attributes, family background, and school context relate to global competence across six countries/regions (Chile, Panama, Croatia, Malta, Korea, Hong Kong). Global competence is measured via a cognitive test and scaled using 10 plausible values, with weighted likelihood estimates (WLE) used as participant scores; the paper reports country-specific HLM coefficients rather than ML predictive accuracy. Across all six regions, gender, student self-efficacy in global issues, family ESCS, and teachers’ intercultural attitudes show statistically significant associations with global competence (e.g., gender β ranges from −7.26 to −21.97; self-efficacy β ranges from 10.62 to 22.90; ESCS β ranges from 4.11 to 17.37; teacher attitudes β ranges from 18.14 to 32.91). The authors apply student- and school-level sampling weights and use multiple imputation for missing data, but the design is explicitly correlational, so causal claims are limited.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Global competence (15-year-olds; OECD global citizenship framework)
all_target_variables: Global competence performance (WLE from 10 plausible values)

title: Indiscipline: The school climate of Brazilian schools and the impact on student performance
authors: Júlia Sbroglio Rizzotto, Marco Túlio Aniceto França
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes PISA 2018 for Brazil (15-year-olds) and defines a disciplinary/school climate index from five student questionnaire items about classroom disruptions in language-of-instruction classes. Students are classified into negative vs positive climate groups, and the study estimates the effect on PISA reading, mathematics, and science scale scores using propensity score matching (nearest neighbor with replacement, plus Kernel and Radius), inverse probability-weighted regression adjustment (IPWRA), and robustness checks including Rosenbaum bounds and an OLS model with school fixed effects. Across matching methods, negative school climate is associated with lower achievement by about 12–15 points in math/reading and about 10–13 points in science; the dose-response function shows smaller but still negative effects (e.g., reading −9.06, math −8.3, science −6.72). The analysis uses complete cases only and does not document the use of PISA sampling/replicate weights, and the authors acknowledge potential reverse causality between climate and performance.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Grade 10+ Reading (Brazil, 15-year-olds) | PISA 2018 Grade 10+ Mathematics (Brazil, 15-year-olds) | PISA 2018 Grade 10+ Science (Brazil, 15-year-olds)
all_target_variables: Reading grade (PISA scale score) | Math grade (PISA scale score) | Science grade (PISA scale score)

title: 1-s2.0-S0742051X25001106-main
authors: Leilei Liang, Chengbin Zheng, Kai Liu, Jiayuan Xu, Junsong Fei, Songli Mei
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-olds from 52 countries/regions that completed the ICT usage questionnaire, focusing on reading, mathematics, and science literacy. Outcomes are based on plausible values, but the authors select PV1READ, PV1MATH, and PV1SCIE after reporting identical centrality metrics across the 10 PVs. The analysis estimates mixed graphical model networks (with LASSO-penalized estimation and 10-fold cross-validation) and evaluates node centrality (expected influence, strength, closeness, betweenness) plus flow-network associations; no conventional ML predictive metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/R²) are reported. The most central ICT-related predictors include perceived ICT competence and learning-oriented out-of-school ICT use (Homesch), while assessing credibility (Metaspam) shows the strongest flow association. Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal inference) and reliance on network centrality rather than predictive performance, with missing data handled via complete-case deletion.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (PV1READ), 15-year-olds | PISA 2018 Mathematics (PV1MATH), 15-year-olds | PISA 2018 Science (PV1SCIE), 15-year-olds
all_target_variables: Reading literacy (PISA 2018 PV1READ) | Mathematical literacy (PISA 2018 PV1MATH) | Scientific literacy (PISA 2018 PV1SCIE)

title: Equity’s diverse pathways: How collectivism shapes the link between home possessions and scientific literacy
authors: M. Wen, Yunbing Liu, Mingqi Wen, Qingke Guo
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2022 scientific literacy (PV1SCIE) for 230,078 students nested in 37 countries/economies, using a two-level hierarchical linear modeling approach with random intercepts and random slopes. The unconditional model shows substantial between-country variation (ICC=0.228). Across the global baseline, fixed effects are positive and significant for family wealth (γ10=1.15, p<.001), cultural possessions (γ10=4.89, p<.001), home educational resources (γ10=2.15, p<.001), and books in the home (γ10=29.75, p<.001). Cross-level interactions reveal three culturally contingent pathways: Latin America amplifies wealth and cultural possessions but weakens home educational resources; Muslim-majority contexts attenuate PISA-defined cultural assets (books and cultural possessions) and home educational resources; East/Southeast Asia shows a paradox where wealth is marginally stronger (γ13=1.48, p=.054) while home educational resources are weaker (γ13=-3.31, p<.05). Limitations include the cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling and survey-weight use.

title: Need supportive teaching is associated with greater reading achievement: What the Philippines can learn from PISA 2018
authors: J.Y. Haw, R.B. King, J.E.R. Trinidad
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Philippines data for 15-year-old students, focusing on reading as the primary domain and using a Rasch-scaled reading achievement score standardized to the PISA international scale. From 7233 students, the authors retained 7050 students with complete data from 187 schools. In a multilevel (hierarchical) linear model, need supportive teaching (a composite of three language-teacher questionnaire items reflecting autonomy, competence, and relatedness support) showed a positive association with reading achievement (β=18.20, SE=1.06, p<.001), with an ICC of 0.34 indicating substantial between-school clustering. Interaction tests indicated that this association was not significantly moderated by school type (public/private), urbanicity, family SES quartiles, or school mean SES. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and the absence of reported PISA sampling/replicate weights in the estimation details.

title: How teachers’ enthusiasm influences Chinese students’ school belonging: The mediation role of teaching practices
authors: Mingfeng Xue
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Chinese students from four participating cities (Beijing, Shanghai, Zhejiang, Jiangsu; N=12,057 students across 360 schools) to examine how teacher enthusiasm relates to students’ school belonging and whether four teaching practices mediate this relationship. School belonging (SCHBLNG) and the teacher-related scales are IRT-scaled using weighted likelihood estimates (WLE), with OECD-referenced scaling (mean 0, SD 1). The analysis applies multilevel mediation models (1–1–1) to account for students nested within schools and reports that teacher enthusiasm has a significant positive total effect on school belonging (est.=0.272, se.=0.010, p<.01) and a smaller direct effect after mediators (est.=0.179, se.=0.012, p<.01). Teaching practices jointly mediate 33.14% of the total effect, with teacher feedback the largest mediator (average mediation effect=0.033). Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling and the cross-sectional design, which constrains causal claims about the mediation pathways.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (China; four cities) — school belonging (SCHBLNG) scale (WLE)
all_target_variables: School belonging (SCHBLNG; WLE score) | School belonging (SCHBLNG; WLE score) — mediator effects (Model 2) | Mediation effects of teaching practices between teacher enthusiasm and school belonging

title: ICT and Digital Reading Achievement: A Cross-national Comparison using PISA 2018 Data
authors: Yiren Kong, Young Sik Seo, Ling Zhai
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 reading achievement in a digital context for three countries (United States, Singapore, Finland), using ten plausible values for reading achievement and multilevel linear models to account for students nested within schools. The final analytic samples were USA N=3,645, Singapore N=6,090, and Finland N=4,352 after excluding cases with missing values on variables used. Across all three education systems, students’ attitude toward digital devices was positively associated with digital reading achievement (e.g., USA B=20.22, p<.001; SGP B=9.83, p<.001; FIN B=20.09, p<.001), while frequency of using digital devices was negatively associated (e.g., USA B=-25.23, p<.001). Frequency of reading on digital devices showed a positive association with achievement in all countries (e.g., FIN B=22.41, p<.001). Gender moderation was present for some relationships (attitude effects in USA/Finland; reading-frequency effect in Singapore). The paper does not use ML algorithms; therefore, results are correlational/associational rather than predictive-model performance.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (digital context), cross-national (USA, SGP, FIN)
all_target_variables: Digital reading achievement (PISA reading achievement plausible values)

title: How teacher collaboration profiles connect to literacy instructional practices: evidence from PISA 2018 outcomes for Korea
authors: K. Rubadeau, J. Jang
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 Teacher Questionnaire data for Korean middle school literacy teachers (n=1,266) to identify latent profiles of teacher collaboration and to compare instructional-practice use across profiles. Using latent profile analysis (LPA) in MPlus 8.3, the authors tested 2–5 profile solutions and selected a four-profile model based on fit indices (AIC/BIC/SABIC), likelihood ratio tests (BLRT significant), and high classification quality (entropy reported around .961 for the four-profile solution). They then applied the BCH method to test differences in five instructional practices (direct instruction, adaptive instruction, initiation of reading strategies, stimulation of reading engagement, feedback provision) across the four collaboration profiles. The results show that teachers in the High Collaboration profile reported higher use of all five practices than other profiles, while the Assessment-centered Collaboration profile differed from Low Collaboration mainly in assessment-related instructional patterns. The study is correlational (no regression-based causal identification) and relies on self-report questionnaire measures; it also does not document the use of PISA complex survey weights.

title: 1-s2.0-S0883035520318218-main
authors: M.R. Harwell, Q. Zhao
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2012 microdata for the United States (analytic N=2,968 after listwise deletion of missing cases) to examine how socio-economic status (SES) relates to mathematics achievement through direct and indirect pathways using path analysis in AMOS. Mathematics achievement is computed as the average of the first three plausible mathematics achievement values for each student, and the authors report model fit indices (chi-square p<.01; NFI/CFI around .95/.93; RMSEA <.05 for the simpler model and ~.08 for the more complex model). In the simpler model, SESHP shows the largest direct effect on mathematics achievement (.31 SD), and parent education has a sizable positive indirect effect (.20 SD). In the more complex model, PISA SES has the strongest direct effect (.32 SD) and multiple indirect effects suggest SES influences achievement via home possessions and teacher support/relations. Limitations include the use of complete cases (potential bias if data are not missing at random) and the absence of reported survey-weight handling.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2012 (United States) — Mathematics achievement (Grade 7th or equivalent, 15-year-olds)
all_target_variables: Mathematics achievement (average of first three plausible values)

title: The relationship between cultural capital and the students’ perception of feedback across 75 countries: Evidence from PISA 2018
authors: N. Eryilmaz, A. Sandoval-Hernández
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 student questionnaire data for 15-year-olds in reading classes across 75 countries/economies, modeling PERFEED (students’ perceived frequency of directive teacher feedback) with multilevel random-intercept regression (students nested within schools). It reports country-specific regression coefficients (Table 3) rather than a single predictive accuracy metric, showing a consistent positive pattern for home educational resources (HEDRES) and reading enjoyment (JOYREAD) on perceived feedback, with non-significant exceptions (e.g., Thailand for HEDRES; Netherlands and Moscow region for JOYREAD). Parental education (PARED) is significant in only six countries with mixed directions, while parents’ occupational status (HISEI) is significantly negative in 20 countries. Gender is consistently significant across all countries, with boys perceiving more feedback than girls. The analysis is cross-sectional and does not establish causality; additionally, missing-data handling for predictors at the individual level is not fully specified beyond excluding four countries with missing PERFEED.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (lower secondary; directive feedback perception; 75 countries)

title: A social network analysis of student-perceived teaching practices in top-performing countries and regions in reading literacy: Insights from PISA 2018
authors: Ping Li, Diya Dou, Ningning Zhao, Guoxing Xiang, Jieqi Li, Xiaoqin Zhu
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 Reading (Student Survey) data for 16 top-performing countries/regions in reading literacy, using IRT to synthesize students’ perceived teaching-practice items into latent variables (theta-values) for six constructs: disciplinary climate, teacher support, teacher-directed instruction, cognitive stimulation, adaptive instruction, and teacher enthusiasm. For the social network analysis, the authors draw a stratified simple random sample of 1,000 students per country/region (16,000 total) and estimate partial-correlation networks, applying LASSO regularization (gamma=0.5) to obtain sparser networks. Network stability is evaluated via nonparametric bootstrap (1000 resamples), reporting strength centrality stability (CS cor=0.70). Across countries/regions, teacher support is the most central practice (mean strength=0.90), and clustering yields four typologies with significant inter-cluster differences for all six practices. Limitations include the descriptive nature of network/clustering results (no PV-based achievement outcome modeling) and missing-data handling not being reported.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (Student Survey) — perceived teaching practices (IRT latent variables)

title: Reading instruction and reading engagement and their relationship with Chinese students’ PISA reading performance: Evidence from B-S-J-Z, Hong Kong, and Chinese Taipei
authors: Y.-x. Gu, K.-l. Lau
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 computer-based reading literacy for 15-year-olds from three Chinese societies (B-S-J-Z, Hong Kong, Chinese Taipei; total N=25,338 across 720 schools). Using a two-level hierarchical linear model (students nested in schools), the authors first estimate effects of background controls and seven instruction indices (TMQT-based: cognitive activation, classroom management/structure, supportive climate), then add six reading engagement indices (cognitive and non-cognitive engagement). In Model 1, disciplinary climate and teacher support are significant positive predictors, while teacher-directed instruction is a significant negative predictor across all three regions; teacher enthusiasm is not significant. In Model 2, metacognition of assessing credibility is the strongest positive engagement predictor across regions, while perceived reading difficulty is a significant negative predictor; joy of reading and metacognitive strategies (understanding/remembering and summarizing) are also positive. The paper reports variance explained and coefficients but does not document PV handling or missing-data treatment, and HLM provides associations rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (computer-based), 15-year-olds (B-S-J-Z, Hong Kong, Chinese Taipei)

title: Bridging Between Us and Them: Cultivating inclusive attitudes toward immigrants through global citizenship education and intergroup contact in South Korea
authors: Soobin Choi
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for Korea (15-year-olds; analytic sample N=6570 across 188 schools) to examine whether global citizenship education (GCE) fosters inclusive attitudes toward immigrants (IATI) and whether it moderates intergroup contact in school and community. IATI is measured as a Likert-based composite scale (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.89), while GCE exposure is operationalized as four binary items summed into dummy variables for exposure to 1–4 types. Using multilevel regression with school-fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors, the authors report that GCE shows positive, non-linear associations with IATI (+0.130 to +0.295 SD across 1–4 types, all significant), and that the interaction between school contact and GCE is significant only for students exposed to all four GCE types (+0.272 SD, p<.01). Intergroup contact in the community is not significantly associated with IATI, and no significant community-contact interactions emerge. Missing data are handled via multiple imputation (50 datasets pooled), but the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 (Korea, 15-year-olds) Inclusive attitudes toward immigrants (IATI) scale

title: Does the relationship between competitiveness and student achievement vary based on the culture of competitiveness? Evidence from PISA 2018
authors: Seijoon Park
outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 mathematics achievement for 15-year-olds using ten plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) combined with multilevel multiple imputation for missing data, and estimates three-level hierarchical linear models (students nested in schools nested in countries). The analytic sample includes 436,343 students from 57 PISA countries/economies for which both competitiveness climate items and a country-level culture-of-competitiveness index (from the World Values Survey) were available. In the final cross-level interaction model, student competitiveness showed a positive association with mathematics achievement (B=8.916, p<0.001), and competitiveness climate at school level was also positively related (B=14.194, p<0.01). The culture of competitiveness significantly moderated the student-competitiveness effect (interaction B=1.056, p<0.05), while the school-competitiveness climate moderation was not significant. Because the design is cross-sectional and the analysis is correlational (not causal), the results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.

title: PISA Maths-Reading index and its relationship with gender and levels of performance
authors: Susana Nieto-Isidro, Fernando Martínez-Abad
outcome_summary: This study conducts a secondary, non-experimental cross-sectional analysis of PISA 2018 microdata for Spain (n=35,943 15-year-olds) to build an individual Maths-Reading Index (MRI) defined as mathematics minus reading performance, computed across the 10 plausible values for each domain. The authors then examine correlations between the MRI and a wide set of contextual and educational factors, using PISA’s adjusted student weights (W_FSTUWT) and 80 replicate weights (Fay’s BRR) to obtain conservative standard errors and p-values. To refine interpretation, they create three performance-based groups (low/medium/high) using k-means clustering (k=3) on maths and reading performance for each plausible-value pair, and then analyze how correlations differ by performance level and by gender. The paper reports correlation coefficients (r) and p-values rather than predictive accuracy metrics, and it explicitly notes that correlations do not imply causality. Overall, the results suggest that gender-linked patterns and reading engagement/self-concept variables are strongly associated with students’ maths-versus-reading orientation, informing targeted STEM-support strategies.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Spain (15-year-olds) Mathematics and Reading (plausible values)

title: Perceived teacher support, self-concept, enjoyment and achievement in reading: A multilevel mediation model based on PISA 2018
authors: L. Ma
outcome_summary: The study analyzes mainland China PISA 2018 data for 15-year-old students (N=12,058; 362 schools) to test a multilevel mediation model grounded in expectancy-value theory. The outcome is reading literacy from the PISA 2018 reading assessment, and the mediators are reading enjoyment and reading self-concept measured via Likert scales. The authors estimate multilevel mediation in Mplus and handle missing continuous variables using EM; reading literacy parameters are combined across the ten plausible-value datasets using Rubin’s combination rules. In the mediation results, student-level perceived teacher support significantly predicts reading literacy (B=5.511, SE=1.177, p<0.001), but school-level teacher support does not (p>0.05). Reading enjoyment (B=23.999, SE=1.584, p<0.001) and reading self-concept (B=18.073, SE=2.297, p<0.001) remain significant when included, while direct teacher-support effects become non-significant. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature of PISA and the fact that the analysis is mediation modeling rather than ML prediction.

title: What teachers can do to enhance students’ well-being: Discussion
authors: Bernhard Schmitz
outcome_summary: This article is a discussion piece that synthesizes evidence from studies in a special issue on student well-being and the role of teaching. It does not conduct an original machine-learning analysis, nor does it estimate predictive models on PISA microdata; instead, it reviews how included studies conceptualize well-being (e.g., hedonic/eudaimonic, social belonging) and how they relate teacher- or teaching-related variables to well-being outcomes. The manuscript highlights that several included studies use large PISA datasets (e.g., PISA 2018 with hundreds of thousands of students across many countries) and that methodological approaches in the included papers include longitudinal designs and multilevel analyses, but it does not report ML model performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) for any single predictive task. Limitations discussed focus on common-method bias from student self-reports, cross-sectional designs, and the lack of intervention evidence for causal mechanisms.

title: Do intercultural education and attitudes promote student wellbeing and social outcomes? An examination across PISA countries
authors: Geetanjali Basarkod, Theresa Dicke, Kelly-Ann Allen, Philip D. Parker, Mary Ryan, Herbert W. Marsh, Zoe T. Carrick, Jiesi Guo
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 cross-national data on 15-year-olds across up to 80 countries/economic regions to examine whether intercultural education practices and teachers’ intercultural attitudes are associated with wellbeing (eudaimonia, life satisfaction, positive affect) and social outcomes (school belonging, victimization). The authors fit weighted three-level multilevel models (students within schools within countries) and apply multiple imputation (10 imputations) for missing questionnaire data, combining results via Rubin’s rules. Across outcomes, the strongest and most consistent associations come from student perceptions: student-reported intercultural education practices predict higher wellbeing and belonging (e.g., β≈0.07–0.12) and slightly lower victimization (β≈-0.02), while student-reported teacher intercultural attitudes show a medium negative association with victimization (β=-0.21) and a small positive association with belonging (β=0.08). Principal- and teacher self-reports are mostly near zero. Because the design is cross-sectional and the models are not ML predictive pipelines, the findings support correlational policy guidance rather than causal claims.

all_target_variables: Eudaimonia (PISA scale score) | Life satisfaction (PISA scale score) | Positive affect (PISA scale score) | School belonging (PISA scale score) | Victimization (PISA scale score)

title: Growth mindset mediates perceptions of teachers' and parents' process feedback in digital reading performance: Evidence from 32 OECD countries
authors: Jie Hu, Yiwei Zhang
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 computer-based reading data for students in 32 OECD countries, using digital reading literacy measured through plausible values (PV1READ; first of 10 PVs). The authors estimate a multilevel mediation model (SEM with maximum likelihood) to test whether students’ perceptions of teachers’ and parents’ process feedback (TEACHSUP, EMOSUPS) promote growth mindset (GM), which in turn predicts digital reading performance. Across countries, growth mindset shows a consistently positive direct association with PV1READ (path b βs ranging from 0.074 to 0.392), while total effects of process feedback are small but significant in many countries (TEACHSUP significant in 20; EMOSUPS significant in 30). Mediation proportions vary by country (teacher path 4.8%–53.6% in 18 countries; parent path 2.8%–46.8% in 25 countries). Limitations include mild effect sizes, correlational mediation (not causal), and reliance on a single-item growth mindset measure.

title: Competition or cooperation: Which is better for students’ academic performance? A multi‑level analysis across cultures based on PISA 2018
authors: Y. Li
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-olds across 76 countries/economies (after excluding Canada, Cyprus, and Vietnam) to examine how student-perceived and school-level competition and cooperation relate to achievement in reading, mathematics, and science. Outcomes are PISA plausible values: 10 PVs per subject are analyzed jointly using Stata’s pv command, and the authors estimate two-level hierarchical regression models to account for the nested student–school structure (ICC around 49–52% in the null models). In the pooled models, student perceived competition is consistently negatively associated with achievement (e.g., reading β = −1.588, p < .01), while student perceived cooperation is positive (reading β = 0.971, p < .001) and school cooperation shows the strongest positive associations (reading β = 21.312, p < .001; mathematics β = 19.744, p < .001; science β = 19.321, p < .001). Missing data are imputed using school- and country-level means with imputation dummies, and robustness checks use non-imputed data with OLS standard errors via Fay’s BRR. Because the design is cross-sectional and student perceptions may reflect reverse causality, the results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (10 plausible values, student-level; multilevel across 76 countries/economies) | PISA 2018 Mathematics (10 plausible values, student-level; multilevel across 76 countries/economies) | PISA 2018 Science (10 plausible values, student-level; multilevel across 76 countries/economies)
all_target_variables: Reading achievement (PVs) | Mathematics achievement (PVs) | Science achievement (PVs)

title: Need-supportive teaching is associated with reading achievement via intrinsic motivation across eight cultures
authors: J.Y. Haw, R.B. King
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 reading-focused data for 15-year-olds across 76 regions (after excluding Canada, Lebanon, and Northern Macedonia) and groups them into Schwartz’s eight cultural value orientations. It models perceived need-supportive teaching (NST) as a three-item latent construct and uses reading intrinsic motivation as the mediator, with reading achievement represented by PISA’s ten plausible values. Using PISA’s complex sampling approach (80 replicate weights) and multiple imputation for missingness (<6% per case), the SEM results show that intrinsic motivation positively predicts reading achievement across all eight cultures, with the largest standardized paths reported in the range of about 0.24–0.42. The indirect pathway from NST to achievement via intrinsic motivation is statistically significant across all eight groups but with small effect sizes, while the direct NST→achievement link is only partially supported. The authors emphasize that PISA is cross-sectional, so causal claims are limited, and the study relies on self-reported teaching perceptions rather than objective classroom observations.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (15-year-olds), Schwartz eight cultural groups (76 regions)

title: Need-supportive teaching is positively associated with students' well-being: A cross-cultural study
authors: Y. Wang, R. B. King
outcome_summary: This cross-cultural study used PISA 2018 (OECD) secondary data for 513,295 students across 70 economies to examine whether need-supportive teaching is associated with three subjective well-being components (positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction) and two additional well-being components (meaning in life and school belonging). The authors estimated two-level HLM models (students nested in schools) after testing a six-factor measurement model and measurement invariance across eight Schwartz (2009) cultural groups. Need-supportive teaching showed small but statistically significant standardized associations with positive affect (β = 0.11), life satisfaction (β = 0.11), meaning in life (β = 0.12), and school belonging (β = 0.10), and a negative association with negative affect (β = −0.04), with ICCs around 0.08–0.10. Missing data were addressed via MCMC multiple imputation. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and reliance on self-reported PISA items; the manuscript excerpt does not report whether PISA sampling weights were applied.
