all_target_variables: Self-efficacy in digital competencies (SEC) | Use of digital resources for support of feedback (USF) | Use of digital resources for subjective learning (USL)

title: Which educational approaches predict students’ generative AI confidence and responsibility?
authors: Tessa Consoli, Dominik Petko
outcome_summary: This exploratory survey study collected student-reported experiences of three GenAI media literacy education approaches (protective-preventive, critical-reflective, creative-productive) and measured two outcomes—GenAI confidence and GenAI responsibility—among 1157 upper secondary students in 15 highly digitized Swiss schools (German-speaking Switzerland). Using hierarchical multilevel multiple regression with class-level grouping, the authors found that the critical-reflective approach significantly predicted both outcomes (confidence β=0.11, p<.001; responsibility β=0.16, p<.001), while the protective-preventive approach did not significantly predict either outcome. The creative-productive approach predicted GenAI confidence only (β=0.08, p<.01). Model fit improved from Model 1 to Model 2 in both cases (confidence marginal R2 0.06→0.09; responsibility 0.02→0.05), with likelihood ratio tests p<.001. Limitations include self-report measures, listwise exclusion for missing data, collapsed school/class variance due to only 15 schools, and cross-sectional associations rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2022 (not used); Switzerland upper secondary student GenAI survey (2023-2024), multilevel regression
all_target_variables: GenAI confidence (Likert scale) | GenAI responsibility (Likert scale)

file_name: Hernández-Ramos & Araya. (2025). Do School Activities Foster Creative Thinking? An Analysis of PISA Results.pdf
title: Do School Activities Foster Creative Thinking? An Analysis of PISA Results
authors: Hernández-Ramos, Araya
outcome_summary: This study analyzes associations between students’ participation in school activities and PISA 2022 creative thinking outcomes, using country/economy-level records derived from PISA 2022 creative thinking means and its four domains (written, visual, social problem solving, scientific problem solving), plus PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 reading/mathematics/science scores. The analytic sample is 54 OECD countries and associated economies after excluding economies with sampling-standard issues; the paper does not report student-level modeling or complex-survey estimation. The strongest relationships are descriptive and regression-based: for overall creative thinking, Var 1 (writing/critical activities) shows a strong negative association (adjusted R²=0.721 in Model 1; adjusted R²=0.768 in Model 2), while reading scores are the most consistent positive predictors (adjusted R²=0.829 for PISA 2018 reading; 0.883 for PISA 2022 reading). For the scientific problem-solving domain, science club and programming participation are negatively correlated (r=−0.666 and r=−0.438). Limitations include the absence of documented plausible-value/missing-data procedures at the student level and the correlational, country-aggregate design, so causality cannot be inferred.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (country mean; four domains aggregated to overall mean score) | PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (Scientific Problem Solving domain; country mean) | PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (country mean; overall creative thinking score)
all_target_variables: Creative thinking mean score (PISA 2022) | Scientific problem-solving domain score (PISA 2022) | Scientific problem-solving domain score predicted from PISA 2018/2022 reading | Creative thinking mean score predicted from PISA 2018/2022 reading and other domain scores | Creative thinking mean score predicted from PISA 2022 reading and other domain scores

title: What makes teachers stay? A cross-sectional exploration of the individual and contextual factors associated with teacher retention in Sweden.
authors: Jeffrey Casely-Hayford, Christina Björklund, Gunnar Bergström, Per Lindqvist, Lydia Kwak
outcome_summary: This cross-sectional study analyzed AFA-insurance questionnaire data collected in Sweden between 2004 and 2011 from 5903 qualified elementary-year teachers (ISCED 1–2) working in public schools across 25 municipalities. Teachers’ retention intention was measured using the WAI-6 item (a 3-point prognosis about being able to continue in the profession two years later). The authors used hierarchical multiple regression (with stepwise/backward selection for exploratory model building) rather than machine learning, and found that individual-level factors explained most of the variance in retention intention, with the final hierarchical model explaining R² = 0.202 (F(14, 4415) = 81.2, p < .001). The strongest standardized associations were health-related quality of life (b = 0.29, p < .001) and exhaustion (b = -0.14, p < .001), followed by work motivation (b = 0.10, p < .001) and support from colleagues (b = 0.06, p < .001). Limitations include reliance on self-report and the absence of reported missing-data handling; causality cannot be inferred from the cross-sectional design.
all_datasets_used: Sweden AFA-insurance teacher questionnaire (2004–2011), elementary-year teachers (ISCED 1–2), public schools

title: Teacher innovation: Conceptualizations, methodologies, and theoretical framework
authors: Shengnan Liu, Hongbiao Yin, Yuning Wang, Jiafang Lu
outcome_summary: This article is a systematic review (PRISMA-guided) synthesizing 109 studies on teacher innovation, including 96 empirical studies (69 quantitative, 22 qualitative, 5 mixed-methods) plus 13 additional excluded/quality-screened records during selection. It does not train or evaluate machine-learning models on TALIS or any other ILSA microdata; instead, it reports descriptive synthesis results about how teacher innovation is conceptualized, measured, and studied. The review finds that teacher innovation definitions are inconsistent (with 23.7% of reviewed papers not providing a definition), that measurement often relies on self-report scales with variable psychometric rigor, and that quantitative studies heavily favor cross-sectional designs and advanced statistical approaches while underusing longitudinal designs. It also highlights limited theoretical integration (only 7.3% explicitly used theories) and calls for stronger measurement, more diverse data sources, and better theoretical grounding. Limitations include potential omission of relevant non-English or non-journal sources and manual coding subjectivity.

title: Teaching quality and student reading outcomes: Evidence from a longitudinal study from grade 5 to 7
outcome_summary: This longitudinal study uses NEPS data from Germany, following a grade 5 cohort to grade 7 (2010/2011 to 2012/2013) and analyzing students in main regular schools who stayed in the same schools between grades 5 and 7. Reading competence is measured with linked paper-pencil tests in grades 5 and 7 and analyzed using WLE scores (with reliabilities reported for grade 5 and grade 7). The authors estimate school-fixed effect regression models with a rich set of student controls measured in grade 5 and 10 teacher- and student-reported teaching quality scales aggregated across grades 5–7. Across specifications, teaching quality components show mostly non-significant effects on grade 7 reading competence and reading attitudes; the only small effect for attitudes (evaluation) disappears after Bonferroni correction. Missing data are handled via predictive mean matching with multiple imputations combined using Rubin’s rules, and sampling weights (w_t_cal) are used for population generalization. The study is not an ML prediction paper and therefore does not report ML metrics or model selection.
all_datasets_used: NEPS longitudinal cohort (Germany) Grade 5→7 Reading competence (WLE scores), grade 7 outcome | NEPS longitudinal cohort (Germany) Grade 5→7 Attitudes towards reading (mean scale), grade 7 outcome

title: Measuring different types and domains of AI knowledge: Developing and validating a performance-based scale
authors: Inbal Klein-Avraham, Rut Ston, Osnat Atias, Ido Roll, Ayelet Baram-Tsabari
outcome_summary: This study developed and validated a performance-based two-axial AI/GenAI knowledge scale using an online quota-sampled survey of adult internet users in Israel (n=800; Oct–Nov 2024). The instrument measured overall AI knowledge (0–27) and sub-scores for knowledge types (content, procedural, epistemic) and knowledge domains (technology-related, user-related, society-related), using true/false/“I don’t know” items plus a separate analytic AI knowledge task. Psychometric validation relied on CFA (DWLS) and SEM with reported fit indices (e.g., overall SEM model CFI=.819, RMSEA=.06, SRMSR=.067) and known-group differences by GenAI experience, age, education, and gender (e.g., overall score GenAI experience F=47.24, p<.001, η2=.106). The study found that trust in GenAI was negatively associated with epistemic and society-related knowledge, while attitudes toward AI showed small positive associations with content/procedural/user-related knowledge. Limitations include the absence of documented survey-weight usage and missing-data handling, and the fact that the paper uses psychometric modeling rather than ML prediction.
all_datasets_used: Custom AI/GenAI knowledge inventory (Israel, Oct–Nov 2024 adult internet users)

title: Scientific reasoning scale in Italy: Validation studies
authors: Rossella Caliciuri, Margherita Lanz
outcome_summary: This paper provides validity evidence for the Italian adaptation of the Scientific Reasoning Scale (SRS) using a quota-sampled online survey of 897 Italian adults aged 18–60. The study does not use ILSA/PISA microdata; instead, it validates a psychometric instrument via CFA/SEM in Mplus, testing a unidimensional structure, reliability (McDonald’s omega), measurement invariance across demographic/ideological groups, and convergent/criterion-related validity. The CFA retained 10 of 11 dichotomous items after removing an item with low factor loading, yielding good fit (e.g., RMSEA = 0.029; CFI = 0.966) and composite reliability ω = 0.612. Measurement invariance results indicate full invariance across gender, age, employment status, political orientation, and religious affiliation, with partial non-invariance for educational level (higher latent means for university degree holders). Convergent validity showed moderate-to-strong correlations with CRT-Long (r = 0.523) and PRS (r = 0.578), while criterion-related validity showed small positive associations with climate change awareness/belief and negative associations with paranormal health belief factors. Limitations include the artificial “lab-oriented” scenarios and the response-format adaptation from the original SRS, which may affect cross-national comparability.

title: Motivation towards mathematics from 1980 to 2015: Exploring the feasibility of trend scaling
authors: E. Majoros, et al.
outcome_summary: This paper investigates how to construct comparable trend scales for two affective mathematics motivation constructs (intrinsic and extrinsic motivation) across decades using grade 8 (or equivalent) questionnaire data from SIMS 1980 and TIMSS cycles 1995–2015. The analytic systems were England (GBR), Hong Kong (HKG), Hungary (HUN), Israel (ISR), Japan (JPN), and the United States (USA), with Japan excluded from latent-variable analyses after cross-cultural measurement invariance did not hold. The authors compare three scaling approaches: (1) CFA-based scaling with MGCFA invariance testing, (2) IRT-based scaling using PCM vs GPCM (GPCM selected for better fit), and (3) a market-basket approach that generates plausible responses five times per respondent using country-specific measurement models and then computes standardized sum scores. Across methods, correlations between individual scores were very high (0.96 to 1.00), and country-level trends from CFA/IRT under invariance assumptions closely matched observed scores. A key limitation is that standard errors of means may be underestimated because TIMSS’s stratified multistage sampling design is not fully reflected when standard errors are computed under simple random sampling assumptions.

title: Correlation analysis using teaching and learning analytics
authors: P.A.N. Prestes, Pedro Alexandre Nery Prestes
outcome_summary: The paper uses TALIS questionnaire data (teacher/principal perceptions and practices) from the INEP open database in Brazil, organized into OECD themes and sub-themes with item codes (e.g., TT3G06D1, TT3G19A1, TT3G32A, TT3G34J). Instead of predictive modeling, it applies correlation analysis—primarily Pearson’s correlation and Spearman’s rank correlation—to examine relationships among assertions within and across themes, reporting that many cross-theme correlations are weak and that some within-theme correlations are moderate to strong. The authors also discuss feature-importance-style checks and mention additional techniques (e.g., DecisionTreeClassifier, RandomForestClassifier, f_classif, RFE, and Chi-2) as reinforcement, but the core empirical results are correlation coefficients and significance thresholds (e.g., ρ > 0.05). The study does not report PV-based achievement outcomes, survey-weight usage, or a formal ML predictive evaluation (no accuracy/AUC/R² metrics), limiting direct policy claims about causal effects or predictive performance.

title: Systematic review of Erasmus+ projects labelled as good practice and related to e-learning and ICT: Some case studies
authors: María Goretti Alonso de Castro, Francisco José García-Peñalvo
outcome_summary: This paper is a systematic review of Erasmus+ projects labeled as good practice and related to e-learning and/or ICT, using a PRISMA-adapted four-stage review process (project definition, selection definition, project selection, and analysis). Evidence is gathered from the Erasmus+ Project Results Platform (E+PRP), a coordinator questionnaire (21 items; ~15–20 minutes; sent Dec 2020–Jan 2021; responses collected until May 2021; response rate 22%), semi-structured interviews (Dec 2021–May 2022; 22 projects), and focus groups (July 2022; 13 projects). The results are synthesized as success factors and examples of project practices (e.g., needs-driven design, partner coordination, usefulness beyond funding, teacher/student participation, and ICT/eLearning integration), rather than as predictive modeling of student outcomes. No ILSA assessment cycle, grade/domain, plausible values, survey weights, or ML prediction metrics are reported, and the study does not train or evaluate machine learning models.

title: Developing the Teacher mentoring self-efficacy scale (TMSES) using the Delphi method and exploratory factor analysis
authors: Rebecca M. Tickell, Robert M. Klassen
outcome_summary: This paper develops the Teacher Mentoring Self-Efficacy Scale (TMSES) through a two-phase mixed-methods design: a UK-based three-round Delphi study (N=26 experts) to generate 44 mentoring competencies, followed by a UK-based online survey of teacher mentors (N=239 fully completed responses) to test the underlying scale structure. The quantitative phase uses exploratory factor analysis with principal axis factoring and direct oblimin rotation, after checking normality, Bartlett’s test of sphericity, and KMO (KMO=0.954). The final solution is a 16-item two-factor model accounting for 61.07% of total variance, with strong loadings (e.g., item 1 loading=0.96; item 29 loading=0.83). Reliability is high (Cronbach’s alpha: total scale α=0.94; factor alphas α=0.94 and α=0.84). Because this is psychometric scale development (not predictive ML on ILSA achievement PVs), there are no ML performance metrics, no survey-weighted estimation, and no PV handling; generalizability is limited by UK-only and COVID-19-era data collection.

title: What kind of individual support activities in interventions foster pre-service and beginning teachers’ self-efficacy? A meta-analysis
authors: Sog Yee Mok, Daniela Rupp, Doris Holzberger
outcome_summary: This article is a systematic review and meta-analysis (not an ILSA microdata study) synthesizing 28 intervention studies (49 effects) on how individual support activities in mentoring/coaching/supervision/program interventions affect teacher self-efficacy for pre-service teachers (PSTs) and beginning teachers (BTs). The authors computed Hedges’ g for each effect size (using pooled pretest SDs for designs without control groups; using reported means/SDs or ANOVA statistics for control-group designs) and then estimated an overall random-effects model with robust variance estimation (RVE) to handle multiple dependent effects per study. The overall intervention effect was medium and statistically significant: Hedges’ g = 0.678 (SE = 0.064, p < .001, CI [0.547, 0.809], I2 = 90.133). In moderator analyses, providing feedback on lesson plans showed the largest effect size (Model 1: g = 1.033, SE = 0.273, p = .056; Model 2: g = 0.849, SE = 0.785, p = .082), though it did not reach conventional significance after additional controls. Limitations include reliance on study-level coding of intervention components, small numbers for some moderators, and no country-level moderator testing despite cross-country inclusion.

title: Students’ growth mindset: Relation to teacher beliefs, teaching practices, and school climate
authors: Junlin Yu, Pia Kreijkes, Katarina Salmela-Aro
outcome_summary: This study used OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills (SSES) data collected in 2018–2020 from the city of Helsinki, Finland, focusing on 10-year-old students and linking student, teacher, and principal reports (final sample: 2200 students, 358 teachers, 65 principals). The authors estimated multilevel Bayesian probit models to predict students’ intelligence growth mindset measured by a single reverse-coded 5-point Likert item, accounting for the nested structure (students within classrooms within schools). In the random-intercept model, guided inquiry showed a positive association with growth mindset (β=0.41, 95% CI [0.11, 0.68], p<.01), task differentiation showed a negative association (β=-0.56, 95% CI [-0.79, -0.22], p<.01), and schools’ holistic development emphasis was positively associated (β=0.43, 95% CI [0.01, 0.73], p=.04). Classroom and school contexts explained about 4.7% and 5.5% of variance, respectively. Limitations include cross-sectional correlational inference and the use of a single-item outcome, with missing-data handling described qualitatively rather than via a formal imputation/deletion method.
all_datasets_used: OECD SSES 2018-2020 (Finland, Helsinki) Grade/age: 10-year-olds (elementary) — student mindset (single-item Likert)

title: The effectiveness of mentoring, coaching, and induction practices for early career teachers: A scoping review
authors: Gia-Yen Luong
outcome_summary: This article is a scoping review of mentoring, coaching, and induction practices for early career teachers (ECTs), not an empirical machine-learning study using TALIS or other ILSA microdata. The review synthesizes 78 included studies identified through a registered protocol (IDESR000154) and organizes evidence into four outcome themes: teacher development of self, retention, teaching practice, and student achievement. Across the included studies, the review finds substantial inconsistency in how “induction,” “mentoring,” and “coaching” are defined and operationalized, which limits comparability of effectiveness results. The review also reports that correlational conclusions are the strongest form of evidence most frequently available, and that study designs vary widely (observational, experiments, quasi-experiments, secondary analyses, and programme evaluations). Because no predictive modeling, PV scoring, or survey-weighted estimation is performed, the findings are best interpreted as evidence about definitional and measurement coherence rather than as quantified causal effects.

title: Self-reported teaching effectiveness and job satisfaction among teachers: the role of subject matter and other demographic variables
authors: Karim Sadeghi, Farah Ghaderi, Zahra Abdollahpour
outcome_summary: This Heliyon study used a convenience sample of 173 Iranian teachers (104 English teachers and 69 non-English teachers) and analyzed self-reported job satisfaction (Lester Teacher Job Satisfaction Questionnaire; 66 Likert items) and self-rated teaching effectiveness (Kulsum Teacher Effectiveness Scale; 60 items rated 1–10). The study reports no statistically significant associations between job satisfaction and teaching experience for either group (English: r=0.040, p>0.05; non-English: r=-0.004, p=0.971) and no significant gender or employment-status differences in job satisfaction (Mann–Whitney U p>0.05; Table 7 and Table 9). However, it finds a positive relationship between job satisfaction and teaching effectiveness for English teachers (Spearman rho=0.628, p<0.01) and a smaller but significant positive relationship for non-English teachers (rho=0.288, p=0.017). Limitations include reliance on self-report questionnaires and correlational (non-causal) interpretation, with no ML modeling or ILSA PV framework involved.
all_datasets_used: TALIS-style teacher survey (Iranian convenience sample; no ILSA cycle/grade/domain)
all_target_variables: Job satisfaction (English teachers) | Job satisfaction (non-English teachers) | Teaching effectiveness (English teachers) | Teaching effectiveness (non-English teachers)

title: Exploring Factors associated with the implementation of student-centered instructional practices in U.S. classrooms
authors: L. Zhang, J.D. Basham, R.A. Carter Jr., et al.
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2013 U.S. lower-secondary teacher and principal questionnaire data from 89 public schools (1112 teachers after applying response-rate, public-school, target-classroom, and PD-information inclusion criteria). The dependent variables are ordinal frequencies (never/occasionally/frequently/all lessons) for four student-centered practices: adaptive instruction, ICT-enhanced learning, collaborative small-group learning, and project-based learning. The analysis fits multilevel ordinal logistic models with teachers nested within schools and uses listwise deletion for missingness (<2% per variable). Reported effects are odds ratios from final models: ICT-focused PD and formative assessment/feedback are consistently associated with higher implementation of ICT-enhanced learning and project-based learning, while PD in individualized learning and formative assessment/feedback relate to small-group learning. The study is correlational (no causal identification) and relies on self-reported instructional practices, limiting causal interpretation and generalizability beyond the analyzed U.S. public-school subset.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2013 U.S. lower secondary (teacher questionnaire) — Adaptive instruction frequency | TALIS 2013 U.S. lower secondary (teacher questionnaire) — ICT-enhanced learning frequency | TALIS 2013 U.S. lower secondary (teacher questionnaire) — Collaborative small-group learning frequency | TALIS 2013 U.S. lower secondary (teacher questionnaire) — Project-based learning frequency
all_target_variables: Adaptive instruction (ordinal frequency) | ICT-enhanced learning (ordinal frequency) | Collaborative small-group learning (ordinal frequency) | Project-based learning (ordinal frequency)

title: Developing a shared cluster construct of instructional leadership in TALIS
authors: Jelena Veletić, Rolf Vegar Olsen
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2013 (lower-secondary) secondary data from Denmark, Finland, Sweden, and Norway (10,688 teachers clustered in 676 schools) to develop and validate a shared-cluster measurement approach for instructional leadership. The authors first test the existing TALIS instructional leadership scale based on principals’ three-item measure (PQ2–PQ4) and find acceptable model fit (SRMRb = 0.027–0.044) but essentially no between-school explanatory power (R2 < 0.02, not statistically different from zero). They then construct two teacher-based shared cluster dimensions—managing the instructional program and developing the school learning climate—using multilevel CFA/SEM with WLSMV and sampling weights (school weight at cluster level; pure teacher weight at teacher level). The strongest and most stable associations with teacher job satisfaction with current work environment are for developing the school learning climate (β = 0.505–0.609; R2 ≈ 0.255–0.370). Limitations include construct underrepresentation in the principal measure, strong collinearity between the two teacher-based dimensions, and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling beyond Mplus default behavior.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2013 (lower-secondary) Nordic countries: Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Norway
all_target_variables: Teacher job satisfaction with current work environment (school level)

title: Contextual influence on formal and informal teacher leadership
authors: Y. Liu
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2013 lower-secondary teacher and school-leader survey data from 32 countries/regions (104,358 teachers nested in 6,045 schools). It operationalizes informal and formal teacher leadership using dichotomous leadership-responsibility items: overall constructs are estimated as latent variables in Mplus with reported fit indices (informal: CFI=0.962, TLI=0.940, RMSEA=0.004; formal: CFI=0.983, TLI=0.974, RMSEA=0.004). For task-specific leadership responsibilities, the authors estimate design-based population means and multiple logistic regressions with BRR (100 replicate weights) to adjust standard errors under the complex survey design. Across countries, formal teacher leaders are more likely accountable for most leadership tasks, while informal leaders are more concentrated in instructional materials and student performance/data analysis. The paper does not report any missing-data handling strategy and does not use ML prediction; therefore, results are correlational associations rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2013 Lower secondary (teacher + school leader surveys), 32 countries/regions
all_target_variables: Overall informal teacher leadership (latent variable) | Overall formal teacher leadership (latent variable) | Informal teacher leadership for leadership tasks (binary items) | Formal teacher leadership for leadership tasks (binary items)

title: Profiles of teaching practices and teacher co-operation: A person-centered approach in multilevel context
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 Turkey upper-secondary (ISCED 3) teacher questionnaire data to identify five latent teacher profiles based on instructional practices (clarity of instruction, cognitive activation, classroom management) and teacher co-operation, using multilevel latent profile analysis (MLPA) to account for teachers nested within schools. The analytic sample includes 6861 teachers from 443 schools after excluding teachers with missing responses on the instructional-practices indicators and excluding schools lacking school-characteristics data. The optimal solution was a five-profile model selected using AIC/BIC/aBIC, entropy, and the adjusted Lo-Mendell-Rubin test; posterior probabilities indicated low misclassification. Profile membership differences were examined with multinomial logistic regression using teacher-level predictors (gender, teaching experience, team innovativeness) and school-level covariates (school location, school size, support and administrative personnel ratios). The paper reports significant associations of team innovativeness with membership across profiles and significant effects of school location for some comparisons, while teacher experience showed no significant relationship with profile membership. Limitations include reliance on teacher self-reports for instructional practices and the absence of documented survey-weight application.

title: Teacher collaboration networks as a function of type of collaboration and schools’ structural environment
authors: Johannes Schuster, Ulrike Hartmann, Nina Kolleck
outcome_summary: This paper analyzes teacher collaboration networks using a 2019 survey from nine German secondary schools (N=366 teachers; after excluding seven schools with network-question response rates below 60%). Collaboration ties were constructed from directed nominations (up to five colleagues) and dichotomized from Likert-type frequency responses (monthly to almost daily coded as ties), producing a general collaboration network plus two type-specific networks: exchange of teaching materials and mutual classroom observations. The authors estimate exponential random graph models (ERGMs) and report log-odds ratio effects with significance tests. Across networks, reciprocity and transitivity (GWESP/GWDSP) are consistently strong for general collaboration and exchange, while classroom observations show strong reciprocity but weaker/non-significant transitivity. The study finds that formal role and subject similarity predict general collaboration, attitude predicts exchange ties, and structural environment moderates whether individual attributes matter. Limitations include small sample size, dichotomization of tie strength, and no causal identification or PV/weighting framework because the data are not ILSA achievement PVs.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (not used; school-based teacher survey in 2019, Germany, secondary schools)
all_target_variables: General teacher collaboration tie formation (directed network) | Exchange of teaching materials tie formation (directed network) | Mutual classroom observations tie formation (directed network) | General teacher collaboration tie formation moderated by schools’ structural environment

title: Do teachers’ years of experience make a difference in the quality of teaching?
authors: Linda J. Graham, Sonia L. J. White, Kathy Cologon, Robert C. Pianta
outcome_summary: This paper is not an ML predictive study; it uses standard statistical comparisons (descriptive statistics and ANCOVA with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons) to test whether teachers’ years of experience are associated with observed teaching quality. The dataset consists of CLASS K-3 classroom observation scores (Emotional Support, Classroom Organisation, Instructional Support) from 80 Queensland primary-school teachers teaching Prep to Grade 3, with grade level taught included as a covariate. Across two experience groupings (0–3 vs. >3 years), there were no significant differences in any CLASS domain or dimension. Across three groupings (0–3, 4–5, >5 years), Classroom Organisation differed significantly, with the 4–5 “transitioning” group scoring lower; at the dimension level, Negative Climate, Behaviour Management, and Instructional Learning Formats showed significant differences. The study’s limitation is that it is a small, non-representative convenience sample and does not report missing-data handling; additionally, the CLASS instrument is US-developed and may be culturally bounded.

title: Improving teaching, teamwork, and school organization: Collaboration networks in school teams
authors: A. Wullschleger, A. Vörös, B. Rechsteiner, et al.
outcome_summary: This study uses a school-improvement collaboration network survey (not TALIS microdata) administered in September 2017 to principals, teachers, and specialist teachers in four lower secondary schools in the German-speaking part of Switzerland. Participants reported with whom they explored new ideas on three improvement areas: teaching, teamwork, and school organization, and also provided trust relations. The authors quantified overlap across the three networks using Venn diagrams and QAP correlations, finding moderate overlap with about half of ties not overlapping across areas, and then compared network structure using density, centralization, reciprocity, and transitivity. To explain structural differences, they estimated exponential random graph models (ERGMs) on 100 multiple-imputed datasets, combining estimates via meta-analytic weighted least squares. No predictive ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/R²/AUC) are reported because the analysis targets network tie formation rather than achievement prediction; results are therefore associational and constrained by the small number of schools.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (not used; school network survey in Switzerland, lower secondary)
all_target_variables: Collaboration network ties: new ideas on teaching | Collaboration network ties: new ideas on teamwork | Collaboration network ties: new ideas on school organization

title: Understanding the relationship between teacher collaboration and instructional clarity via teacher self-efficacy: A moderated mediation model of organizational commitment
outcome_summary: This study analyzes nationally representative U.S. TALIS 2018 data from lower secondary schools (grades 7–9), using a multilevel latent moderated structural equation modeling framework with teachers nested within schools. The analytic sample includes 1,897 teachers across 156 schools after excluding teachers who exclusively/primarily taught special needs students and removing schools with fewer than three teachers; missingness (up to ~4%) is handled using FIML. The results show that teacher collaboration is positively associated with clarity of instruction both directly (β=0.156, p<0.001) and indirectly via teacher self-efficacy in instruction (β=0.148, p<0.001), yielding a total standardized effect of β=0.304 (p<0.001). Organizational commitment moderates the mediated pathway, with stronger conditional indirect effects at higher commitment (+1 SD OC B=0.119) than at lower commitment (−1 SD OC B=0.064). Because the study relies on teacher self-reports and cross-sectional data, findings should not be interpreted as causal.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (U.S., lower secondary grades 7–9) — teacher-level multilevel latent moderated mediation

title: Teachers’ emotional exhaustion and job satisfaction: How much does the school context matter?
authors: Tabea Schulze-Hagenest, Bastian Carstensen, Kira Weber, Thorben Jansen, Jennifer Meyer, Olaf Köller, Uta Klusmann
outcome_summary: This paper is not an ILSA-based machine learning study; it analyzes two German teacher survey datasets (Study 1: DiScH, N=1022 teachers in 120 schools in Schleswig-Holstein; Study 2: SchuMaS, N=2886 teachers in 196 schools across Germany) to quantify between-school versus within-school variation in emotional exhaustion and job satisfaction. The authors use multilevel regression with random intercepts to separate teacher-level from school-level effects and report intraclass correlations (ICC(1), ICC(2)) and standardized regression coefficients (β). In Study 1, between-school variance in emotional exhaustion was low (ICC(1)=3.7%), while social interaction indicators showed substantial between-school variance (principals’ support ICC(1)=22.6%; cooperation ICC(1)=20.7%). Emotional exhaustion was predicted at the teacher level by health concerns (β≈0.29–0.34) and extra workload (β≈0.25–0.33), and negatively by principal support, cooperation, and digital competency. In Study 2, between-school variance in emotional exhaustion was higher (ICC(1)=9.9%), and school-level exchange was associated with lower exhaustion (β≈−0.99), while job satisfaction showed weaker school-level effects and more teacher-level associations with digital competency and professional collaboration. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and reliance on self-reported measures aggregated to the school level.
