title: Teacher wellbeing in rural, regional, and metropolitan schools: Examining resources and demands across locations
authors: A.A. Kingsford-Smith, R.J. Collie, T. Loughland, Hoa Thi Mai Nguyen
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 Australia (ISCED 2) Teacher Questionnaire data to examine how job demands/resources and personal resources relate to teacher self-efficacy, strain, and job satisfaction across rural, regional, and metropolitan school locations. The authors fit multigroup CFA/SEM models in Mplus (complex command for nested teachers-in-schools) and use teacher weights to account for the two-stage sampling design. Missing data were handled with Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML). The multigroup SEM (M1) explained 27–49% of self-efficacy variance, 42–67% of strain variance, and 31–51% of job satisfaction variance, with student behavior stress emerging as the only consistent predictor across all outcomes and locations. The paper is cross-sectional, so associations cannot be interpreted causally, and the modeling is not ML-based prediction (no PVs are involved).

title: A critical evaluation of alignment optimization for improving cross-national comparability in international large-scale assessments
authors: A. Sandoval-Hernández, Andres Sandoval-Hernandez, Nurullah Eryilmaz
outcome_summary: This paper critically evaluates alignment optimization (invariance alignment) as an alternative to traditional multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MGCFA) for cross-national comparability in TALIS 2018. Using TALIS 2018 teacher and principal questionnaire scales at the ISCED 2 level (23 teacher scales and 15 principal scales), the authors first assess unidimensionality (parallel analysis) and reliability (Cronbach’s alpha and person separation reliability), then test measurement invariance with ordinal graded response model (GRM) CFA using DWLS estimation and RMSEA/CFI/SRMR benchmarks. Under strict scalar invariance criteria (RMSEA < 0.055), almost all teacher and all principal scales fail to achieve scalar invariance or do not converge. Alignment optimization, using an invariance parameter threshold of 0.75, yields comparability for only one teacher scale (Effective professional development) but for all principal scales. The study emphasizes that alignment improves parameter-level comparability, yet results may be sensitive to sample size and response sparsity, and missing-data handling is not reported.

title: A multilevel investigation into teacher-supported student use of technology in East Asian classroom: Examining teacher and school characteristics
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher and principal data from five East Asian economies (Chinese Shanghai, Chinese Taipei, Singapore, Korea, Japan) to explain teacher-supported student use of technology in secondary schools (ISCED level 2). Two teacher-reported Likert outcomes were used: TSSUT1 (ICT for projects/class work) and TSSUT2 (supporting learning through digital technology). The authors estimate two-level structural equation models with robust maximum-likelihood estimation, incorporating TALIS complex-sampling weights at the teacher (TCHWGT) and school (SCHWGT) levels, and handling missingness via full-information maximum likelihood. Across the full sample, teacher self-efficacy in student engagement was the most consistent positive predictor for both outcomes (TSSUT1 β=0.150, p<0.001; TSSUT2 β=0.285, p<0.001), while lack of material resources was significantly negative at the school level (TSSUT1 β=−0.201, p=0.004; TSSUT2 β=−0.163, p=0.010). The explained variance was modest-to-moderate (e.g., school-level R2=0.324 for TSSUT1 and 0.267 for TSSUT2), and the cross-sectional design plus mono-source teacher reporting limit causal interpretation.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (teachers, ISCED level 2) — Teacher-supported student use of information technology (TSSUT1) | TALIS 2018 (teachers, ISCED level 2) — Teacher-supported student use of digital technology (TSSUT2)
all_target_variables: Teacher-supported student use of information technology (TSSUT1) | Teacher-supported student use of digital technology (TSSUT2)

title: How can an innovative teaching force be developed? The empowering role of distributed leadership
authors: Yuan Teng, Rui Pu, Yipu Hao
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data from Shanghai, China (junior high schools) and verifies the model in South Korea and Singapore. It models two outcomes—team innovation (4 items) and individual innovation (4 items)—as functions of perceived distributed leadership, with teacher collaboration and teacher self-efficacy as mediators, using stepwise OLS regressions (clustered standard errors) and structural equation modeling with bias-corrected bootstrap (5000 resamples). In Shanghai, distributed leadership shows a significant positive association with both team and individual innovation (team: β=0.332 in the control-only model; individual: β=0.184), and SEM fit is acceptable (team: χ2/df=14.061, RMSEA=0.058, CFI=0.959; individual: χ2/df=12.586, RMSEA=0.060, CFI=0.934). Mediation results indicate that team innovation is driven more by the direct path (79.49% of total effect), whereas individual innovation is driven more by indirect effects (69.37%), especially via self-efficacy (35.14%). Limitations include lack of longitudinal/quasi-experimental design for causal inference and limited transparency on survey-weight application and missingness proportions.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China; junior high teachers) — Team innovation scale | TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China; junior high teachers) — Individual innovation scale

title: Teacher self-efficacy and self-reported cognitive activation and classroom management: A multilevel perspective on the role of school characteristics
authors: Doris Holzberger, Elisabeth Prestele
outcome_summary: This study re-analysed TALIS 2018 teacher and principal questionnaire data for Austria (ISCED level 2), focusing on multilevel associations between teacher self-efficacy and two indicators of self-reported instructional quality: cognitive activation and classroom management. Using multilevel random-intercept and random-slope regression models in Mplus (with TALIS-provided teacher and school weights) and listwise deletion for missing values, the authors found significant positive relationships between teacher self-efficacy and both instructional-quality facets at the teacher level and, more strongly, at the school level. For cognitive activation, school-level efficacy in instruction showed significant between-school associations, but unique context effects of school characteristics were not significant. For classroom management, unique school-level efficacy in classroom management was strongly associated with higher classroom management, and principal leadership showed a significant (negative) association. The study is cross-sectional and relies on teacher self-reports, so directionality and causal claims cannot be inferred.
all_target_variables: Cognitive activation (teacher-reported instructional quality) | Classroom management (teacher-reported instructional quality)

title: Associations between time spent communicating with parents, teacher self-efficacy, and stress: The role of professional development
authors: Hyunwoo Yang, Haram Jeon, Soobin Choi
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data pooled across 45 countries to examine how time spent communicating with parents relates to teacher self-efficacy and parent-related stress, and whether professional development (PD) moderates these associations. Using school fixed-effects regression with teacher sample weights and school-clustered standard errors, the authors find that each additional hour of parent communication is associated with a +0.031 SD increase in self-efficacy (p < .001) and a +0.062 SD increase in parent-related stress (p < .001). PD participation in parent-collaboration topics shows positive main effects for self-efficacy and stress, but the key moderation result is that PD significantly weakens the communication–stress link (PD×Time = -0.040 SD, p < .001) while not significantly moderating communication–self-efficacy. The results are correlational (cross-sectional TALIS) and rely on self-reported outcomes, so causal claims cannot be made.
all_target_variables: Teacher self-efficacy (standardized composite) | Parent-related stress (standardized stress item) | Moderating effect of professional development (PD) on communication–self-efficacy and communication–stress associations

title: Cultivating collective teacher innovativeness in high power distance settings: The role of empowering leadership and collective teacher efficacy
authors: Hasan Kavgacı, Gökhan Savaş, Nedim Özdemir, Ali Çağatay Kılınç
outcome_summary: The study uses a Türkiye 2025 K-12 school survey (73 schools; 926 teachers) to examine how empowering leadership relates to collective teacher innovativeness, mediated by collective teacher efficacy and moderated by school power distance. The authors estimate a two-level Bayesian multilevel SEM in Mplus 8.7 with latent constructs measured from Likert-type items (EL, CTE, CTI, SPD), using Gibbs sampling and convergence diagnostics (PSR<1.05; PSR=1.043). Results show that collective teacher efficacy is positively associated with collective teacher innovativeness (γ=0.799, 95% CrI [0.453, 1.057]), while the direct effect of empowering leadership on innovativeness is weak (γ=0.206, 95% CrI [-0.213, 0.580]). However, the indirect effect via collective teacher efficacy is supported (γ=0.416, 95% CrI [0.169, 0.741]) and is stronger at higher school power distance (+1 SD SPD: γ=0.569; −1 SD SPD: γ=0.252). Limitations include cross-sectional self-report data, no sampling weights, and missing-data handling not reported.
all_datasets_used: Türkiye 2025 school survey (K-12 teachers); TALIS-aligned constructs (EL, CTE, CTI, SPD)

title: Digital ambitions vs. classroom reality in Norwegian lower secondary schools: What digital competencies are students developing over time?
authors: Astrid Elisabeth Kure, Marte Blikstad-Balas, Lisbeth M. Brevik
outcome_summary: This paper reports a longitudinal, naturalistic video study of English teaching in Norwegian lower secondary schools (Years 9–10, ages 13–15) rather than an ILSA-based predictive modeling study. Across 29 recorded lessons, the authors identified 24 ICT lessons and coded 76 15-minute ICT segments using the Norwegian Framework for Digital Skills (NDET, 2017b), scoring each segment on five digital subskills (levels 1–5) and selecting the most advanced level when multiple were observed. The results show a “digital divide” across five schools in 2019–20: three schools provided frequent, multi-subskill opportunities (scored in 75%–100% of segments) while two schools provided infrequent opportunities (35%–50%), with no observed digital responsibility. When revisiting one school three years later (2021–23), opportunities increased substantially (e.g., ICT segments rising to 89%), but opportunities to develop beyond basic digital skills remained limited, with only rare advanced-level evidence. The study is limited by reliance on what is visible/expressed in video recordings and by the absence of survey-weighted, PV-based achievement outcomes.

title: Collective teacher innovativeness in 48 countries: Effects of teacher autonomy, collaborative culture, and professional learning
authors: D. Nguyen, M. Pietsch, S. Gümüs¸
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data from 48 countries (241,426 teachers nested in 15,672 schools) to examine how teacher classroom autonomy and collaborative school culture relate to collective teacher innovativeness, and whether integrated professional learning mediates these relationships. The authors estimate a multilevel structural equation model in Mplus 8.3 and handle missingness using Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML), with model fit reported as c2=20677.383 (df=190), CFI=0.99, RMSEA=0.02, SRMRw=0.01, SRMRb=0.04. At the teacher level, Collaborative Culture strongly predicts innovativeness (b=0.433, p<.001) and Teacher Autonomy has a small positive effect (b=0.016, p<.001). At the school level, Collaborative Culture (b=0.641, p<.001) and Teacher Autonomy (b=0.179, p<.001) are both positive, while integrated professional learning is positive at the school level (b=0.133, p<.001) but negative at the teacher level (b=-0.011, p<.001). The mediation pattern is therefore mixed and the study is cross-sectional and perception-based, limiting causal interpretation.
all_target_variables: Collective Teacher Innovativeness (latent scale) | Integrated Professional Learning (binary: formal + job-embedded participation)

title: Classroom heterogeneity and assessment for learning: Evidence from 47 countries using TALIS 2018
authors: Youngshin Lim
outcome_summary: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data from 47 countries (126,330 teachers across 9,024 secondary schools) to examine how teachers’ perceptions of classroom heterogeneity relate to their Assessment for Learning (AfL) frequency. AfL is constructed as a continuous composite (mean 0, SD 1) from four TALIS items about administering assessments, providing written feedback, enabling self-evaluation, and observing students with immediate feedback; CFA fit is reported as CFI = 0.905 and SRMR = 0.046. The authors estimate three-level multilevel regression models and school- and country-fixed effects models, applying TALIS estimation weights and BRR replicate weights, and using listwise deletion for missingness. Results show positive associations between AfL and most heterogeneity domains (e.g., academically gifted, immigrant background), but a consistent negative association for low achievers (e.g., coefficients around -0.03 to -0.05 with statistical significance). The paper is cross-sectional and relies on self-reported perceptions, so causal claims are not supported.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (teacher survey; 47 countries; secondary school context)
all_target_variables: Assessment for Learning frequency (composite AfL scale)

title: Early career teacher retention intention: Individual, school and country characteristics
authors: Laura Van den Borre, Bram Spruyt, Frederik Van Droogenbroeck
outcome_summary: This peer-reviewed study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for lower secondary education (ISCED 2) to model expected career duration as a proxy for early-career teacher (ECT) retention intention. The analytic sample comprises 11,613 ECTs nested in 3,998 lower secondary schools across 31 countries/regions (Belgium’s two communities analyzed separately), with listwise deletion of cases missing any analysis variables and an additional reduction to 25 countries for model 9 due to missing country-level part-A indicators. The authors estimate nine-stage multilevel linear regression models (teacher, school, and country levels) rather than machine-learning prediction; therefore, no ML accuracy/AUC metrics are reported. Key results show that selection mechanisms (“becoming a teacher”) explain the largest share of variance, with model 9 explaining 17.2% overall variance (teacher 14.0%, school 13.1%, country 48.9% relative to the restricted unconditional model). Notably, higher starting salaries (b=0.25, p<0.001) and mandatory competitive exams (b=0.15, p<0.05) at the country level, and intrinsic motivation and teaching as first choice at the teacher level, are associated with longer expected teaching careers. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal claims) and reliance on subjective intention measures.

title: Exploring teacher job satisfaction in five Latin American countries: A Multi-level analysis using TALIS 2018
authors: Christian Lazcano, Sara Galilea, Stefanie Wenderoth, Armando Rojas, María Soledad Ortúzar
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data for five Latin American systems (Chile, Argentina/Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, Colombia, Mexico, and Brazil) to explain teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA) using a two-level multilevel framework estimated in Mplus with the WLSMV estimator. The authors report country-specific fixed-effect coefficients (γ) and significance levels rather than ML predictive accuracy, with R2L1 (teacher level) ranging from 0.161 to 0.269 and R2L2 (school level) ranging from 0.533 to 0.755. Across countries, teacher cooperation and teacher self-efficacy show positive associations with job satisfaction, while workplace well-being and stress show robust negative associations. At the school level, participation among stakeholders is consistently one of the strongest positive predictors, whereas workload stress is significantly negative in several countries. Limitations include cross-sectional TALIS data (no causal inference) and the inability to use TALIS stratum weights due to confidentiality, which may affect precision of variance estimates.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (teacher questionnaire) — teacher job satisfaction composite (T3JOBSA)

title: Exploring how institutional structures shape instructional quality: The roles of teacher education, employment, and development in fostering higher-order thinking skills
authors: Ari Kim
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data to examine how institutional structures relate to instructional quality for higher-order thinking in the United States (N = 2,560 teachers nested in 165 schools). The dependent variables are teacher-reported instructional practices for critical thinking, knowledge transfer, and problem-solving, each measured on a 1–4 frequency scale. The analysis applies weighted multilevel regression with replicate sample weights and multiple imputation for missing data, reporting coefficient estimates and model R-squared values (up to 0.05 for critical thinking and 0.04 for knowledge transfer/problem-solving). Across outcomes, general pedagogy is consistently positive, while subject content knowledge shows a negative association with problem-solving instruction. Informal, observation- and coaching-based PD is especially important for critical thinking, whereas both formal qualification programs and full-time working hours relate to knowledge transfer; formal and informal PD formats show positive links to problem-solving. Limitations include reliance on self-reports and the absence of student-level achievement measures, so results reflect instructional practice rather than verified HOTS outcomes.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (U.S. teachers) — instructional quality for higher-order thinking (critical thinking item) | TALIS 2018 (U.S. teachers) — instructional quality for higher-order thinking (knowledge transfer item) | TALIS 2018 (U.S. teachers) — instructional quality for higher-order thinking (problem-solving item)
all_target_variables: Critical thinking instructional quality | Knowledge transfer instructional quality | Problem-solving instructional quality

title: Examining the relationship between instructional practice and social studies teacher training: A TALIS study
authors: Peter D. Wiens, Leona Calkins, Paul J. Yoder, Andromeda Hightower
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data restricted to U.S. secondary social studies teachers (n=240) to describe instructional practice frequencies and to test whether initial teacher education (ITE) quality ratings are associated with later instructional practices. Instructional practices are summarized into three TALIS composites—clarity of instruction, cognitive activation, and classroom management—based on teacher-reported frequency on a 4-point scale. Using linear regression, the authors report that ITE-related predictors explain modest variance in instructional practices (Adjusted R2: 0.157 for clarity, 0.051 for classroom management, 0.037 for cognitive activation), with model R2 values of 0.452***, 0.324*, and 0.303þ respectively. The strongest associations for clarity involve ITE subject content, ICT, and monitoring students’ learning, while classroom management is more strongly related to gender and teaching experience. Limitations include cross-sectional self-report measurement and lack of documented missing-data handling and survey-weight use.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (U.S. secondary social studies teachers) — instructional practice composites
all_target_variables: Clarity of instruction (composite) | Classroom management (composite) | Cognitive activation (composite)

title: How stress predicts work engagement among primary and secondary school teachers: The mediating role of emotional labor and burnout, and the moderating role of school support
authors: Yinghua Ye, Yang Jiang, Manliu Wang
outcome_summary: The study analyzed a stratified sample of 5,400 primary and secondary school teachers in China, using questionnaire measures of teacher stress (22 items across six stress factors including workload, student academics, social/school evaluation, professional development, student problem behavior, and technology stress), emotional labor (surface acting, deep acting, expression of naturally felt emotions), burnout (7 items), work engagement (6 items on a 7-point scale), and school support (8 items on a 7-point scale). The authors estimated relationships using structural equation modeling in SPSS/AMOS/Mplus, reporting model fit for the mediation model (CFI=0.842, RMSEA=0.084, PNFI=0.774). Teacher stress significantly predicted lower work engagement (β=-0.316, p<.01), with mediation through burnout (indirect β=-0.247, p<.01) and a chained pathway involving surface acting and burnout (indirect β=-0.038, p<.01). School support also showed significant associations with emotional labor, burnout, and work engagement, but the manuscript does not report any missing-data handling strategy and the design is cross-sectional self-report, limiting causal claims.
all_datasets_used: Teacher questionnaire survey (China; primary & secondary teachers)

title: How perceived teaching autonomy predicts job satisfaction in China: The mediating role of self-efficacy and the moderating role of school climate
authors: Z. Xie, Xueqiang Zou
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for Shanghai (China), focusing on lower-secondary teachers (analytic N=3,944; 198 schools). Using BRR-weighted maximum likelihood estimation in Mplus 8.3, the authors test a triple moderated mediation model where teaching autonomy predicts job satisfaction directly and indirectly via teacher self-efficacy, while school climate moderates the direct and mediated pathways. Teaching autonomy shows a significant total effect on job satisfaction (β=0.272, t=5.192, p<0.001) with partial mediation by self-efficacy (indirect effect β=0.063, t=2.736, p=0.006) and a significant direct effect (β=0.209, t=3.669, p<0.001). School climate significantly moderates all pathways, including the direct interaction (β=0.135, t=2.753, p=0.006), and the model explains 24.4% of variance in job satisfaction (R²=0.244). Limitations include reliance on self-reports, cross-sectional data (no causal inference), and the need for multilevel modeling to better address school-level clustering.

title: Exploring the predictors of teachers’ teaching autonomy: A three-level international study
authors: Q. Lin, X. Gao
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 (Wave 3) data for lower secondary education (ISCED 2) across 27 countries/regions, using a three-level hierarchical linear model (teachers within schools within countries). The dependent variable is teachers’ teaching autonomy measured on a 4-point Likert scale from five items (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.826). After excluding cases with missing values for included variables, the analytic sample comprises 118,347 teachers from 8,262 schools. In the null model, 82.7% of variance is at the teacher level, 10.43% at the school level, and 6.87% at the country level; in the full conditional model, total R2 reaches 9.41%. The strongest positive associations come from professionalism and culture of individualism mechanisms (e.g., self-efficacy β≈0.174, instructional quality β≈0.058, individual vs collaboration time ratio β≈0.114), while complexity-of-practice indicators are mostly non-significant. Limitations include cross-sectional TALIS timing, and the manuscript does not report explicit sampling-weight usage in the provided text.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (Wave 3) Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — teachers’ teaching autonomy (4-point Likert, 5 items)

title: How to promote intrinsically versus extrinsically motivated teachers’ job satisfaction: Exploring individual and school factors
authors: Wonjoon Cha, Eric M. Anderman, Minjung Kim
outcome_summary: The study analyzes KELS 2013 teacher questionnaire data from 242 Korean elementary schools (3677 teachers; extrinsically motivated n=1655, intrinsically motivated n=1882) using sequential linear regression and multigroup CFA/SEM in Mplus with clustering accounted for at the school level. In the sequential regression, the final model explained R²=0.244 of job satisfaction variance, with self-efficacy in classroom management (β=0.20) and colleague teachers’ passion (β=0.19) as positive predictors, while years of teaching experience (β=-0.09) and conflicts with colleagues (β=-0.05) were negative. In multigroup SEM, model fit was acceptable (multigroup SEM CFI=0.920, RMSEA=0.049), and classroom-management self-efficacy predicted job satisfaction for both groups (βEXT=0.23; βINT=0.25). Self-efficacy in teaching mattered only for intrinsically motivated teachers, and colleague passion was the sole significant school-level predictor, stronger for extrinsically motivated teachers (βEXT=0.30 vs βINT=0.17). Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and no explicit reporting of PVs or survey weights beyond complex-sample clustering handling.
all_datasets_used: KELS 2013 (teacher questionnaire), elementary schools (2013–2014 waves) | KELS 2013 (teacher questionnaire), multigroup SEM (extrinsically vs intrinsically motivated teachers)
all_target_variables: Teachers’ job satisfaction (overall) | Teachers’ job satisfaction (moderated by job selection motive)

title: Institutional characteristics moderating the relationship between classroom socioeconomic composition and teacher qualifications: Evidence from 46 education systems in TALIS 2018
authors: L.N. Glassow, E.F., K.Y.H.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 (46 education systems; 9063 schools; 153,682 teachers) for lower secondary (ISCED 2), focusing on whether classroom socioeconomic composition predicts teacher qualification status. Teacher qualification is operationalized as novice (≤5 years experience) and unspecialized (no formal subject study but currently teaching the subject), with classroom SES measured via teacher perceptions of the share of socioeconomically disadvantaged students. The authors estimate within-country logistic regressions and then three-level random-slope generalized linear models in Mplus (classrooms/teachers nested in schools nested in education systems), using teacher/school weights where possible and imputing missing institutional variables via mice (mice package) with country dummies. Results are reported as odds ratios/coefficients with clustered SEs and show significant cross-system heterogeneity in the SES–qualification slopes, with system-level HDI relating more consistently to specialization sorting and system-level autonomy (staffing) and competition relating to novice sorting. Limitations include reliance on teacher-reported classroom SES and the absence of a single predictive ML performance metric (e.g., AUC/RMSE), as the models are regression-based rather than ML predictive modeling.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — teacher/classroom level (all subject domains)
all_target_variables: Teacher with no specialization (math/science teaching mismatch) | Teacher in the first 5 years of their career (novice teacher)

title: Investigating the sources of teacher intercultural self-efficacy: A three-level study using TALIS 2018
authors: M. Schwarzenthal, M. Daumiller, S. Civitillo
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher intercultural self-efficacy using a three-level multilevel framework (teachers nested in schools nested in countries) across 46 countries, focusing on lower and upper secondary teachers. The outcome is teacher intercultural self-efficacy measured with TALIS Likert-scale items about coping with multicultural classrooms and related classroom practices. The authors use teacher final survey weights to address TALIS’s stratified sampling design and handle missingness with FIML in Mplus. They report that intercultural self-efficacy varies significantly across schools and countries (ICC1: 0.046 for schools; 0.157 for countries). In the multilevel models, intercultural professional development and teacher mobility are positively associated with intercultural self-efficacy, while multicultural climate at the school level is also positive (small effect), and multicultural education policy at the country level is negatively associated (moderate effect) but not robust in robustness checks with listwise deletion. The paper is cross-sectional, so associations cannot be interpreted causally.

title: Professional learning communities and teacher outcomes. A cross-national analysis
authors: Anders Astrup Christensen, John Jerrim
outcome_summary: This cross-national study uses TALIS 2018 teacher data for ISCED level 2 to examine whether engagement in professional learning communities (PLCs) is associated with teacher job satisfaction, self-efficacy in instruction, and clarity of instruction. The authors construct a school-level PLC measure as a shared cluster construct with three subdimensions (CPL, SVR, SC) and estimate survey-weighted generalized linear models at the teacher level, using TALIS sampling weights and replicate weights (rescaled to senate weights for pooled estimates). In the pooled analysis across 40 countries/economies, PLCs show the strongest relationship with job satisfaction (0.197 SD; SVR = 0.248 SD), while associations with self-efficacy (0.059–0.062 SD) and clarity of instruction (0.041–0.048 SD) are weak. Country results show substantial heterogeneity: PLCs predict job satisfaction in nearly all countries except Cyprus, but self-efficacy and clarity are significant in only subsets of countries. The study is cross-sectional, relies on teacher self-reports (especially for clarity), and uses multiple imputation as a robustness check; therefore, causal effects cannot be inferred.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 (teacher-level) — job satisfaction with work environment (T3JSENV) | TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 (teacher-level) — self-efficacy in instruction (T3SEINS) | TALIS 2018 ISCED level 2 (teacher-level) — clarity of instruction (T3CLAIN)
all_target_variables: Teacher job satisfaction (T3JSENV) | Teacher self-efficacy (T3SEINS) | Clarity of instruction (T3CLAIN)

title: Patterns of teacher collaboration, professional development and teaching practices: A multiple correspondence analysis of TALIS 2018
authors: M. Methlagl
outcome_summary: This open-access study uses TALIS 2018 lower-secondary (ISCED 2) teacher questionnaire data from participating OECD countries (73,172 teachers) to explore how professional development participation, teacher collaboration, feedback, and classroom characteristics co-occur with teaching practices. The authors apply an exploratory multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) using FactoMineR in R, selecting a two-dimensional solution where Dimension 1 explains 43.3% and Dimension 2 explains 22.7% of total variance. The analysis shows that teachers who report more frequent clear instruction, cognitive activation, and everyday-life problem tasks are positioned differently from teachers who collaborate less and rely more on disciplinary classroom management. Supplementary projections indicate notable links between classroom composition (e.g., problem behaviour, refugees, socioeconomic disadvantage, low achievers) and these teaching-practice patterns, and feedback based on self-assessment versus observation is associated with different dimensions. Limitations include self-report measurement and an exploratory design without causal identification.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (Lower secondary, ISCED 2) teacher questionnaire (OECD countries)
all_target_variables: Teaching practices pattern (MCA dimension 1) | Teaching practices pattern (MCA dimension 2)

title: Job satisfaction predicts teacher self-efficacy and the association is invariant: Examinations using TALIS 2018 data and longitudinal Croatian data
authors: Irena Burić, L.E. Kim
outcome_summary: This paper is not an ML prediction study; it uses TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data (Study 1) and a three-wave longitudinal convenience sample of Croatian teachers (Study 2) to test cross-sectional associations and longitudinal cross-lagged relations between teacher self-efficacy (TSE) and job satisfaction (JS). In Study 1, the authors used confirmatory factor analysis and multi-group CFA to establish measurement and covariance invariance across gender, career stage, and educational level, reporting that the TSE–JS association is invariant across these moderators (fit indices such as CFI/TLI > .90 and RMSEA around .056–.059 in the reported models). In Study 2, they estimated autoregressive cross-lagged panel models (CLPM) with robust maximum likelihood (MLR) and found that JS at Time 1 and Time 2 significantly predicted TSE at subsequent waves (b=0.088 and b=0.142, p<.01), while TSE did not significantly predict future JS (b=-0.063 and b=0.029, p>.05). The study relies on self-report measures and uses FIML for missingness, but it does not report explicit survey-weight application for TALIS.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 data and longitudinal Croatian data

title: Investigating factors affecting teachers’ instructional practices: Evid e nce from TALIS 2018 Turkish data
authors: Ays¸egül Altun, Esra Kuduz, Irem Nur Akkan
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 Turkish teacher data (teachers from ISCED 1, ISCED 2, and ISCED 3) and models teaching practices as the dependent variable, constructed from clarity of instruction, cognitive activation, and classroom management. Missing data were imputed using predictive mean matching before analysis. Although the authors initially considered multilevel modeling due to TALIS’s nested structure, low ICC led them to use multiple regression; they then applied stepwise selection and removed 35 influential outlier cases based on Mahalanobis distance. The best stepwise model (Model 14) achieved R² = 0.360 (Adjusted R² = 0.359) with Durbin–Watson = 1.96, indicating no autocorrelation. The strongest predictors were teacher self-efficacy and related multicultural self-efficacy, followed by teacher cooperation/collaboration, diversity practices, and perceived disciplinary climate; several other TALIS domains (e.g., job satisfaction, school leadership) were not significant. Limitations include the lack of reported survey-weight usage and the fact that regression-based associations cannot establish causality.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 Turkish data (teachers; ISCED 1-3) — instructional practices
all_target_variables: Teaching practices (clarity, cognitive activation, classroom management)

title: Profiles of occupational well-being among Chinese teachers: Associations with basic psychological needs satisfaction and teaching quality
authors: Yanghua Huang, Ma Jenina N. Nalipay, Hui Wang
outcome_summary: This study analyzed TALIS 2018 China teacher data restricted to Shanghai middle school teachers (Grades 7–9), with a total analytic sample of 3,976 teachers. The authors used a person-centered approach (latent profile analysis) to identify four occupational well-being profiles—highly satisfied (n=507), balanced (n=2,726), highly unsatisfied (n=399), and highly stressed (n=320)—and then examined how basic psychological needs satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and demographics related to profile membership. They reported significant profile differences in teaching quality: clarity of instruction (χ2(3)=132.602, p<.001), cognitive activation (χ2(3)=59.424, p<.001), and classroom management (χ2(3)=117.624, p<.001), with highly satisfied teachers highest on clarity and cognitive activation and highly stressed teachers lowest on classroom management. Missing data were handled via FIML under a missing-completely-at-random assumption, but the paper does not report PV handling or explicit TALIS sampling weights, and the cross-sectional design prevents causal inference.

title: Profiles of facilitators’ beliefs about collaboration and how they relate to experience, job satisfaction, self-efficacy, and willingness to innovate
outcome_summary: This study used a QuaMath facilitator survey in Germany (Aug 2023) with 190 experienced mathematics teacher PD facilitators to identify person-centred profiles of collaboration beliefs and to examine how these profiles relate to facilitator characteristics. The best-fitting three-class latent profile analysis (AIC = 759.80; BIC = 805.26; entropy = 0.82) distinguished Selective Collaborators, Moderate Collaborators, and Collaboration Enthusiasts based on collaboration beliefs with teachers, with facilitators, and among teachers during PD. Group differences were tested with MANOVA, which was significant for the combined dependent variables (F(16,356)=39.506, p<.001, partial η2=0.64). Follow-up tests showed significant profile differences for self-efficacy and willingness to innovate, but not for teaching experience, facilitator experience, or job satisfaction. The analysis is not an ILSA/PV-based achievement ML study, uses no survey weights, and willingness-to-innovate has low reliability (ω=0.52), limiting precision and causal interpretation.
all_datasets_used: QuaMath facilitator survey (Germany, Aug 2023; mathematics teacher PD facilitators)
all_target_variables: Latent profiles of collaboration beliefs (3-class LPA)

title: Teacher clusters of emotions and self-efficacy in curriculum reform: Effects on collaboration and learner-centered teaching
authors: Hui-Ling Wendy Pan, Jui-Hsuan Hung, Thi Minh Thu Truong
outcome_summary: This study used a stratified cluster sampling survey of 624 upper secondary teachers in Taiwan (June 2023) and employed TALIS 2018-based scales (with modifications) alongside newly developed emotion and learner-centered teaching measures. Teachers were clustered into three profiles using Ward hierarchical clustering followed by K-means on standardized joy, fatigue, and self-efficacy, and then cluster differences were tested with ANOVA and associations were quantified with cluster-specific regressions. For teacher collaboration, joy and self-efficacy predicted higher collaboration in Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 (e.g., Cluster 1 R2=0.312; Cluster 2 R2=0.254), while fatigue only showed a significant effect in Cluster 2 and no predictors were significant in Cluster 3. For learner-centered teaching, self-efficacy was significant across all clusters (Cluster R2≈0.47–0.51), and fatigue negatively predicted learner-centered teaching only in Cluster 3 (β=-0.241, p<0.05). The paper does not report missing-data handling or any survey-weight application, and the design is correlational rather than causal.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018-based teacher scales (Taiwan upper secondary teachers, June 2023 survey)

title: Teacher job satisfaction: International evidence on the role of school working conditions and teacher characteristics
authors: N. Eryilmaz, Alec Kennedy, Rolf Strietholt, Stefan Johansson
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics teacher questionnaire data from 13,048 teachers across 46 education systems to examine how school working conditions and teacher characteristics relate to teacher job satisfaction. Teacher job satisfaction is measured as an affective latent scale from five Likert-type items, with Cronbach’s alpha of 0.907 for pooled data. The authors first validate the measurement models via CFA and test measurement invariance across countries (metric invariance achieved; scalar invariance not reached, so mean comparisons are limited). In pooled regression models, leadership support (β=0.266***), student discipline (β=0.356***), and professional development (β=0.084***) are positively associated with job satisfaction, while teacher workload (β=−0.113***), teaching years (β=−0.006***), and gender show smaller effects (gender β=0.071**). The analysis uses listwise deletion for ~10% item missingness and explicitly does not apply teacher weights; coefficients are reported rather than ML performance metrics, and the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Teacher questionnaire; 46 education systems)
all_target_variables: Teacher job satisfaction (latent scale from 5 items)

title: Teacher collaboration, school innovativeness and innovative teaching in Taiwan: Evidence from TALIS
authors: H.-L. Pan, Yi-Chun Lin, Chih-Hung Chung
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for lower secondary teachers in Taiwan (N=3835 valid responses) to examine how two forms of teacher collaboration relate to innovative teaching, with school innovativeness as a mediator. Using confirmatory factor analysis and a structural equation model (AMOS) with EM-based missing value estimation and 5000-sample bootstrapping for mediation, the model fit was good (RMSEA=0.04; CFI=0.98; SRMR=0.03). Professional collaboration showed a significant direct positive effect on innovative teaching (β=0.44, p<0.001), whereas exchange and coordination for teaching did not show a significant direct association and instead influenced innovative teaching through school innovativeness (full mediation). School innovativeness had a small but significant positive effect on innovative teaching (β=0.05, p<0.05). Limitations include reliance on self-reported Likert measures and the absence of explicit reporting on TALIS sampling weights and replicate-weight procedures.

title: Teacher and school stress profiles: A multilevel examination and associations with work-related outcomes
authors: Rebecca J. Collie, Caroline F. Mansfield
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 Australian teacher and school questionnaire data (3117 teachers in 225 schools; ISCED Level 2) to identify person-centered teacher stress profiles and then multilevel school profiles based on the prevalence of teacher profiles. The authors estimate five teacher latent profiles (Low-Burden, Mixed-Burden-Workload, Mixed-Burden-Behavior, Average-Burden, High-Burden) and three school profiles (Lower Pressure Climate—Workload, Lower Pressure Climate—Behavior, Higher Pressure Climate) using latent profile analysis in Mplus with complex survey handling and teacher/school weights (TCHWGT, SCHWGT). Outcomes are teacher-level strain and occupational commitment and school-average versions of these outcomes; missing data are handled with full information maximum likelihood (FIML). The results show a clear ordering: Low-Burden and Mixed-Burden-Behavior typically have the lowest strain and highest occupational commitment, while High-Burden shows the highest strain and lowest commitment. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no profile transitions over time) and reliance on person-centered modeling rather than predictive ML performance metrics.

title: Research on the influence of teachers’ ICT Capacity on classroom teaching quality: An intermediary model based on self-efficacy
authors: F. Zhang, Q. Li
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for the Shanghai region of China (N=2945 teachers after excluding missing values) to examine how teachers’ ICT capacity relates to classroom teaching quality and whether self-efficacy mediates this relationship. Using multiple linear regression, Shapley value decomposition, quantile regression (quantiles 0.1/0.3/0.5/0.7/0.9), and Hansen-style threshold regression, the authors find that ICT capacity has a significant positive association with overall classroom teaching quality (coefficient 0.297, p<0.01) and with all three sub-dimensions, with the largest effect on cognitive mobilization (1.365, p<0.01). Heterogeneity appears across quantiles (ICT effects up to 0.372) and a double-threshold pattern emerges (0.201/0.280/0.357 across ICT capacity intervals). Mediation tests show partial mediation via self-efficacy (indirect effect 0.088; 95% CIs exclude zero). Limitations include cross-sectional data and no explicit reporting of TALIS sampling-weight use, so population-representative inference and causal claims are constrained.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), classroom teaching quality (overall) | TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), classroom teaching quality (sub-dimension: clear teaching) | TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), classroom teaching quality (sub-dimension: cognitive mobilization) | TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), classroom teaching quality (sub-dimension: classroom management) | TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) — teacher survey (junior high teachers), mediation pathway
all_target_variables: Classroom teaching quality (overall) | Clear teaching | Cognitive mobilization | Classroom management | Mediation: ICT capacity → teachers’ self-efficacy → classroom teaching quality

title: Relationships between teacher education mechanisms and teacher practices, self-efficacy, and job satisfaction in the U.S.: An analysis of TALIS 2018
authors: T.D. Reeves, V. Hamilton
outcome_summary: This associational study used TALIS 2018’s U.S. lower-secondary teacher data, filtered to full-time, core-content, single-school teachers and excluding special education teachers (final analytic sample: 1175 teachers in 164 schools). The authors estimated weighted multilevel regression models (TCHWGT; results pooled across five multiply imputed datasets) for three outcomes: teacher practices (T3TPRA), teacher self-efficacy (T3SELF), and teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA). No machine-learning algorithms or predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) were reported; instead, Table 2 provides standardized regression coefficients and standard errors. Key predictors included teacher cooperation, specific pre-service content foci (e.g., student behavior/classroom management; monitoring learning), in-service professional development activities (online courses/seminars; conferences; peer/self-observation and coaching; teacher networks), and feedback sources (especially principal/management team). Limitations include observational design (no causal identification), potential measurement error in self-reported practices, and the possibility of reverse causality for mentoring-related findings.
all_target_variables: Teacher practices (T3TPRA) | Teacher self-efficacy (T3SELF) | Teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA)

title: Teachers’ engaging messages, students’ motivation to learn and academic performance: The moderating role of emotional intensity in speech
authors: S. Falcon, J. Leon
outcome_summary: This study is not an ILSA-based machine-learning paper: it uses transcript-based lesson analysis (TBLA) and acoustic scoring to examine how teachers’ engaging messages relate to students’ motivation to learn and subsequent math grades. The sample comprises 36 Spanish secondary teachers and 807 students (Grades 9–12) from 16 schools in Gran Canaria, Tenerife, and Santander. Teachers’ engaging messages were coded into gain/loss frames and motivational appeal types; emotional intensity was computed from audio clips using the Emotional Temperature model (0–100) and averaged per teacher-group. The authors estimated moderated mediation models in MPlus with a counterfactual mediation approach, segmenting emotional intensity into 10-point bins. Results show significant direct and total effects of engaging messages on academic performance for most message types, with emotional intensity often showing an inverse (diminishing) effect on performance; however, indirect effects through motivation to learn were not significant. Limitations include the small, localized sample and the absence of reported missing-data handling and any survey-weighting strategy.

title: Teacher mentorship and job satisfaction: A cross-national econometric analysis of mentees and mentors
authors: Mike Smet
outcome_summary: The study uses TALIS 2018 lower secondary (ISCED 2) teacher data (123,299 teachers in 8,848 schools across 54 regions/language settings) to examine whether teachers’ job satisfaction is associated with (i) having a mentor and (ii) being a mentor. The authors apply a two-stage econometric control-function approach to address self-selection into mentoring roles: a first-stage probit for mentor status followed by a second-stage job satisfaction equation with school fixed effects and school-clustered standard errors. They then treat 49 remaining regions (after excluding regions with <250 observations) as independent studies and aggregate region-specific effects using random-effects meta-analysis with inverse-variance weighting. Results show a consistent positive association for mentees (effect 0.13, 95% CI [0.09; 0.16], I² ≈ 0%) and a stronger but more heterogeneous association for mentors (effect 0.82, 95% CI [0.62; 1.02], I² = 56.1%). Limitations include cross-sectional self-reported measures and no explicit missing-data strategy reported; additionally, the analysis is not a machine-learning predictive pipeline.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 Lower secondary (ISCED 2) teacher job satisfaction (54 regions/language settings)
all_target_variables: Teacher job satisfaction (continuous Likert score, 0–20) — having a mentor | Teacher job satisfaction (continuous Likert score, 0–20) — being a mentor

title: Teachers’ pathways to the profession and their attitudes toward diverse classrooms
authors: Praveen K. Dubey, Jessica Nadzam, Todd D. Little
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data for the United States, focusing on lower secondary teachers (grades 7–9). The authors build four latent constructs—TIP (importance/attitudes), TCT (training/coping for culturally diverse teaching), TPD (diversity implementation practices), and TCC (class composition)—from 19 selected TALIS items and estimate a four-factor CFA model with strong fit (χ²(59)=224.58, CFI=.974, TLI=.966, RMSEA=.033, SRMR=.028). Missing data were handled with full information maximum likelihood (FIML). Measurement invariance across first-career teachers (FCT) vs second-career teachers (SCT) was supported (ΔCFI=.001 for weak and ΔCFI=.003 for strong). The study reports gender-linked differences in TIP and TCT (female higher) and TPD (male higher), while TCC shows no significant gender effect; however, the analysis is based on self-reported perceptions and does not involve ML prediction or PV-based achievement outcomes.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 United States (lower secondary teachers, grades 7–9)
all_target_variables: Teachers’ Importance for Profession (TIP) latent construct

title: The development of student teachers’ teacher self-efficacy before and during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Wendy Symes, Rebecca Lazarides, Isabell Hußner
outcome_summary: This paper analyzes longitudinal change in student teachers’ teacher self-efficacy across three waves (T1, T2, T3) during a single semester in Germany (Brandenburg). The analytic sample comprised N=201 student teachers from one university, split into a face-to-face group (n=80; summer 2019 and winter 2019/20 combined) and a COVID-19 group (n=121; summer 2020 taught entirely online). Using latent growth curve models with an additional growth factor, the authors found that self-efficacy for instructional strategies showed little within-group change but significantly less developmental change in the COVID-19 group relative to face-to-face. For classroom management, self-efficacy increased in the face-to-face group but stayed constant in the COVID-19 group (AGF mean negative and significant). For student engagement, self-efficacy increased face-to-face but declined under COVID-19 (AGF mean negative and significant), with moderation effects involving gender and prior pedagogical experience. Limitations include unequal group sizes and incomplete documentation of missing-data handling beyond inclusion criteria.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (not used); student-teacher longitudinal self-efficacy (Germany, Brandenburg; T1-T3 across one semester)
all_target_variables: Self-efficacy for instructional strategies (latent growth slope / AGF)

title: The effect of teacher collaboration on teachers' career well-being in China: A moderated mediation model of teacher self-efficacy and distributed leadership
authors: Guangqiang Wang, Hui Bai, Kwok Kuen Tsang, Jinjin Bian
outcome_summary: This Acta Psychologica study uses TALIS 2018 data restricted to a Shanghai subsample of 3159 junior high school teachers. Rather than machine learning, the authors estimate mediation and moderated mediation using SPSS PROCESS (Model 4 for mediation; Model 59 for moderation) with bias-corrected percentile bootstrapping (5000 replications) and control variables (gender, teaching experience, educational background). Teacher collaboration shows a significant positive association with both career well-being and self-efficacy (e.g., TC → CWE β=0.117, p<0.001; TC → SE β=0.166, p<0.001), and self-efficacy significantly mediates the TC–career well-being relationship (indirect effect=0.018, 95% CI excludes 0). Distributed leadership further moderates the collaboration effects (TC × DL → career well-being β=0.030, p<0.05; TC × DL → self-efficacy β=0.066, p<0.001) and moderates the mediation pathway, with stronger effects at high distributed leadership. Limitations include cross-sectional data and no documented missing-data handling or survey-weight application.
all_target_variables: Career well-being | Self-efficacy | Career well-being (moderated mediation)

title: The digital divide in online education: Inequality in digital readiness of students and schools
authors: H.G. van de Werfhorst, et al.
outcome_summary: This study uses ICILS 2018 (grade 8) and TALIS 2018 to examine pre-pandemic digital readiness gaps across seven and 45 countries, respectively. In ICILS, the authors construct student ICT-use factor scores and ICT-skill factor scores (from five plausible values) and school ICT infrastructure/competencies from principal/ICT coordinator evaluations, then estimate linear regression models with school-clustered standard errors. The results show that digital readiness inequalities are strongest for students’ ICT skills and are most pronounced by SES (up to 1.3 SD in Chile), with additional migration and gender patterns (e.g., migrants up to 0.54 SD lower in skills in some countries; girls up to 0.44 SD higher). In TALIS, multilevel country-specific models indicate that school composition has very weak explanatory power for teachers’ ICT readiness, with only sporadic significant relationships (e.g., England −24 percentage points; Norway +28 percentage points for ICT professional development). The paper does not report ML model performance metrics because it uses regression-based approaches rather than predictive ML, and it does not document a complete missing-data strategy beyond row-mean imputation for one factor score, limiting full transparency.
