title: The development and validation of the Multidimensional Assessment of Teacher Social-Emotional Competence (MATSEC) in East Asian school contexts
authors: J. Lee, Linyun Fu, Hui Hu, Chenxiao Wang, Eunkyung Chung, Se-na Choi, Changyong Choi, Seungmin Lee, Ingrid D. Lui, Min Sang Yoo
outcome_summary: This paper develops and validates the Multidimensional Assessment of Teacher Social-Emotional Competence (MATSEC) using teacher self-report survey data collected in Spring 2024 from 859 teachers in China (CHN, n=602; elementary) and South Korea (KOR, n=257; elementary). The authors used a psychometric pipeline (EFA on n=430 and CFA on n=429 via the SOLOMON split) and compared non-hierarchical, second-order, and bifactor models, reporting strong model fit (e.g., bifactor Model 6 on the full sample: χ2=688.97, df=297, CFI=0.96, TLI=0.95, RMSEA=0.05, SRMR=0.04). Reliability was high for the general factor (ω=0.97; ωH=0.92) and dimensionality indices supported unidimensional measurement of the overarching construct (ECV=0.75, PUC=0.85, ARPB=3%). Concurrent validity correlations were moderate-to-strong (overall T-SEC r≈0.42–0.65 with most anchors; negative with depression/anxiety and burnout). Limitations include self-report measurement, cross-sectional design, and Korea’s convenience sampling, which constrain generalizability.
all_datasets_used: MATSEC teacher survey (Spring 2024) — China (elementary) and South Korea (elementary) — T-SEC scale validation

title: The impact of teacher deep collaboration on job satisfaction: Evidence from Chinese lower secondary teachers
authors: Haoran Ma, Peng Liu, Min Zhu, Kang Min
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data restricted to Shanghai, China, covering 3,976 junior high school teachers from 198 schools. It tests a multilevel structural equation modeling framework (Mplus 8.3, robust maximum likelihood MLR) to estimate direct and indirect relationships among teacher deep collaboration (T3COLES), team innovation (T3TEAM), teacher self-efficacy (T3SEENG), and teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA). The model fit is strong (SRMRwithin = 0.002; SRMRbetween = 0.03), and teacher deep collaboration shows a significant positive direct effect on job satisfaction (β = 0.087, p < 0.001). Mediation results indicate partial indirect effects via team innovation (β = 0.054, p < 0.001; MP = 29.2%) and via self-efficacy (β = 0.026, p < 0.001; MP = 14.3%), with a smaller chain effect (β = 0.006, p < 0.001; MP = 3.1%). Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal inference) and no reported missing-data handling strategy.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) Junior high school teachers
all_target_variables: Teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA) | Team innovation (T3TEAM) | Teacher self-efficacy (T3SEENG) | Teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA) via mediation

title: The role of openness to experience in innovating teaching and instruction through leader-member exchange and teacher creativity
outcome_summary: This study used a Malaysia teacher questionnaire (Feb–May 2024) with 3016 teachers from 148 schools to examine how openness to experience relates to innovative teaching practices, with leader-member exchange (LMX) and teacher creativity as mediators and moderators. The authors estimated latent moderated structural equation models in Mplus 8.5 using the WLSMV estimator and cluster-robust standard errors (TYPE=COMPLEX) to account for teachers nested within schools. Model fit for the main SEM was acceptable (CFI=0.938, SRMR=0.028). Openness to experience strongly predicted teacher creativity (β=0.956, p<.001) and positively predicted LMX (β=0.397, p<.001). Innovation (binary process innovation in the last 12 months) was predicted by teacher creativity (β=0.271, p<.001) and LMX (β=0.132, p<.001), and openness showed a significant total indirect effect on innovation (β=0.309, 95%CI [0.265, 0.351], p<.001). Limitations include cross-sectional self-report measurement, no documented missing-data handling, and no PV-based achievement framework (so PV methods are not applicable).
all_datasets_used: Non-ILSA teacher survey in Malaysia (Feb–May 2024), latent moderated SEM
all_target_variables: LMX (latent construct) | Teacher creativity (latent construct) | Individual teacher innovation (binary: implemented process innovation in last 12 months)

title: Teachers' expectancy-value-cost profiles in professional development to support students’ self-regulated learning
outcome_summary: This study used a longitudinal teacher-survey design embedded in a year-long SRL-focused professional development program in Estonia (2023/24), collecting data at four waves (T1–T4) from teachers nested in 10 schools. The analytic sample comprised 171 teachers initially, with wave-specific Ns of 136 (T1), 138 (T2), 116 (T3), and 118 (T4). Teachers’ SRL-related teaching practices increased significantly from T1 to T4 across all five practice factors (e.g., promoting metacognition: t(86)=8.67, p<.001, d=0.93; emotional support: t(86)=5.01, p<.001, d=0.54). Motivation and perceived costs showed mostly positive associations for expectancies/values and sporadic negative associations for cost dimensions, with outside effort showing particularly strong negative correlations with end-of-program practices. The study relies on self-reports and has no control group, so effects cannot be interpreted causally; additionally, it does not use ILSA plausible values or survey weights.
all_datasets_used: Longitudinal SRL-focused PD (Estonia, 2023/24; teacher questionnaire; waves T1–T4) | Longitudinal SRL-focused PD (Estonia, 2023/24; teacher questionnaire; LPA at T1 and T4)
all_target_variables: SRL-related teaching practices (T1 vs T4) | Associations between motivation/cost and SRL-related teaching practices | Motivational profile membership and SRL-related teaching practices

title: What drives and drains teachers in Taiwan? Exploring the motivational roots of job satisfaction through stress pathways
authors: Chih-Wei Li, Chien-Chih Chen, Ying-Pei Huang
outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data for 3,598 lower secondary (junior high) teachers in Taiwan, using a complex survey design with final teacher weights and 80 replicate weights (BRR with Fay’s adjustment factor 0.5). Missing responses across key constructs were handled via multiple imputation using Markov chain Monte Carlo (20 imputed datasets), with pooled estimates using Rubin’s combination rules. The authors estimate a multiple-mediator SEM in AMOS (maximum likelihood) and report strong model fit (structural model: χ2(132)=764.174, CFI=0.979, TLI=0.972, RMSEA=0.035, SRMR=0.018). Job satisfaction (T3JSENV) is positively predicted by personal utility (β=0.07), social utility (β=0.16), and intrinsic career value (β=0.13), while workload (β=-0.18) and student behavior stress (β=-0.20) are negative predictors. Mediation is supported by significant indirect paths (e.g., personal utility via student behavior stress β=-0.02; social utility via workload β=0.01 and via student behavior stress β=0.02). Limitations include correlational inference due to cross-sectional self-report measures and the absence of ML-based predictive evaluation.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 Lower secondary (junior high) teachers, Taiwan

title: Teaching quality as a dynamic system: How school support, psychological needs, and motivation interact across needs–skills configurations
authors: Y. Ning
outcome_summary: This study uses OECD TALIS 2024 teacher survey data restricted to Shanghai, China (N=3976 teachers) to model teaching performance as a dynamic, multi-dimensional network of TALIS “teaching practices” (T1–T4) alongside school support, basic psychological needs, and motivation. Rather than training a predictive ML model, the authors estimate cross-factor networks using partial correlations and compare network structure across three needs–performance configurations (HNG, BNPG, HPG) derived from standardized difference scores. The overall network shows self-efficacy as proximal: the strongest edges include T1–M1 (r=0.209) and T3–C2 (r=0.243), while instructional leadership (S2) and trust in school (R2) function as distal correlates. Network comparisons indicate significant structural invariance across configurations (all p<0.01) and configuration-specific edge reversals (e.g., M2–M3: ~0.000, 0.009, −0.044). Limitations include cross-sectional design (no temporal ordering/causality), self-report measurement, and no documented use of TALIS sampling weights.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2024 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey network (no grade/domain restriction stated) | TALIS 2024 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey network by needs–performance configuration (HNG/BNPG/HPG)
all_target_variables: Teaching performance (overall network; teaching practices T1–T4) | Teaching performance network structure differences across needs–performance configurations

title: Understanding teacher leadership: Development and testing of the survey of teacher leadership
authors: Peter D. Wiens, Vanessa Vongkulluksn, Jori Beck, Brenda Pearson
outcome_summary: This paper develops and validates a new instrument—the Survey of Teacher Leadership (STL)—for measuring five teacher leadership subtypes: professional growth, professional development leadership, collaboration, shared leadership, and equity leadership. Data were collected from 1,274 non-charter public-school teachers in Nevada (USA) via an email/Qualtrics survey in fall 2022, with item responses captured as both self-efficacy (4-point Likert) and behavioral frequency (6-point Likert). The authors used a two-phase approach: CFA with WLSMV estimation for construct validity and scale refinement, followed by graded response IRT models to examine item and scale functioning; model fit was evaluated using CFI/TLI/RMSEA/SRMR and item-level fit indices. Missing item responses were handled with listwise deletion, and the final measurement models were validated on an independent even/odd split. Reliability was supported with Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega exceeding 0.77 across subscales, and the final CFA/IRT models showed adequate-to-excellent fit (e.g., RMSEA≤0.07, CFI≥0.97, TLI≥0.98). Because the study is instrument validation rather than predictive modeling, it does not estimate ML performance metrics or causal effects.
all_datasets_used: ILSA literature synthesis (systematic review; no single student-level analytic micro-dataset)

title: Measurement invariance of non-cognitive measures in TIMSS across countries and across time. An application and comparison of Multigroup Confirmatory Factor Analysis, Bayesian approximate measurement invariance and alignment optimization approach
authors: S. Wurster
outcome_summary: This paper is a methodological application comparing three measurement-invariance approaches for TIMSS non-cognitive questionnaire constructs across 26 countries and across time (TIMSS 2007, 2011, 2015; fourth grade). It evaluates exact measurement invariance using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis (MGCFA) and approximate measurement invariance using Bayesian approximate measurement invariance and the alignment optimization method. Across countries, MGCFA fit is generally poor for the School Emphasis on Academic Success scale and for the Students Confident in Science scale, leading to mostly configural (and rarely metric) invariance conclusions; Bayesian approximate invariance similarly indicates configural-level invariance with poor posterior predictive p-values. In contrast, the alignment optimization method often supports approximate invariance and enables more defensible comparisons of latent means across countries and within-country trends over time, provided the proportion of non-invariant parameters is below a 25% threshold and R2 values are sufficiently high. Limitations include convergence/computation constraints for Bayesian student models and the fact that approximate invariance does not guarantee content validity or unbiased comparisons if non-invariance is substantial.

title: 1-s2.0-S0191886923000715-main
authors: Yuan Liu, Xin Zheng, Kit-Tai Hau
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2015 and TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 mathematics and science to test whether instrumental value (task utility) helps students differently depending on intrinsic motivation and cultural individualism/collectivism. The authors restrict analyses to representative top-performing economies (10 in the main analyses; 16 in robustness) and use multilevel modeling to account for clustering of students within schools and economies. Across both waves, intrinsic motivation shows medium-to-large positive effects on achievement (effect sizes reported from about d=0.33 to d=0.68), while instrumental value’s effects are conditional: instrumental value improves achievement for collectivistic students with low intrinsic motivation, with significant interaction terms (e.g., TIMSS 2015 math In×Istr beta=-3.23, p<.001; TIMSS 2019 math beta=-5.76, p<.001). The paper does not report any machine-learning algorithms, survey-weight usage, or plausible-value handling details; therefore, results should be interpreted as multilevel regression evidence rather than predictive ML performance, and causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional associations.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Mathematics (Study 1, representative 10 economies) | TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Science (Study 1, representative 10 economies) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Study 2, representative 10 economies) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (Study 2, representative 10 economies)

title: Exploring measurement invariance in TIMSS: A longitudinal perspective with an emphasis on gender effects
authors: Norman Verhelst, Hüseyin H. Yıldırım
outcome_summary: This paper is a methodological reanalysis of TIMSS grade 8 mathematics data (SWE, USA, HUN, ENG) across six cycles (2003–2023) to study longitudinal measurement invariance and gender-related differential functioning. The authors download TIMSS item responses and test design information, then run country-wise IRT calibrations using a restricted one-parameter logistic model (OPLM) and apply Profile Analysis (PA) to compare observed vs expected performance within item content domains (Algebra, Number, Geometry, Data) across 12 groups defined by cycle and gender. For trend estimation, they compare TIMSS official plausible-value (PV) trends to trends computed from weighted maximum likelihood (WML) estimates derived from the national calibrations, using TIMSS-provided total student weights. The results show that international calibration item parameters are not appropriate for describing country-specific data (scalar invariance not fulfilled), and that gender differences are highly significant and domain-specific (girls advantaged in Algebra; boys advantaged in Number) across all six cycles. The study also finds that the shift to digital administration in 2019 further jeopardizes scalar invariance, suggesting that score-based trend comparisons may be misleading when invariance assumptions fail.

title: Trends in mathematics motivation between 1980 and 2015: Exploring the educational-gender-equality paradox over time
authors: Erika Majoros
outcome_summary: The study investigates the educational-gender-equality paradox in mathematics motivation using longitudinal, system-level panel data built from SIMS 1980, TIMSS 1995, and TIMSS 2015. It constructs cross-culturally comparable intrinsic and extrinsic motivation scales via a market-basket approach and country-specific IRT measurement, generating five plausible sum scores per student and pooling to country means using Rubin’s rules; missing parental education data lead to excluding England from subgroup analyses. The main results come from two-way fixed-effects panel regressions (robust SE clustered by country) on country-level gender gaps. For intrinsic motivation, HDI significantly predicts changes from 1980 to 1995 (notably for students with lower-than-median parental education), while HDI shows no effect from 1995 to 2015; GDP shows a significant narrowing pattern from 1995 to 2015 for the lower parental-education group. For extrinsic motivation, neither HDI nor GDP significantly predicts gender-gap change in either panel. Limitations include aggregation to country-level gaps, subgroup analyses with substantial missingness, and the fact that the paper uses causal language despite relying on observational panel assumptions rather than randomized identification.
all_datasets_used: SIMS 1980 & TIMSS 1995 (Panel A), grade 8/7 systems, mathematics motivation (intrinsic) gender gap | TIMSS 1995 & TIMSS 2015 (Panel B), grade 8 systems, mathematics motivation (intrinsic) gender gap | SIMS 1980 & TIMSS 1995 (Panel A), grade 8/7 systems, mathematics motivation (extrinsic) gender gap | TIMSS 1995 & TIMSS 2015 (Panel B), grade 8 systems, mathematics motivation (extrinsic) gender gap
all_target_variables: Intrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls) | Intrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls) — GDP sensitivity | Extrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls)

title: Circumventing construct-irrelevant variance in international assessments using cognitive diagnostic modeling: A curriculum-sensitive measure
authors: H. Heister, Rolf Strietholt, Hannah Heister, Purya Baghaei, Philipp Doebler
outcome_summary: This study proposes a curriculum-sensitive scaling statistic, Tc, within cognitive diagnostic modeling (CDM) to address construct-irrelevant variance in international assessments when teachers do not cover all tested topics. The empirical demonstration uses TIMSS 1995 mathematics data for secondary students (seventh–ninth graders) across 19 educational systems/countries, combining student item responses with teacher survey reports of which of 32 math topics were taught in class. The authors estimate an MG-DINA model (with an 11-skill Q-matrix) and compute Tc as the average proportion of taught topics that students did not master, then rank countries by Tc (ascending). For comparison, they compute conventional IRT-based country means using sampling weights and all five plausible values. The resulting Tc ranking is highly consistent with the official IRT-based ranking (country-mean correlation r = −0.95; full-sample vs reduced-sample IRT correlation r = 0.99), with only two countries differing by more than one rank. Limitations include substantial missing teacher information requiring sample reduction and potential mismatch between teacher questionnaire topics and the test’s skill/Q-matrix structure.

title: Are schools becoming more unequal? Insights from exploratory data mining of international large-scale assessment, TIMSS 2003-2019
authors: Ali Farhan, Ow-Yeong Yook Kit, Tilley Jacqueline L.
outcome_summary: This exploratory data-mining study uses TIMSS science achievement data from 10 countries across five cycles (2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019) for Grade 4 and Grade 8 general science. The authors compute school-level achievement using five plausible values (PV-based weighted means) and then decompose total achievement inequality into between-school and within-school variance components, filtering out schools with fewer than 10 tested students (7474 schools at Grade 4; 7567 at Grade 8). They report that within-school inequality is consistently much larger than between-school inequality and that between-school inequality does not show a clear worsening over nearly two decades. They further find a stable moderate-to-large negative relationship between within-school average achievement and within-school inequality, and they use Gaussian mixture modeling to show that lower-achieving schools often display bimodality (multiple student subpopulations), especially in Grade 4. Limitations include the lack of explicit missing-data handling documentation and the absence of numeric ML performance metrics because the work is descriptive/exploratory rather than supervised prediction.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 General Science (5 cycles) | TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 8 General Science (5 cycles) | TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 General Science (5 cycles; school-level aggregation) | TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 8 General Science (5 cycles; school-level aggregation)
all_target_variables: Between-school vs within-school inequality (SD of science PV scale scores) | Within-school inequality nature (SD vs within-school average; bimodality via Gaussian mixtures)

title: Does socioeconomic sorting of teacher qualifications exacerbate mathematics achievement inequity? Panel data estimates from 20 years of TIMSS
outcome_summary: The study uses six waves of TIMSS (1999–2019) for grade-8 mathematics, constructing an unbalanced cross-country panel across 32 education systems that participated in at least four cycles. The dependent variable is TIMSS mathematics achievement (standardized to a 500/100 scale) and the key inequity mechanism is tested by interacting student SES with system-level teacher qualification gaps (novice experience vs mathematics education specialization) and with socioeconomic school segregation. Missing data are addressed with multivariate imputation by chained equations (mice) producing five imputed datasets per country-year, and results are pooled using Rubin-style combining rules across plausible values. In fixed-effects panel regressions with country and year fixed effects and country-clustered robust SEs, out-of-subject (mathematics-education) teacher sorting significantly increases the SES–achievement association (Model 3: SES × out-of-subject sorting coefficient ≈ 44.30; SES × segregation ≈ 34.81), while novice sorting is null. The paper reports student weights applied and uses teacher weights for exposure/gap construction; however, the approach remains observational and fixed-effects estimates can still be sensitive to time-varying confounding and measurement error in teacher qualification proxies.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 1999–2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (panel; 32 education systems with ≥4 waves)
all_target_variables: Mathematics achievement (TIMSS mathematics score; inequity via SES interaction)

title: The progression of achievement gap between immigrant and native-born students from primary to secondary education
authors: Aigul Alieva, Vincent A. Hildebrand, Philippe Van Kerm
outcome_summary: This study constructs three synthetic cohorts to measure how the immigrant–native achievement gap evolves from primary to secondary education by pooling PIRLS, PISA, and TIMSS cross-sections. It focuses on reading (Cohorts 1 and 2: PIRLS Grade 4 to PISA age 15) and mathematics (Cohort 3: TIMSS Grade 4 to Grade 8) across 12 Western European countries and 4 traditional immigration countries (Australia, Canada, New Zealand, United States). Because test-score scaling across surveys is not assumed cardinally comparable, the paper uses Gastwirth’s PROB index (ordinal) and also reports raw mean-score gaps; adjusted gaps are computed via direct standardization reweighting using gender, parental education, books at home, and computer/desk. Results show persistent immigrant lags in many European countries in reading and more heterogeneous patterns in mathematics, with convergence or advantage more common in traditional immigration countries. Limitations include the absence of explicit missing-data handling documentation for covariates and the fact that the approach is not a causal design.
all_datasets_used: PIRLS 2001 & PISA 2006 (Cohort 1) Reading (Grade 4 to age 15) | PIRLS 2006 & PISA 2012 (Cohort 2) Reading (Grade 4 to age 15) | TIMSS 2015 & TIMSS 2019 (Cohort 3) Mathematics (Grade 4 to Grade 8)

title: Science and mathematics preservice teachers’ perceptions and experiences of practicing dialogic teaching in generative AI-powered virtual reality simulation
authors: Nuodi Zhang, Fengfeng Ke, Chih-Pu Dai, Sherry A. Southerland, Alex Barrett
outcome_summary: This qualitative multi-case study examines science and mathematics preservice teachers’ perceptions and experiences of practicing dialogic teaching with generative AI-powered virtual students in the EVETeach virtual reality simulation. The study uses a purposive sample of 34 preservice secondary teachers (U.S.-based) who completed a 2-hour Zoom session with text-based interaction, followed by semi-structured interviews; data sources included recorded videos, field notes, dialogue logs, and interviews. Analysis employed inductive thematic coding with within-case thematic analysis and cross-case comparisons, reporting interrater reliability (Cohen’s kappa κ = 0.82) and 100% interrater agreement after peer debriefing. Results are reported as four qualitative themes (engagement dynamics; authenticity/variances; pedagogical sandbox; supplement to teacher preparation) and descriptive frequencies of dialogic talk moves (e.g., open-ended questions n = 509; dialogic talk moves overall n = 1,274). Limitations include the qualitative design (findings as trends), subject-area specificity (science/math), and that the think-aloud protocol may affect perceived realism.

title: A systematic review of the use of log-based process data in computer-based assessments
authors: Surina He, Ying Cui
outcome_summary: This PRISMA systematic review synthesizes how log-based process data are used in computer-based assessments, focusing on data-driven reasoning within an evidence-centered design perspective. Across 330 included peer-reviewed publications (searched in Nov 2022 and Mar 2024; records published through Dec 31, 2023), the review reports trends in adoption and summarizes common process indicators: time indicators (used in 82% of studies), count indicators (32%), and sequence indicators (25%), with the most common indicator usage being time-only (51%). It also categorizes how process indicators infer latent constructs into four inferential levels, with level 4 (36%) most prevalent, and notes that many level-4 studies focus on latent response speed via log-normal response time models. The review does not estimate predictive models or report ML performance metrics because it does not conduct original student-level analysis; instead, it aggregates reported constructs (e.g., cheating, rapid guessing, persistence, planning, speed, latent engagement) and discusses benefits, challenges, and recommendations, including validity grounding and fairness/bias concerns in advanced AI methods.

title: What students learn depends on what we teach: Curriculum content coverage and student achievement in mathematics and science
authors: Marlen Holtmann, Alec I. Kennedy, Rolf Strietholt
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS cycles 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019, and 2023 to model how intended curriculum content coverage relates to attained student achievement in mathematics and science for Grades 4 and 8. The attained curriculum is constructed from TIMSS domain achievement using plausible values (scaled to a mean of 500, SD=100) and aggregated to country-by-domain averages with sampling weights. The authors estimate fixed-effects mediation models (country and domain fixed effects) and synthesize cycle-specific coefficients via a one-step meta-analytic procedure. Across subjects and grades, the synthesized total effect of intended coverage is positive (e.g., γ=0.19, s.e.=0.01, p<.001), with implemented coverage showing a significant mediation pathway (indirect effect αβ=0.07, s.e.=0.01, Sobel Z=10.04, p<.001). Limitations include reliance on expert and teacher questionnaire measures for intended/implemented coverage, low but nonzero missingness handled by listwise deletion, and observational identification that cannot fully rule out reverse causality within cycles.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2003-2023 Grade 4 Mathematics (domain-specific achievement; attained curriculum) | TIMSS 2003-2023 Grade 8 Mathematics (domain-specific achievement; attained curriculum) | TIMSS 2003-2023 Grade 4 Science (domain-specific achievement; attained curriculum) | TIMSS 2003-2023 Grade 8 Science (domain-specific achievement; attained curriculum)
all_target_variables: Attained curriculum (domain achievement, PV-based country average)

title: Investigating preservice teachers’ emotions and dialogic teaching practices in simulation-based learning with artificial intelligence-powered virtual student agents
authors: Chih-Pu Dai, Fengfeng Ke, Nuodi Zhang, Alex Barrett, Luke West, Saptarshi Bhowmik, Sherry A. Southerland, Xin Yuan
outcome_summary: This open-access Learning and Instruction study examined preservice teachers’ emotions and dialogic talk during VR-supported simulation-based teaching with AI-powered virtual student agents (EVETeach). The quantitative component used association rule mining with the Apriori algorithm on sentence-level coded interaction data, extracting co-occurrence patterns among emotion states (e.g., neutral, joy, satisfaction, anxiety/uncertainty) and dialogic talk moves (e.g., explores, probes, orchestrates) across initiation vs consensus-building stages. The study reports descriptive frequencies (e.g., neutral n=404; joy n=371; satisfaction n=311; anxiety/uncertainty n=141) and association-rule strength using support and lift (e.g., satisfaction/frustration→excitement lift=1.99; builds-on-ideas/counter-argues→orchestrates lift=1.30). No PV-based achievement outcomes, survey weights, or missing-data imputation/deletion procedures are described, and the association-rule approach cannot establish causal effects or temporal dynamics beyond co-occurrence. The findings nonetheless suggest design levers for AI virtual students that elicit progress and support idea uptake to promote emotionally balanced, ambitious dialogic teaching.
all_datasets_used: EVETeach VR simulation with AI-powered virtual students (TIMSS/AST fine-tuning; sentence-level coded emotions) | EVETeach VR simulation with AI-powered virtual students (TIMSS/AST fine-tuning; sentence-level coded dialogic talk moves)
all_target_variables: Preservice teachers’ emotions (coded states) | Dialogic teacher talk patterns (coded talk moves by stage)

title: How effective is the professional development in which teachers typically participate? Quasi-experimental analyses of effects on student achievement based on TIMSS 2003-2019
authors: Nils Kirsten, Johan Lindvall, Anders Ryve, et al.
outcome_summary: The study uses TIMSS 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, and 2019 nationally representative data from OECD countries, analyzing grade 4 and grade 8 mathematics and science achievement in a within-student between-subjects fixed-effects design. Teachers’ typical PD participation is measured from teacher questionnaires across five PD topics (content, pedagogy, curriculum, IT integration, assessment), recoded into dummy indicators and summarized as a latent PD participation variable. Student achievement is modeled using TIMSS plausible values (five PVs per student) with TYPE=IMPUTATION in Mplus, and missing data are handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML). Across cycles, the main model estimates PD effects close to zero and slightly negative: for grade 4, about -0.017 SD (p=0.002), and for grade 8, about -0.020 SD (p=0.010) after including student fixed effects and controls. The paper also finds heterogeneity, with negative effects concentrated among higher-achieving students, and it emphasizes that these are quasi-experimental observational estimates where causality cannot be fully guaranteed despite robustness checks.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2003-2019 (pooled) Grade 4 Mathematics and Science | TIMSS 2003-2019 (pooled) Grade 8 Mathematics and Science

title: Opportunity to learn: A comparison of analytical approaches and relations to student achievement
authors: Victoria Rolfe, Nani Teig
outcome_summary: This study compares four operationalizations of opportunity to learn (OTL) as content coverage—composite, domain-general, domain-specific, and a latent-variable factor—using TIMSS 2015 and 2019 microdata for Grade 4 mathematics and science in Norway and Sweden. Achievement is modeled with five plausible values per score, incorporated in Mplus via TYPE=IMPUTATION, and the analysis uses two-level SEM with student and classroom-level weights to reflect the nested sampling structure. Across 32 country-by-subject-by-cycle models, SES (books at home) is consistently a significant predictor at both student and classroom levels, while OTL’s explanatory power is highly context-dependent: composite OTL is significant for Norway mathematics (2015/2019), domain-specific links are strongest when content and achievement domains align, and the latent OTL factor yields the most consistent significant results, including OTL significantly predicting science achievement in Sweden 2019. Reported model fit is summarized via classroom-level R² (Table 3), but the paper does not provide a missing-data method beyond marking derived content-coverage variables as missing when teacher subdomain responses are insufficient, limiting transparency about missingness handling.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics (Norway) | TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Science (Norway) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics (Sweden) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Science (Sweden)

title: Age differences in bullying victimisation and perpetration: Evidence from cross-cultural surveys
outcome_summary: This paper is a cross-cultural synthesis of age-trend patterns in bullying victimisation and perpetration using three large-scale surveys: HBSC (1993/94–2017/18; ages 11/13/15), EU Kids Online (2010 and 2018/19; ages 9–16, with 9–10 dropped for comparability), and TIMSS (2011/2015/2019; grades 4 and 8). The authors do not train machine-learning models; instead, they classify each country’s age pattern into U/D/P/V/S categories and test gender differences in trend distributions using chi-square tests in SPSS. Across HBSC and TIMSS, victimisation most often shows a downward (D) trend (e.g., HBSC: 334/504 or 66% D; TIMSS: 145/185 or 78% D), while perpetration shows more mixed patterns (HBSC: predominant P and U; EUKO: predominantly U). Cyberbullying trends are more complex, with greater variability across surveys and genders. Limitations include reliance on self-report, restricted age range (~10–16), and comparability issues across survey procedures; the study uses trends rather than exact prevalence to mitigate these biases.

title: Peer Effects in Education: Theoretical Synthesis of Frame Factor Theory and Opportunity to Learn using TIMSS 2011
outcome_summary: The study analyzes Swedish TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 mathematics using student plausible values (BSMMATH01–05) and teacher/student survey items to test a synthesized Frame Factor Theory (FFT) and Opportunity to Learn (OTL) model of peer effects. The analytic sample is 3,928 students in 207 classes after excluding outlier class sizes (<10 or >40 students) and classes with more than one mathematics teacher; teacher limitation indicators with extensive missingness (lack of nutrition; lack of sleep) are omitted from the latent construct. The authors estimate a multilevel structural equation model (M-SEM) in Mplus with MLR and handle plausible values by running the model across each PV and reporting mean effects. Results show that the latent “Limitations on instruction” is strongly negatively related to mathematics achievement (standardized about -0.54 to -0.65, p < .05), while “Advanced content coverage” has a small positive relation (about 0.15–0.19, p < .05). Because the design is cross-sectional and the paper does not fully specify non-PV missing-data handling, causal claims are limited and should be interpreted as theory-consistent evidence rather than causal proof.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2011 Sweden Grade 8 Mathematics (BSMMATH01–05 plausible values)

title: From teacher quality to teaching quality: Instructional productivity and teaching practices
authors: S. Briole
outcome_summary: The paper uses TIMSS 2011 8th-grade mathematics data to estimate the causal effect of topic-specific instructional time on student math achievement in the U.S. (main sample: 7,258 students) and to replicate internationally across 43 countries (587,100 observations). The identification strategy exploits within-student variation across math topics taught by the same teacher and uses TIMSS’s matrix sampling and teacher-reported coverage to focus on taught subtopics, with a falsification test on untaught subtopics showing no instructional-time effect. The main U.S. results indicate that one additional weekly hour of instructional time devoted to a math topic increases math test scores by about 4.3% of a standard deviation on average, and the effect is moderated by teaching practices: moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of the Active Learning index increases instructional productivity (e.g., 0.030 to 0.056 SD per weekly hour). Internationally, instructional time effects are smaller (0.7%–1.0% SD per weekly hour) but active learning remains strongly and positively associated with instructional productivity. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight handling and missing-data rules beyond excluding observations with missing instructional time; moreover, the study is not an ML prediction paper, so ML metrics and PV handling are not applicable.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) — taught vs untaught subtopics falsification test | TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) — taught subtopics main estimates | TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) — heterogeneity by AL index percentile | TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (International sample, 43 countries)
all_target_variables: Math achievement (topic score) on untaught subtopics | Math achievement (topic score) on taught subtopics | Math achievement (topic score) productivity across Active Learning index

title: Linking the first, second and third IEA science studies
authors: Yuriko K. Sosa Paredes, Björn Andersson
outcome_summary: This paper is a linking and scaling methodology study that constructs a comparable long-term science achievement scale for upper primary students by linking the IEA First International Science Study (FISS, 1970–71), Second International Science Study (SISS, 1983–84), and TIMSS 1995. The authors first assess comparability by evaluating measurement invariance using item response theory (fitting 1-PL/2-PL/3-PL for binary items and a graded response model for TIMSS polytomous items), then identify anchor items via configural invariance, differential item functioning (DIF) testing, and partial invariance selection using traditional stepwise, alignment, and RMSD-based approaches. They then fit latent regression models with contextual questionnaire information (after contrast coding missingness and PCA dimensionality reduction) to generate five plausible values per system and compute weighted mean trends. The results show that linking is feasible but varies by system, with the number of anchor items and the strength of invariance differing across countries; the paper reports BIC-based model selection and fit indices for invariance, and presents adjusted mean science trends across selected grade/age groups. Limitations include sensitivity to population definition shifts (age-based to grade-based), incomplete comparability in some systems, and the fact that the output is a constructed scale rather than a predictive ML model with accuracy metrics.

title: The relationship between student engagement and dropout risk in early adolescence
authors: L. Szabó, A. Zsolnai, A. Fehérvári
outcome_summary: This study used a locally administered questionnaire study in Hungary (fall 2020/2021) with grade 7 students from 117 at-risk primary schools (initial N=5975; analytic N=3230 after listwise deletion; SEM/path models used N=2124 with complete cases). The dependent variable was students’ self-reported grade point average (GPA) from the previous academic year, treated as a continuous achievement indicator, while student engagement was measured using an adapted Student Engagement Instrument (SEI) covering affective, cognitive, behavioral, and academic engagement dimensions. The authors estimated associations using Pearson correlations and linear regression, and tested hypothesized mediation/hierarchy using structural equation modeling and path analysis (SPSS AMOS 27). In regression, the comprehensive model explained 41% of GPA variance (Adjusted R²=0.41), with the strongest effects from failure/grade repeat (B=-0.794) and homework completion (B=0.106), alongside maternal education (B=0.099). The hypothesized mediation model was not supported, with poor model fit (e.g., structural model CFI=0.47, RMSEA=0.17), and the authors note potential common-method variance due to self-report measures. Limitations include non-representative sampling of at-risk regions and no imputation for missing variables in SEM.

title: Research on personalized assessment Information of students’ mathematical competency based on cognitive diagnosis
authors: Xiaopeng Wu, Tianshu Xu, Rongxiu Wu
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 mathematics test items to construct a cognitive diagnosis assessment framework with eight basic mathematics attributes (NC, AT, SO, SR, PR, FI, WG, DE). The main empirical dataset is 4,733 Grade 8 students from four mainland China provinces/cities (Gansu, Guizhou, Guangdong, Shanghai), and the paper also compares attribute mastery against Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Hong Kong using the same TIMSS-based attribute framework. For model selection, the Mixed Model is chosen as best fit using AIC/BIC (AIC=14848.97; BIC=16228.02) and absolute fit RMSEA2=0.0348 (<0.05), with high reliability (Cronbach’s alpha=0.9079; attribute reliabilities mostly >0.91). The learning path covers 93.9% of students (4,444 included; 289 excluded) and suggests a dominant progression beginning with Spatial Reasoning. Limitations include the lack of reported missing-data handling and the fact that the “learning path/progression” is constructive and not yet validated in practice.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Mathematics (mainland China sample; four provinces/cities)
all_target_variables: Personalized diagnostic report recommendations (attribute mastery + follow-up sequences)

title: The paradoxical relationship between students’ non-cognitive factors and mathematics & science achievement using TIMSS 2015 dataset
authors: M. Chen, D. Hastedt
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2015 data to examine a “paradoxical” relationship between students’ non-cognitive factors (academic interest and confidence/self-concept) and mathematics/science achievement. The authors first test measurement invariance of eight non-cognitive scales using multiple-group categorical CFA in Mplus (configural → metric/equal slopes → scalar/equal thresholds) and report that all scales meet at least metric invariance, enabling cross-country correlational comparisons. Using IDB Analyzer to respect TIMSS complex survey design (weights, replication, and plausible values for achievement), they compute correlations at the individual level and at ecological levels (country and class). At the country level, student interest and confidence show positive associations with achievement at the individual level but negative aggregated correlations at the country level (e.g., for fourth graders’ Students Like Learning Mathematics: r_cnt level = −0.621, p < .01). At the class level, the paradox appears for some countries and more often for mathematics than science, while self-concept scales show no paradox. The authors emphasize that remaining analyses are correlational/descriptive rather than inferential, and they note that a multilevel modeling approach would better separate within- vs. between-level variation.

title: Motivational components in TIMSS 2015 and their effects on engaging teaching practices and mathematics performance
authors: M. Ivanova, M.P. Michaelides
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2015 Student Context Questionnaire (SCQ) data from the United States for both fourth and eighth grades, modeling motivational constructs (enjoyment, self-concept, and importance/usefulness where available) and engaging teaching as latent factors. Mathematics achievement is the dependent variable, estimated using TIMSS plausible values; the authors enter all five plausible values simultaneously in the SEM and report model fit using CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR under the WLSMV estimator. For Grade 8, the structural model fit was adequate (CFI=0.945, RMSEA=0.075, SRMR=0.061) and self-concept strongly predicted performance (β=0.785, p<.001), while enjoyment and engaging teaching showed negative conditional effects (E→β=-0.331; ET→β=-0.107). For Grade 4, fit was also adequate (CFI=0.962, RMSEA=0.064, SRMR=0.058) with an even stronger self-concept effect (β=0.881, p<.001) and negative conditional effects for enjoyment (β=-0.467) and engaging teaching (β=-0.050). The study explicitly does not apply sampling weights (model-based approach) and uses cross-sectional SEM, so the mediation results do not establish causal direction.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Mathematics (USA) — Student Context Questionnaire (SCQ) latent model with plausible values | TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics (USA) — Student Context Questionnaire (SCQ) latent model with plausible values

title: School bullying: Prevalence and variation in and between school systems in TIMSS 2015
authors: S. Johansson, S. Johansson et al.
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2015 bullying items to construct a continuous bullying scale (IRT partial credit scaling) for 4th-grade students across 50 participating school systems. The authors first describe bullying prevalence using a three-category index derived from the continuous scale, reporting that about 43% of students experience bullying at least monthly and about 15% experience bullying weekly on average across countries. They then estimate multilevel null models to quantify between-school variation via the intraclass correlation (ICC), and select eight countries with relatively high between-school bullying variation for covariate models. In separate multilevel models by country, students’ sense of school belonging shows significant negative associations with bullying both within and between schools in most countries (e.g., UAE belonging_w estimate 0.43, p<0.001; Bulgaria belonging_w estimate 0.40, p<0.001, where higher bullying-scale values indicate lower prevalence). The paper does not report a missing-data handling strategy and uses multilevel modeling rather than ML prediction, so results are correlational and not causal.

title: Teaching with confidence: How a skill-based intervention develops teacher self-efficacy and improves educational outcomes
authors: Danling Huang, Johnmarshall Reeve, Hye-Ryen Jang, Herbert W. Marsh, Theresa Dicke, Sung Hyeon Cheon
outcome_summary: This paper reports a year-long randomized controlled trial in South Korea with 91 full-time PE teachers (91 schools; 48 experimental, 43 control) who completed measures at three time points (T1 baseline in August, T2 end of fall, T3 end of spring). The intervention trained teachers in autonomy-supportive teaching (AST) through three face-to-face sessions, and the study modeled teacher self-efficacy (TSE for student engagement), job satisfaction, and class-average PE grades. Using structural equation modeling in Mplus with MLR and FIML for 1.1% missing data, the experimental condition significantly increased T2 TSE for student engagement (β = 0.46, p < .001). T2 TSE for student engagement then predicted T3 job satisfaction (β = 0.20, p = .002) and T3 student achievement (β = 0.24, p = .005), with full mediation of the intervention effects. Limitations include teacher-report measurement for AST and student achievement, modest sample size for SEM, and no PV-based ILSA achievement framework; thus, results are not directly generalizable beyond PE teachers in this training context.
all_datasets_used: South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention (T1/T2/T3) — PE teacher self-efficacy for student engagement | South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention (T1/T2/T3) — PE teacher job satisfaction | South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention (T1/T2/T3) — PE class-average student achievement
all_target_domains: Non-Cognitive / Process Output | Other / Unspecified | Composite / Multi-Domain
all_target_variables: T2 teacher self-efficacy (TSE) for student engagement | T3 job satisfaction | T3 student achievement (class-average PE grade)

title: School leadership matters: Evidence from TIMSS on teacher job satisfaction and students’ academic outcomes
authors: Nurullah Eryilmaz, Rolf Strietholt
outcome_summary: This open-access study uses TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 mathematics and science data across 45 countries to examine how school leadership support relates to teacher job satisfaction and student achievement. The authors estimate separate country-level regression models (RQ1: leadership → teacher job satisfaction; RQ2: leadership and teacher job satisfaction → student achievement) and then integrate country coefficients using random-effects meta-analysis (REML) in R. For teacher outcomes, leadership support shows small positive pooled associations with mathematics teacher job satisfaction (0.20, 95% CI [0.18, 0.22], I²=7%) and science teacher job satisfaction (0.22, 95% CI [0.19, 0.24], I²=74%). For student outcomes, leadership support is negatively associated with mathematics (−0.05, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.03]) and science achievement (−0.04, 95% CI [−0.05, −0.02]), while teacher job satisfaction is not significantly related to either domain. The analysis is cross-sectional, so causal direction cannot be established, and the manuscript does not report missing-data handling or the exact PV strategy used for achievement scoring.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Mathematics (teacher questionnaire; teacher job satisfaction outcome) | TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Science (teacher questionnaire; teacher job satisfaction outcome) | TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Mathematics (student achievement outcome) | TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Science (student achievement outcome)
all_target_variables: Mathematics teacher job satisfaction | Science teacher job satisfaction | Mathematics achievement | Science achievement

title: Mathematics Teachers’ Professional Traits that Affect Mathematical Achievement for Fourth-grade Students according to the TIMSS 2015 Results: A Comparative Study among Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, and Saudi Arabia
authors: M.S. Alharbi, M.S. Alharbi et al.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 mathematics achievement for students taught by mathematics teachers in Singapore, Hong Kong SAR, Japan, and Saudi Arabia (total N=14,971 students; Table 2). It links teacher questionnaire variables—gender, teaching experience, educational qualification, specialization, and professional development course exposure—and tests associations using two-way ANOVA with partial eta-squared (Tables 3–10) plus effect-size comparisons (Table 11). No machine learning models are trained; therefore, there are no ML metrics such as accuracy or AUC. Key results include significant teacher gender effects in Saudi Arabia (favoring female teachers) and Japan (favoring female teachers), and a significant gender-by-specialization interaction in Hong Kong. Limitations include the absence of reported plausible-value handling and missing-data strategy, and the use of ANOVA/associational inference rather than causal identification.
