all_target_variables: Mathematical achievement (fourth grade) | Mathematical achievement (fourth grade) variance explained by teacher traits

title: School belonging and math attitudes among high school students in advanced math
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics data for students in the final year of secondary school enrolled in advanced mathematics/science courses across nine countries/regions (France, Italy, Lebanon, Norway, Portugal, Russian Federation, Slovenia, Sweden, and the U.S.). It predicts two TIMSS attitude scales—Students Like Learning Advanced Mathematics (SLM) and Students Value Advanced Mathematics (SVM)—using multiple regression with sampling weights and jackknife replicate-based standard errors, while handling the TIMSS math achievement covariate via five plausible values (five regressions with averaged parameter estimates). Across all countries, students’ sense of school belonging is a statistically significant positive predictor of both SLM and SVM (each p < .001), with math achievement often the most important predictor by Pratt indices, except where belonging dominates (e.g., SVM in Italy, Lebanon, Norway, Russia). Gender shows significant main effects in some countries and limited moderation overall. Limitations include reliance on self-reported attitudes and a correlational design, so significant predictors should not be interpreted as causal effects.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics (final year secondary) — Students Like Learning Advanced Mathematics (SLM) scale | TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics (final year secondary) — Students Value Advanced Mathematics (SVM) scale
all_target_variables: Students Like Learning Advanced Mathematics (SLM) | Students Value Advanced Mathematics (SVM)

title: Instruction time and student achievement: The moderating role of teacher qualifications
authors: K. Wedel
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes TIMSS 2015 fourth-grade students in math and science (each student observed twice) using senate weights and a student fixed-effects design with subject fixed effects. The main outcome is standardized test scores measured as the first plausible value for math and science; the key regressor is weekly instruction time aggregated at the school-by-subject level. Across 39 countries (108,358 students; 216,716 subject observations), one additional hour of instruction time increases test scores by 0.030 standard deviations (p<0.01). The positive effect is moderated by teacher formal qualifications: interaction coefficients with instruction time range from 0.025 to 0.034 SD for PD, subject specialization, and major degree, while experience is not significant. The study also finds instruction time improves the like-subject attitude index (0.046–0.059 SD), with teacher qualifications showing little moderation for attitudes. Limitations include reliance on fixed-effects identification (not randomized assignment) and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics & Science (student test scores; first plausible value) | TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics & Science (motivation/attitude index; factor-analytic index)
all_target_variables: Test score (math/science plausible value, standardized) | Like subject index (motivation/attitude, standardized)

title: Re-imagining educational quality. The need for a multidimensional approach in evaluating educational quality through TIMSS data
authors: L. Appels, Sven De Maeyer, Peter Van Petegem
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 grade-four data to construct country clusters representing multidimensional educational quality configurations. The clustering is based on country-level aggregates of teacher quality (e.g., teacher specialization in education/mathematics and job satisfaction), instructional quality (instructional clarity in mathematics lessons), and quality of school life (principal-reported emphasis on academic success, students’ sense of belonging, and safety). The authors use the IEA IDB Analyzer to compute weighted country percentages/means and to incorporate TIMSS plausible values by averaging across the five plausible-value analyses. They exclude benchmarking systems and two participating systems (Austria and Belgium Flanders), while approximating missing data for Belgium using uncleaned Flemish datasets. Six clusters emerge (e.g., “aware valued content educators” and “focused detached doubtful specialists”), and the paper reports standardized z-score differences in intrinsic motivation, self-esteem, and mathematics achievement across clusters, but it does not train predictive ML models or report ML performance metrics such as accuracy or RMSE.

title: The effects of individual- and class-level achievement on attitudes towards mathematics: An analysis of Hong Kong students using TIMSS 2019
outcome_summary: This study analyzed TIMSS 2019 Hong Kong mathematics data for fourth- and eighth-graders (N = 2,947 and 3,265, respectively) to examine how individual and class-level achievement relate to attitudes toward mathematics (enjoyment, boredom, perceived value, and self-concept). Mathematics achievement was based on five TIMSS plausible values, operationalized as the mean across the five PVs, while attitudes were measured with TIMSS SLM/SCM/SVM items on 4-point Likert scales. Using two-level hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) with listwise deletion for missing data, the authors found a consistent pattern: individual achievement positively predicted all ATM constructs, whereas class average achievement negatively predicted self-concept, value, and enjoyment and positively predicted boredom. The big-fish-little-pond effect was stronger in eighth grade than fourth grade, and moderation showed that gender and individual performance further shaped the class-level achievement–boredom relationship. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight usage and the use of cross-sectional associations (no causal identification).
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics (Hong Kong) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Hong Kong)
all_target_variables: Self-concept (ATM scale) | Enjoyment (ATM scale) | Boredom (ATM scale) | Perceived value (ATM scale)

title: School closures, shelter-use and learning outcomes in the philippines: evidence from 2019 TIMSS
authors: Michael R.M. Abrigo, Kris A. Francisco, Kevin Carl P. Santos
outcome_summary: The study combines Grade 4 TIMSS 2019 Mathematics and Science assessment data from the Philippines with administrative measures of school-as-shelter use and typhoon warnings, then estimates the causal impact of school closure days using an instrumental-variables (two-stage least squares) framework. The analytic sample includes Grade 4 public school students in 156 public schools (with 9 schools used as shelters), and the outcomes are TIMSS IRT-scaled achievement scores handled via five plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules. In the full IV models, one additional school closure day reduces Mathematics by about 12.7 points and Science by about 14.1 points (≈0.12–0.14 SD), with inference based on Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument robust Wald tests. The paper reports robustness and falsification checks (including using 2019–2020 closures and alternative covariate sets), but the provided text does not specify a missing-data strategy beyond noting sample-size declines from nonresponse. No machine-learning predictive models are trained; results come from econometric IV estimation rather than ML.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Philippines Mathematics (plausible values) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Philippines Science (plausible values)
all_target_variables: Mathematics achievement (IV outcome) | Science achievement (IV outcome)

title: A latent profile analysis of achievement emotions and their relationships with students’ perceived teaching quality in mathematics classrooms
outcome_summary: This study used student questionnaire data from 76 mathematics classrooms in 11 secondary schools in Jiangsu, China (N=1900 collected; N=1762 after excluding outliers/invalid data and classrooms with size <5). It modeled the structure of perceived teaching quality with confirmatory factor analysis and then identified three latent profiles of seven achievement emotions (enjoyment, pride, relaxation, anxiety, shame, boredom, anger) using latent profile analysis; the three-profile solution was selected with entropy = .90 and improved fit over one- and two-profile models. To examine links between teaching and profile membership, the authors used R3STEP with a multilevel estimator (Estimator = MLR) and reported odds ratios from logistic regression. Students perceiving more teacher support, cognitive activation, classroom management, and mathematical richness were more likely to be in positive/medium profiles, whereas perceived errors and imprecision were associated with lower odds of positive/medium membership (e.g., OR=0.39 for P3 vs P1). Limitations include reliance on student perceptions, no reported missing-data strategy, and a cross-sectional design that cannot establish causality.
all_datasets_used: Student questionnaire in Jiangsu, China (secondary grades 7–9), mathematics classroom teaching perceptions and achievement emotions (7 emotions)
all_target_variables: Latent emotion profile membership (positive vs medium vs negative)

title: Profiles of teachers built on cognitive-activation teaching strategies and its effect on student’s outcomes in TIMSS 2019
authors: Z. Chen, D. Carrasco, A. Sandoval-Hernandez
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 grade 8 science data, combining teacher questionnaire indicators of general and science-specific inquiry-related cognitive-activation teaching with student science achievement estimated via IRT scaling and five plausible values. Teacher profiles are identified using structurally homogeneous multigroup latent class analysis across 14 countries, selecting a four-class solution based on AIC/BIC/SABIC and entropy. The subsequent two-level modeling compares student science achievement across the four teacher profiles while controlling for socioeconomic status using the Home Educational Resources scale aggregated at the classroom level, and it combines results across plausible values using Rubin’s rules. The reported evidence shows significant profile–achievement differences in some countries (notably for Low-Engagement Experimentalists in several contexts), but overall effects are described as modest and inconsistent across national settings. Limitations include reliance on teacher self-reports, classroom-based teacher sampling, and cross-sectional design, which restricts causal interpretation.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (teacher questionnaire + student science achievement PVs)

title: Construct validity of a mixed-worded mathematics confidence scale: Relations with mathematics achievement in TIMSS 2019
authors: Lena Asp
outcome_summary: This study uses Swedish Grade 4 TIMSS 2019 data to evaluate the construct validity of the “student confident in mathematics” mixed-worded scale and to test how different measurement operationalisations relate to mathematics achievement. The mathematics confidence scale comprises nine 4-point Likert items (four positive, five negative), with positively worded items recoded so higher values reflect higher confidence. Mathematics achievement is modeled using TIMSS plausible values (five PVs) within Mplus, and missing item responses are handled with full-information maximum likelihood (FIML). Across four structural equation models, the three-item positively worded operationalisation (items 1, 4, 6) showed good fit (CFI=.990, RMSEA=.053) and a significant positive association with achievement (β=0.322, p<.001). In contrast, the target-rotated bifactor ESEM model fit well (CFI=.994, RMSEA=.027) but yielded counterintuitive factor–achievement relations, suggesting method effects and caution against using the full mixed-worded scale without validation. The paper is cross-sectional, so causal claims are not supported.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Swedish Grade 4 Mathematics confidence scale (9 items; mixed-worded) and Mathematics achievement (PVs) | TIMSS 2019 Swedish Grade 4 Mathematics confidence scale (operationalisations B1–B4) and Mathematics achievement (PVs)
all_target_variables: Mathematics confidence construct validity (measurement model fit and factor structure) | Mathematics achievement (regressed on latent mathematics confidence operationalisations)

title: How classroom management and instructional clarity relate to students' academic emotions in Hong Kong and England: A multi-group analysis based on the control-value theory
authors: X. Chen, L. Lu
outcome_summary: This study analyzed TIMSS 2019 grade 8 mathematics data from Hong Kong and England, focusing on two teaching characteristics (classroom management and instructional clarity) and their links to two academic emotions (enjoyment and boredom) via cognitive appraisals (mathematics self-concept and value). The analytic sample was restricted to students with native-born parents (Hong Kong: 1146; England: 1981) and missing item responses (0.4%–2.9% per item) were handled with FIML in Mplus. The authors used a latent multi-group SEM with TYPE = COMPLEX and integrated results across five plausible values for mathematics achievement. Model fit was acceptable (e.g., χ2(792)=4004.398, RMSEA=0.051, CFI=0.930), and the model explained substantial variance in enjoyment (63.7% HK; 59.9% England) and boredom (21.7% HK; 43.3% England). Key limitations are that the study is not an ML predictive modeling paper (no ML algorithms or ML metrics like AUC/RMSE are reported) and that causal claims are not warranted from cross-sectional SEM paths.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Hong Kong vs England) — mathematics achievement (Plausible Values) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Hong Kong vs England) — enjoyment (Likert-scale latent factor) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Hong Kong vs England) — boredom (Likert-scale latent factor)
all_target_variables: Mathematics achievement (PVs) | Mathematics enjoyment | Mathematics boredom

title: The Relationship between the School Resources index; Gender; Age and Mathematics Achievement in TIMSS 2019 survey: Multilevel analysis
authors: Khalid Boulifaa, Abdelali Kaaouachib
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Moroccan fourth-grade students (7500 students across 257 schools) and models mathematics achievement using multilevel random-intercept/slope models. The dependent variable is the average mathematics achievement score derived from the five plausible values, and missing data are imputed using the R mice package. The empty model shows substantial between-school variation (ICC=0.3941; school-level variance explained 39.41%), justifying hierarchical modeling. In the full models, age is negatively associated with mathematics achievement (γ10=-4.84, p<.05), and girls outperform boys (γ20=-4.42, p<.05, girls as reference). Mathematics-specific resources (RMI) show a positive association (γ30=8.23, p<.05), while general school resources (GSR) are positive but only marginally significant (γ40=14.37, p=.08). The manuscript does not report the use of TIMSS sampling/replicate weights, so results may not be fully representative under complex survey design.

title: Teaching for near transfer: Is maths instruction aimed at schema formation and abstraction associated with pupils' ability to answer unfamiliar maths questions?
authors: J. Jerrim, Luis Alejandro Lopez-Agudo, Sam Sims, Oscar David Marcenaro-Gutierrez
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 mathematics data from 47 countries (280,083 pupils; 16,050 teachers) to test whether teacher-reported instructional practices aligned with schema formation and abstraction are associated with pupils’ near transfer to off-curriculum (unfamiliar) mathematics items. The primary outcome is percent correct on off-curriculum items, modeled with OLS specifications that include country fixed effects and TIMSS senate weights with Jackknife clustered standard errors by school. Across models, coefficients for the Teaching for transfer scale are small (generally <1 percentage point per 1 SD) and are not statistically significant at 5% once on-curriculum performance is controlled (R-squared up to 0.396). Near-transfer question-level logistic regressions similarly show that any initial association with unfamiliar items largely vanishes after controlling for within-domain familiar performance. The results are correlational and rely on self-reported teaching measures, so measurement error and the lack of causal identification limit policy conclusions.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics (pooled across 47 countries) — off-curriculum items | TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics (pooled across 47 countries) — item-level off-curriculum questions
all_target_variables: Novel/unfamiliar mathematics achievement (percent correct on off-curriculum items) | Near transfer within mathematics domains (probability of correct response to off-curriculum items)

title: Attitudes towards science in higher education: Validation of questionnaire among science teacher candidates and engineering students in Indonesia
authors: A.G.C. Wicaksono, E. Korom
outcome_summary: This Heliyon study validates an Indonesian version of the Attitude Towards Science Questionnaire (ATSQ) for higher-education students (second-year science teacher candidates and food engineering students) using psychometric methods rather than predictive machine learning. The sample includes 296 students from three universities in Central Java, Indonesia. Construct validity was evaluated with CFA (WLSMV) reporting CMIN/df = 2.61, CFI = 0.98, TLI = 0.98, RMSEA = 0.07, and SRMR = 0.04, and Rasch analysis showed good item fit (infit MNSQ minfit ≈ 0.99; outfit MNSQ moutfit ≈ 0.98) with acceptable dimensionality (average variance explained ≥ 30%). Reliability was high overall (Cronbach alpha = 0.95; McDonald omega = 0.95), while the anxiety/difficulty dimension showed lower item reliability (≈ 0.38). Group comparisons indicated no significant differences between science teacher candidates and engineering students across the four attitude dimensions and total attitude, with moderate overall attitude levels (mean ≈ 0.54 logit). Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling and the absence of ML prediction performance metrics; findings support questionnaire validity and descriptive group patterns within this sampled context.

title: Effectiveness of integrated STEM and problem-based learning in improving students’ conceptual understanding in science
authors: A.A. Funa
outcome_summary: This quasi-experimental one-group pretest–posttest study evaluated a six-week integrated STEM delivered through problem-based learning (I-STEM-PBL) for Grade 11 General Biology 1 (biomolecules) in a single public SHS classroom in the Philippines (n = 38). The outcome was a researcher-developed 20-item two-tier Meaningful Conceptual Understanding (MCU) test scored 0–20, with conceptual understanding operationalized across concept connections, explanation/justification, application/transfer, and misconception diagnosis. Students’ total MCU scores increased from M = 4.81 (SD = 2.00) to M = 6.14 (SD = 2.43), t(37) = 2.89, p = .007, Cohen’s d = 0.48, with a normalized gain g = 0.08; the Proteins & Enzymes facet improved significantly (t(37) = 2.65, p = .012) while Carbohydrates & Lipids did not (t(37) = 1.37, p = .180). The study reports no machine-learning models, no survey weights, and no missing-data handling procedure, so results are context-bound and causal claims are limited by the lack of random assignment.

title: The impact of science teaching strategies in the Arabic-speaking countries: A multilevel analysis of TIMSS 2019 data
authors: M. AlSalouli, M. AlGhamdi, F. AlShaya, A. AlMufti, B. Aldarwani, S. Pagliarani
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 science achievement in seven Arabic-speaking countries (Bahrain, Kuwait, Morocco, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates) using multilevel random-intercept and random-coefficient models. The outcome is the first plausible value for science performance, and the authors apply TIMSS complex-survey weights (student and classroom probability weights) in Stata. Results show substantial between-classroom variation (ICC≈0.486 in the empty model), with about half of classroom-level variance explained by classroom averages of home resources, attitudes, and bullying, and about 14% of individual-level variance explained by student-level variables. Teaching strategies are associated with achievement: emphasis on academic success and active instruction have positive coefficients, while emphasis on science investigation has a small negative coefficient. The moderation analysis indicates that emphasis on academic success strengthens the home-resources effect (≈+2.6 points per 1 SD, ~11% change), suggesting potential equity trade-offs. Limitations include lack of explicit missing-data handling reporting and the fact that the paper uses multilevel modeling rather than ML algorithms.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Science (first plausible value) | TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Science (random-coefficient interaction models)
all_target_variables: Science achievement (Plausible Values) | Science achievement moderation of home resources effect

title: School leadership support and socioeconomic status inequalities in mathematics and science achievement: Evidence from TIMSS 2019
authors: Nurullah Eryilmaz
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 mathematics and science achievement across 46 countries, using student and teacher questionnaire variables to estimate country-specific regression models and then combine the coefficients via random-effects meta-analysis. The key outcomes are mathematics and science scale scores, benchmarked to TIMSS international benchmarks (e.g., 625/550/475/400 for mathematics at Grade 8). Across countries, SES shows a strong positive association with both mathematics (β=0.28, p<0.001) and science (β=0.29, p<0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I²≈66%). Leadership support has a small negative direct association with mathematics (β=-0.0593, p<0.05) but no significant direct or moderating effects for science (leadership and Lead×SES p=0.10). The study uses listwise deletion for missing data and applies student weights via IDB Analyzer; however, it does not document a PV-combining procedure, and the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims about leadership reducing SES gaps.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics | TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science
all_target_variables: Mathematics achievement (scale score) | Science achievement (scale score)

title: Studying the comparability of student perceptions of teaching quality across 38 countries
authors: B. Senden, Bas Senden
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 student questionnaire data to assess cross-national comparability of two latent teaching-quality constructs—behavioral management and instructional clarity—across 38 countries (Singapore excluded). The authors first fit a two-factor measurement model and evaluate exact measurement invariance using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (configural, then metric, then scalar), reporting fit indices such as CFI/TLI/RMSEA/SRMR. Metric invariance was supported (ΔCFI=0.007; ΔRMSEA=0.002), but scalar invariance was not (ΔCFI=0.036; ΔRMSEA=0.015), implying that mean comparisons across countries are not justified under exact invariance. They then applied the alignment method for approximate invariance and used Monte Carlo simulation to assess reliability of factor-mean/variance recovery. Despite improved interpretability for instructional clarity, the alignment method did not substantially increase comparability for mean-score use; the authors caution that TIMSS international mean scores may be misleading for substantive cross-country interpretation.

title: Effect of school climate on fourth-grade students’ science achievement in the United Arab Emirates: Insights from the 2023 TIMSS Dataset
authors: Hassan Tairab, Latifa Alketbi, Ahmad Qablan, Laurent Gabriel Ndijuye, Maxwell Peprah Opoku
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2023 cycle data for fourth-grade students in the UAE (n=34,217; variable-specific Ns reported by questionnaire item) to examine whether school climate predicts science achievement. Science achievement was operationalized using TIMSS science plausible values (five PVs), and the authors imputed missing questionnaire data using the expectation maximization algorithm after confirming missingness was <10%. In hierarchical regression, the three school-climate domains—science classroom environment, social and emotional safety, and attitude toward science—explained 12% of variance in science achievement (R²=0.12), and adding demographics increased explained variance to 18% (R²=0.18). Social and emotional safety contributed most uniquely (β=0.25, p=.001), and absenteeism also showed a strong direct association (β=0.22, p=.001). The paper does not report the use of TIMSS complex-sampling weights, and the analysis is not ML-based despite being framed around prediction; therefore, results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal impacts.
all_target_variables: Science achievement (Plausible Values; total of five PVs)

title: Enhancing middle school science education: Evaluating a competency-based STEM training program for teachers
authors: Mohamed A. Shahat, Mahmoud M. Emam, Marwa Alhinai, Ehab M. Omara, Nabil Alhabsi, Khoula Alhosni, Amur Al-Yahmedi, Mohammed Al-Amri, Sameh S. Ismail, Sulaiman M. Al-Balushi
outcome_summary: This quasi-experimental teacher program evaluation used a scenario-based STEM Pedagogical Content Knowledge test (TPCKST) administered to 48 science teachers in Oman’s capital (grades 5–7 focus). Teachers were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=24) receiving a three-week competency-based STEM training program (engineering design, inquiry-based learning, collaborative workshops, and reflection) or a control group (n=24) continuing regular professional development without STEM integration emphasis. Baseline equivalence was supported by non-significant pretest differences across six TPCKST domains. Post-intervention, a two-way MANOVA showed a significant overall group effect (Wilks’ Lambda=0.52, F(6,39)=5.99, p<0.001, partial η2=0.48), with univariate ANOVAs indicating significant improvements for Q1–Q4 and Q6 (largest effect for correcting misconceptions, Q4: partial η2=0.28). The study reports no survey weights and does not document missing-data handling, so robustness and external validity beyond the capital-city sample should be interpreted cautiously.
all_datasets_used: Oman teacher PCK (TPCKST) pretest–posttest; grades 5–7 science; scenario-based STEM PCK test
all_target_variables: Teaching procedures (Q1) score | Teaching planning (Q2) score | Content knowledge (Q3) score | Methods of correcting misconceptions (Q4) score | Methods of teaching (Q5) score | Assessment (Q6) score

title: Optimizing automated scoring in ILSAs with prompt compression
authors: J.Y. Jung, Ummugul Bezirhan, Matthias von Davier
outcome_summary: This study evaluates GPT-4o-based automated scoring for five secured 1-point constructed-response items from digital PIRLS 2021 (Grade 4) across 27 countries and 29 languages, using a randomly selected 20% subset per country for feasibility. It compares a baseline prompt (original passages and original scoring guides) against three prompt-compression configurations: refined scoring guides (Model 1), passage summarization plus extractive SG refinement (Model 2), and passage summarization plus abstractive SG refinement (Model 3). Model 3 achieved the highest average accuracy (92.87%) with κ=0.80, closely approximating the baseline (92.62%, κ=0.82), while keeping hallucination rates low (0.12% vs 0.05% baseline). The paper also reports a major efficiency gain: average cost about $3.62 per item versus $15–17 for the baseline (~76% reduction). Limitations include heuristic hallucination detection, lack of reported missing-data handling, and no explicit use of PIRLS sampling/replicate weights for generalizing agreement rates.
all_datasets_used: PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading — 1-point Constructed-Response (CR) items (5 items; multilingual, 27 countries)

title: Using convolutional neural networks to automatically score eight TIMSS 2019 graphical response items
authors: Lillian Tyack, Lale Khorramdel, Matthias von Davier
outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether convolutional neural networks can automatically score TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items by matching CNN classifications to human rater score categories. The authors selected eight graphical items (five Grade 4 and three Grade 8, including one trichotomous partial-credit item) and trained CNNs on preprocessed student response images (greyscale conversion, contrast/saturation adjustment, resizing to fixed dimensions, and pixelation; plus augmentation for the trichotomous item). Performance was assessed using hold-out validation and five cross-validation splits, reporting exact match accuracy, loss, and F1-scores to address class imbalance. Across seven dichotomous items, best models achieved average accuracy ~99.37%–99.92% with F1 ~0.9948–0.9992, and for the trichotomous item ME62300 accuracy was ~97.99% with F1 ~0.9766. The paper does not report applying TIMSS survey weights and provides limited transparency on missing-data handling, so results primarily support scoring reliability rather than population-representative inference.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 4 Mathematics (Graphical response items; dichotomous scoring) | TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 Mathematics (Graphical response items; trichotomous scoring)
all_target_variables: CNN classification of graphical responses (incorrect vs correct/partial) | CNN classification of graphical responses (incorrect vs partial vs full credit)

title: The relationship between differences in students’ computer and information literacy and response times: an analysis of IEA-ICILS data
authors: Heldt, et al.
outcome_summary: This secondary analysis uses ICILS 2013 Grade 8 data from the Czech Republic (N=3066), Denmark (N=1767), and Germany (N=2225) to examine whether response times can explain differences in computer and information literacy (CIL). The authors standardize timing items (z-scores) and estimate two processing profiles (fast vs slow) via latent profile analysis, then compare CIL across profiles and within background groups (gender, cultural capital/books at home, parental occupational status/HISEI, and immigrant background via language at home and parents’ country of birth). In the Czech Republic and Germany, the fast profile is associated with higher CIL (Czech: 558 vs 541; Germany: 526 vs 510; p<0.05), while Denmark shows no significant profile differences. The study reports no predictive ML performance metrics and relies on descriptive profile comparisons; it also does not report missing-data handling, and Denmark’s sampling participation constraints may affect results. Overall, the findings support using process data (time-on-task effects) as an explanatory lens for competence gaps, with caution about methodological transparency and country-specific effects.
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2013 Grade 8 Computer and information literacy (CIL) — process data (response times)

title: Examination of Turkish Middle School STEM Teachers' Knowledge about Computational Thinking and Views
authors: Kaan Bati, M. I. Yetisir
outcome_summary: This study used an online teacher survey in Turkey (n=121) drawing adapted scales from the ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire and a translated QCT computational thinking test (17 items after removing two poorly functioning items). The analyses were descriptive and inferential (MANOVA for group differences and Pearson correlations), not machine-learning prediction; therefore, no PV handling, ML model metrics, or survey-weighted estimation are reported. Teachers’ QCT conceptual development scores (M=8.80, SD=2.9) did not significantly differ by educational discipline, teaching experience, graduation level, attending ICT–CT training, or ICT level in schools (Table 5). In contrast, teachers’ positive and negative ICT views differed significantly by ICT availability and ICT use in schools (e.g., positive views: ICT in schools F=4.073, p=0.018; negative views: using ICT in schools F=9.139, p=0.001). Correlational results showed collaboration and positive ICT views were associated with greater CT teaching emphasis (r=.501 and r=.489, p<.01), but the cross-sectional design prevents causal interpretation.

title: Finnish teachers' and students' programming motivation and their role in teaching and learning computational thinking
outcome_summary: This study analyzes ICILS 2018 Finland data for Grade 8 students’ computational thinking (CT) and teachers’ CT instruction emphasis, using complex survey sampling with sampling weights and jackknife repeated replication. Students completed two of five 30-minute CIL modules and two 25-minute CT modules; CT test scores were aggregated across CT tasks and reported using five plausible values, with analyses performed separately per plausible value and then averaged. The study reports weighted descriptive statistics and linear regression associations rather than machine-learning prediction. Key results show that teachers’ intrinsic programming motivation is positively related to their CT instruction emphasis (both international CT items and programming-specific items), while extrinsic motivation shows no significant effects for experienced teachers. For students, intrinsic motivation predicts higher CT scores only among those with prior programming experience, whereas extrinsic motivation predicts higher CT scores only among those without prior experience; effect sizes are modest and the design is correlational.
all_datasets_used: ICILS 2018 Finland Grade 8 (CT modules; plausible values) — Computational thinking (CT) test scores

title: How to improve the design of experimental studies in computing education: Evidence from the international assessments
authors: Mehmet Kara
outcome_summary: This paper uses ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 Grade 8 data to improve the design of cluster randomized trials (CRTs) for computer and information literacy (CIL) and computational thinking (CT). The authors fit two-level multilevel models (students nested in schools) to estimate intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), variance explained (R2) at level 1 and level 2, and minimum detectable effect sizes (MDES) under power assumptions (two-tailed test, power=0.80, balanced design P=0.50). They use five plausible values for CIL/CT and average variance components across plausible values, then compute MDES using Hedges and Hedberg’s method. Results show strong country specificity in ICCs (CIL ICC difference 0.44 in 2013 and 0.46 in 2018; CT ICC difference 0.38 in 2018) and that increasing the number of schools (J) substantially lowers MDES, while adding both student and school/teacher covariates (Model 3) yields the most precise effects. title: School leaders’ expectations of AI’s impact on students and teachers: Insights from ICILS 2023
authors: Nurullah Eryilmaz, Mehmet Sükrü Bellibas, Marcus Pietsch
outcome_summary: This study analyzes principals’ Likert-scale expectations about ChatGPT/AI impacts on students’ learning and teachers’ work using the optional principals’ generative-AI module in ICILS 2023. The analytic sample comprises N = 1134 schools nested within 12 countries (Chile, Cyprus, Denmark, Greece, Korea, Norway, Romania, Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Sweden, Taiwan, and Uruguay), using ICILS’ complex two-stage stratified cluster sampling weights for nationally representative cross-country comparisons. Rather than predicting an outcome with supervised ML, the authors estimate latent network models (LNMs) to examine how five pre-defined perception constructs interrelate, validate internal structure via Walktrap community detection, and assess robustness using the Partial Correlation Likelihood Test, then pool country-specific edges using random-effects meta-analytic aggregation (Fisher-z). They report model fit indices (e.g., CFI = 0.865 initially; improved CFI = 0.905 after removing low-loading items; RMSEA = 0.067 with 90% CI 0.064–0.070; SRMR = 0.084, improved to 0.070). The study finds coherent within-construct clustering and a central “increased workload” bridge linking student- and teacher-focused perceptions, with substantial cross-country stability for most edges (88.4% low heterogeneity). title: Towards the implementation of automated scoring in international large-scale assessments: Scalability and quality control
authors: Ji Yoon Jung, Lillian Tyack, Matthias von Davier
outcome_summary: This study evaluates automated scoring for three TIMSS 2023 science constructed-response items (Grade 4 Physical Science, Grade 4 Life Science, and Grade 8 Physics) across participating countries and 42 languages. Responses were dichotomously scored (correct=1/incorrect=0) and filtered to exclude aberrant responses and untranslated outputs; the remaining data were split 80:20 into training and test sets. The best-performing approach was MMT_ANNs, which combine Google Translate and ChatGPT-based translation with a feed-forward neural network trained on bag-of-words features. On the test set, MMT_ANNs achieved the highest agreement with human scoring across items, with average EA and Cohen’s kappa of 93.85% and 0.86, respectively, and the lowest standardized mean score differences (SMD) (average SMD=0). Limitations include reliance on bag-of-words (ignoring word order/context), sensitivity to translation quality for misspellings and low-resource languages, and lack of reported complex-survey weighting or a formal missing-data strategy beyond explicit exclusions.

title: Evolution of the computational science community: The dynamics of topics and collaborations in 24 years of ICCS and JoCS publications
authors: Lijing Luo, Klavdiya Bochenina, Tesfamariam M. Abuhay, Nachyn Dorzhu, George Kampis, Sergey Kovalchuk, Valeria Krzhizhanovskaya, Maciej Paszynski, Clélia de Mulatier, Jack Dongarra, Peter M.A. Sloot
outcome_summary: This paper is a bibliometric/science-of-science study rather than an ILSA-based predictive ML study: it analyzes the evolution of computational science topics and collaboration networks using ICCS proceedings (2001–2009 & 2010–2017 & 2018–2024) and JoCS journal articles (2010–2023). The authors build a discipline classification library (15 first-level disciplines, 213 second-level disciplines) and represent papers with TF-IDF vectors, then compute cosine similarity to assign discipline relevance and derive standardized popularity scores normalized per 100 papers per year. They report validation of the topic-discovery approach via Pearson correlations between topic assignments under different numbers of selected disciplines (e.g., Table 3), and they characterize network structure using scale-free distribution fits, clustering coefficients, and edge-weighted co-occurrence networks (e.g., Tables 6–8). No student-level outcomes, survey weights, PVs, or supervised ML models are trained; therefore, there are no predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) for a target variable.

title: Asymptotic Parallel Solver in Compressible DNS Code
authors: Mitsuo Yokokawa, Taiki Matsumoto, Ryo Takegami, Yukiya Sugiura, Naoki Watanabe, Yoshiki Sakurai, Takashi Ishihara, Kazuhiko Komatsu, Hiroaki Kobayashi
outcome_summary: This paper proposes an asymptotic parallel linear solver for reduced matrices arising from an eighth-order compact finite-difference scheme used inside a direct numerical simulation (DNS) code for compressible isothermal turbulence. The computational domain is a cube with periodic boundary conditions, discretized on a uniform N×N×N grid; spatial derivatives are computed using CD8 for convection terms and FD8 for viscous terms. The solver is applied when the number of grid points per subdomain in a Cartesian direction satisfies M≥64, otherwise a normal Mattor-based parallel solver is used. Performance is evaluated on the SX-Aurora TSUBASA vector supercomputer using MPI cuboid decomposition and halo exchange. Reported results include a 1.7× speedup of the optimized code versus the original for a DNS with 2048^3 grid points, and an approximately 4-fold speedup of the asymptotic solver compared to the Mattor solver for a single solver call. The study also reports excellent weak scalability, with communication overhead increasing for larger MPI decompositions but remaining manageable.

title: Stališča osmošolcev v Sloveniji o vlogi vere pri vplivu na družbo: analiza podatkov ICCS
authors: Eva Klemenčič Mirazchiyski, Plamen V. Mirazchiyski
outcome_summary: This paper reports secondary analyses of ICCS 2016 student questionnaire data focused on 8th graders in Slovenia (N = 2844). The reported results are correlation-based (Spearman and Pearson), showing a positive association between religious-service attendance and S_RELINF (ρ = 0.53, SE = 0.02, p < 0.001), weak but significant associations with volunteering (ρ = 0.11 and 0.14, both p < 0.001), and weak associations with future political participation (ρ = 0.12, p < 0.001; ρ = 0.05, p = 0.033). title: The claim that personality is more important than intelligence in predicting important life outcomes has been greatly exaggerated
authors: C. Zisman, Y. Ganzach
outcome_summary: This paper compares the predictive validity of intelligence versus Big Five personality for educational and occupational success using six representative datasets: NLSY79, NLSY97, ADD Health, MIDUS, WLS, and OECD PIAAC 2012 (with Germany’s PIAAC-L follow-up for Big Five traits). The authors do not apply machine learning; instead, they compute squared correlations (R²) and regression R² to quantify how much variance in outcomes is explained by intelligence versus personality, reporting ratios of R² as a relative-validity metric. title: Subtask analysis of process data through a predictive model
authors: Zhi Wang, Xueying Tang, Jingchen Liu, Zhiliang Ying
outcome_summary: This paper proposes a computationally efficient exploratory method for analyzing PIAAC 2012 PSTRE process-log data by segmenting long action sequences into shorter “subtasks.” The pipeline first trains a GRU-based action prediction model (with a multinomial logistic layer) to estimate next-action uncertainty, then computes Shannon entropy over time and uses an entropy-depth criterion (λ) to identify U-shaped entropy segments as subprocess boundaries. Subprocesses are labeled as subtasks via k-means clustering on action-frequency profiles, producing interpretable subtask sequences. In simulations (N=5000, M=26), the proposed SIP substantially outperforms HMM and eHMM on transition estimation metrics (Precision/Recall/Precision+/Recall+/Overlap), and in the PIAAC case study it identifies meaningful subtasks for 9 of 14 items. For item U19a, SEARCH strategies show higher correctness (91.6%) than SORT-only strategies (83.1%), and subtask-sequence features improve out-of-sample prediction of literacy, numeracy, and age versus a baseline. Limitations include lack of reported survey-weight usage and missing-data handling, and the method is designed for exploratory interpretation rather than causal inference.

title: Selecting or rewarding teachers? International evidence from primary schools
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes PIRLS Grade 4 reading literacy microdata from four waves (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016) pooled across 70 country/state/region entities, linking classes to the teacher’s year of entry into the profession. The outcome is PIRLS standardized reading achievement, and the empirical strategy estimates an educational production function with country, wave, and country×wave fixed effects, clustering standard errors at the country and year of teacher hiring. In the baseline (Table 5), recruitment reforms are positively and significantly associated with student achievement (e.g., 3.33*** in the full sample; 2.53** in the restricted OECD sample), while working-conditions reforms show a negative and significant association (−4.82***; −2.38**). Salary reforms are not significant in baseline specifications, and retirement reforms are not significant. For a subset of OECD countries with pay data, the teacher pay index relative to GDP is positive and significant (24.95***), suggesting compensation matters for attracting teacher quality, but not necessarily through the reform indicators alone. Limitations include observational identification, measurement error in NATLEX-based reform proxies, and incomplete documentation of survey-weight usage.

title: Continuation Ratio Model for Polytomous Responses with Censored Like Latent Classes
authors: Diego Carrasco, David Torres Irribarra, Jorge González
outcome_summary: This chapter proposes a mixture continuation ratio response model (M-CRM) to handle polytomous bullying victimization responses with a censored-like latent distribution, motivated by the high accumulation of “not at all” responses across bullying items in ICCS 2016. The empirical application uses ICCS 2016 bullying items (bul1–bul6) from five Latin American countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru) and expands each polytomous item into continuation-ratio pseudo-items for modeling. The authors fit the model in Mplus using pseudo maximum likelihood with complex sampling adjustments (WEIGHT=ws, CLUSTER=id_j, STRATIFICATION=id_s) and select the number of latent classes using the Vuong–Lo–Mendell–Rubin likelihood ratio test (favoring three classes). The results are used to describe item-side bullying event frequencies, person-side bullying risk profiles via mixture classes, and class differences in expected response proportions, while also enabling estimation of population prevalence of bullying events. The chapter emphasizes modeling advantages over sum-score approaches, but it does not report predictive ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) in the provided excerpt.

Results show positive effects in 18 countries (2SLS effects reported as roughly 0.64 SD to 3.13 SD) and null effects in 16 countries, while the instrument is weak in French-speaking Belgium, Canada, France, Ireland, and Northern Ireland based on Stock and Yogo (2005). The authors compare an IRTree Skip model (a multidimensional IRT framework that jointly estimates ability and skipping propensity) against a Rasch reference model using PIRLS’s standard missing-response handling (skipped items treated as incorrect for ability estimation; not-reached items treated as not administered). title: SURVEYHLM: Multilevel Analysis with Large-Scale Assessment Data in SAS
outcome_summary: This article is a methodology paper that develops the SAS macro SURVEYHLM for multilevel analysis of large-scale assessment (LSA) data, focusing on technical requirements such as plausible values, complex sampling weights, and replication-based standard errors. It explains that LSA datasets (e.g., TIMSS, PIRLS, PISA) use matrix-sampling designs and IRT-based scaling, producing plausible values that can be used as dependent variables; it also describes how ordinal benchmark/proficiency outcomes can be modeled via appropriate GLMM distribution/link choices. The paper’s worked examples use TIMSS 2015 Dutch fourth-grade mathematics achievement (continuous plausible values) and PIRLS 2011 German reading achievement (benchmark-based categorical outcomes), demonstrating two-level and three-level multilevel specifications and alternative covariance structures. It reports example model outputs including fit statistics and fixed-effect significance tests, but it does not frame the work as machine-learning prediction with accuracy/AUC-style metrics. The key implication is that secondary analysts need software that correctly combines PV handling (Rubin’s rules) with multilevel modeling and LSA sampling/replication design features to avoid biased standard errors and incorrect inference.

title: Importance of students’ social resources for their academic achievement and well-being in elementary school
authors: Jakob Schwerter, J. Schwerter et al.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes representative German PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 data (N=3959) to examine how two social interaction resources—experienced bullying and perceived teacher support—relate to academic track recommendation (a dichotomous proxy for achievement) and enjoyment of school (a standardized well-being measure). Using a double machine learning approach for variable selection (stacked adaptive LASSO across 50 multiple imputations) and OLS with school-clustered robust standard errors, the authors compare baseline and “many-worlds” sensitivity models that expand controls and apply PCA-based dimensionality reduction. For academic track recommendation, the bullying effect shrank from β=-0.062 (Model 1) to β=-0.011 (Model 3) and became non-significant in richer specifications, while teacher support also attenuated. For enjoyment of school, both bullying (e.g., β=-0.185 in Model 3) and teacher support (β=0.361 in Model 3) remained significant across models, with R2 ranging roughly from 0.406 to 0.544. Limitations include observational design, use of track recommendation rather than standardized test scores, and reliance on proxy well-being components (positive affect only).

title: Synergistic effects of instruction and affect factors on high- and low-ability disparities in elementary students’ reading literacy
authors: Jie Hu, J. Chen
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading literacy for 9,748 students from seven English- and Chinese-speaking education systems, restricting the sample to binary high vs low achievers using PIRLS benchmarks (advanced ≥625 vs intermediate <475). It trains four supervised ML classifiers—logistic regression, linear SVM, decision tree, and XGBoost—separately for English-speaking and Chinese-speaking system groups, using a 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation and grid search for tuning. Missing values from invalid Likert codes were imputed using nearest-neighbor averaging after removing cases with high missingness; features were normalized to [0,1] but left unscaled for tree-based models. Across both system groups, XGBoost achieved the best testing performance (English: Accuracy 88.19%, F-score 88.19%; Chinese: Accuracy 88.01%, Recall 91.72%). The most influential predictors were affective constructs—especially reading self-concepts—suggesting that improving students’ reading confidence and related beliefs may be central to reducing high–low disparities, though the approach is predictive (not causal) and does not report complex survey weighting.

file_name: Imputing PIRLS s home socioeconomic status from students  and schools  questionnaire data  a simulation with MICE.pdf
title: Imputing PIRLS’s home socioeconomic status from students’ and schools’ questionnaire data: a simulat
authors: João Marôco, Matthias von Davier
outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether PIRLS 2021 Home Socioeconomic Status (HSES) can be imputed from student and school questionnaire data using MICE, focusing on how accuracy changes under different missingness conditions. Using a simulation sample of 5,500 students drawn from PIRLS 2021 (with complete predictor records), the authors compare six MICE-based imputation algorithms (PMM, weighted PMM, CART, Random Forest, Bayesian linear regression, and Lasso) and assess recovery using Pearson correlation and explained variance. Under MCAR seeded only in HSES (RQ1), correlation drops from about r≈0.6 (≈36% explained variance) at 10% missingness to below r<0.4 (≈16%) at 60% missingness, with PMM best at low missingness but showing shrinkage (overestimating low HSES and underestimating high HSES). When predictors are also missing (RQ2), correlations decline to around 0.45 at 60% missingness for most methods, while Random Forest performs worse (~0.32, SE=0.008). Across countries/territories (RQ3), recovery ranges from <0.2 to ~0.7 at 10% MCAR, and weighted PMM using totwgt improves stability, highlighting that distributional non-normality and questionnaire nonresponse patterns limit imputation reliability. The paper uses Rasch reading scores rather than PIRLS plausible values for reading, and it simulates MCAR/MNAR-like scenarios rather than estimating causal effects.

title: ICT, Motivation, and Academic Performance in Elementary Education: Meta-analysis, Literature Review, and State of the Art
authors: Francisco Ábalos-Aguilera, Luis M. Romero-Rodríguez, César Bernal Bravo
outcome_summary: This paper synthesizes evidence (2019–2023) on how ICT use in elementary/primary education relates to student motivation/engagement and academic performance. It follows PRISMA-based procedures and uses Scopus and Web of Science searches, yielding 19 eligible studies after screening and full-text eligibility checks. The results are reported as a predominance of positive associations in quasi-experimental studies (n=10) between digital resources, engagement, and academic performance, with stronger benefits when ICT is paired with active methodologies such as gamification, flipped classroom, or project-based learning. The review also highlights implementation conditions—digital resource design, teacher age, and lack of effective training—as determinants of whether ICT adoption translates into improved outcomes. Limitations include the small number of included studies and heterogeneity across interventions and measures, so effect sizes and causal claims cannot be directly inferred from this synthesis.

title: The Dual Role of Digital Self-Efficacy in Reading Engagement from a Nonlinear Dynamics Perspective
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade data from Saudi Arabia (N=4386) to model reading engagement as a nonlinear outcome using the cusp catastrophe model in R. Reading engagement is measured with nine PIRLS questionnaire items on a 4-point scale, and digital self-efficacy and liking reading are each measured via PIRLS scales; participants with fewer than two digital self-efficacy responses were deleted from measurement. The cusp model was strongly favored over a linear and logistic comparison using information criteria (AIC 8392.269 for cusp vs 13,993.596 for linear) and a nested-model chi-square difference test (χ2(2)=5605.000, p<0.001). The bifurcation term for digital self-efficacy was significant (b1=0.224, p<0.001), and the outcome distribution supported the cusp assumption of multimodality (Hartigan D=0.974, p<0.001; six modes). The paper does not report a missing-data strategy for engagement/self-efficacy items and does not specify whether PIRLS sampling weights were applied in the cusp estimation, limiting generalizability of effect magnitudes.
all_datasets_used: PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 Reading (Saudi Arabia) — Reading engagement scale

title: Development of the reading literacy questionnaire for EFL learners at primary schools
authors: Li W, Kang S, Shao Y
outcome_summary: This paper is not an ILSA/PISA-style predictive ML study; it develops and validates a self-report English Reading Literacy Questionnaire (ERLQ) for EFL learners in primary schools. Using a two-stage sample of Chinese Grade 3–6 students (Stage 1: N=420 split into two groups of 210 for EFA and CFA; Stage 2: N=364 for criterion validation), the authors used psychometric validation procedures rather than machine learning prediction. For the initial 21-item version, item analysis showed significant item discrimination (item-total correlations r=0.591 to 0.852, p<0.01), and EFA led to a revised 14-item, three-dimension structure with cumulative explained variance of 59.876%. For the revised instrument, CFA fit indices were acceptable (CMIN/DF=1.508, GFI=0.935, AGFI=0.907, NFI=0.909, IFI=0.968, RMSEA=0.049), reliability was high (Cronbach’s alpha=0.904), and criterion validity was strong (Pearson r=0.871, p<0.01). Limitations include a relatively small, localized sample and no reported missing-data handling or survey-weighting strategy.

title: EM-JWLJ210074 388..402
outcome_summary: The study uses PIAAC first-cycle microdata (2011–2012, 2014–2015, 2017–2018) and extracts a working subsample of 122,897 adults aged 16–65 who answered all ILB-related items. It first re-estimates the measurement structure of ILBs and antecedents using EFA and CFA, selecting an 18-item, four-factor model (after excluding two items) with reported fit indices (e.g., CFA for the 18-item model: CFI=0.94, TLI=0.93, RMSEA=0.05, SRMR=0.04). For prediction, it applies hierarchical multiple regression: R² increases from 0.093 (controls only) to 0.212 after adding the three antecedent factors, with Interaction in the workplace showing the largest standardized effect (b≈0.29, p<0.001) and Readiness to learn also significant (b≈0.26, p<0.001). The paper does not report survey-weight usage or missing-data handling, and the analysis is not a machine-learning predictive pipeline; therefore, results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal impacts.

title: A cross‑country study of skills and unemployment flows
authors: D. Stijepic
outcome_summary: This paper uses OECD’s Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to study how adult cognitive skills relate to unemployment flows across 37 countries. The analytic sample is restricted to adults aged 25–54 who are classified as unemployed or in paid work, and the author estimates entry and exit rates into unemployment using a maximum-likelihood framework with country fixed effects by PIAAC round; sampling weights are used and pooled specifications give equal weight to each country. At the country level, numeracy shows a strong unconditional correlation with the log-risk-ratio of exiting to entering unemployment (0.68), and in the baseline country-level SUR estimates the implied exit-to-entry risk-ratio effect of numeracy is 1.969*** (Table 1 spec 1). However, the relationship does not extend to seven skill-scarce economies (exit-entry coefficient -0.273, not significant in Table 2 spec 1). The study does not use machine learning models; therefore, “ML” metrics are not applicable, and causal interpretation depends on the instrumental-variable design rather than on predictive modeling.

title: Work-in-Progress: Implementing and Evaluating a Competency-Oriented Assessment in an Innovative Application-Oriented Course of Mechanical Engineering
authors: Iris Groß, Alexandra Reher, Leona Brust, Doerthe Vieten
outcome_summary: This work-in-progress paper presents a competency-oriented assessment design for an advanced mechanical engineering course, evaluated through Teaching Analysis Poll (TAP) and student questionnaires. The assessment consists of a written test (30%) and a group presentation of practical results (70%), with grading based on weighted scoring of requirements aligned to intended competencies. The authors report prior evidence from earlier course evaluations (e.g., self-estimated ability shifts from low to high after the course) and anticipate that the new evaluation will show higher subjective competence gains and a stronger increase in “scientific self-image and professionalism.” No ILSA program/cycle, achievement domain, or PV-based outcome is used; therefore, no PV handling or ML predictive performance metrics are applicable. The paper does not provide final end-of-semester questionnaire results yet (planned for August), and it does not document missing-data procedures, limiting the strength of any conclusions.

file_name: Review of Income and Wealth - 2024 - Cammeraat - Organizational Capital  Skills and Productivity.pdf
title: Organizational Capital, Skills and Productivity
authors: Emile Cammeraat
outcome_summary: The paper links organizational capital (OC) and workforce skills to industry-level labor productivity using OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) skill indicators (numeracy plus task-based ICT and STEM measures) aggregated to country–industry cells. It includes 21 countries (AUT, BEL, CAN, CZE, DEU, DNK, EST, FIN, FRA, GBR, GRC, HUN, IRL, ITA, LTU, NLD, NOR, POL, SVK, SVN, SWE, and the first wave of USA) and estimates OLS models with country and industry-cluster fixed effects, using 260 observations in the preferred specification (R² ≈ 0.917). The results show that a one-point increase in numeracy is associated with roughly a 1.8–2.4% higher productivity, STEM (non-OC) is positively related to productivity, and the ICT ratio (OC/non-OC) is negatively correlated with productivity (a 0.1 increase corresponds to about 2.34% less productivity). A three-step Heckman selection plus instrumental variables approach yields broadly similar coefficient magnitudes, but the authors caution that exclusion restrictions may be violated, so causal interpretation remains limited. The study also uses a bespoke cluster-based imputation for missing skill coverage and drops industries with insufficient coverage, which may affect comparability across cells.

title: Adult Literacy Skills and Risk of Job Automation Among Middle-Aged and Older Workers in the United States
authors: Donnette Narine, Takashi Yamashita, Runcie C. W. Chidebe, Phyllis A. Cummins, Jenna W. Kramer, Rita Karam
outcome_summary: The study analyzes a nationally representative PIAAC U.S. Restricted Use File sample of employed adults aged 50+ (n=1,880) using PIAAC adult literacy skills (0–500, estimated with 10 plausible values) to predict job automation risk for occupations (0%–100%). Job automation risk is constructed by mapping 43 PIAAC occupation sub-major groups to 31 sub-major groups and then to broader occupational categories using Frey and Osborne’s approach adapted by Yamashita and Cummins. The authors run survey-weighted linear regression and report that adult literacy skills are negatively associated with job automation risk in the final model (b = −0.052, SE = 0.016, p = .002), with R-squared = .189; the mean job automation risk is 37.75%. Limitations include reliance on an occupation-level automation-risk classification and the inability of regression on observational data to infer causal effects.

title: Updated IQ and Well-Being Scores for the 50 U.S. States
outcome_summary: This paper updates previously published state-level IQ and well-being estimates for the 50 U.S. states by combining aggregate results from two large-scale assessments: PIAAC (adult Literacy and Numeracy; 2012–2017) and NAEP (fourth/eighth grade Math and Reading; 2015, 2017, 2019). It constructs state IQ by averaging PIAAC- and NAEP-derived state IQ components, then builds well-being from four subdomains (crime, education, health, income) using principal components analyses and a hierarchical PCA to obtain a global well-being index. The reported results are correlations and variance-explained statistics (e.g., global well-being explaining 75% of variance across subdomains; state IQ correlating 0.80 with global well-being; state IQ correlating up to 0.87 with FICO credit scores). No machine learning model is trained; therefore, there are no predictive performance metrics, no PV handling for student-level outcomes, and no survey-weighted estimation. The main limitation is ecological inference risk: state-level correlations may not translate to individual-level causal effects.

title: 1-s2.0-S0191491X21001279-main
authors: H. Luyten
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2009 and PISA 2018 reading literacy and questionnaire measures for 15-year-olds, aggregating to the country level and analyzing per-country change over 2009–2018. It reports that the rise in online chatting frequency is strongly negatively correlated with change in reading literacy (r = −0.718, p = .000) and with change in awareness of reading strategies (r = −0.494, p = .000). Regression results show that online chatting change predicts reading literacy change with beta = −0.718 and R² = 0.515 in the bivariate model, and beta = −0.491 with R² = 0.674 when jointly modeled with strategy awareness change. Structural equation modeling further indicates mediation: the total effect (−0.718) is split into a direct effect (−0.491) and an indirect effect (−0.226). The analysis is correlational (no individual-level change), and the excerpt does not document PV handling or missing-data procedures for the underlying PISA cognitive scores.

title: FINANCIAL AND CREDIT ACTIVITY: PROBLEMS OF THEORY AND PRACTICE
authors: Sergiy Londar, Oleksandr Bosenko, Lidia Londar, Marcus Pietsch
outcome_summary: This article evaluates the effectiveness of general secondary education financing by relating country-level PISA outcomes to education expenditure measures and broader societal indicators. It uses PISA 2015, PISA 2018, and PISA 2022 average scores across mathematics, reading, and science, and tests curve approximations (including inverse quadratic/polynomial forms) to characterize a non-linear relationship between cumulative 9-year education spending (USD at PPP) and PISA performance. For PISA 2022, it identifies leading and lagging countries (e.g., Vietnam, Singapore, Macao, Japan vs. Qatar, Panama, Cyprus, Dominican Republic, Thailand) based on deviations from the fitted curve beyond standard deviation/standard error limits. For long-term system success, it models HDI as a function of R&D expenditure (% GDP) and per-student educational spending adjusted for PISA scores in the high-R&D group, reporting R² = 69.7% and a significant Fisher test. Limitations include the absence of student-level PV handling, no reported missing-data strategy, and no ML model comparison/validation framework because the analysis is primarily regression/correlation and curve fitting on aggregated indicators.

authors: Antoniya Baltova, Albena Vutsova
outcome_summary: This article conducts a cross-country comparative analysis using OECD Education at a Glance (UOE) indicators and OECD PISA country-level averages for Austria, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, and Bulgaria over 2000–2022 (with figures referencing up to 2023). The study models the relationship between per-student public spending (PPP-adjusted) and PISA performance (math/reading/science averaged) using linear and quadratic regression, reporting R² = 0.702 for the simple association and R² = 0.916 (Adjusted R² = 0.895) for a multiple regression with ESCS and early childhood enrolment controls (N=16). It finds diminishing returns beyond about $14,000 per student (quadratic model R² = 0.817). Finally, PCA on spending, PISA averages, efficiency ratios, and student–teacher ratios explains >97% of variation via a resource–performance gradient (PC1=89.9%) and a teacher deployment–efficiency axis (PC2=7.89%). Limitations include a correlational design, omission of key confounders (e.g., deeper SES/cultural factors), and no reported survey-weight or PV handling because the analysis is based on aggregated country metrics rather than student-level PV outcomes.

title: The comparison of PISA 2015-2018 mathematics trend items based on item response times
authors: Muhsin Polat, Hülya Kelecioğlu
outcome_summary: The study analyzes Türkiye’s PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 computer-based mathematics trend items (69 common items) using item-level response times and response-time effort indices (RTE/RTF). Across the 69 items, mean response time increased from 99.38 seconds (2015) to 118.26 seconds (2018), with a statistically significant t-test (t=3.49, p<.05). Item format strongly shaped response times: open-ended items—especially human-coded open responses—had the highest mean response times, and all item-format comparisons across cycles were significant using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (p=0.00 in Table 2). Response time correlated positively with item difficulty in both cycles (Spearman r=0.26 and r=0.27, p<0.01) but not with item discrimination. Using NT10/NT20 thresholds, mean RTF rose (0.97→0.98; 0.94→0.96) and rapid-guessing proportions declined (3%→2%; 6%→4%). Limitations include the absence of documented survey-weight handling and missing-data strategy for item-level recoding, and the fact that the analysis is descriptive/nonparametric rather than PV-based achievement modeling.

title: Error Performance of Relay-Assisted Free-Space Optical Communication Links Over Atmospheric Turbulence Channels
authors: Rahat Ara, I. E. Lee, Zabih Ghassemlooy, Gwo Chin Chung, Wai Leong Pang
outcome_summary: This paper evaluates the error performance of free-space optical (FSO) communication links over atmospheric turbulence using MATLAB simulation. It compares a conventional single-hop SISO configuration with relay-assisted multi-hop configurations (N = {1,2,3} relays) and studies BER versus transmit optical power under multiple weather scenarios (clear air, haze, light fog, moderate rain, heavy rain) at link distance L = 12 km, with additional aperture-averaging experiments at L = 8 km and L = 3 km. The key benchmark is a maximum BER threshold of 10^-9 for seamless communication, with telecommunications-relevant ranges up to 10^-12. Results show that SISO can approach outage (BER near 1) under haze/light fog, while multi-hop relaying can reduce the required transmit power by more than 9 dB while maintaining BER ≤ 10^-9 under clear weather and improving performance under haze and rain. The study also finds that increasing receiver aperture diameter (D up to 150 mm) substantially improves BER, enabling large power reductions (overall ~38 dB improvement) for triple-hop links in clear weather. Because this is physics-based simulation rather than data-driven ML on human outcomes, there are no survey weights, PVs, or missing-response handling steps.

authors: Carme Garcia Yeste, Teresa Morlà-Folch, Garazi Lopez de Aguileta, Laura Natividad Sancho, Ane Lopez de Aguileta, Ariadna Munté-Pascual
outcome_summary: This article is a qualitative-quantitative case study rather than an empirical machine-learning prediction paper. It uses school documentary data from a marginalized neighbourhood in Catalonia, Spain, focusing on absenteeism and Basic Competences outcomes in 6th grade primary across three school years (2013–2014, 2020–2021, 2022–2023). The paper reports improvements in pass rates in language (Catalan, Spanish, English) and in mathematics and natural sciences, alongside a reduction in absenteeism from 50% (2009–2010) to 16% (2022–2023), and it links these changes to the implementation of Successful Educational Actions (SEA) and dialogic learning principles. No ML model training, PV-based achievement modeling, or survey-weighted estimation is described; therefore, no predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE/AUC) are available. The main limitation is that the evidence is not based on a controlled design and does not provide student-level sample sizes or missing-data handling procedures.

title: A meta-analysis on the relationship between school characteristics and student outcomes in science and maths: evidence from large-scale studies
authors: Doris Holzberger, Sarah Reinhold, Oliver Lüdtke, Tina Seidel
outcome_summary: This study is a meta-analysis (not an ML prediction study) synthesizing 285 effect sizes from 71 international/national large-scale studies, covering 3,960,281 students across 260,390 schools. The authors extracted relationships between school characteristics (e.g., academic press, school climate, material and personnel resources, classroom climate, instructional practices, and out-of-school activities) and student outcomes in science and maths, distinguishing cognitive versus motivational-aﬀective outcomes and science versus maths. They transformed diverse primary-study effect metrics into correlation coefficients and estimated multilevel random-effects meta-analytic models using metaSEM, clustering at the sample level to address dependency among effect sizes. Overall, the mean effect was r = .15 (95% CI [.12, .17], p < .01), with heterogeneity (I2 = .89 within-sample). The strongest positive associations were for SES composition (r = .30), followed by out-of-school activities (r = .18), academic press (r = .14), instructional practices (r = .13), and classroom climate (r = .13), while material and personnel resources were near zero. The authors emphasize that effects are correlational and cannot support causal claims.

title: Evaluating scientific thinking among Shanghai’s students of high and low-performing schools
authors: Irfan Ahmed Rind, Bo Ning
outcome_summary: This study used specially designed, previously validated science-thinking assessments administered to 55 Shanghai 15-year-old Grade 9 students from two schools (one high-performing and one low-performing). The outcomes were not ILSA PV-based achievement scores; instead, they were scored from (1) a Control of Variables (CoV) task requiring consistent controlled comparisons and justifications, (2) a multivariable causal reasoning task coded into causal-variable categories and context-comparison behavior, and (3) a multivariable analysis/prediction task requiring correct predictions across nine countries and correct attribution of contributing vs noncontributing factors. Across all three tasks, there were no statistically significant between-school differences (e.g., CoV controlled comparisons: X2(1)=0.525, p=0.469; prediction score: t=0.322, p=0.714). However, multivariable causal reasoning and prediction performance were comparatively weak, with most students favoring single-variable explanations and showing limited consistency in selecting all contributing factors. The paper does not report any missing-data handling strategy and does not use survey weights, so results should be interpreted cautiously and cannot be generalized to all Shanghai students.

title: LOS DEBERES ESCOLARES. UN ANÁLISIS SISTEMATIZADO CON ESPECIAL REFERENCIA AL CASO ESPAÑOL
authors: Rafael Feito Alonso
outcome_summary: This paper provides a systematic, narrative analysis of the homework debate with special reference to Spain, drawing on prior meta-analyses (e.g., Cooper) and on descriptive evidence from international large-scale assessments such as PISA and TIMSS. It does not run an original machine-learning or predictive modeling study on ILSA microdata; instead, it summarizes reported patterns: a moderate association between homework and school outcomes in secondary education, little to no association in primary education, and potential counterproductive effects when homework time exceeds roughly two hours per day. For Spain, it reports that students spend relatively more time on homework than in many other countries, while achievement is not necessarily higher. Methodologically, the paper emphasizes the correlational nature of much of the evidence and highlights limitations such as confounding (e.g., prior achievement, school quality) and the difficulty of isolating homework effects from other factors.

outcome_summary: The study investigates how language skills relate to mathematics success by combining (i) content analysis of Singapore and Hong Kong native-language and mathematics curricula and (ii) AI modeling that links curriculum-derived language-theme frequencies to published PISA 2018 outcomes for the two countries. It builds two predictive models: an ANN (Model 1) and an ANFIS hybrid model (Model 2), both implemented in MATLAB 2019a, with a 70%/15%/15% train–test–validation split. Model fit is modest: ANN yields RMSE = 17.6385 and R² = 0.353954, while ANFIS yields RMSE = 12.42771 and R² = 0.397867, and both are interpreted as insufficient relationships. The analysis is limited because it does not use student-level PISA microdata (no PVs or survey weights) and relies on a very small effective dataset (two countries), which the authors also cite as a likely reason for poor performance. Consequently, the results should be read as descriptive associations between curriculum content and country-level PISA outcomes rather than causal effects.

title: Test scores and economic growth: update and extension
authors: Gabriel Heller-Sahlgren, Henrik Jordahl
outcome_summary: This paper updates cross-country evidence linking international education test performance to economic growth. It uses country-level test-score indicators from Hanushek and Woessmann (2012a) (international math/science in primary and secondary schooling, 1963–2003) and Maddison Project GDP per-capita growth for 1960–2016, reporting that a one standard deviation higher test score is associated with about a 1.3 percentage-point higher growth rate (Table 1; Adjusted R2 up to 0.80 in the main specification excluding Zimbabwe). It further tests upper-secondary quality using TIMSS 1995 final-year scores for 21 countries and finds a weaker but positive association with 1990–2016 growth (Table 2; TIMSS 1995 score coefficient 0.006***). Finally, it shows that the share of top-performing students (≥600 points) correlates with growth about five times more strongly than the share reaching basic literacy (≥400 points) (Table 3). The study does not perform ML and does not establish causality; it also relies on already-constructed cross-country indicators rather than student-level PV-based modeling.
