file_name: The Linkage between School Autonomy and Inequality in Achievement in 69 Countries  Does Development Level Matter .pdf
title: The Linkage between School Autonomy and Inequality in Achievement in 69 Countries: Does Development
authors: Mobarak Hossain
outcome_summary: The study constructs a country-level panel using six PISA waves (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015) for 69 countries/territories, focusing on 15-year-olds’ mathematics achievement and estimating SES-based achievement inequality at the country-wave level. Achievement inequality is operationalized as the SES gradient on mathematics achievement, with plausible values incorporated via repest and weighted by student and school survey weights. In pooled weighted mixed-effects models (322 country-waves; 69 countries), none of the four autonomy domains (academic, budget, hiring, salary) shows a statistically significant association with inequality (p > .05). However, interaction models show that only academic autonomy differs by development level: academic autonomy × upper-middle-income (109.5, p < .001) and × high-income (70.6, p < .01) are significantly steeper than low/lower-middle-income groups, while budget and personnel autonomy interactions are not significant. The authors emphasize that results are robust to several specifications but cannot be interpreted causally due to potential endogeneity.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2000–2015 (15-year-olds), Mathematics achievement inequality by SES (country-wave panel; 69 countries)
all_target_variables: Maths achievement inequality (SES gradient) and school autonomy (pooled models) | Moderation of autonomy effects by development level (interaction models)

title: Socioeconomic Status and Academic Achievement in Primary and Secondary Education: a Meta-analytic Review
authors: Juan Liu, Peng Peng, Baobao Zhao, Liang Luo
outcome_summary: This paper reports two meta-analyses: one synthesizing 326 empirical studies (348 independent samples; 1,587 effect sizes; 949,699 participants) and another synthesizing SES–achievement relations computed from three international large-scale assessments (PISA, TIMSS, PIRLS) across 105 countries/areas (1230 independent samples; 9,883 effect sizes; 5,095,283 participants). Across both components, the overall SES–academic achievement association is moderate (empirical studies: r = 0.22, 95% CI [0.20, 0.23]; ILSAs: r = 0.28, 95% CI [0.28, 0.29]). Moderation analyses show that the SES–achievement relation strengthened over time (empirical: Years2 vs Years1 β = 0.05, p = 0.04; ILSAs: Years3 vs Years1 β = 0.06, p < 0.001) and that educational expansion indicators (net enrollment ratio; duration of compulsory education) were associated with stronger SES–achievement correlations in the ILSA meta-analysis. The authors emphasize correlational evidence and caution against causal interpretation, and they argue that educational equity policies should prioritize quality alongside access.

title: Assessing AI in Educational Evaluation: A Comprehensive Analysis of ChatGPT’s Performance on PISA Reading Skills
authors: Mehmet Başaran, Ömer Faruk Vural, Cennet Tandırcı
outcome_summary: This study evaluates ChatGPT’s ability to answer PISA reading literacy questions by administering 90 OECD-released items (45 from PISA 2000 and 45 from PISA 2009) to ChatGPT twice within one week and scoring responses against OECD answer keys. Across both rounds, ChatGPT achieved an overall accuracy of about 91% for the selected PISA reading items. Performance varied systematically by item characteristics: accuracy was higher for continuous texts than non-continuous texts (e.g., in 2000: 93.9% vs 83.3%; in 2009: 95.7% vs 80.0%), and complex multiple-choice items showed the lowest success in 2000 (50%). Accuracy also depended on difficulty and Bloom’s taxonomy, with weaker results at higher difficulty levels and in analytical/evaluative domains. The study is not a student-based PISA analysis (no PVs, no survey weights) and does not train ML models; therefore, results reflect AI item-response behavior rather than population achievement, and inconsistency across rounds limits reliability for high-stakes assessment.

title: Inductive and combinatorial reasoning in international educational context: assessment, measurement invariance, and latent mean differences
authors: Hao Wu, et al.
outcome_summary: The study compares inductive reasoning (IR) and combinatorial reasoning (CR) development between Indonesian and Hungarian students using online eDia assessments administered in two sessions (CR + learning strategies, then IR) to Grades 8 and 11. The analytic sample comprised 250 Indonesian students and 864 Hungarian students after excluding Indonesian cases with >80% missingness and applying data cleaning in Hungary. Measurement invariance was evaluated with multi-group confirmatory factor analysis in Mplus: IR showed strong invariance across nationalities and grades (in both countries), while CR showed partial invariance across nationalities and failed across grades in Hungary. Latent mean comparisons indicated stagnation for Indonesian reasoning skills from Grade 8 to 11 and a Grade-11 disadvantage versus Hungary for both IR and CR. Learning strategies were modeled via SEM: control strategies predicted IR in Indonesia (β=.46, p<.01), and elaboration strategies predicted CR in Hungary (β=.18, p<.05), with memorization not significant. The study does not use PV-based achievement or ML prediction; therefore, causal claims about strategy effects are limited.

all_target_variables: Inductive reasoning (IR) latent achievement | Combinatorial reasoning (CR) latent achievement

title: Practical significance of item misfit and its manifestations in constructs assessed in large-scale studies
authors: Fährmann, Köhler, Hartig
outcome_summary: This paper is not an ML prediction study; it develops and applies criteria for the practical significance of item misfit in IRT scaling. Using German PISA 2018 field trial data, the authors analyze reading literacy (cognitive example) with a 2PL/GPCM scaling approach and evaluate item misfit using RMSD, then rescale the test after removing misfitting items (RMSD>0.06 and RMSD>0.08). They estimate proficiency using PVs (with PVs transformed to the PISA score scale) and compare trait distributions and proficiency-level allocations with and without misfitting items; they report high rank correlations (r=0.92 and r=0.93), no significant mean PV differences (t(1889)=-0.79, p=0.43; t(1889)=0.76, p=0.45) and negligible effect sizes (d<0.001). For non-cognitive/metacognitive scales (ST183, ST223), they use WLE and find no meaningful gender-correlation changes and only small practical effects (e.g., ST223 mean difference Cohen’s d=0.154). Limitations include the absence of an explicit missing-data handling description and the fact that results are based on a single country and one field-trial cycle, limiting generalizability.

file_name: Robitzsch & Lüdtke. (2022). Some thoughts on analytical choices in the scaling model for test scores in international large‑scale assessment studies.pdf
title: Some thoughts on analytical choices in the scaling model for test scores in international large‑scale assessment studies
authors: Robitzsch, Lüdtke
outcome_summary: This article is a methodological discussion of analytical choices in the scaling models used to estimate proficiency distributions in international large-scale assessments, with particular emphasis on PISA. It distinguishes design-based inference (targeting a clearly defined population quantity such as a country mean) from model-based inference (depending on statistical model assumptions), and argues that official reporting should prefer design-based inference because it is less sensitive to modeling choices. The paper explains how plausible values are generated using an IRT measurement model combined with a latent background model, and how misspecification of the IRT functional form or the LBM can affect the meaning of ability and the resulting distributional statistics. It also reviews operational and proposed treatments of local dependence, multidimensionality, test-taking behavior (speed/omission), and country differential item functioning (DIF) including partial invariance and linking errors for cross-sectional comparisons and trend estimation. No empirical predictive modeling results are reported.

file_name: Governance - 2020 - Davies - How global performance assessments shape attitudes toward government decision‐making  Survey.pdf
title: How global performance assessments shape attitudes toward government decision‐making: Survey experimental evidence
authors: Emmerich Davies, Thomas Gift, Carlos X. Lastra-Anadón
outcome_summary: The paper reports a U.S. survey experiment (DLABSS) with 555 respondents, randomly assigned to fictitious news vignettes that varied the source of performance monitoring (PISA as a GPA with cross-country comparisons vs. NAEP as a domestic NPA) and the framing of underperformance (scare vs. shame). The dependent variable is a dichotomous attitude: whether respondents think the federal government should assume the largest responsibility for K-12 education. In linear probability models, the GPA×scare interaction shows the strongest effect on federal control (marginal effect 0.122, SE 0.0516, p<.05), while other interaction combinations are smaller and not statistically significant. The study also finds subgroup heterogeneity (e.g., larger effects among parents, left-leaners, and respondents prioritizing education), and placebo tests show no significant prime effects on alternative education attitudes (funding, school grades, reform support). Limitations include reliance on fictitious vignettes and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling in the excerpt; additionally, the analysis is not an ML/PV-based achievement study.
all_datasets_used: PISA (GPA framing; fictitious news vignette based on PISA) vs NAEP (NPA control; fictitious news vignette based on NAEP) — U.S. survey experiment (no ILSA cycle/grade reported)
all_target_variables: Federal control preference for K-12 education (binary)

title: An Extended Dataset of Educational Quality Across Countries (1970–2023)
authors: H. Lee, J.-W. Lee
outcome_summary: This paper constructs an extended cross-country dataset of educational quality for 101 countries from 1970 to 2023 by harmonizing mathematics and science test scores from TIMSS, PISA, and earlier IEA/IAEP assessments onto the TIMSS 1995 metric (mean=500, SD=100). It then imputes missing country-year observations (48% missing; 581 of 1212 potential) using two approaches: linear interpolation/extrapolation (Tscore_INT) and a machine-learning prediction model based on LASSO regression (Tscore_ML) trained on 501 fully observed World Bank education and economic indicators. Model selection uses an 80/20 train/validation split with grid search and 10-fold cross-validation, yielding RMSE=17.5 and R²=0.912 (out-of-sample RMSE=15.7, R²=0.905). The two imputation methods agree closely (correlation=0.967), and the dataset further derives annual 15–19 educational quality indicators and working-age (15–64) quality indexes using population weights and an assumed return to test-score gains. Because this is a dataset construction study (not student-level PV modeling), results should be interpreted as imputation accuracy for harmonized country-year indicators rather than causal effects on individual achievement.
all_datasets_used: Harmonized cross-country test scores (TIMSS 1995 scale; 1970–2023; country-year panel)
all_target_variables: Tscore_ML (harmonized test scores imputed via LASSO)

title: Thematic Analysis of Indonesian Physics Education Research Literature Using Machine Learning
outcome_summary: This paper is a data-driven thematic analysis of Indonesian physics education research (PER) literature using unsupervised NLP. The authors manually collected 852 open-access conference proceeding papers from five Indonesian PER international conferences (ICRIEMS, ISSE, ICMSE, ICMScE, ICoMSE) published between 2014 and 2021, then scraped and cleaned the PDFs (removing headers, names, affiliations, references, acknowledgments; removing punctuation/numbers/stopwords; lemmatizing and detecting bigrams). They trained Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) models over a grid of topic numbers (K=4–14), alpha values (1, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5), and random seeds, selecting K=8 based on coherence (0.31–0.42) and an elbow plot, with expert face validity. They then quantified topic development using topic prevalence (within-year mixture proportions) and visualized cumulative and rolling-window trends with jackknife-based variability bands. Because this is topic modeling on text (not ILSA achievement PVs), there are no PVs, survey weights, or student-level missing-data procedures; results are interpretive and depend on preprocessing and expert validation.
all_datasets_used: Indonesian PER conference proceedings (2014–2021; ICRIEMS, ISSE, ICMSE, ICMScE, ICoMSE)
all_target_variables: Indonesian PER topic structure (8 latent topics) | Topic development over time (topic prevalence, 2014–2021)

title: Investigating the relationship between teacher efficacy, job satisfaction, and digital resource utilization in assessment practices: Insights from PISA 2018 and 2022
authors: Dirgha Raj Joshi, Bishnu Maya Joshi, Jeevan Khanal
outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 (pre-pandemic) and PISA 2022 (post-pandemic) teacher questionnaire data for 128,866 teachers across 24 countries (excluding low-income economies). It models five constructs—teacher efficacy (TE), job satisfaction (JS), assessment practices (AP), use of instructional technology tools (UIT), and use of digital learning/communication tools (UDT)—using SEM and a regularized regression “machine learning” component with item-wise effects. Predictive performance is strongest for UDT (R² = 0.55; RMSE = 0.40; MAPE = 16.74%) and weakest for UIT (R² = 0.10; RMSE = 0.59; MAPE = 29.26%), while AP shows moderate fit (R² = 0.27; RMSE = 0.52). SEM indicates TE strongly predicts UDT (Beta = 0.88) and AP (Beta = 0.37), whereas JS has a strong effect on TE (Beta = 0.40) but minimal direct effect on AP (Beta = 0.01) and a negative association with UIT (Beta = −0.32). Limitations include unreported missing-data handling and unclear use of PISA sampling weights, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (pre-pandemic) and PISA 2022 Teacher Questionnaire (post-pandemic), 24 countries
all_target_variables: Assessment practices (AP) | Use of digital learning & communication tools (UDT) | Use of instructional technology tools (UIT) | Teacher efficacy (TE)

title: Educational participation, cultural resources, and social inequality: Have social inequalities in reading literacy increased or decreased between 2000 and 2022?
authors: Markus Lörz
outcome_summary: The study analyzes Germany using PISA reading literacy data from 2000 to 2022, restricting to students aged 15–16 and excluding special needs schools, vocational schools, and out-of-range ages. Reading literacy is scaled using PISA’s multi-matrix design with five plausible values, estimated in separate analyses and pooled using Rubin’s rules; missing item responses are handled via multiple imputation by chained equations across five imputed datasets, with clustering at school level. The authors report inequality trends using OLS regression coefficients and Chi-square tests for changes over time, and they quantify mechanisms using R² (explained variance) and KHB effect decompositions. They find that SES-related reading differences are not significantly different between 2000 and 2022 overall, but they decrease from 2000 to 2012 and increase after 2015. The decomposition suggests the early decline is largely linked to more equitable educational participation, whereas the later increase is driven more by the growing influence of cultural resources at home; however, the descriptive cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

title: Standardization and Low Reading Performance
authors: Teltemann, Schunck
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2009 and 2015 reading data for 15-year-olds pooled across 30 OECD countries (422,172 students) to model the risk of low reading performance, defined as scoring below PISA reading proficiency level 2 (dummy created from the first five plausible values and averaged across five models). The authors estimate four-level linear probability models with students nested in schools, country-years, and countries, using normalized student weights and cluster-robust standard errors (clustering at country, country-year, and school). They find that standardized testing alone (regular mandatory tests) is not statistically significant, while making aggregated achievement data publicly available is associated with lower risk of low reading performance (b = −0.158, s.e. = 0.067), with stronger negative interactions for first-generation immigrants (b = −0.160, s.e. = 0.036). Providing achievement data to administrative authorities shows smaller and less robust effects. Limitations include only two waves for longitudinal country fixed effects and potential residual time-varying confounding.
all_target_variables: Low reading performance (below PISA reading proficiency level 2)

title: The impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on academic performance are still a debated topic in public and empirical educational research, as the pandemic-related school closures have impacted approximately 90% of students globally (UNESCO, 2020).
authors: Kastorff, Heine
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA scientific literacy for 15-year-olds using pooled data from the 2018 and 2022 cycles across 69 countries (N = 1,060,311), treating each country as an independent “study” in a random-effects meta-analytic framework. Scientific literacy is modeled using PISA’s ten plausible values, and sampling weights are incorporated via OECD-aligned procedures implemented in R (BIFIEsurvey and metafor). The main effect shows a positive SES–science association (β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.25, 0.31]) with substantial between-country heterogeneity (I2 = 68.72). The SES×cycle interaction is also significant (β = 0.06, 95% CI [0.03, 0.09]), suggesting the SES gradient was more pronounced in 2022 than in 2018. Country-level moderation by HDI and DRI is not significant, and the authors emphasize that PISA is cross-sectional, so changes cannot be interpreted as causal pandemic effects for individuals.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 & 2022 (Science) — scientific literacy (15-year-olds, pooled across 69 countries)
all_target_variables: Scientific literacy (Plausible Values) — main effect of SES | Scientific literacy (Plausible Values) — interaction of SES with PISA cycle

title: Artificial Intelligence Potential in Higher Education Institutions Enhanced Learning Environment in Romania and Serbia
outcome_summary: This paper is an exploratory teacher-survey study about perceived opportunities, challenges, and utility of AI in higher education institutions in Romania and Serbia. The authors used SmartPLS 3.0 to estimate a measurement/structural model with four latent constructs (AIopp, AIChallenge, AIutility, Contribution) and evaluated reliability and validity (Cronbach’s alpha, rho_A, composite reliability, AVE), discriminant validity (Fornell–Larcker and HTMT), and model fit (SRMR, d_ULS, d_G, AIC/BIC, chi-square comparisons). Reported quantitative results are primarily construct loadings (e.g., AIutility loadings up to 0.978 for AIteachacc) and path/association statistics (e.g., AIopp–AIutility correlation 0.511; AIopp→Contribution path coefficient 0.469; AIChallenge→Contribution −0.140). The study does not use ILSA microdata, does not report ML predictive performance metrics, and does not document a missing-data handling strategy for questionnaire items, limiting interpretability and generalizability.
all_datasets_used: ILSA assessment context not specified in extraction (heuristic migration)

title: Pitsia Large-scale Assessments in Education (2022) 10:14
outcome_summary: This study uses secondary PISA microdata for Ireland from the 2012 and 2015 cycles, focusing on 15-year-olds and defining “high achievement” as proficiency levels 5–6 in mathematics (2012) and science (2015). Because PISA uses rotated test designs, the authors create PV-based binary outcomes for each plausible value and estimate multilevel two-level binary logistic regression models in Mplus, accounting for the nested student-within-school structure and applying sampling and replicate weights. For mathematics (PISA 2012), the final model shows that ESCS and non-cognitive factors—especially mathematics self-efficacy and openness for problem-solving—raise the odds of high achievement, while mathematics anxiety lowers it; the model explains 41.8% (student level) and 36.4% (school level) of variance. For science (PISA 2015), interest in broad science topics and science self-efficacy increase odds, whereas test anxiety and value of co-operation decrease odds; the model explains 50.6% (student level) and 83.6% (school level). The study is non-experimental, so relationships may be reciprocal and causality cannot be inferred.

all_target_variables: High achievement in mathematics (binary; PV-based cut-off) | High achievement in science (binary; PV-based cut-off)

title: Using machine learning to improve Q-matrix validation
authors: Lei Guo, Haijiang Qin
outcome_summary: This paper proposes four ML-based Q-matrix validation methods for cognitive diagnostic models, using random forest and feed-forward neural networks trained on features derived from PVAF and McFadden pseudo-R2. Because the task is Q-matrix validation (classifying item q-vectors) rather than predicting PV-based achievement, plausible values are not part of the outcome. In two simulation studies under a G-DINA data-generating process, the ML-based methods achieved higher Q-matrix recovery rates than the GDI and generally outperformed the Hull method, with RF-P showing the highest average QRR across both studies. In a real-data illustration using a PISA 2000 reading sub-dataset for German students (20 items; 1095 students), the RF-P suggested Q-matrix showed the best fit (M2 test p=.428 and RMSEA2=0.004), while FNN-based suggestions could not compute some fit indices due to low degrees of freedom. A key limitation is that the empirical analysis does not report survey-weighting or missing-data handling beyond stating non-missing dichotomized responses, and the ML is used to assist expert review rather than to establish causal correctness of attribute-item mappings.
ml_all_techniques: Random Forest, Neural Network (feed-forward neural network)

all_target_variables: Q-matrix validation outcome (suggested Q-matrix fit) | Q-matrix recovery rate (QRR)

title: Relationships Between Response Styles and the Hofstede and GLOBE Dimensions of Culture in a Sample of Adolescents From 33 Countries
authors: Hana Vonkova
outcome_summary: The study conducts secondary, country-level analyses using PISA 2006 (15-year-olds) response-style estimates (ERS, ARS, DARS, NONC) from Buckley (2009) for 33 countries. It reports Pearson correlations between response styles and country GDP per capita, and correlations between response styles and Hofstede (6) and GLOBE (9) cultural indices, then repeats these relationships as partial correlations holding GDP per capita constant. Across Table 1 and Table 2, GDP per capita is negatively associated with ARS (r = −.377, p<.05) and positively associated with DARS (r = .430, p<.05), while it is not significantly related to ERS or NONC. Several cultural associations weaken or change sign after GDP adjustment (notably Hofstede individualism with DARS and some GLOBE uncertainty/future orientation links), while others remain robust (e.g., Hofstede uncertainty avoidance with NONC; GLOBE power distance with ERS/ARS). The paper uses correlation/partial-correlation rather than ML, so no predictive performance metrics or survey-weighted estimation are reported, and the findings are associational and country-aggregated.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2006 (15-year-olds) — country-level response styles (Buckley 2009) across 33 countries

title: Relating teenagers’ science interest network characteristics to later science course enrolment: An analysis of Australian PISA 2006 and Longitudinal Surveys of Australian Youth data
authors: Maien S. M. Sachisthal
outcome_summary: The study combines Australian PISA 2006 science literacy data with LSAY 2008 (wave 3) for the 2006 cohort, following Year 10 students to their Year 12 science course enrolment decision (chemistry, physics, biology). The analytic sample is 4,758 students after excluding International Baccalaureate students and those not on the same Year 10→Year 12 trajectory; missing data were handled via casewise deletion after MCAR checks. Science knowledge indicators used PISA plausible values with PV1 for each science knowledge indicator, and all network indicators were dichotomized to improve centrality stability. Using bootnet/IsingFit psychometric network estimation, the authors found positive, significant correlations between centrality and course enrolment (r=.36–.74, all p<.05). Forecast regressions showed significant predictive relationships for both strength and closeness centrality, with the strongest explained variance for chemistry (R2_adj≈.56/.54) and physics (≈.31/.35) and weaker but significant effects for biology (≈.25/.27). Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight use and the correlational nature of the predictive associations.

all_target_variables: Chemistry course enrolment (Year 12) | Physics course enrolment (Year 12) | Biology course enrolment (Year 12)

title: Teacher vs. Machine Correction: Comparing Assessments of Students’ Reading Comprehension and Written Summaries
authors: Vázquez-Cano, E., Ramírez-Hurtado, J. M., Díez-Arcón, P.
outcome_summary: This study experimentally compares human teacher scoring with the automatic correction system G-Rubric on a Spanish reading comprehension task drawn from PISA 2009. Thirty Spanish students (aged 14–16) wrote 60–100 word summaries of a 385-word text; 30 teachers then scored the summaries on style and content, while G-Rubric produced corresponding rubric-based scores. The analysis uses Euclidean distance between each teacher’s 30 style and 30 content scores and the system’s scores, categorizing dissimilarity into low/medium/high via quartiles, and then applying latent class analysis (Latent Gold 4.5) and correspondence analysis (SPSS) to identify teacher profiles. The best-fitting latent class solution is a three-cluster model (lowest BIC among 1–4 clusters), with dissimilarity explained at R²=0.5729 and cluster membership associated with teacher age and experience (sex not significant at conventional levels). The study reports cluster sizes of 41.26% (Cluster 1), 34.48% (Cluster 2, lowest dissimilarity), and 24.26% (Cluster 3, highest dissimilarity), and concludes that scoring similarity varies by teacher demographics, suggesting G-Rubric may be more aligned with certain teacher profiles. Limitations include the small, non-representative sample and the absence of PV-based achievement modeling or survey-weighted inference.

file_name: Brit J of Edu Psychol - 2023 - Qin - Learning strategies and reading achievement in primary schools  Longitudinal.pdf
title: Learning strategies and reading achievement in primary schools: Longitudinal relationship and gender differences
authors: Kexin Qin, Ji Zhou, Yehui Wang
outcome_summary: This longitudinal study followed Chinese primary students across two waves (Grade 4 to Grade 6), measuring reading achievement with a self-developed 33-item multiple-choice test linked across waves using a Rasch model and scored via EAP, and measuring learning strategies (memorization, elaboration, control) using scales adapted from PISA 2009. The analytic sample included 3878 students from 99 schools in four provinces, with attrition at T2 handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) and clustering accounted for in Mplus via the type=complex option. The cross-lagged model fit well (e.g., χ2(14)=102.739, CFI=0.992, RMSEA=0.040), and the key predictive pattern was that only prior memorization significantly predicted later reading achievement (β=0.138, p<.001), while prior reading achievement predicted later strategies. Gender moderation tests showed stronger achievement-to-strategy effects for boys than girls. Limitations include the absence of PV-based ILSA achievement modeling and the correlational nature of cross-lagged paths, so causal claims cannot be made.

title: Análisis del sentido espacial en estudiantes de secundaria en actividades PISA
authors: María Isabel Elvas Fernández, Rafael Ramírez Uclés
outcome_summary: This descriptive didactic study analyzes spatial sense in secondary students using selected PISA 2012 released tasks from the space and shape domain and compares coded spatial-sense manifestations with teachers’ classroom-test performance. The analytic sample is 122 Uruguayan 15-year-olds in first-year bachillerato from a single private school in Montevideo. The authors operationalize spatial sense through two sets of indicators: management of geometric concepts and visualization skills, coded as binary manifestations across 13 PISA questions (with sums such as H2_C and H2_H) and then relate these indicators to the teachers’ grades (“nota”). Using correlation analyses, they find statistically significant positive associations between teachers’ performance and multiple spatial-sense indicators (e.g., note correlates with several concept-management and visualization variables). They further run regression analyses and report that performance is significantly predicted (p<.05) only by one concept-management variable and one visualization variable, specifically linked to question H2. Limitations include the local, single-institution sample and the absence of reported missing-data rules and any PV/weighting strategy.

file_name: J Educational Measurement - 2026 - Xue - Evaluating General‐Purpose Multimodal AI for Q‐Matrix Generation from Math Items .pdf
title: Evaluating General‐Purpose Multimodal AI for Q‐Matrix Generation from Math Items: A Cognitive Diagnostic Modeling Exploration
authors: Kang Xue, James J. Appleton
outcome_summary: This study evaluates multimodal LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Claude-sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-pro) as an Attribute-based Automatic Q-Matrix Generator for cognitive diagnostic modeling. It uses TIMSS 2007 (25 items; 698 students), TIMSS 2011 (26 items; 1,010 students), and PISA 2012 mathematics items (6 attributes; 12 items; 6,561 students across Shanghai, Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan) to compare AI-generated Q-matrices against expert benchmarks. Across datasets, AI-generated Q-matrices show strong chatbot-human matching accuracy (e.g., TIMSS 2011 best matching rate 0.905 with precision 0.861 and F1 0.630; PISA 2012 best precision/F1 0.846 with G-mean 0.879). In exploratory CDM fit analyses using DINA, DINO, RRUM, GDINA, and LLM, AI-generated matrices often achieve competitive or improved AIC/BIC/log-likelihood and consistently low SRMSR values, indicating adequate residual-based fit. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weighting and missing-data handling, and the fact that Q-matrix fidelity is assessed via matching and fit indices rather than causal effects on learning outcomes.

file_name: Mathematics anxiety and self-efficacy as predictors of mathematics literacy.pdf
title: Mathematics anxiety and self-efficacy as predictors of mathematics literacy
authors: Suzanne E. Hiller, et al.
outcome_summary: The study analyzed two nationally representative Greek samples from PISA 2003 and PISA 2012, focusing on mathematics literacy for 15-year-olds. Mathematics literacy was treated as a PV-based achievement score (five plausible values), and the authors followed the single-PV approach by conducting analyses with one plausible value at random. They estimated two OLS multiple regression models: Model 1 with demographic controls (R² = 20.4%) and Model 2 adding mathematics anxiety, mathematics self-efficacy, and their interaction (R² = 34.1%). In Model 2, mathematics self-efficacy was positively related to literacy (B=26.94, p<.001), mathematics anxiety was negatively related (B=-20.46, p<.001), and the Anxiety×Self-efficacy interaction was significant (B=-3.66, p<.001). The paper reports that computations used appropriate sampling weights and imputes missing data via iterative Markov Chain Maximum Likelihood; however, the design is observational and the regression framework is not ML, so predictive performance should not be interpreted as causal effects.

This study uses PISA 2012 data for 151,745 fifteen-year-old students across 65 countries and economies to test expectancy-value theory (EVT) and control-value theory (CVT) predictions about mathematics anxiety (MA). The authors construct latent EVT/CVT constructs from PISA questionnaire items: Control (perceived control and failure attributions), Value (maths interest, instrumental motivation, and parents’/friends’ valuation), and Success Expectancy (maths self-efficacy and maths self-concept). MA is modeled as the dependent variable in linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts for country, and the analysis controls for maths achievement using the first of PISA’s five plausible values (PV1). They apply PISA student sampling weights to account for oversampling of target subpopulations and use country clustering via multilevel random effects. Key results show that Success Expectancy and Control are strongly negatively associated with MA, while Value shows a weak positive association once Control and Success Expectancy are held constant; interactions and nonlinearities are statistically detectable but practically small. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature of PISA and the use of self-report anxiety measures, so causal directions cannot be inferred.

title: International Comparative Study on PISA Mathematics Achievement Test Based on Cognitive Diagnostic Models
outcome_summary: This study conducts an international cognitive diagnostic analysis of PISA 2012 mathematics using 12 publicly available items that were jointly tested across 10 countries (GBR, FIN, RUS, CHN, JPN, SGP, USA, CAN, AUS, and Saudi Arabia). Students were included if they completed all 12 items, yielding 24,512 students total. The authors evaluated eight cognitive diagnostic model families (DINA, DINO, RRUM, ACDM, LCDM, LLM, G-DINA, and a Mixtures Model) and selected the LLM because it had the smallest Deviation, AIC, and BIC. Using LLM with Bayesian EAP estimation, they reported attribute mastery probabilities for content (N1–N4), process (P1–P3), and context (C1–C4), plus knowledge-state patterns and prerequisite learning trajectories (e.g., N4→N3→N2→N1; P3→P2→P1). The paper does not document survey-weight use or missing-data handling, and the learning trajectories are derived from cross-sectional data, so associations cannot be interpreted causally.

title: Investigating response behavior through TF-IDF and Word2vec text analysis: A case study of PISA 2012 problem-solving process data
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2012 computer-based complex problem-solving process data for the single task “climate control (CP02501)”, using 16,763 task-level samples with a binary correctness outcome (0/1). It applies TF-IDF and Word2vec to convert action sequences into numerical representations, then trains supervised models (logistic regression, KNN, SVM, random forest) and evaluates them with 5-fold cross-validation and grid-searched hyperparameters using F1, accuracy, precision, and recall. For predicting correctness, Random Forest with TF-IDF features performs best (F1=0.8419; Accuracy=0.8231; Recall=0.8572). For unsupervised profiling, k-means with K=3 yields clusters with markedly different correct rates (TF-IDF: 81% vs 42% vs 36%; Word2vec: 78% vs 27% vs 26%). Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weighting and missing-data handling, and the fact that the dependent variable is task-level correctness rather than PV-based achievement.

title: Thinking Skills in Teaching Practices: Relationship with Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
authors: G. Larina, A. Kapuza
outcome_summary: The study examines how teacher-reported mathematics teaching practices relate to students’ mathematics achievement in the eighth grade (TIMSS) and ninth grade (PISA), using SEM/confirmatory factor analysis to construct lower-order (LO) and higher-order (HO) teaching practice scales. It reports that HO practices show a strong positive association with TIMSS scores (coefficients around 0.70–0.78 SD) and with PISA scores (around 0.71–0.75 SD), while LO practices are not significant in TIMSS and become negative in PISA when HO is included. When PISA is modeled while controlling for TIMSS performance, HO remains significant (about 0.31–0.32 SD), whereas LO loses significance, suggesting effects persist beyond prior achievement. The paper uses Huber–White robust standard errors for clustered data but does not report PV handling or a missing-data strategy in the provided text, limiting interpretability and reproducibility.

title: What are the Factors Affecting Turkish Students’ Science Literacy? A Hierarchical Linear Modelling Study Using PISA 2015 Data
authors: Ulaş ÜSTÜN, Ertuğrul ÖZDEMİR, Mustafa CANSIZ, Nurcan CANSIZ
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 science literacy for Turkey (15-year-olds; N=5895 students from 187 schools) using hierarchical linear modeling (HLM 7) to address the nested student-within-school structure (ICC=0.52). The authors report that averaging across the 10 science plausible values yields a single PV-based science literacy score per student. In the level-1 (student) model, nine student-level variables explain 12.77% of within-school variance; the strongest student predictor is weekly science learning time, while out-of-school study time is significantly negative and inquiry-based science teaching is also negative. In the level-2 (school) model, four school-level variables explain 32.74% of between-school variance; science-specific resources are the strongest positive school predictor. The paper does not report a missing-data strategy or whether PISA sampling/replicate weights were applied, limiting interpretability of effect sizes and generalizability.

title: Exploring Differences in Financial Literacy Across Countries: The Role of Individual Characteristics and Institutions
authors: Andrej Cupák, Pirmin Fessler, Maria Silgoner, Elisabeth Ulbrich
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes OECD/INFE adult financial literacy microdata collected in 2014–2016 for 12 countries (total N=15,388; analytic N=12,298 for baseline controls; N=10,810 when adding experience variables). It models financial literacy (0–7) using weighted OLS with country fixed effects and then applies Blinder–Oaxaca decompositions at the mean and RIF-based quantile decompositions at the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles, using survey weights and robust standard errors. At the mean, income buffer and university education are positively associated with literacy, while women and singles score lower; adjusted R² is 0.144 with fixed effects. Decomposition results show that individual characteristics explain a substantial share of gaps in some countries but leave a large unexplained remainder, and that lower-tail gaps are less explained by individual characteristics than upper-tail gaps. Finally, the unexplained components correlate negatively with institutional indicators such as PISA 2012 math scores, internet usage, secondary enrolment, stock market capitalization, social contributions, life expectancy, and GDP per capita; the authors emphasize that these country-level associations do not imply causality.

title: Epistemic beliefs in science socio-economic status and mathematics and science test results in lower secondary education a multilevel perspective
authors: Karin Taht, D. Rozgonjuk, et al.
outcome_summary: This study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2015 Estonia (Grade 9; 3991 students from 81 schools) to examine how epistemic beliefs in science (EBS) and socio-economic status (SES; ESCS) relate to mathematics and science achievement. The authors use two-level regression models with school as a random effect and pool estimates across the 10 plausible values using Rubins multiple-imputation approach. For mathematics, the pooled total R2 is 0.175; student SES and student EBS are significant positive predictors, school SES is significant, and school EBS is not significant (p = .127). For science, the pooled total R2 is 0.181; both student and school EBS and SES significantly predict higher science scores. Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal identification) and the possibility of partial conceptual overlap between the EBS questionnaire and science achievement content.

title: Examining key capitals contributing to students' science-related career expectations and their relationship patterns: A machine learning approach
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 519,334 15-year-old students from 72 countries/economies, predicting a binary indicator of science-related career expectations (science/ICT/health/science technician occupations vs other jobs). A Random Forest classifier was trained after deleting students who did not report career aspirations and those with missingness in more than half of selected contextual features, then imputing remaining missing contextual variables via KNN; features were standardized prior to imputation. For achievement-related predictors, the authors used PISA’s 10 plausible values by repeating analyses across all 10 PVs and aggregating results. In the global model (top 25 features), performance was AUC=0.7419 with test accuracy=0.6818; in Hong Kong (top 10 features), test AUC was about 0.766–0.769. The paper uses ALE plots for relationship-shape interpretation (increasing, S-shaped, inverted-U, decreasing) but, because PISA is cross-sectional, the findings support predictive importance and associations rather than causal effects.

title: Exploring the Relationship Between Students' Physical Activity and Academic Achievement in Different Social Environments
authors: Lu Ye, Zaiju Tai
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 student data (397,388 students across 52 countries/territories) to examine how physical activity intensity and timing relate to academic achievement in mathematics, reading, and science. Using OLS regressions with school fixed effects and PISA-provided weighting, the authors report statistically significant associations (Table 3) where moderate physical activity outside school (MPA) is positively related to achievement (Math β=0.048; Read β=0.067; Science β=0.063; all p<0.01), while vigorous activity (VPA) and physical education days (PES) are negatively related (e.g., Math VPA β=−0.020; PES β=−0.031). Exercise before school (EBS) shows the strongest negative associations across subjects (Math β=−0.124; Read β=−0.158; Science β=−0.154). The paper emphasizes cross-context heterogeneity (Tables 4–6) and explicitly notes that results reflect correlations rather than causality; it also does not provide replicate-weight uncertainty estimates.

file_name: The mediating moderating model of inquiry-based learning and science self-efficacy  evidence from PISA 2015.pdf
title: The mediating–moderating model of inquiry-based learning and science self-efficacy: evidence from PISA 2015
authors: Y. Liu, J. Wang
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) Science data from 57 participating countries and economies (N=346,109) to test a mediating–moderating model linking inquiry-based learning to science self-efficacy. Using WLE-scaled PISA questionnaire constructs—science self-efficacy (SCIEEFF) as the outcome, inquiry-based learning (IBTEACH) as the predictor, science interest (INTBRSCI) as the mediator, and teacher support (TEACHSUP) as the moderator—authors estimate mediation and moderated mediation with PROCESS in SPSS using 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results show a significant positive total effect (B=0.194, p<.001) with partial mediation: the indirect effect via science interest is B=0.039, representing 20.1% of the total effect. Teacher support strengthens the direct effect (direct effect rises from 0.087 to 0.185 from low to high teacher support) but reduces the indirect effect (from 0.034 to 0.021). The paper reports correlations/standardized regression coefficients rather than causal effects, and it does not document missing-data handling or whether PISA complex survey weights were applied in the estimation.

title: The socio-familiar context and its impact on student reading performance in PISA
authors: Esteban Vázquez-Cano, Ana-María De-la-Calle-Cabrera, Carlos Hervás-Gómez, Eloy López-Meneses
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 reading performance among 30,000 16-year-old students selected by mother tongue (Spanish vs English) across six countries: Spain, Chile, Uruguay, Great Britain, United States, and Ireland. The authors use multilevel analysis and binary logistic regression in SPSS, treating reading performance as a dependent variable derived from 10 reading items and an overall summation, and recoding parental education/occupation and parental educational-role items into nominal predictors. Results indicate that the socio-familiar context predicts roughly 20% of reading performance variability in Spanish-speaking countries and 15% in English-speaking countries, with the strongest incidence attributed to average parental education and parents’ interest in school activities and educational support. The paper reports significant differences between language blocks and provides p-values and model fit statistics (e.g., R² ranges in multilevel models and omnibus/Wald tests in logistic regression). Limitations include lack of documented plausible-value combination and missing-data strategy, and the absence of explicit survey-weight handling details, which constrains interpretability for population-level inference.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 Reading (students aged 16; mother tongue: Spanish vs English; 6 countries)

title: Teachers Collaborating as a Professional Learning Network and Learning How to Implement Collaborative Problem Solving in the Primary Math’s Classroom
outcome_summary: This paper reports a qualitative case study rather than an empirical ML prediction study. It examines how a small team of five primary teachers in one NSW public/state school used a professional learning network (PLN) and an action-research cycle to implement collaborative problem solving (CPS) in primary mathematics. Data come from a focus-group session (recorded and transcribed) and teacher reflections, analyzed using reflective thematic analysis, yielding five themes: Collaborative Leadership, Common Vision, Collective Vision with Students, Trust, and Deeper Understanding of CL and CPS. No quantitative performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, RMSE, AUC) are reported because there is no model training or predictive target. The study is not generalisable beyond the single school context, and it does not use ILSA microdata or survey-weighted estimation.

title: Predicting science achievement scores with machine learning algorithms: a case study of OECD PISA 2015–2018 data
authors: Cafer Mert Yesilkanat, Sibel Acıslı-Celik
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 science literacy data (PV2SCIE) from 13 randomly selected countries (N=67,329) and predicts both (i) students’ PISA-2015 science scores and (ii) students’ PISA-2018 science scores using the same 18 predictors. For each country, the authors split PISA-2015 data into training (75%) and testing (25%) sets, tune hyperparameters via grid search with 10-fold cross-validation, and evaluate models using Pearson’s r, RMSE, and MAE. Across all countries, XGBoost consistently outperformed MLR, SVR, and Random Forest; for PISA-2018, Luxembourg achieved the highest predictive correlation (r=0.600, RMSE=75.06, MAE=59.97) and Finland the lowest (r=0.467, RMSE=79.38, MAE=63.24), with correlations generally in the moderate range (0.40<r<0.69). Missing values were excluded during preprocessing, and the manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than population-representative causal effects. The authors also note reduced accuracy at extreme achievement values.

title: Counterfactual Graph Representation Learning for Fairness-Aware Cognitive Diagnosis
outcome_summary: The study proposes FACD, a fairness-aware cognitive diagnosis model using counterfactual graph representation learning, and evaluates it on PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) data. After filtering to students with at least 20 response records, the authors train on a 70/10/20 split and compare FACD against IRT, MIRT, NeuralCDM, and KaNCD as well as fairness variants (Base+ and Reg). Across frameworks, FACD attains the strongest overall predictive performance, with improvements in ACC/AUC and reductions in RMSE (e.g., under MIRT: AUC 0.7334 and RMSE 0.4638). For fairness, FACD consistently yields the lowest GD-RMSE and EOD values across backbones (e.g., IRT: GD-RMSE 0.0214, EOD 0.0305). Limitations include missing reporting on survey-weight usage and missing-data handling, and the fairness objective targets representation invariance rather than establishing causal effects.

title: The Effect of Inquiry-Based Practices on Scientific Literacy: the Mediating Role of Science Attitudes
authors: Yue Ma
outcome_summary: This study used PISA 2015 science data for eight countries (China, Japan, Korea, Singapore, USA, Germany, Australia, Finland; total N=60,812 students) to test a two-level mediation model in Mplus (students nested in schools). Scientific literacy was operationalized as the mean of the ten PISA plausible values for science. The model fit was acceptable across countries (RMSEA ≈ 0.036–0.056; CFI ≈ 0.909–0.959; TLI ≈ 0.899–0.954). Results showed a consistently negative direct path from perceived inquiry-based practices to scientific literacy (standardized β from −0.319 to −0.136), but positive indirect effects through interest in science and science self-efficacy, and a negative indirect effect through instrumental motivation for six countries (China and Finland were exceptions). The study also used sampling weights “considered” in analyses and omitted cases with missing values for MSEM, and it interprets associations rather than causal effects due to cross-sectional PISA data.

title: The Relationship Between Students’ Awareness of Environmental Issues and Attitudes Toward Science and Epistemological Beliefs—Moderating Effect of Informal Science Activities
authors: Yong Xie, Yonghe Zheng, Yang Yang
outcome_summary: This study used PISA 2015 science data for 15-year-old students from the BSJG subset of China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Guangdong; N=9841; weighted N reported as 1,331,794). Students’ environmental awareness, informal science activities, and ESCS were related to four science attitude/epistemology outcomes using correlation and multiple regression models in SPSS 25, with multiple imputation for missing values (5 imputations). Environmental awareness showed significant positive correlations with enjoyment (r=0.340), interest (r=0.373), self-efficacy (r=0.401), and epistemological beliefs (r=0.290). In regression, environmental awareness predicted all four outcomes (R²: 0.332 enjoyment; 0.303 interest; 0.284 self-efficacy; 0.194 epistemological beliefs), while informal science activities significantly moderated only the enjoyment and self-efficacy relationships (interaction β=0.016, p<0.05) and not interest or epistemological beliefs (interaction not significant after Bonferroni). Limitations include cross-sectional design and self-reported measures, so findings indicate associations and moderation rather than causal effects.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds), BSJG subset (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Guangdong), China

title: Student test-taking effort in low-stakes assessments: evidence from the English version of the PISA 2015 science test
authors: Elodie Pools, Catherine Monseur
outcome_summary: This study analyzes test-taking engagement in the PISA 2015 science assessment (computer-based, English version) using response times from science items administered in four cluster positions. The authors selected six English-speaking countries (AUS, CAN, GBR, IRL, NZL, USA) and derived an effort index by fitting a two-class finite mixture model to item RT distributions (99% trimmed RTs), then aggregating posterior probabilities of belonging to the effortful class into a global effort measure. Effort decreased toward the end of the test (mean effort probability dropping from about 0.94 to 0.88 in session 1, and from 0.90 to 0.85 in session 2). Expectancy-value proxies explained only a trivial amount of effort variability (average pseudo R² up to ~0.07). Critically, effort correlated strongly with science achievement and the association increased across clusters (from ~0.39 to ~0.56), with gross variance explained rising from ~11.79% to ~26.68% by the last cluster. The study uses house weighting and PISA replicate-based standard errors; however, the effort–achievement link is correlational and the effort measure may conflate disengagement with fatigue or perseverance.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2015 Science (computer-based), English version; cluster positions 1-4
all_target_variables: Test-taking effort (average posterior probability of being effortful)

title: ICT Engagement: a new construct and its assessment in PISA 2015
authors: Kunina-Habenicht, Goldhammer
outcome_summary: This study provides construct validity evidence for the newly introduced PISA 2015 ICT Engagement scale, using PISA 2015 main-study questionnaire data from Switzerland (n=5860) and Germany (n=6504). The authors estimated SEM measurement models in Mplus (WLSMV for ordinal indicators) and confirmed a four-dimensional ICT Engagement structure (ICT interest, perceived ICT competence, perceived autonomy in ICT use, and ICT as a topic in social interaction) with acceptable fit in Switzerland (CFI=0.929; RMSEA=0.087). In a latent regression model, ICT Engagement explained substantially more variance in outside-of-school entertainment use (74.1%) than in learning-related home use (10.8%) and only modest variance in ICT use at school (8.7%). Gender comparisons showed lower latent means for girls on competence, autonomy, and social-interaction engagement (with scalar invariance not fully supported). Correlations with PISA literacy performance were small; notably, ICT social interaction topic correlated negatively with reading (r=-0.20 in Switzerland; r=-0.12 in Germany). Limitations include the absence of documented survey-weight application and the cross-sectional design, so results support validity and associations rather than causal effects.

title: Kindergarten pre-reading skills predict Grade 9 reading comprehension (PISA Reading) but fail to explain gender difference
authors: Minna Torppa, M. Manu
outcome_summary: The study uses a Finnish longitudinal sample from the First Steps Study to examine whether Kindergarten pre-reading skills (age 6) predict Grade 9 reading comprehension using PISA Reading tasks (administered in fall 2017). The analytic sample included 1010 adolescents (FIN; 480 girls, 530 boys) and the outcome was a total reading comprehension score computed from PISA Reading link items administered in classrooms (60 minutes). The authors estimated multigroup and mediation path models in Mplus using robust maximum likelihood (MLR) due to skewed predictors; no machine learning algorithms were trained. Results show that Kindergarten pre-reading skills explained 27% of Grade 9 reading variance for boys and 18% for girls, with letter knowledge, rapid naming, vocabulary, and listening comprehension predicting reading depending on gender. Gender differences in PISA Reading were only partially mediated by Kindergarten skills, with indirect effects totaling about 5% of the reading variance, indicating that the adolescent gender gap emerges through pathways beyond early pre-reading measures. Limitations include attrition and the exclusion of students in special-needs education classes, and the fact that the analysis uses a single score rather than PV-based PISA achievement estimates.

title: s11092-020-09328-6
authors: Anindito Aditomo, Carmen Köhler
outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether PISA 2015 science teaching scales—aggregated from students to the school level—yield reliable and valid measures of school-level teaching quality. Using multilevel CFA/SEM in Mplus (robust maximum likelihood), the authors estimated two-level unidimensional factor structures for six teaching scales and computed school-level reliability via ICC-1 and ICC-2, plus predictive validity by regressing school-level teaching factors on school-level intrinsic motivation. Across 69 countries/regions (503,146 students; 17,678 schools), classroom management showed the strongest school-level reliability (mean ICC-1=0.12; ICC-2=0.76) and positive predictive validity (average beta=0.58; significant in 86.2% of regions). Emotional support, adaptive instruction, and teacher-directed instruction showed low-to-marginal reliability but meaningful predictive validity in many regions, whereas personal feedback and inquiry-based instruction showed weak or inconsistent predictive validity. The paper does not report missing-data handling and does not document whether PISA complex-survey weights were applied, so results should be interpreted with caution for cross-country policy use.

title: Algorithmic Fairness in Automatic Short Answer Scoring
authors: Nico Andersen, Julia Mang, Frank Goldhammer, Fabian Zehner
outcome_summary: The study analyzed German PISA 2015 reading literacy constructed-response items with dichotomous human scoring (correct/incorrect), using n = 4,060 students and 37 selected items. It compared four feature–classifier combinations and found the best-performing approach to be an SVM trained on RoBERTa sentence embeddings, with κ = 0.82 and ACC = 0.93 (TPR = 0.96; FPR = 0.16), evaluated via 5-fold cross-validation stratified by score distribution. At the fairness level, aggregate gender differences were not detected, but a minor significant bias emerged for language spoken at home: foreign-language speakers received about 1% more false-positive correct classifications than native speakers (DD = −0.011; D ≈ 0.03). The paper does not report plausible-value handling because the outcome is item-level correctness rather than PV-based achievement, and it does not fully document missing-data handling for the language variable, which limits certainty about the robustness of group disparity estimates.

title: Large-scale Assessments in Education (2024) 12:11

outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2012 mathematics data for South Korea (analytic sample N=3,310) to examine how learning-strategy use relates to mathematics achievement. The authors first compare two IRT-based scoring models for four nominal learning-strategy items—NRM versus GPCM—using model fit indices (AIC/BIC, likelihood ratio test) and item-level fit (Q1, RMSEA), concluding that NRM fits better overall and yields higher empirical reliability (0.365 vs 0.214). For the achievement relationship, they use plausible values for mathematics and compute correlations and a quadratic regression between the NRM-based learning strategy score and mathematics achievement. The mean correlation is ρ=0.18 (p<.05), and the quadratic term is significantly negative (β=-0.0667, p<.001), indicating an inverted-U pattern with small effect size (R2=0.03572). Limitations include reliance on self-reported strategy items, listwise deletion after rotation-design missingness, and no explicit reporting of survey-weight application.

title: A graphically based machine learning approach to predict secondary schools performance in Tunisia
authors: Sonia Rebai, Fatma Ben Yahia, Hedi Essid
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2012 school and student data for Tunisia, restricting the analytic sample to 105 public secondary schools after excluding private schools and removing observations with missing data. In a first stage, it computes school-level inefficiency using a directional distance function (DEA) that combines three desirable outputs (school-average PISA mathematics, reading, and science scores summarized across plausible values) and one undesirable output (principal-reported dropout proportion), with three inputs (weekly learning time in mathematics, science, and language). In the second stage, it trains regression trees and random forests in R to predict the continuous inefficiency score and to visualize nonlinear interactions; random forests use 1000 trees and report variable importance shares (notably school size and proportion of girls). Robustness is assessed with OLS and Tobit models, where competition and school location are significant at the 5% level. Limitations include lack of reported survey-weight usage and the fact that ML feature importance and tree splits are predictive associations rather than causal effects.

title: The impact of reading metacognitive strategies on mathematics learning efficiency and performance: An analysis using PISA 2018 data in China
authors: Weizhong Zhang, Rong Lian
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata from 361 schools in four Chinese provinces, focusing on 15-year-old students (final analytic sample N=11,993 after removing 65 cases with missing key variables). Reading metacognitive strategies were measured using 16 PISA items across three dimensions (Understanding & remembering, Summarizing, Assessing credibility), summarized as UNDREM, METASUM, and METASPAM, and students were grouped into six latent profiles via latent profile analysis. Mathematics performance was derived from PV1MATH–PV10MATH by averaging the ten plausible values (MATHACH), and weekly mathematics learning time (MMINS) was used to examine learning efficiency within each profile. The study reports that Gender and ESCS primarily shape profile membership, and that weekly learning time significantly predicts mathematics performance for Novice-indifferent, Veteran-average, Novice-low evaluating, and Novice-arbitrary profiles, but not for Veteran-skilled and Novice-mixed. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and lack of reported PISA sampling-weight usage and PV/missing-data transparency beyond the stated case deletion.

title: Influence of students’ perceptions of instruction quality on their digital reading performance in 29 OECD countries: A multilevel analysis
authors: Jie Hu, Yanyu Wang
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 computer-based digital reading performance for 223,807 students (15-year-olds) across 29 OECD countries, using 10 plausible values for the outcome and pooling estimates with Rubin’s rules. It applies three-level hierarchical linear models (students within schools within countries) with normalized student weights and stepwise model building to retain statistically significant controls. Multiple imputation with predictive mean matching is used for missing LMINS (23.60%), generating 10 imputed datasets that are combined with PVs. In the final model, adaptation of instruction and stimulation of reading engagement show positive associations with digital reading (β=0.067, p<0.001), whereas teacher-directed instruction and training exercises for reading skills show negative associations (β=-0.084 and β=-0.094, p<0.001). Random effects indicate substantial school-level variance explained (f2=45.706%), and the authors caution that effect sizes are small and the design is correlational rather than causal.
all_target_variables: Digital reading performance (PVs pooled via Rubin’s rules)

title: General or specific abilities? Evidence from 33 countries participating in the PISA assessments
authors: A. Pokropek, G. N. Marks, F. Borgonovi, P. Koc, S. Greiff
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 item-level responses from 33 OECD countries (total N=226,434 for the major reading domain) to test whether PISA primarily measures general ability or distinct domain-specific abilities. The authors compare three psychometric measurement models—(i) a standard three-dimensional correlated-factor model, (ii) a symmetrical bifactor model with a general ability factor, and (iii) an S-1 bifactor reading model—using AIC for model fit and bifactor indices (ECV, ω, ωH, and omega subscale coefficients) for reliability and explained common variance. The symmetrical bifactor model yields the best fit in all countries with very large ΔAIC differences, and the general factor explains most common variance (ECV around 0.8+), while specific-factor contributions are small and often too unreliable for interpretable domain subscores. Covariate SEM results show ESCS and gender relationships consistent with general ability, and learning-time effects are weak or sometimes counter to theoretical expectations. Limitations include reliance on latent-factor modeling rather than PV-based achievement scores and the use of FIML for missingness, without reporting a PV-handling strategy.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Reading (major domain), OECD countries (33 countries)

title: Evaluación de un juego serio que contribuye a fortalecer el razonamiento lógico-matemático en estudiantes de nivel medio superior
authors: Alicia López Sánchez, Aída González Lara
outcome_summary: This paper evaluates a serious game (“MathLogic - La Leyenda de YuZhen”) designed to strengthen logical-mathematical reasoning in Mexican upper-secondary students. The study uses a pre/post design: students took a first multiple-choice exam, then used the game for two weeks, and finally took a second exam; performance was analyzed using response time and correctness, and game progression (advance/regress) was determined by a fuzzy inference system based on time and correctness. The reported results show that students who used the game (and/or advanced levels) improved more than those who did not: average exam performance increased from 52 to 58 for game users versus 66 to 60 for non-users (time=0 group). The paper also reports that students who advanced at least to the next level (level 2) showed improvement in the second evaluation, with Welch hypothesis tests reported at 95% probability. Limitations include the absence of ML model training/validation, no survey-weighting framework, and limited transparency on missing-data handling.

outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 reading literacy for Spain, where low reading comprehension is defined as not reaching level 2 and is dichotomized (0=medium/high, 1=low). For predictor selection, it trains a Random Forest classifier on a 70% training / 30% validation split and reports validation accuracy of 86% for the student-level model (VP 6) and 81% for the school-level model (VP 5), using the top 15 variables selected via the Gini index. For probability modeling, it estimates multilevel binary logistic regression models (student-only, school-only, and combined), reporting marginal/conditional R² values of 35%/23% (Model 1), 1%/46% (Model 2), and 38%/47% (Model 3), with grade repetition and educational expectations showing the largest odds-ratio effects. The authors note a limitation that sampling weights were not applied in the Random Forest step and that the cross-sectional PISA design prevents causal inference.

title: Validating School-based Measures of Educational Disadvantage in Ireland
outcome_summary: The study validates Ireland’s school-based disadvantage measure (HP index) by comparing it with two alternative socio-economic indicators derived from PISA 2018: school-average ESCS and the percentage of students with an examination fee-waiver (2015, matched to PISA schools). Using PISA 2018 reading achievement for Ireland (5,577 students in 157 schools), the authors compute school-average reading and school-average ESCS using plausible values and then estimate multilevel random-intercept models in MPlus to explain variation in reading achievement. They report strong bivariate correlations among school-level indicators (e.g., HP mean vs ESCS r = .73; ESCS vs fee-waiver r = −.82) and quantify associations in multilevel models: a 1 SD increase in student ESCS corresponds to +19.68 points, while a 1 SD increase in school-average ESCS corresponds to +21.80 points (Model 1). In school-only models, HP mean shows +25.13 points per 1 SD, but explains less variance than ESCS and fee-waiver (between-school variance explained: 45.10% for HP vs 76.17% for ESCS and 68.82% for fee-waiver). The analysis is not an ML predictive modeling study; it uses multilevel modeling and correlations, and the paper presents unweighted correlations for exploratory purposes despite describing school-weighted preparation for MPlus.

title: The role of computer game playing and reading attitudes in digital reading achievement: evidence from Hong Kong 15-year-olds
authors: Wenrui Zhang, Lei Gu
outcome_summary: This study analyzed the Hong Kong subset of PISA 2018 (N = 6,037 15-year-olds) to examine how computer game playing and reading attitudes relate to digital reading achievement, and whether reading attitudes mediate the gaming–achievement relationship under gender control. Digital reading achievement was modeled using the three PISA digital reading components (RCLI, RCUN, RCER) represented by all ten plausible values, while computer game playing and reading attitudes were latent factors measured from ICT familiarity and student questionnaire items. Using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling (lavaan/lavaan.survey) with PISA’s final weight (W_FSTUWT) and 80 replicate weights, the authors found that computer game playing was negatively associated with both reading attitudes and digital reading achievement, and that reading attitudes positively predicted digital reading achievement. In Model 2, both direct and indirect effects were significant; in Model 3, the direct effect of gaming on achievement became non-significant while the indirect effect through reading attitudes remained significant (βa*b = -0.03, p < .001). Limitations include reliance on cross-sectional PISA data and SEM mediation assumptions rather than causal identification.

title: Socially Jetlagged and Late for School: Chronotypes, Achievement and Truancy among 15-Year-Old Stude
authors: Jörg-Henrik Heine, Christine Sälzer
outcome_summary: The study analyzes the German PISA 2018 subsample (n=5451 students in 223 schools) and uses a nationally added chronotype module to construct social jet lag (CHRONOSJL) from an adapted Munich Chronotype Questionnaire. Truancy is measured via a formative index combining three self-reported items (skipping whole days, skipping lessons, arriving late) and is modeled with stepwise linear regression separately for Gymnasium versus non-Gymnasium school types. The authors account for PISA’s stratified sampling structure and use all ten plausible values for the PISA reading domain via BIFIEsurvey. In the final models, social jet lag significantly predicts higher truancy in both school groups (non-Gymnasium: b=0.0985, p=0.0015; Gymnasium: b=0.0769, p=0.0440), while PISA reading proficiency significantly predicts lower truancy (non-Gymnasium: b=-0.2593, p<0.001; Gymnasium: b=-0.1808, p<0.001). Explained variance remains modest (R² up to 0.0923), and the paper emphasizes that PISA’s design does not allow causal inference; additionally, missing-data handling for non-PV variables is not reported in the provided text.
all_datasets_used: PISA 2018 Germany (15-year-olds) — Reading literacy (PVs) + German grade + BEFKI figural intelligence; outcome: truancy index

file_name: The OECD s  Well-being 2030  agenda  how PISA s affective turn gets lost in translation.pdf
title: The OECD’s ‘Well-being 2030’ agenda: how PISA's affective turn gets lost in translation
authors: Jeremy Rappleye, Hikaru Komatsu, Yukiko Uchida, Jeanne Tsai, Hazel Markus
outcome_summary: This article is a conceptual/interpretive critique of how the OECD operationalizes the Well-being 2030 agenda through PISA 2018’s “students’ feelings” measures. Rather than training or evaluating machine-learning models, the authors compare cross-economy patterns in reported emotion-related item responses and argue that translation equivalence is not achieved even within the same written language (China, Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan), citing differences in the Chinese terms used for emotions such as “proud,” “afraid,” and “sad.” The paper also situates these measurement issues within broader Western psychological frameworks (e.g., independent vs. interdependent self-construal) and argues that the OECD’s approach treats equivalence as a technical engineering problem. Methodologically, the study does not report sampling-weighted estimation, PV handling, missing-data procedures, or quantitative model performance metrics, limiting any causal or statistical generalization beyond the authors’ interpretive claims.

title: Child poverty and academic skills at the national level: A longitudinal analysis of four waves of PISA
authors: Dennis J Condron, Joseph J Merry
outcome_summary: The study links OECD/UN child poverty rates to national PISA outcomes across four waves (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018), analyzing 40 nations (N=160 nation-years; N=159 for reading after excluding Spain from reading due to implausible responses). Using pooled time-series two-way fixed-effects models with nation and year controls, the authors find that within-nation increases in child poverty are associated with lower mean academic skills in reading, math, and science (e.g., reading mean: −0.843; math mean: −1.030; science mean: −1.030). Child poverty also increases the share of low-skilled students in all three subjects (reading: +0.266; math: +0.305; science: +0.358). For high-skilled students, the association is negative for math only (−0.270) and not significant for reading or science. The analysis is correlational despite fixed effects, and child poverty missingness is handled via interpolation/averaging rather than a fully specified statistical imputation framework.

title: The role of metacognitive strategies for the development of digital competence in students of Compulsory...
authors: Beatriz Ortega-Ruipérez, Enrique Navarro Asencio
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 language teacher questionnaire data (20,205 teachers) from selected countries/regions (Spain, Portugal, Germany, United States, United Kingdom, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Korea, Macau, Brazil, Chile, Dominican Republic, Peru) to test an explanatory structural model linking teachers’ metacognitive strategy use to teaching good Internet use. The authors validate the measurement model with confirmatory factor analysis using polychoric correlations and WLSMV for ordinal items, reporting RMSEA=0.076, TLI=0.951, and CFI=0.958. In the structural regression, metacognitive use in reading comprehension is the best predictor of teaching media literacy (beta=0.540, p=0.000), learning support is also significant (beta=0.187, p=0.000), while metacognitive use for learning shows no significant direct effect (beta=-0.055). The model explains 41.5% of the variance (R²=0.415). Limitations include the absence of a documented missing-data strategy and the cross-sectional, self-report nature of the constructs, so causal claims are not warranted.
