title: Perceived teacher autonomy support for adolescents' reading achievement: The mediation roles of control-value appraisals and emotions
authors: Wang and Hu
outcome_summary: This study analyzed a China subset of PISA 2018 reading for 15-year-old students (n=12,058) and modeled reading achievement using PV1 reading, normalized to an OECD scale (mean 500, SD 100). The authors estimated a serial multiple mediation model in R (lavaan) with maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors (MLR), reporting acceptable fit (CFI=0.990, TLI=0.947, RMSEA=0.078, SRMR=0.045). Teacher autonomy support showed a positive direct effect on reading achievement (B=2.790, p<0.05) and a significant positive indirect effect via reading enjoyment (B=1.660, p<0.001). In contrast, the indirect path through control-value appraisals alone was negative (B=-2.280, p<0.05), while the full serial chain through appraisals and then enjoyment to achievement was positive (B=7.270, p<0.001). Limitations include cross-sectional mediation assumptions, self-report measures for autonomy support and emotions, and limited reporting of how PISA complex sampling weights were applied in the mediation estimation.

title: Self-Concept and Feeling of Belonging as a Predictor Variable of the Attitude towards the Study from the PISA 2018 Report
authors: N.G., I.M., J.J.C., R.T.
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 questionnaire items (Likert-type, 0–5) to examine how educational self-concept and personal self-concept relate to students’ sense of belonging in Spanish Compulsory Secondary Education. The sample includes 35,943 students from Spain, and the authors report positive, statistically significant associations among the constructs using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha reliability, bivariate correlations, and a structural equation model (SEM) estimated with maximum likelihood and bootstrapping (6000 iterations). Model fit is reported as χ²(74, n=35,943)=191.98 (χ²/df=2.59), IFI=0.96, TLI=0.96, CFI=0.96, RMSEA=0.052 (90% CI=0.050–0.061), and SRMR=0.033. The paper does not report any machine-learning model, survey-weight usage, or a missing-data handling procedure, so the results should be interpreted as correlational evidence within the analysed sample rather than population-representative or causal effects.

title: Methodological aspects of the highly adaptive testing design for PISA
authors: Fink A, König C, Frey A
outcome_summary: This methods paper formalizes the highly adaptive testing (HAT) design for PISA, building on computerized adaptive testing (CAT) with shadow testing and multidimensional IRT (M2PL for dichotomous items and GPCM for polytomous items). It targets PISA 2018 reading as the main worked example, with four 30-minute clusters and domain-specific adaptive clusters for mathematics and science, while keeping within-cluster unidimensional administration. The paper specifies how item selection is constrained by PISA requirements: unit-level structure with within-unit adaptation, content/process coverage constraints, item exposure control via progressive item exposure, item position effects handled through a continuous calibration strategy, and constraint satisfaction through mixed-integer programming. It reports that, in a referenced simulation study, HAT increases test information by ~30% relative to the PISA 2018 MST reading design, improves ability estimation accuracy (lower RMSE), and eliminates average constraint violations (vs ~four violated constraints for MST). Limitations: this paper itself does not estimate student-level predictive models or report PV/missing-data handling for an empirical dataset; it is an algorithmic and implementation-focused contribution.

title: Teacher workload and intensifying demands: Lessons from the Chinese double reduction policy
authors: Ji, Chan, Kalogeropoulos
outcome_summary: This article is an empirical qualitative study examining teacher workload and related challenges under China’s Chinese Double Reduction Policy (DRP). It does not use PISA (or any other ILSA) micro-data, and it does not train or evaluate machine learning models. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with school leadership and teachers at a public school in Zhejiang Province, supplemented by focus groups with parents and junior secondary students. The findings are presented as thematic results: teachers report increased workload and longer working hours, inequitable or insufficient compensation, and tensions arising from mismatched expectations between parents and teachers. The study emphasizes school-level strategies (e.g., flexible teaching arrangements, temporary accommodation, parent-child cloud platforms) and argues for clearer remuneration guidelines and greater stakeholder collaboration. Because the design is qualitative, the results are not intended to estimate causal effects or population-wide achievement impacts.

outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 student data to examine whether teacher support moderates the association between a constructed cultural capital index and reading performance, and whether this moderation differs across education systems. Countries were first ranked by the cultural capital–reading correlation across 37 OECD countries (294,527 students), then six countries were grouped into “strongest” (Hungary, France, Czech Republic) and “weakest” (Israel, Canada, Norway) correlation sets for separate moderation analyses. The authors report hierarchical multiple regression results: in the strongest-correlation group, Step 1 R² = 0.184 and the interaction adds ΔR² = 0.001 (p < .001), with an enhancing pattern; in the weakest-correlation group, Step 1 R² = 0.052 and the interaction adds ΔR² = 0.0002 (p = .006), with a decreasing pattern. No machine-learning models are evaluated (the analysis is moderation via regression), and the paper does not report missing-data handling or whether PISA sampling weights were applied, limiting interpretability for policy inference.

authors: Luca Bonacini, Irene Brunetti, Giovanni Gallo
outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 student data for eight EU countries (Austria, Croatia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia) and models reading and mathematics outcomes using OLS regressions with school-clustered standard errors. The dependent variables are the average of the ten plausible values for each cognitive domain, and the analytic sample (N=45,285) is obtained after dropping observations with missing values on the variables used. For model specification, the authors apply efficient best-subsets selection (Furnival & Wilson) and then estimate effects; they report R-squared by country (e.g., Total R²=0.331 for reading and 0.325 for maths) rather than ML prediction metrics like accuracy or AUC. Across both domains, the strongest predictors are books at home and the school type/localization composite, while vocational tracking is associated with significantly lower performance. The Gelbach decomposition further suggests that family socio-economic characteristics explain most of the general-vocational gap, whereas school quality (notably class size) explains more of the big vs small city gap. Limitations include the absence of explicit survey-weight variable naming and the fact that the approach is predictive/correlational rather than causal.

file_name: Brit J of Edu Psychol - 2023 - Pan - Using machine learning to predict UK and Japanese secondary students  life.pdf
title: Using machine learning to predict UK and Japanese secondary students' life satisfaction in PISA 2018
authors: Zexuan Pan, Maria Cutumisu
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 student questionnaire and well-being questionnaire data to predict secondary students’ life satisfaction (ST016Q01NA) separately for the United Kingdom and Japan. Two supervised ML regression models—Random Forest and k-nearest neighbours (KNN)—were trained using 26 individual-level predictors and evaluated with nested cross-validation (five outer folds, five inner folds) and grid-search hyperparameter tuning. Missing values (<10%) were handled by series-mean imputation, and performance was assessed with MSE, RMSE, MAE, and R². Across both countries, Random Forest performed better than KNN: for the UK, test R² was 0.187 (RF) vs 0.103 (KNN), and for Japan, 0.138 (RF) vs 0.055 (KNN). The most important predictors included meaning in life, student competition/cooperation, teacher support, exposure to bullying, and ICT resources, but the findings are correlational (cross-sectional questionnaire data) and the paper does not document the use of PISA complex survey weights.

title: CONCEPTUAL CONSTRUCTION OF GLOBAL COMPETENCE IN EDUCATION
authors: MARÍA SANZ LEAL, MARTHA LUCÍA OROZCO GÓMEZ, RADU BOGDAN TOMA
outcome_summary: This paper is a critical review and discourse analysis of how “global competence” has been conceptualized, with special attention to intercultural education as an inclusion-oriented educational approach. It discusses the OECD/PISA 2018 definition of global competence and contrasts conceptual “background ideas” (often aligned with social efficiency/human capital) versus “foreground ideas” (often aligned with social reconstructionism). The review highlights that global competence and intercultural competence are frequently used interchangeably, while global competence is argued to be more comprehensive for addressing globalisation challenges. It also emphasizes conceptual and measurement challenges that limit international comparability, including critiques of PISA 2018’s framework and the difficulty of standardizing assessment of a construct that is not purely science-based. The study does not report ML model performance metrics because it does not conduct predictive modeling on ILSA microdata.

title: Hierarchical clustering of the pre-exam anxiety levels in physically inactive and active adolescent students from 56 countries: an observational study using PISA program data
authors: Encarnação, JT, PF, LL, AS, LB, RF, PA, PV, AM
outcome_summary: This observational study uses PISA 2018 (15-year-old students) from 56 countries to examine pre-exam anxiety patterns separately for two habitual physical-activity groups: physically inactive (no regular activity) and physically active (moderate-to-vigorous activity). Because the authors do not access microdata, they cluster countries using country-level mean percentages of pre-exam anxiety for each physical-activity group, treating each country as one data point. The hierarchical clustering quality is evaluated with silhouette score (0.60 for the low-activity clustering with five clusters; 0.56 for the high-activity clustering with four clusters), within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), between-cluster sum of squares (BCSS), explained variation (96% for low activity; 92% for high activity), and BCSS/WCSS ratios (22.10 and 11.18). The paper reports statistically significant within-country differences in anxiety between activity groups for multiple countries (e.g., Austria, Belgium, Chile, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Israel, Korea, Mexico, Turkey, United States), while Russia and the UAE show increases. Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling, lack of documented survey-weighted estimation for country means, and the fact that clustering is descriptive rather than a predictive model of individual anxiety.

outcome_summary: The paper analyzes the relationship between financial education and financial literacy using PISA 2018 financial literacy data for 15-year-old students in 20 countries (Bulgaria, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Estonia, Finland, Georgia, Indonesia, Italy, Lithuania, Latvia, Netherlands, Peru, Poland, Portugal, Russia, Serbia, Slovak Republic, Spain, USA). It estimates a student fixed-effects model that differences each student’s standardized administrative scores between financial literacy and mathematics, using PISA recommended practices: final student weights, balanced repeated replication (BRR) replicate weights, and 10 plausible values. In the main fixed-effects results (Table 1, equation 4), financial education encountered during mathematics classes is associated with higher financial literacy in most countries, with effects reported from roughly 0.12 to 0.37 SD depending on the country, while other delivery modalities show no consistent positive gains. The study cautions that unobserved confounding may remain and that the financial education exposure is self-reported, so findings should be interpreted as conditional associations rather than fully causal impacts.

title: ijced-02-2023-0011
outcome_summary: This study evaluates the validity of socioeconomic deprivation (SED) measures in PISA 2018 by comparing the standard ESCS index with a newly derived local SES measure (SES_LOCAL) constructed via PCA on three country-specific household items. Using PISA 2018 data for 15-year-olds in grades seven and above, the authors report that ESCS and SES_LOCAL show weak convergent validity: correlations vary widely by country, with the highest correlation around r=0.68 (Peru) and the lowest around r=0.10 (Romania). For predictive validity, country-wise regressions show that ESCS consistently outperforms SES_LOCAL in predicting achievement in reading, science, and mathematics using PISA plausible values (PV_READ, PV_SCIE, PV_MATH). The manuscript does not provide a full missing-data strategy for the analytic stage beyond excluding regions with missing ESCS/SES_LOCAL, and it does not report model-based performance metrics beyond regression coefficients, limiting precision about effect sizes and uncertainty.

title: Motivational Profile, Future Expectations, and Attitudes toward Study of Secondary School Students in Spain: Results of the PISA Report 2018
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for Spain (N=35,943; mean age 15.83) focusing on compulsory secondary students’ motivational reasons for studying/not studying and their future expectations for 5 years ahead. The paper reports descriptive chi-square associations by sex and grade repetition, then estimates a multinomial logistic regression to predict future-expectation categories from sex, grade repetition, discouraging reasons (not interested in content; never studying), and influences on expectations (school grades and subject mastery). The final multinomial model was significant (χ2(50)=1042.79, p<0.001) with Nagelkerke R2=0.209, and Table 7 reports odds ratios and confidence intervals for multiple outcome categories. Finally, a structural equation model (maximum likelihood estimation) reports good fit indices (e.g., IFI=0.994, RMSEA=0.017) and a pathway where grade repetition predicts discouragement reasons, which in turn relate to future expectations. Limitations include the absence of documented survey-weight use and missing-data handling, and the fact that the analysis is not a machine-learning predictive pipeline.

title: Language exposure and English digital reading achievement in East Asia: Examining the role of students’ socioeconomic status
authors: Shuqiong Luo, Lingyi Fu, Ronnel B King, Shing On Leung
outcome_summary: This study used PISA 2018 microdata for English digital reading, restricting the sample to students who took the computer-based reading assessment in English in Macao (n=679), Hong Kong (n=348), and Singapore (n=6,676), for a total of 7,703 students. The dependent variable was the PISA plausible value PV1READ, and missing data were addressed via MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS. Pearson correlations showed positive associations between SES and English digital reading in all three economies (whole sample r=0.38, p<0.01), while language exposure–reading correlations varied by source and economy. In hierarchical linear regression, SES significantly predicted reading achievement (whole sample Model 1 r2=0.14, β=0.38***), and in Model 2 SES remained significant (r2=0.22, β=0.313***), with LE-mother showing a small negative effect (β=-0.03*, p<0.05) and peer exposures such as siblings (β=0.12***) and best friends (β=0.16***) showing positive effects. The moderation tests in Model 3 indicated that SES did not significantly moderate the language exposure–reading relationship, and the manuscript does not report survey-weighted estimation, limiting generalizability and causal claims.

title: Does ICT involvement really matter? An investigation of Turkey’s case in PISA 2018
authors: Erhan Ünal, Ahmet Murat Uzun, Selcan Kilis
outcome_summary: The study analyzes the Turkish dataset from PISA 2018, focusing on math and science achievement estimated via plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH and PV1SCIE–PV10SCIE) and ICT Familiarity Questionnaire indices. The analytic sample was 6,101 students after excluding non-digital-device users and applying listwise deletion for missing data. Using two-step hierarchical regression in IDB Analyzer (with BRR/Fay replicate weights), the models explained modest variance: math R² increased from 0.11 to 0.20, and science R² increased from 0.11 to 0.21 after adding ICT constructs. ESCS was a consistent positive predictor, while ICT availability at home (ICTHOME) was significantly negative. Among ICT use variables, subject-related ICT use during lessons (ICTCLASS) and leisure ICT use (ENTUSE) were positive, whereas general school ICT use (USESCH) and schoolwork-related outside use (HOMESCH) were negative; ICT competence and interest were positive, while ICT use for social communication (SOIAICT) was negative. The authors caution against causal interpretation because the design is relational and based on self-reported ICT measures.

title: ICT, learning environment and student characteristics as potential cross-country predictors of academic achievement
authors: Funda Erdogdu
outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 data for 41 countries/economies, using country-level mean test scores for 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics, and science as dependent variables. The authors apply stepwise multiple linear regression (backward elimination/forward addition) with robust standard errors to address heteroscedasticity, and they report high model fit across subjects (R²≈0.90; Root MSE <0.05). Across the three models, the strongest and most consistent predictors include average class size (negative association), home internet time (positive), inadequate educational material (negative), and student school-climate variables such as belonging, disciplinary climate, and fear of failure (positive). Teacher enthusiasm and teacher support show negative associations with achievement in all subjects where significant. Limitations include the correlational nature of regression, lack of documented missing-data handling, and no explicit reporting of how PVs and country-level aggregation were handled for the mean-score outcomes.

title: The Protective Factor of Resilience in the Face of Mathematical Anxiety
authors: R.T., J.C., J.M.A.-P., J.M.F.-C., I.M.
outcome_summary: This cross-sectional study analyzed 1742 students from secondary schools in Almeria (Spain) to examine how academic resilience and mathematical anxiety relate to motivation, metacognitive strategies, and end-of-year mathematics performance. The authors used SEM with maximum likelihood estimation and bootstrapping (5000 interactions) to test a hypothesized predictive model, reporting good model fit (χ2/df = 2.41, CFI = 0.96, IFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.96, RMSEA = 0.053, SRMR = 0.041). Key standardized paths showed resilience negatively associated with mathematical anxiety (β = −0.54, p < 0.001), resilience positively predicting SDI (β = 0.43, p < 0.001) and metacognitive strategies (β = 0.57, p < 0.001), and anxiety negatively predicting SDI (β = −0.47, p < 0.001) and metacognitive strategies (β = −0.31, p < 0.01). Motivation (SDI) predicted metacognitive strategies (β = 0.43, p < 0.001) and academic performance (β = 0.48, p < 0.001), and metacognitive strategies predicted performance (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). Limitations include the absence of any reported missing-data handling and the inability to infer causality due to the cross-sectional design.

title: Relationship between students’ ICT interactions and science achievement in PISA 2018: The case of Türkiye
authors: Ernest Afari, Funda Örnek, Shaima Ali Alaam
outcome_summary: This study uses secondary microdata from PISA 2018 for Türkiye (6890 students in 186 schools) to examine how students’ ICT interactions relate to science achievement. Science achievement is modeled using PISA 2018 science plausible values (PV1SCIE–PV10SCIE) and estimated in Mplus with TYPE=IMPUTATION and TYPE=COMPLEX, using the student weight W_FSTUWT and school clustering via CNTSCID. The SEM measurement model shows good fit (e.g., CFI=0.930, RMSEA=0.032), and the structural model fits extremely well (CFI=1.00, RMSEA=0.000, SRMR=0.000) with R²=0.165 for science achievement. ICT use outside school (home availability, leisure use, and ICT for schoolwork) and ICT use in school (subject-related ICTCLASS and school-activity USESCH) are significant positive predictors, as is ICT interest (INTICT) and perceived ICT competence (COMPICT), while ICT availability at school (ICTSCH) and perceived ICT autonomy (AUTICT) are not significant. Because the design is cross-sectional and SEM paths are correlational, the results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal impacts of ICT policies.

title: Predicting teachers’ research reading: A machine learning approach
authors: Maria Cutumisu, Mehrdad Yousefpoori-Naeim, Surina He, Ying Cui
outcome_summary: The study uses the 2018 PISA language teacher questionnaire and analyzes a restricted cross-country subset of 18 countries (final analytic sample N=10,469 teachers) to predict whether teachers are “light” vs “heavy” professional readers based on self-reported weekly reading time. The outcome is dichotomized (<3 hours/week vs >6 hours/week), and features are scaled with RobustScaler; correlated predictors were reduced to mitigate multicollinearity. Two ML classifiers—logistic regression and SVM—were trained using a 5:1 train/test split with 10-fold cross-validation on the training set for hyperparameter tuning. On the hold-out set, accuracy was 0.64 (logistic regression) vs 0.65 (SVM), with ROC AUC of 0.70 for both; precision/recall/F1 were also very similar. The most important predictors in logistic regression were teaching reading comprehension strategies, the length of reading assignments, and teachers’ general reading habits (books and news), with age also contributing. Limitations include modest predictive performance, lack of an explicit missing-data handling description, and no clear reporting on whether PISA complex survey weights were applied; therefore, results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

The authors used SPSS 25.0 and PROCESS Model 6 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples to estimate mediation paths, and they reported regression coefficients (e.g., USESCH direct effect on reading literacy β=-7.106, p<.001; reading enjoyment β=27.710, p<.001; reading metacognition β=54.159, p<.001). They also report bootstrapped indirect effects with 95% confidence intervals for multiple mediation chains, finding significant negative mediation for ENTUSE and a metacognition-driven negative mediation for USESCH. title: A Cross-national Study of Mathematics Anxiety
authors: Z. Yuan, Renmin Ye, Zhenguo Yuan, Jiang Tan

The study reports weighted descriptive comparisons and then uses partial correlations (controlling gender and ESCS) and multiple linear regressions to relate M-Anxiety to student, teacher, and peer-related constructs. Across all economies, M-Anxiety shows significant negative relationships with mathematics test score, interests, and familiarity (e.g., test-score correlations as low as r=-0.42, p<0.001). In regressions, student study efforts (S_Efforts) is the only factor significant across all five economies (e.g., Shanghai -0.27***; Singapore -0.26***), while teacher and peer variables show weak or non-uniform effects. authors: Acun Çelik, Filiz Kalelioğlu, Sıla Acun Çelik
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Turkey data (students in grade 7 or above; N=6890, with 5438 retained after univariate and multivariate outlier removal) to validate a four-dimensional ICT competence construct and to examine how ICT variables relate to mathematics, science, and reading literacy. ICT constructs are measured via Likert-type questionnaire-derived indices (availability, ICT use, interest & perceived competence, and subject-related ICT use), while literacy outcomes use PISA plausible values pooled across 10 PVs using Rubin’s combination criteria and estimated with BRR for the complex survey design. Using SEM path models with ESCS as a control/moderator, the authors report acceptable model fit (e.g., CFI≈0.92–0.93; RMSEA≈0.07–0.08) and find negative associations for ICT availability and entertainment use, alongside positive associations for educational ICT use, ICT interest/competence, and subject-related ICT use. Limitations include the non-causal, correlational nature of SEM and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling beyond PV imputation.

title: The Relationships Among ICT-Related Psychological Factors, School Contextual Factors and Secondary Students’ Reading Performance: A Multilevel Analysis Across 47 Economies
authors: Ya Xiao, Khe Foon Timothy Hew
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 computer-based reading literacy performance (READ) for 222,293 secondary students nested within 10,103 schools across 47 economies, using the optional ICT Familiarity Questionnaire plus student and school questionnaires. The authors fit three-level hierarchical linear models (students within schools within countries) and report statistically significant associations consistent with Self-Determination Theory: ICT interest, autonomy, and competence are positively related to reading performance, whereas perceived social interaction in ICT use is negatively related. Cross-level moderation shows that quantity-oriented school support in ICT devices accentuates both the autonomy benefit and the social-interaction disadvantage, while quality-oriented support via teachers’ capacity to integrate technology strengthens the competence benefit and buffers the social-interaction disadvantage. Model fit is evaluated using deviance, AIC/BIC, and effect sizes (f2), but the paper does not report PV handling or a detailed missing-data strategy beyond country exclusions, and causality cannot be inferred due to the cross-sectional design.

title: How to breakthrough disparities in scientific literacy of different family background: The mediating role of self-directed learning efficacy and the moderating role of family support

outcome_summary: This Acta Psychologica study uses PISA 2022 microdata restricted to six East Asian societies (Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan, Singapore, Japan, and South Korea; total N = 34,968) to examine how family background relates to scientific literacy and through which mechanism. Scientific literacy is modeled using the first plausible value PVSCIE1, while SDL efficacy (ST355) and family support (ST300) are standardized indices. Using SPSS PROCESS (Model 4 for mediation and Model 7 for moderated mediation), the authors report that family background positively predicts scientific literacy (β = 0.211, p < 0.001) and that SDL efficacy significantly mediates the relationship (indirect effect = 2.448; 95% CI excludes 0). They also find that family support strengthens the family background → SDL efficacy link (interaction β = 0.033, p < 0.001; simple slopes 0.103 vs 0.168). Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal identification) and missing-data handling not reported; additionally, the paper does not document whether PISA sampling weights were applied.

title: Teachers’ Frequency of ICT Use in Providing Sustainable Opportunity to Learn: Mediation Analysis Using aReading Database
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 teacher questionnaire data from reading teachers in Hong Kong (HKG), Macau (MAC), and Chinese Taipei (TWN) to test a multilevel mediation model linking teachers’ ICT use frequency to opportunities to learn (OTL) in reading comprehension. The analysis is multilevel (teachers nested in schools/regions) and estimates mediation via two parallel mediators: teacher self-efficacy in instruction (SEFFINS) and teacher adaptive instruction (ADAPTINSTR). Missing data were imputed using expectation maximization (EM), and variables were standardized with Z-scores; the paper does not report any machine-learning model or PV-based achievement metrics. Results show positive total and direct effects of ICT use on OTL across regions and both novice and experienced teachers (direct effects β≈0.22–0.36; total effects β≈0.34–0.47). Mediation is significant for adaptive instruction across groups, while self-efficacy mediation fails for novice teachers in Hong Kong. Because measures are self-reported and the design is correlational/mediation-based, causal claims about ICT improving OTL should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Revisiting educational assumptions: The surprising negative link between creative extracurricular activities and creative thinking in PISA 2022

The creative thinking outcome is based on 10 plausible values, which the authors aggregated using Rubin’s rules, and the models incorporate PISA’s complex sampling design via whole-sample student weights and 80 replicate weights. Weighted Pearson correlations show negative associations between creative thinking and creative activities both inside (r = −0.25) and outside school (r = −0.32), and survey-weighted regression yields negative standardized effects for activities inside (β = −0.06) and outside school (β = −0.27), with pseudo-R² = 0.54 and variance-based R² = 0.27. The outcomes are ordered policy categories (not for any subjects / for some subjects / for all subjects) for ability grouping implemented (a) within the school between classes and (b) within the class. The authors report descriptive statistics and correspondence analyses, then estimate multilevel ordinal regression models with country-varying intercepts; they adjust for school demographics measured as shares of students with special learning needs, socioeconomically disadvantaged homes, and students whose heritage language differs from the test language. They find large welfare-regime differences for ability grouping between classes within schools (social democratic vs liberal), but only weak differences for within-class ability grouping, which appears more strongly associated with school demographics. As a sensitivity check, they compare welfare regimes to Varieties of Capitalism (LME vs CME) using AIC/BIC; both theories show similar conclusions for between-class grouping, while neither strongly explains within-class grouping. outcome_summary: This article is a methods-focused review of AI-powered scoring for PISA 2022 Creative Thinking, motivated by the cost and subjectivity of human raters. It organizes approaches into unsupervised semantic-distance methods, supervised fine-tuning of transformer models, and few-/zero-shot prompting with LLMs, and it discusses how these could map onto PISA scoring criteria such as appropriateness, originality, and flexibility. The paper reports that prior feasibility studies show substantial convergence between AI-based scores and human ratings (e.g., correlations in the ~0.70–0.85 range in the abstract; and a PISA Book Covers case study reporting convergence comparable to human inter-rater reliability). However, the current paper does not present a new student-level ML model trained and evaluated on PISA microdata, nor does it report PV handling, missing-data procedures, or survey-weighted estimation. Therefore, the contribution is primarily conceptual and implementation-oriented, with psychometric safeguards (e.g., Many-Facet Rasch Models and measurement invariance) highlighted as key requirements for cross-cultural validity.

The main quantitative results come from correlation and hierarchical multiple regression (SPSS v28), not from machine learning. Children’s overall creativity performance averaged 47.05 (SD=26.71) percentile points, with significant between-school differences (one-way ANOVA H(11,1052)=39.124, p<0.001). In regression, school context plus teacher EE explained 3.8% of variance (R2=0.038), and adding home climate dimensions did not improve prediction (ΔR2=0.002, p=0.606), with all home dimensions non-significant (all p>0.350). Limitations include convenience sampling, reliance on self-report questionnaires, and no reported missing-data handling strategy.
all_datasets_used: TCI creativity task (Children’s Creativity Test) in Spanish primary schools (ages 6–13)

title: Machine-Learning Applications in Predicting Students’ Non-Cognitive Skills: Evidence from PISA 2022
authors: Dahman Tahri, Ji Liu, Millicent Aziku
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 student data (15-year-olds) restricted to Module 8 to predict a non-cognitive skills outcome defined as an equally weighted composite index across OECD non-cognitive domains. The analytic sample includes 75,217 students from ten OECD countries/partner economies (Australia, Spain, Estonia, Hong Kong, Ireland, Korea, Macao, Singapore, Chinese Taipei, Turkey). After recoding invalid/skipped/not applicable responses as missing, the authors applied listwise deletion and evaluated models using nested 5-fold cross-validation with hyperparameter tuning. Gradient Boosting Machine outperformed OLS, Lasso, and Random Forest, with test performance summarized by MSE ≈ 0.2399 and R² ≈ 0.3038 (vs. RF R² ≈ 0.2898; Lasso R² ≈ 0.2663). SHAP interpretation indicated cognitive-motivational traits as the most influential group, with several math-related beliefs/behaviors contributing positively or negatively. Limitations include cross-sectional prediction (no causal identification) and the absence of reported PISA survey-weight usage.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Computer-Assisted Learning and AI-guided Tutors
authors: Almudena Sevilla, Pilar Cuevas-Ruiz, Luz Rello, Ismael Sanz
outcome_summary: This paper is primarily a review of causal evidence on computer-assisted learning (CAL) and AI-guided tutoring, emphasizing mathematics gains and the importance of pedagogical design (e.g., hint/scaffolding vs. answer-giving). It also provides secondary, non-ML evidence using PISA 2022 school questionnaire indicators on educational and digital resource shortages (EDUSHORT and digital resource lack/quality reported by principals) for OECD countries near Italy, and it reports descriptive regression results on ChatGPT search intensity in Italian regions using Google Trends as a proxy for AI adoption. The paper does not train or evaluate machine learning models on PISA microdata; consequently, there are no PV-based achievement prediction metrics, no ML model comparison, and no survey-weighted ML estimation procedure. The key implication is that equitable adoption depends on digital infrastructure, school capacity, and teacher support, and that unstructured diffusion risks reinforcing existing inequalities.

title: Decoding Singapore’s Mathematics Mastery: Student and School Predictors of PISA 2022 Performance
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2022 microdata for Singapore (6,482 students from 157 schools) to explain mathematics literacy performance using a two-level hierarchical linear model with student-level and school-level predictors. The authors apply PISA sampling weights and handle missing data via list-wise deletion, while mathematics achievement is represented through plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules across the ten PVs. The intercept-only model shows an ICC of 0.3049, indicating substantial between-school variance; in the full model, between-school variance drops from 3190.6 to 1135 and the model explains 64.25% of between-school variance and 26.04% of within-school variance. Significant positive predictors include DISCLIM, EXPO21ST, MATHEFF, FAMCON, and teachers’ full-time totals, whereas some reasoning-focused cognitive activation and reasoning/21st-century self-efficacy coefficients are negative. Limitations include reliance on self-reported questionnaire measures and the fact that the analysis is multilevel modeling rather than machine-learning prediction, so ML-specific claims about “best models” and predictive accuracy are not applicable.
all_target_variables: Mathematics performance (Plausible Values; Rubin’s rules mean estimate)

title: Scientific creativity in secondary students and its relationship with STEM-related attitudes, engagement and work intentions
authors: I. Pont-Niclòs, A. Martín-Ezpeleta, Y. Echegoyen-Sanz
outcome_summary: This open-access study (2021–2022 academic year) used a convenience sample of 780 Spanish compulsory secondary students from four high schools in the Valencian Community to assess scientific creativity and STEM-related attitudes. Scientific creativity was measured with the Hu et al. (2010) questionnaire, producing two total scores: daily scientific creativity (DSCI) and specific scientific creativity (SSCI), scored via fluidity, flexibility, and originality. STEM attitudes were measured with perceptions and engagement Likert composites adapted from a scientific literacy survey, and career expectations using items from PISA 2015 ST113. The study reports descriptive and non-parametric inferential results (Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis, Spearman correlations) rather than ML prediction; no ML algorithms or PV-based achievement modeling were used. Key results include girls scoring higher on both creativity dimensions, perceptions increasing across levels, engagement and career expectations declining in later levels, and a strong engagement–career expectations correlation (rs=0.5, p<0.001). Limitations include non-probabilistic sampling, no documented missing-data handling, and a cross-sectional design that precludes causal interpretation.

title: Assessing the Linguistic Creativity Domain of Last-Year Compulsory Secondary School Students
outcome_summary: This study used a Spanish convenience sample (N=454) of last-year compulsory secondary students (fourth grade; ages 14–17) to assess linguistic creativity through three paper-based tasks: naming unrelated words (semantic distance percentage), metaphor generation (novel/conventional/literal scoring), and the alternate uses task (PIC-J fluency, flexibility, originality). The analysis did not train or evaluate any machine-learning model; instead, it reports descriptive statistics, gender-group comparisons (t-test/Mann–Whitney U), and Pearson correlations among task scores. Key results include moderate performance on naming unrelated words (M=79.3, SD=4.4) and alternate uses total (M=33.6, SD=16.9), while metaphor generation performance was lower (M=11.2, SD=4.6) with only 7% novel metaphors reported in the discussion. Gender differences were found for metaphor generation (p=0.01, g=0.11) and alternate uses total (p<0.001, g=0.17), but not for naming unrelated words (p=0.34). Correlations were significant between metaphor generation and naming unrelated words (p=0.035) and between metaphor generation and alternate uses (p=0.001), while naming unrelated words and alternate uses were not significantly correlated (p=0.030). Limitations include non-representativeness of the sample and lack of explicit missing-data handling documentation.

title: TRÚ NEMENDA Á EIGIN GETU OG FRAMMISTAÐA Í STÆRÐFRÆÐILÆSI PISA 2022
authors: Berglind Gísladóttir, Jóhann Örn Sigurjónsson, Guðmundur Bjarki Þorgrímsson, Freyja Hreinsdóttir
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2022 mathematics literacy performance for Icelandic 15-year-olds (N=3,364) using regression models with PISA-derived scales for mathematics self-efficacy (MATHEFF), mathematics anxiety (ANXMAT), and teacher support (TEACHSUP), alongside ESCS and gender. The authors report nested-model results: ESCS and gender explain 9% of variance (R²=0.09), adding self-efficacy increases explained variance to 24% (self-efficacy β=0.41, p<0.001), and adding anxiety yields R²=0.26 (anxiety β=-0.13, p<0.001). In the full model, teacher support is statistically significant but weak (β=0.11, p<0.001) and the total explained variance is R²=0.27. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature of PISA (no causal identification) and the absence of a documented missing-data handling strategy and explicit complex-survey weighting for the regression inference.

title: Exploring Validity Evidence for Mathematics Self-Concept of Adolescents: Key Findings from PISA 2022
authors: Onur Ramazan, S. D., R. W. D.
outcome_summary: The study examined validity evidence for a PISA 2022 mathematics self-concept construct using only U.S. students (n=4552). Mathematics self-concept was operationalized as a single relative index item (“Mathematics is easy for me” endorsed more than test language and science), and mathematics motivation was similarly coded as a relative index. Concurrent validity was supported by a significant positive association between self-concept and motivation (χ2 = 86008.920, p < .001; φ = 0.153). Discriminant validity was supported by statistically significant but negligible negative point-biserial correlations with two self-efficacy composites (rpb = -0.078 and -0.073, p < .001). Predictive validity was supported via multilevel modeling that accounted for school clustering using replication weights, showing self-concept predicted mathematics performance PVs (β = 20.20, p < .001). Limitations include single-item indices for motivation and self-concept and the non-causal, correlational nature of validity evidence.

title: ‘No words’—Machine‐learning classified nonverbal immediacy and its role in connecting teacher self‐efficacy with perceived teaching and student interest
authors: Rebecca Lazarides, Jonas Frenkel, Uroš Petković, Richard Göllner, Olaf Hellwich
outcome_summary: The study uses the German TALIS video study (mathematics lessons in grades 8–10) with 50 teachers and 1140 students, excluding 4 teachers due to missing/insufficient video and using longitudinal surveys at Time 1 (pre), Time 3 (post-lesson), and Time 4 (6-week follow-up). Teachers’ nonverbal immediacy (NVI) during the lesson (Time 2) is computed via a multimodal computer-vision pipeline that trains a neural-network-based model; its validation shows agreement with human ratings (ICC = .690). In multilevel path models, teacher self-efficacy for student engagement (TSESE) is positively related to NVI, and student-perceived enthusiastic teaching behaviours are positively associated with students’ mathematics interest immediately after the lesson (Time 3) when controlling for prior interest (β=0.29, p=0.021). For longer-term interest, Time 3 interest predicts Time 4 (β=0.47, p=0.002), with an indirect effect from enthusiastic teaching via Time 3 interest. Limitations include the small classroom-level sample (46 teachers), lack of reported survey-weight usage, and the fact that the ML component supports measurement of NVI rather than causal identification.

title: Predicting STEM competencies with machine learning: identifying key determinants among 522,802 adolescents
authors: Ji Liu, Dahman Tahri, Millicent Aziku
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for 15-year-old students across 66 economies (final analytic sample: 522,802) and constructs STEM competencies by averaging mathematics (AVGMATH) and science (AVGSCIE) achievement, then dichotomizing into high vs low using the global mean threshold. Six supervised ML classifiers (Naïve Bayes, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost) were trained on an 80/20 train/test split with hyperparameter tuning via GridSearchCV and feature selection using XGBoost-based elimination and RFECV, evaluated with Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, and AUC. XGBoost outperformed all alternatives, reaching Accuracy 78.3%, F1 77.7%, and AUC 0.85. The most influential predictors (via SHAP) included home possessions, student employment, gender, cognitive activation for reasoning, and mathematics anxiety, with SHAP interaction suggesting a slight moderation by gender for anxiety effects. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature (no causal inference) and unclear incorporation of PISA complex survey weights in the ML pipeline.

authors: Lazarides, et al.
outcome_summary: The study uses the German TALIS video study (2016–2020 international design; national substudy) with mathematics lessons on quadratic equations taught by 50 teachers and their 1,140 students (Grades 8–10). It develops a computer-vision-based ML algorithm to score teachers’ nonverbal immediacy (NVI) from classroom video, using human ratings of 403 segments (3,056 frames) for training/validation and then applying the validated model to additional segments, yielding 623 segments for analysis. In multilevel three-level manifest modeling, the best-supported pattern is that ML-assessed NVI is positively associated with observer-rated socioemotional support (encouragement and warmth) and with both teacher- and student-reported autonomy support, with significant standardized effects at multiple levels (e.g., Level 3 NVI→socioemotional support β=0.43, p=0.001; NVI→teacher autonomy support β=0.36, p=0.001). By contrast, NVI is not significantly related to positive student–teacher relationships. The analysis is correlational (no causal identification) and the manuscript does not report the use of TALIS complex survey weights; missingness for the third lesson is handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML).

title: A global perspective on school leadership: Evidence from a latent class analysis on OECD TALIS data
authors: Mara Soncin, Tommaso Agasisti
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD TALIS 2013 principal questionnaire data (32 countries; N=9,384 principals after complete-case filtering on six leadership indicators) to build a four-class latent class typology based on instructional and distributed leadership. It then links this leadership typology to PISA 2012 school-average test scores (mathematics, reading, science) for a TALIS–PISA subset of eight countries (N=1,215 schools). The results show no statistically significant differences across leadership classes for mathematics, while reading and science show initial between-class differences in Step 3 (e.g., contingent leaders have higher reading and science averages). However, after adjusting for principal, school, and context covariates (Step 3 post hoc ANCOVA), these differences largely disappear, suggesting that contextual composition mediates the leadership–achievement association. The paper relies on self-reported leadership measures and uses listwise deletion for missing covariate data; it also cautions against generalizing beyond the eight TALIS–PISA link countries.

title: Investigating Mathematics Teachers’ Self-Efﬁcacy
authors: Guangbao, Timothy
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2013 Australian secondary mathematics teachers (ISCED 2), using 495 teachers from 120 secondary schools. It models five constructs (constructivist beliefs, classroom climate, and three self-efficacy subscales) with a measurement model assessed via reliability/validity indices and a structural model estimated using maximum likelihood in SPSS/AMOS. The key results show that constructivist beliefs are not significantly associated with classroom climate (CB→CC = −0.04, t = −0.222), but they are strongly and positively associated with self-efficacy in instruction (CB→EI = 0.88***), classroom management (CB→ECM = 0.72***), and student engagement (CB→ESE = 0.69***). Classroom climate also shows positive associations with all three self-efficacy subscales (ECM: 0.40**; EI: 0.35**; ESE: 0.40**), with R² values of 0.65, 0.88, and 0.61 respectively. Limitations include cross-sectional self-report data (no causal inference) and missing-data handling not being reported; survey weighting is also not documented.

title: Comparative indices of the education quality from the opinions of teachers and principals in TALIS 2018
authors: João Sampaio Maia, Vítor Rosa, Daniela Mascarenhas, Vítor Duarte Teodoro
outcome_summary: This study is a comparative, index-based analysis using TALIS 2018 lower secondary questionnaires administered to teachers and school principals across 48 countries/economies. The authors construct two rule-based country indices—TOI (teachers’ opinions) and POI (principals’ opinions)—by classifying each OECD TALIS indicator as favourable, unfavourable, or neutral and then aggregating these classifications within themes and across TALIS Volumes V1 (learning environment) and V2 (working conditions/well-being). They report quartile-based Top–Bottom groupings and compute Pearson correlations between the TALIS indices and PISA 2018 domain scores (Reading, Mathematics, Science) at the country/economy level. No machine-learning models are trained; instead, the paper uses descriptive comparisons, confidence-interval-based classifications, and correlation statistics. Limitations include the absence of microdata-level weighting/missing-data procedures in the manuscript and the fact that correlations between country-level indices and PISA outcomes do not establish causal relationships.

file_name: Determinants of teachers  positive perception on their professional development experience  an application of LASSO-based machine learning approach.pdf
title: Determinants of teachers’ positive perception on their professional development experience: an appli
authors: Iksang Yoon, Minjung Kim
outcome_summary: The study uses TALIS 2018 U.S. teacher survey data (2,418 teachers in 165 lower-secondary schools) and predicts a dichotomous teacher self-report outcome (TT3G25: whether PD had a positive impact on teaching practice). After excluding teachers who reported no PD participation in the past academic year, the authors fit a LASSO model with 132 candidate predictors spanning teacher characteristics, PD activity features, and school organizational environments. Continuous predictors were standardized to Z-scores, and missing values were handled using EM algorithms before model fitting. The optimal tuning parameter λ was selected via 10-fold cross-validation using binomial deviance, with the final model chosen by the one-standard-error rule (log(λ) = −3.73). The paper reports 16 non-zero predictors and identifies workplace stress as the largest individual-characteristic factor, while perceived positive impact of feedback on teaching practice is the strongest overall predictor; however, no explicit classification performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) are reported, and survey-weighted estimation is not described.

title: Factors affecting teacher job satisfaction: a causal inference machine learning approach using data
authors: Nathan McJames, Andrew Parnell, Nikolaos Fotou, Hamilton Institute, Maynooth University
outcome_summary: The study applies a causal inference machine learning approach (bartCause using Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, BART) to the English subset of TALIS 2018, analyzing 4,385 teachers (2009 primary; 2376 lower secondary). Teacher job satisfaction is measured from eight Likert items and converted into a continuous scale (mean 12.42, SD 2.28). Using BRR-based complex survey weighting, the authors estimate average treatment effects (ATEs) for binary “treatments” including CPD (≥4 events), induction, observing, team teaching, mentoring, public school employment, class size (30+), out-of-field teaching, and part-time contracts (<90%). CPD shows a positive ATE with 95% CI [0.035, 0.309], induction is the strongest positive effect with CI [0.107, 0.329], and part-time contracts reduce job satisfaction with ATE CI [-0.388, -0.044]. For team teaching and observing, confidence intervals include zero, so effects are imprecisely estimated; the paper also imputes missing covariate responses with missRanger (single imputation), and causal claims depend on ignorability/overlap assumptions.

title: Exploring the optimal factors influencing teachers’ instructional practices performance using machine learning approaches

outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher microdata for secondary school teachers in Shanghai, China (3,976 teachers across 198 schools in 16 districts) and operationalizes “Teaching Practices” (T3TPRA) as a binary outcome (above-mean = high instructional practices; below-mean = low). After mode imputation for missing values, the authors apply RFECV-based feature selection and then refine to an optimal set of 10 features using domain knowledge. For prediction, they compare Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), and XGBoost, and interpret the GBM model using SHAP. In model comparison, GBM shows the best stability and competitive test accuracy (GBM test accuracy 0.807 vs RF 0.809 and XGBoost 0.786), while the best 10-feature configuration reaches test accuracy 0.845 with validation mean 0.845 and SD 0.015. The study’s SHAP-based interpretation reflects predictive associations rather than causal effects, and the paper does not clearly document whether imputation and feature selection were nested within cross-validation folds.

title: Kernel Causality in TALIS
authors: Zhang et al.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data for lower secondary schools (ISCED 2) in nine TALIS-PISA-linked countries/economies (Australia, CABA–Argentina, Colombia, Czechia, Denmark, Georgia, Malta, Turkey, Vietnam), using 18,571 teachers across 1,512 schools after initial cleaning. Missing responses are handled with listwise deletion. The authors first fit a multi-group unidimensional nominal response model (mirt) with an empirical histogram approach to accommodate extreme response styles and estimate latent traits via EAP, then compute kernel causality using generalized measures of correlation (GMC) on total scale scores (generalCorr). Across the total sample, kernel causality directions are judged acceptable when P(cause)≥0.7; for example, SC→TSE is unconvinced (P(cause)=0.56) while multiple other directions involving WWS and JS are acceptable (P(cause)=1). The paper does not report survey-weight usage, and kernel causality is not equivalent to experimental causal identification, so cross-country policy conclusions should be treated as directional evidence rather than definitive causal effects.

title: Korean Teachers’ Job Satisfaction Predictors
authors: Yoo, Rho
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2013 Korea data for 2,577 middle school teachers (and 165 principals merged into the candidate predictor set) to predict teacher job satisfaction measured as the mean of 10 Likert-type items (TT2G46A–TT2G46J). After removing variables with ≥50% missingness and dummy-coding categorical items, the authors impute remaining missing values using k-NN (k=41, Gower distance). For modeling and variable selection, they compare penalized group methods—Group Mnet (primary), Group MCP, and Group LASSO—using repeated random 7:3 train/test splits with 10-fold cross-validation on the training set and 100 repetitions. Group Mnet yields RMSE mean 0.393 (SD=0.008), with similar RMSE ranges across methods (≈0.368–0.409). The most consistently selected predictors are teacher feedback/appraisal perceptions, classroom climate items, and participatory/caring school climate items. Limitations include unclear use of TALIS sampling weights and the fact that predictive selection does not imply causality.

title: Teacher policies and teacher labor market outcomes: Results from cross-national comparison
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 lower-secondary teacher questionnaire data from 16 cross-nationally selected countries (53,178 teachers in 3,076 schools) to examine how four typological models of teacher profession regulation (Market, Bureaucratic, Training, Professional skills) relate to teachers’ perceived value of the profession, satisfaction with employment conditions, satisfaction with the profession, satisfaction with the work environment, and intention to quit within 5 years. The authors estimate within-country two-level models using TALIS teacher and school weights (tchwgt and schwgt), extract adjusted country means, and then compare regulation models via ANOVA/ANCOVA in SPSS 29. Key results include a strong regulation effect on work-environment satisfaction (F=18.849, R²=0.825) with the Professional skills model showing lower satisfaction, and significant effects on perceived value and employment-condition satisfaction (F≈3.9, R²≈0.49). The intention-to-quit outcome is restricted to teachers with ≤25 years seniority; main ANOVA is not significant (F=1.704) but ANCOVA indicates higher quitting intentions in the Market model than the Bureaucratic model after controlling for economic status. Limitations include reliance on subjective TALIS measures and the absence of any ML modeling (no predictive algorithms), so findings are about statistical associations rather than causal effects.

outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD TALIS 2018 core teacher data for South Africa, focusing on lower secondary teachers (ISCED 2; N=2046). Using Pearson correlations and hierarchical multiple regression in SPSS, it examines how teacher autonomy, school climate subdimensions (disciplinary climate, teacher-student relations, participation among stakeholders), and teachers’ perceptions of value & policy influence relate to job satisfaction (JSENV, JSPRO, and overall). The results show significant associations for all predictors except disciplinary climate in the abstract’s summary, with autonomy explaining roughly 3–5% of variance and school climate explaining substantially more (about 5–28% depending on the satisfaction dimension). Model fit is reported via R² and incremental ΔR² (e.g., overall satisfaction R²≈0.277 in Model 3). outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for Turkey (n=3,953 teachers; SEM mediation results reported for n=3,500) to test whether principals’ classroom observation feedback (POF) is associated with teachers’ instructional practices (TCP) and whether teacher self-efficacy (TSE) mediates this relationship. Using structural equation modeling in Mplus 7 with 2,000 bootstrap samples, the authors report a small but statistically significant positive direct effect of POF on TCP (β=0.052, p<0.01) and a significant indirect effect through overall TSE (β=0.063, p<0.001), with a total effect of β=0.115 (p<0.001). Model fit indices indicate good fit (e.g., RMSEA≈0.042–0.043; CFI≈0.95–0.96). The mediation-by-dimension results show that only self-efficacy in instruction (SEINS) significantly mediates the relationship, while classroom-management self-efficacy does not. title: A machine learning analysis of school-level drivers of organisational innovativeness
authors: Hayri İncekara, Ahmet Göçen, Mehmet Tufan Yalçın
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD TALIS 2018 principal data from 47 education systems (ISCED Level 2) to predict organisational innovativeness (T3PORGIN), a scale derived from four principal Likert items. After excluding principals with missing T3PORGIN (final N=8,792) and imputing missing predictor values (−99 to NaN) via KNN (k=5) while standardizing predictors, the authors benchmarked six regression ML algorithms using an 80/20 train/test split and 5-fold CV on the training set. XGBoost achieved the best test performance (RMSE=1.7350, MAE=1.3402, R²=0.2929), outperforming LightGBM, Linear Regression, SVR, Random Forest, and a Decision Tree. SHAP was then used to rank influential TALIS items: school climate dominated (e.g., encouraging staff initiatives, mutual support, shared responsibility, community cooperation), principals’ job satisfaction was a strong secondary block, and time shortage with students showed a negative association. The authors caution that the approach is predictive (not causal), uses pooled-sample patterns, and relies on principals’ self-reports; they also do not report applying TALIS sampling weights in the ML pipeline.

title: School accountability and teacher stress: international evidence from the OECD TALIS study
authors: John Jerrim
outcome_summary: This paper uses OECD TALIS 2018 lower-secondary data (teachers and headteachers) and links it to a PISA 2018 headteacher-derived school system accountability scale to study accountability-induced stress across 42 countries. The analysis is correlational (cross-sectional) and relies on multi-level linear probability models for country-level associations and logistic regression models for within-school relationships, with teacher (senate) and BRR replicate weights applied in key pooled models. The main results show a modest positive association between system accountability and both teacher and headteacher stress (correlations ≈0.3; for teachers, +4.2 percentage points per 1 SD accountability increase). Within schools, emotional contagion is strong among peers: a one-category increase in colleagues’ accountability stress corresponds to odds ratios around two for teachers’ own stress. The study finds little overall evidence that senior leaders’ regular use of test scores in appraisals increases stress, and management practices change only weakly when headteachers report accountability stress. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causality), a single-item stress measure, and missing-data handling not reported.

title: A Cross-National Examination of Teachers’ Multicultural Self-Efficacy: Can Multicultural Education in Initial Teacher Education and Professional Development Make a Difference?
authors: Qin Mou
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for lower secondary teachers who had previously taught in culturally diverse classrooms, excluding Russia, Spain, and Iceland and removing teachers with incomplete responses. Multilevel modeling was used with teachers nested within countries, and TMSE was measured via five Likert items (composited into a mean scale). In Model A, teacher self-efficacy (TSE) showed a strong positive association with TMSE (β = 0.473, p < .001) with a pseudo R2 of 40%, yet 60% of TMSE variance remained unexplained, supporting TMSE as distinct from general efficacy. In Model B, multicultural education in initial teacher education (ITE) and professional development (PD) were both positively related to TMSE (β = 0.129 and 0.123, respectively, p < .001), but the combined explained variance was small (pseudo R2 ≈ 7.14%). The paper uses listwise deletion for missing values and does not report any survey-weight or PV handling because the outcomes are questionnaire composites rather than PV-based achievement scores; additionally, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 (lower secondary teachers; TMSE scale from 5 items)

title: Effects of Teacher Collaboration on Teaching Practices in China and England: A Structural Equation Model With TALIS 2018 Data
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for China (Shanghai) and England, focusing on lower-secondary teachers and modeling three teaching-practice latent constructs: clarity of instruction (CLAIN), cognitive activation (COGAC), and classroom assessment (ASS). The authors estimate confirmatory factor models and a structural equation model using maximum likelihood with robust standard errors in Mplus 7.4, and test mediation via bootstrap confidence intervals (Hayes, 2009). Across both countries, teacher self-efficacy is positively associated with all three teaching-practice subscales (e.g., SELF→CLAIN b=.399 in China; b=.553 in England). Professional collaboration shows significant indirect effects on all three teaching practices through self-efficacy in both countries (e.g., COLES→COGAC via SELF: b=.093 in China; b=.104 in England), while exchange/co-ordination has more mixed direct and no indirect mediation effects. Limitations include the absence of reported missing-data handling and unclear use of TALIS complex-survey weights, so results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

title: Distributed Leadership as a Catalyst for Change: Building Emotional Capital to Enhance Teachers' Beliefs in AI-Integrated Teaching
authors: Jihe Chen, Myduyen Dang, Mengting Zhang
outcome_summary: The study uses TALIS 2024 teacher survey data from Vietnam (junior high/secondary teachers), excluding missing responses to obtain 1,423 valid cases out of 4,348 teachers. It tests a chain mediation model grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, with distributed leadership predicting teachers’ AI teaching beliefs directly and indirectly via teacher stress and enjoyment of teaching. The structural paths show distributed leadership positively predicts AI beliefs (β=0.121, p<0.001) and enjoyment of teaching (β=0.228, p<0.001), while teacher stress does not significantly predict AI beliefs (β=0.026, p=0.383). Mediation results from PROCESS (Model 6, 5,000 bootstrap iterations) indicate the indirect effect through enjoyment is significant (DL→ET→AI beliefs: Effect=0.0644; CI excludes 0), whereas the stress-only mediation is not (DL→TS→AI beliefs CI includes 0). Limitations include the absence of explicit TALIS sampling-weight reporting and the fact that the analysis is not an ML predictive pipeline with PVs.

title: How to square the circle of voluntary participation in controlled samples?
authors: Kristine Kampmane, S and van Staden, A Ozola
outcome_summary: This paper is a mixed-methods follow-up study to TALIS 2024 in Latvia, focusing on how voluntary teacher participation can be achieved under school-level participation requirements. It reports participation dynamics using coordinator-reported teacher participation categories (early birds, late comers, non-respondents) and compares perceptions across groups of schools and teachers with different participation patterns. Quantitatively, it finds that 17% of teachers responded in the first week, 4% in the last week, and 10% did not log into the survey system; reminders were associated with up to a 4% increase in completed questionnaires. It also reports that voluntary participation correlates positively with immediate participation (correlation 0.6, p<0.001) and that postponement with increasing reminders is negatively associated with voluntary participation (correlation −0.6, p<0.001). The study uses descriptive statistics, correlations, and Mann–Whitney U tests, with pairwise deletion for missing values, and does not train or evaluate machine learning models or PV-based achievement outcomes.

title: Peculiarities of the higher education development in a blended learning environment
authors: Pavlo CHERVONYI, Svitlana ALIEKSIEIEVA, Nadiia SENCHYLO-TATLILIOGLU, Oleksandr CHASTNYK, Nataliia DIOMIDOVA
outcome_summary: This paper analyzes secondary TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data for France and the Netherlands to describe higher education teachers’ reported inclusion of blended-learning-relevant components and ICT skills in formal education and professional development, and to examine associations among these questionnaire components. The study reports descriptive proportions (e.g., 50.0% report inclusion of blended-learning teaching components in formal education; 48.4% report inclusion of ICT use elements in further learning activities; 28.9% are “not at all” ready and 36.6% “somewhat” ready for ICT use in teaching). It also reports Pearson correlation results at the 1% level, including a strong negative association between formal education components in blended learning and teachers’ readiness for blended learning (−0.626) and between teacher preparation for ICT use and readiness for ICT use (−0.646). No machine learning models are trained or evaluated; therefore, there are no predictive performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) to report. Limitations include the absence of documented missing-data handling and the lack of explicit survey-weight usage in the analysis.
all_datasets_used: TALIS 2018 teacher survey data were used for France

title: The future of intelligence: A prediction of the FLynn effect based on past student assessment studies until the year 2100
authors: Heiner Rindermann, David Becker
outcome_summary: This paper predicts societal cognitive development (expressed as IQ on a Greenwich-IQ scale) up to 2100 by using past international student achievement results from TIMSS (1995–2019; grades 4 and 8; mathematics and science), PISA (2000–2018; reading, mathematics, science), and PIRLS (2001–2016; reading). The authors convert published study means to a common IQ scale, compute decadal gains via trend subtraction, and estimate country-specific linear (y=a+bx) and nonlinear quadratic (y=a+bx+cx²) regressions using up to 14 measurement years (1995–2019) where available. Across 79 countries, the worldwide corrected mean IQ increases from 91.29 (2020) to 93.51 (2030), 95.69 (2050), and 101.25 (2100), with an average decadal gain of 1.25 IQ points. Model choice strongly affects extremity: nonlinear predictions yield much larger dispersion (uncorrected SD 229.78 vs corrected SD 95.43), and outlier correction substantially reduces implausible values. Limitations include the absence of student-level ML modeling, no PV-based uncertainty quantification, and reliance on extrapolation assumptions that the authors themselves flag as likely to fail over long horizons.

file_name: Rutkowski et al. - 2024 - The limits of inference reassessing causality in international assessments.pdf
title: The limits of inference: reassessing causality in international assessments
authors: David Rutkowski, Leslie Rutkowski, Greg Thompson, Yusuf Canbolat
outcome_summary: This paper is not an empirical ML or causal-estimation study using ILSA microdata; it is a methodological critique and framework-oriented review. It argues that the observational, cross-sectional, and standardized nature of ILSA data makes strong causal inference difficult, even when quasi-experimental designs (e.g., difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, fixed effects) are used. The authors juxtapose examples of quasi-experimental studies that can approximate causal reasoning with RCT-like assumptions against ILSA-based applications that face limitations such as non-exogenous treatment exposure across countries, threats to the parallel trends/equivalence-in-expectation condition, and ambiguity in defining treatments and outcomes across heterogeneous contexts. The paper emphasizes that causal claims require stringent, often untestable assumptions and that standardization can mask heterogeneity, limiting policy interpretation. Because no model training, PV handling, weighting, or missing-data strategy is executed in the paper itself, no predictive performance metrics are reported.

file_name: The  Non Impact of Differential Test Taker Engagement on Aggregated Scores.pdf
title: (The (Non)Impact of Differential Test Taker Engagement on Aggregated Scores)
outcome_summary: This study analyzes pilot computer-based PISA-Based Test for Schools (PBTS) data administered to 5,091 U.S. students (15-year-olds) across 84 schools, using response-time-based engagement measures. Engagement is operationalized via response behavior effort (RBE), defined as the proportion of item responses classified as solution behaviors using response-time thresholds; the study also computes effort-moderated PBTS scores and a distortion score (standard minus effort-moderated) to quantify rapid-guessing-related score distortion. Results show that school-level mean engagement and mean performance are strongly positively correlated (r = 0.56–0.72 by subject), yet effort-moderated scoring produces almost no net shift in school means: standard versus effort-moderated school performance correlations are near-perfect (r > 0.999). A random-intercept multilevel robustness check indicates very small between-school variance in distortion (ICC up to 0.007 in reading), implying that differential disengagement has marginal impact on aggregated scores. The paper does not use machine learning models and does not report PV handling or a missing-data strategy, so findings are best interpreted as evidence about score robustness under low-stakes disengagement rather than predictive performance.

title: A Theoretical Framework for a Mathematical Cognitive Model for Adaptive Learning Systems
authors: S.S., X.W., T.X.
outcome_summary: This paper is a theoretical/methodological construction of a mathematical cognitive model for cognitive diagnostic assessment and adaptive learning systems, grounded in the TIMSS cognitive framework. It does not train predictive machine-learning models on TIMSS student microdata; instead, it uses interpretive structural modeling (ISM) to convert expert judgments about relationships among 16 TIMSS 2015 cognitive attributes into a hierarchical, five-level cognitive model. The model is revised using additional expert input and then qualitatively checked via a verbal report from a single fourth-grade student on two extracted TIMSS items. The study reports no ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, RMSE, AUC) and no PV-based achievement estimation, so there are no benchmark comparisons. Limitations include reliance on expert calibration rather than longitudinal student data and limited generalizability beyond mathematical problem-solving processes.

title: Factors Influencing Students’ Achievements in the Content and Cognitive Domains in TIMSS 4th Grade Science and Mathematics in the United Arab Emirates
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2015 grade 4 secondary data for the UAE (21,177 students; 558 schools) to examine how student factors relate to mathematics and science achievement in both content and cognitive domains. The authors analyze PV-based outcomes using TIMSS’s PV framework and Jackknife Repeated Replication (JRR) with sampling weights, and they handle missingness via listwise deletion. In multiple linear regression, mathematics achievement shows R² = 0.12, with student confidence in math (b=41.07) and engaging teaching in math (b=11.5) as strong positive predictors, while bullying (b=-13.10) is strongly negative. For science, R² = 0.16, with student confidence in science (b=43.40) and liking science (b=21.57) positive and bullying (b=-16.69) negative. SEM results indicate weak/poor model fit (SRMR around 0.40–0.43), and the study is correlational (no causal identification), so policy should be framed as associations rather than effects.

title: Large-scale Assessments in Education
authors: Duggan, Karakolidis, et al.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes inequality in mathematics and science achievement for 4th-grade students in Ireland using TIMSS 2011, TIMSS 2015, and TIMSS 2019. The outcomes are TIMSS IRT-based achievement scale scores summarized via five plausible values, and the study operationalizes inequality of achievement using changes in mean performance, standard deviations, and between-school variance (ICC), while inequality of opportunity is assessed via the strength of associations between achievement and socioeconomic indicators. Across 2011–2015, average mathematics increased by 20 score points and science by 13, alongside reduced standard deviations and lower between-school variance (e.g., mathematics between-school variance from 17.7% to 10.2%; science from 21.3% to 13.9%), indicating reduced inequality of achievement. From 2015–2019, average performance was stable, but inequality of achievement increased slightly (standard deviation increased significantly in science). For opportunity, home resources for learning and school DEIS status were statistically significant predictors in all cycles, and the combined variance explained by these factors increased from 2011 to 2019 (science: overall R² 16.8% to 20.2%; mathematics: 16.3% to 17.6%). Methodologically, the paper uses multilevel regression (not ML prediction), applies complex survey weights in univariate/bivariate analyses and at both levels in multilevel models, and uses FIML to handle missing home resources for learning data; therefore, results describe associations and variance decomposition rather than causal effects.

file_name: Brit J of Edu Psychol - 2023 - Ellis - International comparisons of the home mathematics environment and relations with.pdf
title: International comparisons of the home mathematics environment and relations with children's mathematical achievement
authors: Alexa Ellis, Jimena Cosso, Robert J. Duncan, María Inés Susperreguy, Victoria Simms, David J. Purpura
outcome_summary: This study used TIMSS 2019 fourth-grade data and the TIMSS Early Learning Survey (ELS) to examine the home mathematics environment (HME) across 54 countries, focusing on a nine-item retrospective HME subset. Parents reported the frequency of specific home activities before children began primary/elementary school, and children’s mathematics achievement was measured at fourth grade using an IRT scaling approach with five plausible values. The authors used IEA IDB Analyzer to account for TIMSS sampling design, sampling weights, and plausible values, then computed country-level descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and Pearson correlations. The HME scale showed acceptable internal consistency in all countries (Mα=.79; range .73–.89) while HME frequency varied substantially (e.g., Morocco vs Northern Ireland). The overall HME–achievement association was small but positive (r=.15), with strong cross-country differences (Turkey r=.41 vs Georgia r=.02). Limitations include reliance on retrospective parent reports and correlational (not causal) interpretation.

file_name: Enhancing students  reasoning skills by asking students to provide evidence-based explanations in science classrooms  findings from TIMSS 2019.pdf
title: Enhancing students’ reasoning skills by asking students to provide evidence-based explanations in science classrooms findings from TIMSS 2019
authors: Risa Haridza, Lin Ding
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science data from the United States, linking 8739 students to 456 science teachers across 273 schools. Student performance on TIMSS reasoning questions serves as the outcome, while teachers’ questionnaire responses capture how often they ask students to provide evidence-based explanations; teacher professional development (PD) and school science resource shortage are used to explain and moderate these practices. The authors use multilevel modeling (random-intercept HLM; multilevel logistic regression for ordinal teacher responses) and apply multiple imputation for missing questionnaire data (4.6% student, 15.7% teacher). Key results show that more frequent evidence-based explanation prompts are positively associated with higher student reasoning scores (γ01=12.84, p<.001), and that PD focused on science content and pedagogy—especially longer PD duration—predicts higher teacher use of these prompts. The study is correlational and relies on questionnaire measures, so causal effects and specific PD mechanisms cannot be confirmed.
