file_name: J Res Sci Teach - 2024 - Ogegbo - Factors predicting teachers  implementation of inquiry‐based teaching practices  Analysis.pdf
title: Factors predicting teachers' implementation of inquiry‐based teaching practices: Analysis of South African TIMSS 2019 data from an ecological perspective
authors: Ayodele Abosede Ogegbo, Umesh Ramnarain, Joseph Krajcik
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 South Africa teacher contextual questionnaire data for Grade 9 science teachers (n = 537) to model teachers’ inquiry teaching practice using the Teachers Emphasize Science Investigation (ESI) scale. The outcome is teacher-reported frequency of inquiry activities (4-point Likert), and the analysis fits a weighted hierarchical multiple regression that controls for classroom science achievement using five plausible values. Across nested ecological layers (intrapersonal, microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem), the final model explains 29.3% of the variance in inquiry teaching practice (R2 = 0.293; F(18,253) = 5.838; p < 0.001). The strongest final predictors are teachers’ perceptions of the significance of assessment strategies (β = 0.316, p < 0.001), followed by inquiry-related professional development (β = 0.152, p = 0.006), instructional resource shortage (β = 0.148, p = 0.015), and job satisfaction (β = 0.127, p = 0.037). Limitations include non-experimental design (no causal inference) and reliance on self-reported perceptions rather than observed classroom inquiry quality.

file_name: Overcrowded Classrooms and their Association with South African Learners  Mathematics Achievement.pdf
title: Overcrowded Classrooms and their Association with South African Learners’ Mathematics Achievement
authors: Marien Alet Graham
outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of TIMSS 2019 for South Africa at Grade 9 mathematics, using the TIMSS mathematics plausible values (five PVs) and analyzing associations between class size/overcrowding perceptions and mathematics achievement. Quantitatively, mathematics achievement shows a negative association with class size (BTBG10 correlation r = -0.247, p < 0.001). In group comparisons based on teacher agreement with the statement “There are too many learners in the class” (BTB09A), learners taught by teachers who “agree a lot” scored 34.58 points lower on average than the “disagree a lot” reference group (|t| = 3.15). Qualitatively, interviews in 2020–2021 (eight schools; six principals and 24 teachers) suggest mechanisms including limited individualized interaction, didactic neglect, and time management challenges. Limitations include non-experimental design (no causal identification) and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling and whether complex survey weights were explicitly applied.

file_name: Reassessing urban-rural education disparities  evidence from England.pdf
title: Reassessing urban-rural education disparities: evidence from England
outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 data for England (N=3,365 students across 136 schools) to reassess urban–rural education disparities in mathematics and science. It creates an urban vs rural school geography grouping and a third “missing” group for students whose schools did not respond to the school questionnaire; missing real-valued variables are mean-imputed and missing parental education is handled via an “unknown” category. Achievement outcomes are TIMSS plausible values for math and science, and the regression models use OLS with stepwise forward entry of student background controls followed by a rural-school indicator. The rural-school indicator shows a negative association with achievement in both domains, with small explanatory power: adjusted R-square increases from 0.191 to 0.198 in math (rural coefficient = -0.083) and from 0.202 to 0.206 in science (rural coefficient = -0.050). The study is cross-sectional and does not report design-weighted estimation, so results should be interpreted as correlational rather than causal.

title: Associations Between School Climate and Student Mathematics Achievement: A Multilevel Structural Equation Modeling Approach
outcome_summary: The study analyzed TIMSS 2019 U.S. eighth-grade data (N=7589 students in 235 schools) to examine how nine school-climate factors at both student and school levels relate to mathematics achievement using multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM). The mathematics outcome used five TIMSS plausible values (BSMMAT01–BSMMAT05) and the final MSEM showed good fit (CFI=0.964, TLI=0.961, RMSEA=0.018; within-level SRMR=0.055). At the student level, school belonging and safety (b*=0.192, p<0.001) and mathematics class climate (b*=0.090, p=0.014) were positively associated with achievement, while bullying was negatively associated both directly (b*=-0.087, p=0.001) and indirectly via belonging/safety (b*=-0.072, p<0.001) and class climate (b*=-0.026, p=0.020). At the school level, shortages of mathematics resources (b*=-0.320, p=0.011) and school discipline and safety problems (b*=-0.183, p=0.030) were negatively associated, whereas teacher/parent/student characteristics and school support were not significant. Because the design is cross-sectional and mediation is not time-ordered, the results indicate associations rather than causal effects.

title: Fostering Self-efficacy: Understanding South African Grade 9 Students’ Confidence in their Mathematics Abilities
authors: Sylvia Hannan, Andrea Juan, Jaqueline Harvey
outcome_summary: This open-access study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 9 mathematics data for South Africa (20,829 students from 524 schools) to examine how mathematics self-efficacy relates to mathematics achievement and which contextual factors are associated with self-efficacy. The authors use the IEA International Database Analyser (v5) to account for the complex sampling design and plausible values methodology; mathematics achievement is reported on a common scale centered at 500 with a standard deviation of 100 and is based on five plausible values. In multiple regression, the model explains 15% of the variation in mathematics achievement (adjusted R2 = 0.15), and self-efficacy is reported as significantly and positively associated with achievement even after controlling for age, SES, instructional clarity, and home experiences. For self-efficacy, instructional clarity and parents checking homework show positive associations, while females report lower self-efficacy after controls. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (directionality cannot be established) and the lack of an explicit missing-data handling description.

title: The Relationship Between Weekly Instruction, Homework Time and Students’ Competences
authors: Luis Alejandro Lopez-Agudo, Marcenaro-Gutierrez
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 fourth-grade mathematics and science data for 58 countries (N=276,512) to test whether one additional weekly hour of instruction time and homework time is associated with students’ competences. Using student fixed-effects within-students between-subjects differencing (and constructing standardized cognitive scores from students’ actual responses to avoid bias from TIMSS imputed scores), the authors estimate country-specific effects in SD units per +1 hour. Results in Table 1 show that instruction time is non-significant in most countries (44/58) with coefficients ranging from −0.088 (Armenia) to 0.126 (Poland), while homework time is non-significant in most countries (40/58) with coefficients ranging from −0.037 (Qatar) to 0.166 (England). The paper applies TIMSS recommended sampling weights and jackknife replication for standard errors, but it does not provide a comprehensive missing-data handling protocol beyond excluding students with missing teacher time information. The fixed-effects approach reduces confounding from time-invariant student factors, yet the authors caution against strong causal interpretation.

title: Large-scale Assessments in Education
outcome_summary: This study evaluates AI-based automated scoring for six short TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 science constructed-response items using multilingual student responses from eight countries. Responses are translated into English with either Google Translate or ChatGPT, then converted into a common BoW feature matrix after NLP preprocessing (tokenization, lower-casing, spelling correction, stemming), and scored with a fully-connected feed-forward neural network trained on an 80/20 train/test split with cross-validation on the training set. The authors select ChatGPT as the preferred translation engine based on higher log odds ratio (LOR) for human-machine exact match. For automated scoring using ChatGPT-translated responses, machine scores show strong agreement with human scores: average F1=0.88 and average Cohen’s kappa=0.80, with a small standardized mean score difference (SMD=-0.04). The paper reports item-level weaknesses (notably Item 5 and Item 6 in C6) and does not describe missing-data handling or any survey-weighted analysis, limiting generalizability beyond the constructed evaluation sample.

title: Investigating the Performance of Artificial Neural Networks in Predicting Affective Responses
authors: Aydoğan, İ., Tat, O.
outcome_summary: The study trains artificial neural networks on PISA 2018 Lebanese Awacom (intercultural communicative awareness) item responses to predict two held-out items (Item3 and Item7) from the other six items, after listwise deletion of cases with missing and extreme values (final N=4631). For Item3, the selected single-hidden-layer ANN (Model1) achieved RMSE ≈ 0.619 (all) and ≈ 0.623 (test), with moderate agreement between predicted and actual responses (match ratio 0.63; Kappa 0.42). For Item7, the best ANN (ModelB) showed weaker predictive correspondence (RMSE test ≈ 0.734; match ratio 0.58; Kappa 0.37). Although similarity metrics were only moderate/low, CFA-based validity and reliability analyses indicated that using predicted items with the remaining items improved factor loadings, explained variance, and Cronbach’s alpha, while fit indices were somewhat weakened. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights, and the ANN predictions are evaluated on response overlap and psychometric consequences rather than PV-based achievement.

file_name: 100. Ulitzsch et al. (2021). Combining Clickstream Analyses And Graph-Modeled Data Clustering For Identifying Common Response Processes.pdf
title: Combining Clickstream Analyses and Graph-Modeled Data Clustering for Identifying Common Response Processes
authors: Esther Ulitzsch, et al.
outcome_summary: This paper proposes a two-step exploratory framework for identifying common response processes in interactive assessment tasks by combining clickstream-style action-sequence similarity with graph-modeled clustering (cluster edge deletion). Applied to PIAAC 2012 PSTRE item U01a (US), the authors analyzed a random subset of N=225 correct-response examinees and compared three similarity measures: action-only, a modified time-related measure aggregating timing over the LCS, and the original time-sensitive measure. Incorporating action-level times produced less dense similarity graphs (more edge deletions) and more/smaller cliques, indicating finer differentiation of response processes. For external validation, the authors used PSTRE PV means descriptively: dominant processes based only on performed actions were not predictive of proficiency levels, while within strategy groups, less time on the most common LCS and age-related timing patterns aligned with higher proficiency. The study does not report survey-weight usage or a missing-data handling strategy for the PV-based descriptive comparisons.

file_name: 101. Tang et al. (2021). An exploratory analysis of the latent structure of process data via action sequence.pdf
title: An exploratory analysis of the latent structure of process data via action sequence autoencoders
authors: Xueying Tang, Zhi Wang, Jingchen Liu, Zhiliang Ying
outcome_summary: This paper proposes an action sequence autoencoder to extract latent features from PIAAC 2012 PSTRE action sequences (11,464 respondents; 14 items). The autoencoder (with RNN components using LSTM or GRU) compresses variable-length categorical action sequences into fixed-dimensional features, followed by logistic/linear regression for prediction tasks. In the case study, the extracted features reconstructed 93 derived binary variables with prediction accuracy >0.80 for all variables, >0.90 for 75, and >0.975 for 35. Cross-item prediction showed that process features improved out-of-sample outcome prediction, especially for incorrect-response processes. For competency-related targets, process models outperformed baseline models for literacy and numeracy (higher OSR2) and improved gender prediction accuracy (up to ~0.63) and age prediction (about 2× baseline OSR2 with all 14 items). The manuscript does not report a missing-data strategy and does not document the use of PIAAC survey weights; additionally, the study is predictive rather than causal.

file_name: 119. Cortes et al. (2025). Evaluating uncertainty: the impact of the sampling and assessment design on statistical inference in the context of ILSA.pdf

outcome_summary: This paper is not an ML prediction/classification study; it develops and applies a design-effect framework to decompose design-based uncertainty in ILSA inference. The authors find that for mean achievement, the sampling design effect is often substantially larger than the assessment design effect, but this difference is context dependent (e.g., assessment design effects can exceed sampling design effects in some populations). The paper emphasizes correct variance estimation by combining sampling variance (via JRR) and measurement variance (via plausible values / random multiple imputation) rather than shortcut methods such as using a single plausible value or ignoring complex sampling.

title: Rethinking TIMSS quality assurance: utilizing neural network models with regression‑based bias mitigation strategies for validating country‑level math and science achievement scores

outcome_summary: This study develops and pilots two TIMSS-specific quality assurance indicators that use neural networks plus regression-based bias mitigation to predict country-level Grade 8 mean achievement and compute residuals for screening. It reports an emerging field with exponential growth in publications and citations, identifies leading authors and core journals, and characterizes collaboration networks among authors and countries using co-authorship analyses. The study finds that PISA receives the greatest attention in the literature and that research themes cluster around measurement/testing, educational policy and reform, education quality/effectiveness, equity/inequality, interpersonal relationships, and motivation/beliefs. Methodologically, it relies on bibliometric and social network mapping (Bibliometrix and VOSviewer) rather than predictive ML on student outcomes, so there are no model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) for ML learners.

file_name: 70. Maia et al. (2023). Applications of Artificial Intelligence Models in Educational Analytics and Decision Making: A Systematic Review.pdf
title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence Models in Educational Analytics and Decision Making: A Systematic Review
authors: J. de S. Z. Maia, A. P. A. Bueno, J. R. Sato, A. P. A. Bueno, J. R. Sato
outcome_summary: As a systematic review, the paper does not train or evaluate machine learning models on an original student-level dataset, so no predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, RMSE, AUC) are reported for this review itself. Instead, it reports bibliometric and synthesis results across 70 included studies, including publication trends (peak around 2020), the most frequent dataset origins (e.g., PISA/TIMSS), the most common education levels (elementary most frequent), and the most common AI model families (classificatory models, deep learning/neural networks, regression, and decision-tree-based approaches). It also discusses interpretability concerns (black-box issue) and highlights model-interpretation techniques such as LIME and SHAP as discussed in the included literature. Methodologically, the review’s evidence base is limited by the inclusion criteria (English-only, title/abstract keyword restriction) and by the fact that it synthesizes heterogeneous studies rather than estimating a unified model.

file_name: 71. Huang et al. (2025). The Application of Machine Learning to Educational Process Data Analysis: A Systematic Review.pdf
title: The Application of Machine Learning to Educational Process Data Analysis: A Systematic Review
authors: J. Huang, Y. P. X., H. H. C.
outcome_summary: This paper is a systematic review rather than an empirical ML study on a single dataset. It synthesizes 38 peer-reviewed publications (2013–2024) and reports descriptive findings about the types of educational process data used (clickstream most prevalent) and how ML is applied (procedural feature coding/representation learning vs. instrumental latent-trait/measurement estimation). The review also highlights recurring challenges such as feature extraction/selection and interpretability for practical educational use, and discusses issues like scalability and replicability. No model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are computed by the authors in this review because they do not train or evaluate ML models on a pooled dataset.

file_name: 72. Teig. (2024). Uncovering Student Strategies for Solving Scientific Inquiry Tasks: Insights from Student Process Data in PISA.pdf
title: Uncovering Student Strategies for Solving Scientific Inquiry Tasks: Insights from Student Process Data in PISA
authors: Nani Teig
outcome_summary: This paper demonstrates how PISA process-log data can be used to uncover students’ scientific inquiry strategies by combining product information (response accuracy) with process indicators (exploration behavior, inquiry strategy, and response time). In Example 1 (PISA 2015 Norway field trial, Task 1; N=81), process mining visualized distinct action sequences and showed that although many students used the VOTAT strategy, only about 40.7% of those using VOTAT solved the task correctly; successful students tended to show goal-oriented exploration with higher exploration quantity and longer time before first action and time-on-task. In Example 2 (PISA 2015 Norway, Task 2; N=1222), latent profile analysis identified three profiles (strategic, emergent, disengaged) that differed in interactive strategy use and process-time/exploration patterns, and MANOVA indicated significant associations between profile membership and several inquiry-based teaching/learning practices (notably class debate). The study does not report PV-based achievement modeling or survey-weight usage, and it does not provide explicit missing-data handling details despite stating that preprocessing addressed missingness.

file_name: 74. Ding et al. (2025). Evaluating test-taking motivation based on process data and its influence on academic performance.pdf
title: Evaluating test-taking motivation based on process data and its influence on academic performance
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 science process data from two fixed clusters (S01 and S02; 38 items) to construct a new “behavioral effort” indicator from eight standardized process measures (time to last visit, time to first action, number of actions, and user missingness, separated for MC and CR items). After excluding 28 students with missing target-item responses or total reaction time >3600 s, the analytic sample contained 2853 students from Confucian and Western culture groups. Behavioral effort was validated against self-reported effort and response time effort (RTE) and then used in multilevel regression models predicting science academic performance (PISA PV1). All three effort measures (behavioral effort, self-reported effort, RTE) significantly and positively predicted performance, with behavioral effort showing the largest effect (Est.=87.338, p<0.001, d=1.083). Cultural moderation was significant for behavioral effort and self-reported effort but not for RTE (p=0.083). The paper uses multilevel modeling with PISA sampling weights, but it does not evaluate ML predictive algorithms; thus, “ML techniques” are not applicable here.

file_name: 76. Guo et al. (2024). Human-Centered AI for Discovering Student Engagement Profiles on Large-Scale Educational Assessments.pdf
title: Human-Centered AI for Discovering Student Engagement Profiles on Large-Scale Educational Assessments
authors: Guo, H., Johnson, M., Saldivia, L., Worthington, M., Ercikan, K.
outcome_summary: The study proposes a human-centered AI (HAI) framework to create student engagement profiles by integrating NAEP Grade 8 Mathematics digital process/log data with response information from a single 2022 released item block (14 items). After excluding students with irregular response time and abnormal completion, the analytic sample comprised 14,008 students from the USA. In Step 2, an autoencoder with LSTM compresses sequential navigation/response-time information into a latent space, and K-means clustering supports human annotation of ten preliminary engagement profiles. In Step 3, an active learning semi-supervised loop trains an ensemble voting classifier combining a random forest and an SVC to assign profiles to unlabeled students, using pseudo-label confidence thresholds (e.g., >0.75). The paper reports profile proportions and qualitative descriptors but does not provide standard predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC), and it does not describe a missing-data handling strategy or PV-based achievement handling.

file_name: 78. Salles et al. (2025). When didactics meet data science: process data analysis in large‑scale mathematics assessment in France.pdf
title: When didactics meet data science: process data analysis in large‑scale mathematics assessment in France
authors: Salles, et al.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes CEDRE (France) grade 9 pilot data from May 2017 for one technology-enhanced interactive mathematics item (“Tree growth”), using engineered aggregates from students’ log files. For supervised learning, the authors trained a Random Forest classifier to predict whether the student’s response was correct, reporting ROC AUC = 0.78; the item success rate was 47.3%. Feature-importance results indicate that the number of tested values and the variance of tested values around the target are the most informative, followed by distances from early inputs to the target and alternation behavior (trial-and-error vs. targeted search). In parallel, unsupervised clustering (DBSCAN, with k-means used for stability comparison) yields four student profiles that separate success/failure and two strategic approaches: an operational “trial and error” profile and a structural “pencil-assisted, concentrated inputs” profile. A key limitation is that the model cannot explain achievement beyond the item’s correctness label, and the manuscript does not document missing-data handling for log-derived features or any complex-survey weighting strategy.

file_name: 80. Peters et al. (2025). Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review.pdf
title: Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review
outcome_summary: This systematic review synthesizes 37 articles (46 studies) on text-based item difficulty prediction in large-scale assessment contexts. Across the reviewed literature, item difficulty was most often modeled as continuous outcomes using CTT p-values or transformed p-values, and less often using IRT b parameters or categorical difficulty levels. The review reports benchmark ranges for model performance across heterogeneous datasets and metrics: RMSE as low as 0.165 and Pearson correlation as high as 0.87, with exact accuracy up to 0.806 for classification settings. The review also finds that richer inputs (e.g., item stem plus answer and distractors) and larger training sets generally improve performance, while hand-crafted linguistic features remain competitive despite the rise of transformer-based language models. Methodological caveats include heterogeneity of datasets and evaluation criteria, overrepresentation of BEA/USMLE shared-task studies, and under-reporting of data preprocessing in many primary studies.

file_name: 82. Costa & Chen. (2023). Exploring the relationship between process data and contextual variables among Scandinavian students on PISA 2012 mathematics tasks.pdf
title: Exploring the relationship between process data and contextual variables among Scandinavian students on PISA 2012 mathematics tasks
authors: Denise Reis Costa, Chia-Wen Chen
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics (CBAM) log-file process indicators and questionnaire context for three items (CM015Q01, CM015Q02D, CM015Q03D) from Denmark, Sweden, and Norway (final N=1426). A three-factor CFA model linking response accuracy, log response time, and log frequency of actions fit well (CFI=0.982, TLI=0.957, RMSEA=0.052, SRMR=0.028), and weak measurement invariance across countries was preferred, supporting meaningful cross-country comparisons. In the multigroup latent regression, ESCS showed a consistent positive association with math proficiency across all three countries, while ICT related negatively to math performance in Denmark and showed no effect on the latent factors in Sweden and Norway for some outcomes. Experience with pure mathematics tasks at school predicted higher achievement and more interaction with the platform in Sweden and Norway, and Norway showed no gender differences in proficiency, speed, or exploration. The paper is cross-sectional, so causal claims are not warranted; additionally, the extraction schema does not treat PVs as applicable because the outcomes are item-level accuracy and process indicators rather than PV-based achievement scores.

file_name: 83. Murchan & Siddiq. (2021). A call to action: a systematic review of ethical and regulatory issues in using process data in educational assessment.pdf
title: A call to action: a systematic review of ethical and regulatory issues in using process data in educational assessment
authors: Damian Murchan, Fiona Siddiq
outcome_summary: This paper is a systematic review (not an ML modeling study) examining how ethical, privacy, and regulatory considerations are addressed in research using process/log data in educational assessment. Across 22 eligible studies (from an initial 1349 screened records), the authors find a dearth of work that explicitly and clearly addresses ethics/privacy in K-12 assessment contexts (only three K-12-relevant studies met the initial criteria). Using a modified Sclater (2016) code of practice with eight categories, they report that ethics-related issues feature minimally overall, with comparatively higher attention to Privacy, Transparency & consent, Enabling interventions, and Minimising adverse impact. The review highlights gaps in responsibility/administration of data and in access rights, and argues for developing a bespoke code of ethics for process/log data in educational assessment.

file_name: 84. Gong et al. (2023). Using process features to investigate scientific problem-solving in large-scale assessments.pdf
title: Using process features to investigate scientific problem-solving in large-scale assessments
authors: Tao Gong, L. Shuai, Y. Jiang, B. Arslan
outcome_summary: This open-access study analyzes NAEP 2018 science pilot computer-based scientific inquiry tasks (two fair tests and two exhaustive tests) to determine whether process timestamps relate to rubric-based item scores. The authors define three temporal process features—preparation time (PT), execution time (ET), and mean execution time per answer-related event (MET)—after excluding missing process/response cases and applying 98% winsorization to reduce outlier influence. Across all four testlets, process features significantly differed across score groups: for fair tests, higher scores generally corresponded to shorter ET (and full-score students also showed shorter PT and MET than lowest-score students), while for exhaustive tests, full-score students showed shorter PT and MET but longer ET, consistent with completing more exhaustive conditions. The study uses Kruskal–Wallis/Wilcoxon and cross-validates with omnibus ANOVA/t-tests; no machine-learning predictive models are trained, and survey weighting/replicate-weight procedures are not described in the provided text.

file_name: 87. Kara. (2025). Exploring Test-Taking Disengagement in the Context of PISA 2022: Evidence from Process Data.pdf
title: Exploring Test-Taking Disengagement in the Context of PISA 2022: Evidence from Process Data

outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 process data for the Turkish sample (N=6,560 after listwise deletion) to examine test-taking disengagement using three indicators: response time (RT), number of actions (NA), and self-reported effort (SRE). Using latent profile analysis (LPA), the authors selected a three-profile solution (entropy=0.883; AIC/BIC/aBIC improved; LMR p<.05), yielding Moderately Engaged (82.79%), Highly Engaged (7.20%), and Disengaged (10.01%) groups. Disengagement was characterized by low SRE, minimal interactions, and rapid responses, and it was associated with lower mathematics achievement (Disengaged mean=421.74 vs. Highly Engaged mean=536.453; Moderately Engaged mean=452.689; p<.05). The manuscript does not report any machine-learning predictive model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) and does not document plausible value (PV) handling, limiting direct comparability to PV-based ILSA achievement modeling.

file_name: 89. Lee et al. (2025). Uncovering Behavioral Patterns in Creative Thinking: Utilizing and Interpreting PISA 2022 Process Data.pdf

It describes five process metrics (total time on item, time to first action, number of actions, number of visits, number of short visits) and explains how PISA defines engagement/disengagement-related indicators. It provides an illustrative example using descriptive statistics for two released items (Robot Story and Save the River) and discusses model-based approaches (data mining and IRT-based frameworks) conceptually rather than estimating predictive models in the paper itself. As a result, no ML algorithm is trained/evaluated, and no performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/R²) are reported for an empirical predictive task.

file_name: 90. Han et al. (2023). Behavioral patterns in collaborative problem solving: a latent profile analysis based on response times and actions in PISA 2015.pdf

outcome_summary: This exploratory LPA used PISA 2015 ColPS process data from the Xandar unit, restricting to English test-takers with Xandar as the first cluster (N=2,520 across 11 education systems). The authors modeled four response-time indicators (log-transformed) and four action-count indicators to derive two behavioral profiles (Profile 1: 95%, N=2,395; Profile 2: 5%, N=125). Profile 2 showed more actions and longer response times in most parts, with the largest differentiation in Part 1. Overall performance differed significantly between profiles: Profile 1 had higher PVCLPS (519.11) than Profile 2 (389.70), with a mean gap of 129.41 (S.E.=21.66, p<.01). The study used complex-sample student weights (W_FSTUWT) and analyzed 10 plausible values with Rubin’s rules; however, it did not include covariates predicting profile membership and used a single task unit, limiting generalizability.

file_name: 92. Park et al. (2025). Measurement Invariance for Multilingual Learners Using Item Response and Response Time in PISA 2018.pdf

outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 U.S. data to examine assessment bias for multilingual learners (MLs) versus non-MLs using multigroup IRT DIF (RMSD thresholds) on scored responses and invariance of item response times via LOWESS and the Guo & Ercikan DRT test. Across reading, mathematics, and science, DIF was present for a minority of items (about 14% in reading, 7% in mathematics, and 11% in science), indicating that some items function differently for MLs even after accounting for latent ability. Latent ability estimates (WLE theta) showed non-MLs scoring higher in all three domains; however, the mathematics gap disappeared after controlling for reading ability, while the science gap remained significant. Response-time analyses consistently indicated that MLs spent more time than non-MLs when abilities were matched, with DRT significant for 8% (reading), 10% (math), and 7% (science) of items. The paper does not report a missing-data strategy and does not apply/describe PISA sampling weights, which may affect generalizability.

file_name: 93. Liang et al. (2023). Using Process Data to Improve Classification Accuracy of Cognitive Diagnosis Model.pdf
title: Using Process Data to Improve Classification Accuracy of Cognitive Diagnosis Model
outcome_summary: The paper proposes a joint cognitive diagnosis model (JCDM-RRT) that integrates two process-data sources—response times (RTs) and mouse click/drag traces operationalized as the number of actions—into a DINA-family cognitive diagnosis framework. In the empirical PISA 2018 computer-based reading example (12 items; 2,003 students from 79 countries/districts), the joint model achieved better posterior predictive model checking for response and RT (PPMC_RA = 0.551; PPMC_RT = 0.551) and higher attribute classification reliability (average attribute reliability 0.494 vs 0.437 for response-only and 0.454 for RT-only). In simulation studies, the joint model improved person and attribute classification: PCCR = 0.5193 and ACCR mean = 0.8335, outperforming the two baselines. The study is Bayesian (MCMC via JAGS) and does not report a missing-data handling strategy or any survey-weighting approach, so results should be interpreted as model-based rather than explicitly population-representative.

file_name: 95. Bungaro et al. (2024). Jointly exploring mathematics ability and speed in large‑scale computer‑based testing.pdf
title: Jointly exploring mathematics ability and speed in large-scale computer-based testing
authors: L. Bungaro, Mariagiulia Matteucci
outcome_summary: The study analyzes INVALSI grade 10 mathematics data from Italy (2017–2018) and jointly estimates latent mathematics ability and latent test-taking speed from response accuracy and response times using a Bayesian hierarchical joint model (LNIRT). It finds a significant negative between-person association between ability and speed (correlation at the person level = −0.574; and in the multilevel empty model, student-level correlation = −0.484 and class-level correlation = −0.779). In the final bivariate multilevel regression model (M3), prior achievement and math test anxiety are key predictors of both ability and speed, with test anxiety showing a non-linear pattern: ability peaks at very low anxiety and declines toward very high anxiety, while speed decreases from low to intermediate anxiety and then increases sharply at higher anxiety. Contextual effects are also significant: class average ESCS predicts higher ability and class composition variables relate to speed. The paper does not report any missing-data handling strategy and does not use PVs; results should be interpreted as conditional on the analyzed INVALSI sample and the modeling assumptions (e.g., log-normal RT structure).

file_name: 96. Li et al. (2025). Exploring the Evidence to Interpret Differential Item Functioning via Response Process Data.pdf
title: Exploring the Evidence to Interpret Differential Item Functioning via Response Process Data
authors: Ziying Li, Huan Kuang
outcome_summary: The study used PIAAC 2012 computer-based numeracy data for the United States, focusing on open-ended items and labeling nine items as gender DIF vs DIF-free using Mantel–Haenszel DIF detection with iterative purification across 10 MICE-imputed datasets. It then trained Random Forest and ridge logistic regression classifiers to model the association between DIF item status and response-process features, using 10-fold cross-validation and SMOTE to balance the DIF-free vs DIF item classes in training. Random Forest and ridge logistic regression showed similar performance: RF achieved Accuracy=0.761 and AUC=0.860, while ridge logistic regression achieved Accuracy=0.731 and AUC=0.849; F1 was also similar (RF=0.636 vs LR=0.660). Feature-importance results converged on four key process features—RT, FIRST_TIMING, betweenness centrality, and action-sequence density—suggesting DIF is linked to response efficiency and exploration rather than item scores alone. The authors explicitly frame the results as correlational (not causal) and do not report survey-weight or replicate-weight usage for the ML stage.

file_name: 97. Chen et al. (2023). Using learners’ problem‑solving processes in computer‑based assessments for enhanced learner modeling: A deep learning approach.pdf
title: Using learners’ problem‑solving processes in computer‑based assessments for enhanced learner modeling: A deep learning approach
authors: Fu Chen
outcome_summary: The study proposes a deep learning learner-modeling framework that sequentially predicts learners’ next item-response correctness using both product information (previous correctness) and process information (logged action sequences and associated time durations) from PSLC DataShop “Lab study 2012 (cleanedLogs)”. Across training/test partition ratios (0.3/0.5/0.7), the full model consistently outperformed the DKT baseline and a model variant that excluded process-data learning, improving both classification (ACC, AUC) and regression-style error metrics (MAE, RMSE). For example, at a 0.7 training ratio, the full model reached ACC=0.7225 and AUC=0.7400 with MAE=0.3580 and RMSE=0.4254, while DKT had ACC=0.7037 and AUC=0.7157. The attention variant slightly outperformed the LSTM-only variant. The paper does not report any survey weighting (appropriate for this log dataset) and does not document missing-data handling for incomplete sequences, which limits transparency.

file_name: 98. Zhou & Jiao. (2022). Exploration of the Stacking Ensemble Machine Learning Algorithm for Cheating Detection in Large-Scale Assessment.pdf
title: Exploration of the Stacking Ensemble Machine Learning Algorithm for Cheating Detection in Large-Scale Assessment
authors: Hong Jiao, Zhou
outcome_summary: The study used a large licensure-test dataset (1,636 test-takers; 46 flagged cheaters) and framed cheating detection as an imbalanced binary classification problem. Across 4-fold cross-validation, resampling (SMOTE oversampling, RandomUnderSampler under-sampling, or both) was applied only to the training folds, and models were evaluated on the non-resampled test folds using Recall, Precision, F1, and false-positive rate. At the base-model level, Gradient Boosting and Random Forest were generally top performers, with Random Forest achieving the highest Precision (e.g., 0.838 under dual resampling 10:1 with item responses + summary statistics) and Gradient Boosting achieving the highest F1 (e.g., 0.573). The best overall result was a stacking meta-model using Discriminant Analysis on the top two base models, with under-sampling ratio 10:1 and item responses plus augmented summary statistics, yielding Recall=0.638, Precision=0.551, F1=0.586, and FP rate=0.014. The paper does not report a formal missing-data imputation strategy (scored responses reportedly contain no missing values because missing options are coded as 0s), and it does not discuss survey weights or hierarchical adjustments.

file_name: 99. Jiao et al. (2021). Editorial: Process Data in Educational and Psychological Measurement.pdf
title: Editorial: Process Data in Educational and Psychological Measurement
authors: Jiao, He, Veldkamp
outcome_summary: This editorial does not report model training, predictive performance metrics, or an empirical dataset used for analysis. Instead, it summarizes a collection of papers on process data approaches, including examples such as hidden Markov modeling, data mining with supervised algorithms (e.g., CART, gradient boosting, random forests, SVM), and other joint modeling frameworks for response accuracy and response times. Because no single study’s dataset, target variable, or evaluation results are analyzed within this editorial, there are no extractable findings or performance statistics. Survey weighting, plausible values handling, and missing-data handling are therefore not applicable to the editorial itself.

title: Effects of dimensionality and covariate on items with DIF in mixture models
authors: Ömer Doğan
outcome_summary: This paper is a descriptive DIF-detection study using eTIMSS 2019 booklet 3 item responses (28 four-choice multiple-choice items) rather than a predictive ML study. The author compares MixIRT, multidimensional MixIRT (MMixIRT), and multidimensional MixIRT with a covariate added to latent class membership, using model fit criteria (AIC/BIC/SABIC) and then performs DIF testing via the Mantel–Haenszel (MH) method implemented in R (difR). The best-fitting models by information criteria were the two-class versions: C2 for MixIRT, D-C2 for MMixIRT, and Cov-D-C2 for the covariate-augmented MMixIRT. Across these models, adding multidimensionality and the covariate reduced the number of items flagged with DIF and altered which latent class (focal vs reference) benefited, with the covariate model showing the strongest separation in latent-class achievement means. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight usage and the lack of access to the underlying item content for expert review of DIF sources.

title: Evaluating the alignment between the Grade 9 mathematics Annual National Assessment (ANA) and TIMSS
authors: Dhlamini
outcome_summary: This study evaluates horizontal alignment between South Africa’s Grade 9 mathematics Annual National Assessment (ANA) and the 2011 Grade 8 mathematics TIMSS framework by computing Porter’s alignment index from topic-by-cognitive-level matrices. The analysis uses ANA question papers from 2012 (n=59), 2013 (n=62), and 2014 (n=61) and TIMSS 2011 response items (n=90), mapped by three reviewers into collapsed 4×4 matrices. The Porter’s alignment index indicates moderate-to-perfect alignment overall but still reveals substantial misalignment: 0.657 (34.3% misalignment) for 2012, 0.728 (27.2% misalignment) for 2013, and 0.681 (31.9% misalignment) for 2014. The study also reports mean deviations showing which topic and cognitive-level cells were preferred or underrepresented, with ANA showing irregular cognitive-level testing across years. Limitations include the absence of student-level PV achievement modeling and no ML prediction pipeline; the results are alignment-based and do not establish causal effects on learner performance.

title: Rethinking Item Fairness Using Single World Intervention Graphs
authors: Youmi Suk, Weicong Lyu
outcome_summary: The article proposes a causal framework for differential item functioning (CDIF) using Single-World Intervention Graphs (SWIGs), and it demonstrates the approach with both simulations and an empirical TIMSS application. In the TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 mathematics analysis, the authors restrict to U.S. students who received Booklet 1, use 19 DIF-free items as anchor items to estimate math ability, and then analyze a single dichotomous item response (M032595). For the protected variable sex (ITSEX), traditional DIF methods (standardized D-statistic, Mantel–Haenszel, and logistic regression) flag DIF in favor of boys, but the SWIG-informed regression-adjusted CDIF approach finds no CDIF after adjusting for home educational resources (BSDGHER), reporting p = 0.088. The key limitation is that the causal conclusion depends on the correctness of the assumed SWIG and measured confounders; unmeasured confounding could still bias CDIF estimates.
all_datasets_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S., Booklet 1; item M032595)
all_target_variables: CDIF for item M032595 (binary item response)

title: Comparing Bayesian random coefficient prediction and latent interaction models for multilevel moderated mediation
authors: Lee, Kim
outcome_summary: This paper compares two Bayesian multilevel moderated mediation parameterizations—Bayesian random coefficient prediction (BRCP) and Bayesian latent interaction (BINT)—using TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade U.S. data (273 schools; 8,698 students). The empirical model estimates a 1-1-1 multilevel mediation structure with latent variables for math preference (MP), math class environment (MCE), and math teacher relationship (MTR), and uses school-level relatedness (REL) as a cross-level moderator of the within-level indirect effect. The authors report Bayesian credible intervals and model-fit indices from a multilevel CFA (e.g., CFI/TLI around 0.95/0.93 and RMSEA around 0.07–0.075) and show that BRCP and BINT yield nearly identical posterior distributions (posterior overlap coefficients > 0.9). For moderated mediation, the within-level indirect effect strengthens at +1 SD REL (credible interval excludes zero) but is not statistically reliable at −1 SD REL. A key caveat is that TIMSS sampling weights were not applied due to convergence issues in Blimp, and the paper does not fully document missing-data handling for the Bayesian latent-variable estimation.
